chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.content:
Oh, you who walk the Narrow Way
By Tophet-flare to Judgment Day,
Be gentle when “the heathen” pray
To Buddha at Kamakura!

He sat, in defiance of municipal regulations, astride the cannon Zam-Zammah on its brick platform opposite the old Ajaib-Gher—the Wonder House, as the locals call the Lahore Museum. Those who control Zam-Zammah, that “fire-breathing dragon,” control the Punjab, for this great green-bronze piece is always the first prize of any conqueror.

Kim had some justification for being there—he had just kicked Lala Dinanath’s boy off the gun’s trunnions—especially since the English ruled the Punjab and Kim was English. Yet he was burned as dark as any native; he spoke the local dialects by preference, while his mother tongue came out in a clipped, uncertain sing-song; and he associated on perfectly equal terms with the small boys of the bazaar. Kim was white, but he was a poor white of the very poorest class. The half-caste woman who looked after him—she smoked opium and pretended to run a second-hand furniture shop near the square where cheap carriages wait—told the missionaries that she was Kim’s mother’s sister. In truth, however, his mother had been a nursemaid in a colonel’s family and had married Kimball O’Hara, a young lance-sergeant in the Mavericks, an Irish regiment. O’Hara later took a job on the Sind, Punjab, and Delhi Railway, and his regiment returned home without him. His wife died of cholera in Ferozepore, and O’Hara drifted into heavy drinking, wandering up and down the railway line with his sharp-eyed, three-year-old baby. Well-meaning societies and chaplains tried to rescue the child, but O’Hara kept moving until he met the opium-smoking woman, learned her habit, and died just as poor whites die in India. His entire estate at the time of his death consisted of three papers. One he called his ne varietur because those exact words were written beneath his signature; another was his clearance certificate; and the third was Kim’s birth certificate. O’Hara used to say during his grand opium-induced reveries that these documents would one day make little Kimball a man. Under no circumstances was Kim to part with them, for they belonged to a powerful piece of magic—the kind of magic men practiced across the way behind the Museum, in the large blue-and-white Jadoo-Gher, the Magic House, as they called the Masonic Lodge. He promised that everything would turn out right one day, and that Kim’s honor would rise high between monstrous pillars of beauty and strength. The colonel himself, riding a magnificent horse at the head of the finest regiment in the world, would look after Kim—little Kim, who deserved better than his father. Nine hundred first-class fighting men whose God was a Red Bull on a green field would watch over Kim, provided they had not forgotten O’Hara, the poor gang-foreman from the Ferozepore line. At that point, O’Hara would weep bitterly in his broken wicker chair on the veranda. So it came to pass that after his death, the woman sewed the parchment papers and the birth certificate into a leather amulet case and hung it around Kim’s neck.

“And someday,” she said, vaguely remembering O’Hara’s prophecies, “a great Red Bull on a green field will come for you, and the colonel will ride up on his tall horse, yes, and—” she slipped into English—“nine hundred devils.”

“Ah,” Kim replied, “I will remember. A Red Bull and a colonel on a horse will come, but first, my father said, two men will come to prepare the ground. That is how my father said they always did things, and that is how it always happens when men work magic.”

If the woman had sent Kim up to the local Masonic Lodge with those papers, he would naturally have been taken in by the Provincial Lodge and sent to the Masonic Orphanage in the Hills; but she deeply distrusted anything she heard about magic. Kim also had his own ideas. As he grew older, he learned to avoid missionaries and serious-looking white men who asked who he was and what he did. For Kim did nothing with remarkable success. True, he knew the wonderful walled city of Lahore inside and out, from the Delhi Gate to the outer Fort Ditch. He was on intimate terms with men who led lives stranger than anything Haroun al Raschid ever dreamed of, living an existence as wild as the Arabian Nights, though missionaries and charity secretaries could never appreciate its beauty. His nickname through the neighborhood was the “Little Friend of all the World.” Because he was lithe and went unnoticed, he frequently ran errands at night across crowded rooftops for sleek, well-dressed young men of fashion. It was intrigue—he understood that well enough, having been familiar with all sorts of shadowy dealings since he could speak—but what he loved was the game itself: the stealthy prowl through dark alleys and narrow lanes, the quiet climb up a drainpipe, the sights and sounds of the women’s world on the flat roofs, and the headlong escape from one rooftop to another under the cover of the hot, dark night. He was also on familiar terms with holy men, such as the ash-smeared fakirs sitting by their brick shrines under the trees by the riverside. He would greet them as they returned from their begging tours and, when no one else was watching, share a meal from the same dish with them. The woman who looked after him insisted with tears that he wear European clothes—trousers, a shirt, and a battered hat. But Kim found it much easier to slip into Hindu or Muslim clothing when he was handling certain businesses. One of the young men of fashion—the very one who was found dead at the bottom of a well on the night of the earthquake—had once given him a complete Hindu outfit, the traditional costume of a low-caste street boy. Kim kept this hidden in a secret spot beneath some heavy timbers in Nila Ram’s timber-yard, past the Punjab High Court, where fragrant deodar logs lie seasoning after floating down the Ravi River. Whenever there was business or mischief afoot, Kim would put on his disguise, returning to the veranda at dawn, exhausted from shouting behind a wedding procession or yelling at a Hindu festival. Sometimes there was food in the house, but more often there was not, and then Kim would simply go back out to eat with his native friends.

As he drummed his heels against Zam-Zammah, he would turn away from his king-of-the-castle game with little Chota Lal and Abdullah, the sweetmeat-seller’s son, to shout a teasing remark at the native policeman standing guard over the rows of shoes left at the Museum door. The big Punjabi would grin tolerantly, for he knew Kim of old. So did the water-carrier, who splashed water onto the dry road from his goat-skin bag. So did Jawahir Singh, the Museum carpenter, bending over his new packing-cases. In fact, everyone in sight knew him, except for the country peasants who hurried to the Wonder House to view the crafts made in their own province and beyond. The Museum was dedicated to Indian arts and manufactures, and anyone seeking knowledge was welcome to ask the Curator for an explanation.

“Get off! Get off! Let me up!” cried Abdullah, struggling to climb the wheel of Zam-Zammah.

“Thy father was a pastry-cook, thy mother stole the ghee,” Kim chanted. “All Muslims fell off Zam-Zammah long ago!”

“Let me up!” shrilled little Chota Lal in his gilt-embroidered cap. His father was worth perhaps half a million pounds sterling, but India remains the only truly democratic land in the world.

“The Hindus fell off Zam-Zammah too. The Muslims pushed them off. Thy father was a pastry-cook—”

He stopped mid-sentence. Around the corner from the roaring Motee Bazaar came shuffling a man of a kind Kim had never seen, despite his belief that he knew every caste under the sun. The stranger was nearly six feet tall, draped in fold upon fold of dingy fabric that looked like horse-blanketing, none of which matched any known trade or profession. At his belt hung a long, openwork iron pen-case and a wooden rosary like those carried by holy men. On his head he wore a gigantic sort of tam-o'-shanter cap. His face was yellow and wrinkled, much like Fook Shing’s, the Chinese bootmaker in the bazaar, and his eyes turned up at the corners like narrow slits of onyx.

“Who is that?” Kim asked his companions.

“Perhaps it is a man,” Abdullah said, with a finger in his mouth, staring hard.

“Without a doubt,” Kim replied, “but he is no man of India that I have ever laid eyes on.”

“A priest, perhaps,” suggested Chota Lal, noticing the rosary. “Look! He is going into the Wonder House!”

“No, no,” said the policeman, shaking his head. “I don’t understand your talk.” The constable spoke in Punjabi. “O Friend of all the World, what is he saying?”

“Send him over here,” Kim said, dropping down from Zam-Zammah and waving his bare feet. “He is a foreigner, and you are as thick-headed as a buffalo.”

The old man turned helplessly and drifted toward the boys. His woolen cloak still smelled strongly of the pungent wormwood of the mountain passes.

“O children, what is that big house?” he asked in surprisingly good Urdu.

“The Ajaib-Gher, the Wonder House!” Kim did not give him any respectful title like Lala or Mian, for he could not figure out the man’s religion.

“Ah! The Wonder House! Can anyone go inside?”

“It says right above the door—everyone can enter.”

“Without paying?”

“I go in and out as I please. I’m no banker,” Kim laughed.

“Alas! I am an old man. I did not know.” Then, fingering his rosary, he turned slightly toward the Museum entrance.

“What is your caste? Where is your home? Have you come from far?” Kim asked.

“I came by way of Kulu—from beyond the Kailas mountains—but what do you know of that? From the hills where,” he sighed, “the air and water are fresh and cool.”

“Aha! Khitai [a Chinaman],” said Abdullah proudly. Fook Shing had once chased him out of his shop for spitting at the little idol above the boots.

“Pahari [a hillman],” said little Chota Lal.

“Yes, child—a hillman from hills you will never see. Have you heard of Bhotiyal [Tibet]? I am no Chinaman, but a Bhotiya [Tibetan], if you must know—a lama, or what you would call a guru.”

“A guru from Tibet,” Kim repeated. “I have never seen such a man. Are there Hindus in Tibet, then?”

“We are followers of the Middle Way, living in peace in our monasteries, and I am traveling to see the Four Holy Places before I die. Now you children know as much as I do, though I am old.” He smiled kindly upon the boys.

“Have you eaten?”

He fumbled inside his robe and drew out a worn wooden begging-bowl. The boys nodded; all the priests they knew were beggars.

“I do not wish to eat just yet.” He turned his head like an old tortoise basking in the sunlight. “Is it true that there are many statues in the Wonder House of Lahore?” He repeated the last words carefully, as if making sure of an address.

“That is true,” Abdullah said. “It is full of heathen idols. You are an idolater yourself.”

“Never mind him,” Kim said. “That is the Government’s house, and there is no idolatry inside, only an Englishman with a white beard. Come with me, and I will show you.”

“Strange priests eat little boys,” Chota Lal whispered.

“And he is a foreigner and an idolater,” added Abdullah the Muslim.

Kim laughed. “He is new here. Run back to your mothers’ laps where you’ll be safe. Come along!”

Kim clicked through the self-registering turnstile, and the old man followed, stopping in amazement. In the entrance hall stood large Greco-Buddhist sculptures created long ago by forgotten artisans whose hands were reaching, quite skillfully, for a mysteriously transmitted Greek influence. There were hundreds of pieces: friezes of figures in relief, fragments of statues, and slabs crowded with images that had once decorated the brick walls of northern Buddhist monasteries and shrines, but now, dug up and labeled, formed the pride of the Museum. With his mouth open in wonder, the lama wandered from piece to piece, finally coming to a halt in rapt attention before a large relief representing the coronation or apotheosis of Lord Buddha. The Master was shown seated on a lotus whose petals were carved so deeply they appeared almost detached. Around Him stood an adoring hierarchy of kings, elders, and ancient Buddhas. Below were lotus-covered waters filled with fish and water-birds. Two devas with butterfly wings held a wreath above His head, while another pair above them supported an umbrella topped by the jewelled headdress of a Bodhisattva.

“The Lord! The Lord! It is Shakya Muni himself!” the lama sobbed softly, and under his breath he began the wonderful Buddhist invocation:

“To Him the Way,—the Law,—Apart—
Whom Maya held beneath her heart,
Ananda’s Lord—the Bodhisat.”

“And He is here! The Most Excellent Law is here as well. My pilgrimage is well begun. And what workmanship! What workmanship!”

“Yonder is the Sahib,” Kim said, ducking away sideways among the exhibit cases of arts and manufactures. An elderly Englishman with a white beard was watching the lama, who gravely turned and saluted him, then, after some fumbling, produced a notebook and a scrap of paper.

“Yes, that is my name,” the Englishman said, smiling at the clumsy, childish lettering.

“One of us who made the pilgrimage to the Holy Places—he is now Abbot of the Lung-Cho Monastery—gave this to me,” the lama stammered. “He spoke of these things.” His thin hand waved tremulously around the room.

“Welcome, then, O lama from Tibet. The images are here, and I am here,” he glanced at the lama’s face, “to gather knowledge. Come into my office for a moment.” The old man was trembling with excitement.

The office was simply a small wooden cubicle partitioned off from the sculpture-filled gallery. Kim stretched out flat on the floor, pressing his ear against a crack in the heat-split cedar door, and instinctively prepared to listen and watch.

Most of the conversation was far above his head. The lama spoke haltingly at first to the Curator about his own monastery, the Such-zen, situated opposite the Painted Rocks four months’ march away. The Curator brought out a massive photograph album and showed him that very monastery perched on its cliff, overlooking a gigantic valley of multicolored rock strata.

“Yes, yes!” The lama put on a pair of horn-rimmed spectacles of Chinese workmanship. “Here is the little door through which we bring in firewood before winter. And you—do the Englishmen know of these things? The present Abbot of Lung-Cho told me, but I could not believe it. Does the Lord—the Excellent One—receive honor here as well? And is His life known?”

“It is all carved upon the stones. Come and see, if you are rested.”

The lama shuffled out into the main hall and, accompanied by the Curator, walked through the collection with the reverence of a devotee and the appreciative eye of a craftsman.

Incident by incident, he identified the beautiful story on the weathered stone, occasionally puzzled by the unfamiliar Greek artistic conventions, but as delighted as a child with each new discovery. When the sequence broke off, as it did around the Annunciation, the Curator supplied the missing parts from his towering stack of books—French and German volumes filled with photographs and reproductions.

Here was the devoted Asita, the Buddhist counterpart of Simeon in the Christian story, holding the Holy Child on his knee while the mother and father listened. Here were scenes from the legend of the cousin Devadatta, and the wicked woman who falsely accused the Master of impurity, all of them put to shame. Here was the teaching in the Deer Park; the miracle that astonished the fire-worshipers; the Bodhisattva in royal state as a prince; the miraculous birth; and the death at Kusinagara, where the weak disciple fainted. There were countless repetitions of the meditation under the Bodhi tree, and the worship of the alms-bowl was everywhere. Within a few minutes, the Curator realized that his guest was no ordinary bead-counting beggar, but a scholar of considerable learning. They started over from the beginning, the lama taking snuff, wiping his spectacles, and speaking at breakneck speed in a bewildering mixture of Urdu and Tibetan. He had heard of the travels of the Chinese pilgrims Fa-Hien and Hiuen-Tsiang and was eager to know if any translations of their journals existed. He caught his breath as he eagerly turned the pages translated by Beal and Stanislas Julien. “It is all here. A locked treasure!” Then he reverently settled down to listen to passages hastily translated into Urdu. For the first time, he heard about the tireless work of European scholars who, using these and a hundred other documents, had successfully identified the sacred sites of Buddhism. Next, he was shown a massive map marked and traced in yellow. The lama’s brown finger followed the Curator’s pencil from point to point: here was Kapilavastu, here the Middle Kingdom, here Mahabodhi—the Mecca of Buddhism—and here Kusinagara, the sorrowful place of the Holy One’s death. The old man bowed his head over the papers in silence for a while, and the Curator lit another pipe. Kim had fallen asleep. When he woke up, the conversation, still flowing fast, was easier to follow.

“And so it was, O Fountain of Wisdom, that I decided to visit the Holy Places trodden by His feet—to the Birthplace, even to Kapila; then to Mahabodhi, which is Buddh Gaya; to the Monastery; to the Deer-Park; and to the place of His death.”

The lama lowered his voice. “And I came here alone. For five—seven—eighteen—forty years, it weighed on my mind that the Old Law was no longer properly followed, having become burdened, as you know, with demon-worship, charms, and idolatry. Just as the child outside said a moment ago. Yes, even as the child said, with idol-worship.”

“That is the way with all faiths.”

“Do you think so? I read the books of my monastery, and they were like dried pith; and the later rituals that we of the Reformed Law have piled upon ourselves—they, too, felt worthless to these old eyes. Even the followers of the Excellent One are constantly feuding with one another. It is all an illusion. Yes, maya, mere illusion. But I have another desire—” The weathered yellow face moved within three inches of the Curator’s, and a long fingernail tapped firmly on the table. “Your scholars have followed the Blessed Feet in all their wanderings through these books, but there are things they have not searched for. I know nothing—nothing at all—but I am traveling to free myself from the Wheel of Things along a broad and open road.” He smiled with simple triumph. “As a pilgrim to the Holy Places, I gain spiritual merit. But there is more. Listen to a true thing. When our gracious Lord, while yet a youth, sought a wife, the people in His father’s court said He was too delicate for marriage. You know this?”

The Curator nodded, wondering what would come next.

“So they arranged a triple trial of strength against all challengers. At the test of the bow, our Lord first broke the bow they gave Him, and then demanded a bow so strong that no other man could bend it. You know this?”

“It is written. I have read it.”

“And shooting far past all other marks, His arrow flew beyond the range of sight. At last it landed, and where it touched the earth, a stream broke forth that soon became a river. By our Lord’s grace, and the merit He earned before freeing Himself, anyone who bathes in this river washes away every stain and speckle of sin.”

“So it is written,” the Curator said sadly.

The lama drew a long breath. “Where is that river? Fountain of Wisdom, where did the arrow fall?”

“Alas, my brother, I do not know,” the Curator replied.

“No? Surely you jest—this is the one thing you have not told me. You must know! Look, I am an old man! I ask with my head resting upon your feet, O Fountain of Wisdom. We know He drew the bow! We know the arrow fell! We know the stream gushed forth! Where, then, is the river? My dream told me to find it. So I came. I am here. But where is the river?”

“If I knew, do you think I would not shout it from the rooftops?”

“Through it, one attains freedom from the Wheel of Things,” the lama continued, paying no attention. “The River of the Arrow! Think again! Perhaps it is some small stream—dried up in the summer heat? But the Holy One would never deceive an old man like that.”

“I do not know. I do not know.”

The lama brought his wrinkled face close to the Englishman’s once more. “I see you truly do not know. Since you are not of the Law, the matter is hidden from you.”

“Yes—hidden—hidden.”

“We are both bound, you and I, my brother. But I—” he rose with a sweep of his soft, thick robes—“I am going to cut myself free. Come with me!”

“I am bound here,” the Curator said. “But where are you going?”

“First to Kashi [Benares]; where else? There I will meet one of the pure faith in a Jain temple. He is also a secret seeker, and perhaps I can learn from him. Maybe he will travel with me to Buddh Gaya. From there, north and west to Kapilavastu, and there I will search for the river. Indeed, I will search everywhere along my way—for the exact place where the arrow fell is unknown.”

“And how will you travel? It is a long way to Delhi, and even farther to Benares.”

“By road and by train. From Pathankot, after leaving the hills, I came here in a te-rain. It moves with incredible speed. At first, I was amazed to see the tall poles beside the track constantly snatching at the wires—” he mimicked the stoop and blur of a telegraph pole flashing past the carriage window. “But later, I felt cramped and wanted to walk, as I am accustomed to do.”

“And are you certain of your road?” the Curator asked.

“Oh, for that, one simply asks a question and pays money, and the appointed officials send you straight to the appointed place. I learned as much in my monastery from reliable reports,” the lama said proudly.

“And when do you leave?” The Curator smiled at the blend of ancient piety and modern progress that defines India today.

“As soon as possible. I will follow the places of His life until I reach the River of the Arrow. Besides, I have a written paper listing the departure times of the trains heading south.”

“And for food?” Lamas usually carried a good store of money somewhere about them, but the Curator wanted to be sure.

“For the journey, I will rely upon the Master’s begging-bowl. Yes. Just as He went, so will I, leaving behind the comforts of my monastery. When I left the hills, a disciple was with me who begged for me as our Rule requires, but when we stopped in Kulu for a while, he caught a fever and died. I have no disciple now, but I will take the alms-bowl so that charitable people may earn spiritual merit.” He nodded his head bravely. Learned scholars of a monastery do not normally beg, but the lama was entirely devoted to his quest.

“So be it,” the Curator said, smiling. “Allow me now to earn some merit. We are fellow craftsmen, you and I. Here is a new book of white English paper, and here are two or three sharpened pencils—thick and thin, all good for a scribe. Now, lend me your spectacles.”

The Curator looked through them. They were heavily scratched, but their magnification was almost identical to his own pair, which he slid into the lama’s hand, saying, “Try these.”

“A feather! They feel like nothing at all upon my face.” The old man turned his head delightedly and wrinkled his nose. “I can scarcely feel them! And how clearly I see!”

“They are crystal—pure glass—and will never scratch. May they help you find your river, for they are yours now.”

“I will take them, and the pencils, and the white notebook,” the lama said, “as a token of friendship between priest and priest—and now—” He fumbled at his belt, detached the open-work iron pen-case, and laid it on the Curator’s table. “Keep this as a memory between you and me—my pen-case. It is very old, even as I am.”

It was an ancient Chinese design crafted from an iron that was no longer smelted in modern times, and the collector’s heart in the Curator had fallen in love with it from the very first moment. No amount of persuasion would convince the lama to take it back.

“When I return after finding the river, I will bring you a painted scroll of Padma Sambhava, such as I used to make on silk at the monastery. Yes—and a Wheel of Life,” he chuckled, “for we are fellow craftsmen, you and I.”

The Curator would have liked to keep him longer; there are few people left in the world who preserve the secret of traditional brush-and-ink Buddhist paintings, which are half written and half drawn. But the lama strode out, his head held high, paused for an instant before the great statue of the meditating Bodhisattva, and pushed through the turnstiles.

Kim followed like a shadow. What he had overheard had excited him wildly. This man was completely unlike anyone he had ever met, and he intended to investigate further, exactly as he would have explored a new building or a strange festival in Lahore. The lama was his discovery, and he intended to take charge of him. After all, Kim’s mother had been Irish, too.

The old man stopped by Zam-Zammah and looked around until his eyes found Kim. The initial inspiration of his pilgrimage had faded for a moment, and he suddenly felt old, lonely, and very empty inside.

“Do not sit under that gun,” the policeman said loftily.

“Huh! You owl!” was Kim’s reply on the lama’s behalf. “He’ll sit under the gun if it pleases him. When did you steal the milkwoman’s slippers, Dunnoo?”

It was a completely unfounded accusation tossed out on the spur of the moment, but it instantly silenced Dunnoo, who knew that Kim’s sharp shout could summon a mob of mischievous bazaar boys if necessary.

“And whom did you worship inside?” Kim asked pleasantly, squatting in the shade beside the lama.

“I worshipped no one, child. I bowed before the Excellent Law.”

Kim accepted this new god without missing a beat; he already knew a few score of them.

“And what are you going to do now?”

“I am going to beg. I realize now that it has been a long time since I last ate or drank. What is the custom of charity in this town? Do people give in silence, as we do in Tibet, or do they speak aloud?”

“Those who beg in silence starve in silence,” Kim quoted, reciting a local proverb. The lama tried to stand up, but sank back down, sighing for his disciple who had died far away in Kulu. Kim watched him sideways, thoughtful and intrigued.

“Give me the bowl. I know the people of this city—everyone who is charitable. Hand it over, and I will bring it back full.”

Trusting as a child, the old man handed him the bowl.

“You rest here. I know these people.”

He trotted off to the open stall of a low-caste vegetable-seller across the tramway lines in the Motee Bazaar. She knew Kim well.

*“Oho,* have you turned holy man with a begging-bowl?” she called out.

“No,” Kim said proudly. “There is a new priest in the city—a man unlike any I have ever seen.”

“Old priest, young tiger,” the woman said crossly. “I’m sick of new priests! They settle on our wares like flies. Is my son’s father a bottomless well of charity to give to everyone who asks?”

“No,” Kim admitted. “Your husband is more bad-tempered than holy. But this priest is different. The Sahib in the Wonder House spoke to him like a brother. Come on, mother, fill this bowl for me. He is waiting.”

“That bowl indeed! That cow-bellied basket! You have as much modesty as the sacred bull of Shiva. He has already taken the best of my onions this morning, and now I have to fill your bowl as well? He’ll be coming here next.”

A huge, mouse-colored Brahmin bull belonging to the neighborhood was shouldering his way through the colorful crowd, a stolen plantain hanging from his mouth. He headed straight for the shop, well aware of his privileges as a sacred beast, lowered his head, and sniffed heavily along the rows of vegetable baskets before making his choice. Kim’s hard little heel flew up and caught the bull squarely on its moist blue nose. The beast snorted with indignation and ambled off across the tram tracks, its hump quivering with rage.

“Look! I’ve saved you more than three times the cost of that bowl. Now, mother, some rice with dried fish on top—yes, and some vegetable curry too.”

A deep growl came from the back of the shop, where a man was resting.

“He chased away the bull,” the woman said quietly. “It’s good to give to the poor.” She took the bowl and returned it filled with hot rice.

“But my holy man is no cow,” Kim said seriously, making a hole in the top of the rice mound with his fingers. “A bit of curry would be good, and a fried cake, and a piece of sweetmeat would please him, I think.”

“It’s a hole as big as your head,” the woman grumbled. Nevertheless, she filled it with steaming vegetable curry, slapped a fried cake on top, added a dollop of clarified butter, and placed a lump of sour tamarind preserve on the side. Kim looked at the loaded bowl affectionately.

“That’s wonderful. Whenever I’m in the bazaar, no bull will come near your shop again. He’s a bold beggar, that one.”

“And what about you?” the woman laughed. “You talk big about bulls. Didn’t you tell me that someday a Red Bull would come out of a field to help you? Now carry that carefully and ask the holy man for his blessing on me. Perhaps he knows a cure for my daughter’s sore eyes, too. Ask him that as well, you Little Friend of all the World.”

But Kim had already darted away before she finished, dodging stray dogs and hungry acquaintances.

“This is how we beg when we know the proper way,” Kim told the lama proudly, showing him the contents of the bowl. The lama’s eyes widened at the sight. “Eat now, and I will share it with you. Ohé, bhistie!” he called out to the water-carrier who was splashing the shrubbery by the Museum. “Bring some water here. We men are thirsty.”

“We men!” the water-carrier laughed. “Is one skinful enough for a pair like you? Drink, then, in the name of the Compassionate One.”

He released a thin stream of water into Kim’s hands, and Kim drank in the native fashion. The lama, however, felt obliged to pull a cup from his endless layers of clothing and drink ceremonially.

*“Pardesi* [a foreigner],” Kim explained as the old man muttered what was clearly a blessing in an unknown tongue.

They ate together with great satisfaction, completely emptying the begging-bowl. Afterward, the lama took a pinch of snuff from a massive wooden gourd, fingered his rosary for a while, and drifted into the easy sleep of old age as the shadow of Zam-Zammah lengthened.

Kim sauntered over to the nearest tobacco-seller, a lively young Muslim woman, and begged a harsh cigarette of the kind sold to Punjab University students who liked to imitate English customs. He smoked it while deep in thought, sitting with his knees pulled up to his chin beneath the belly of the great cannon. His thoughts led him to a sudden, stealthy departure toward Nila Ram’s timber-yard.

The lama did not wake until the evening life of the city had begun with the lighting of lamps and the return of white-robed clerks and officials from the Government offices. He stared around him in confusion; no one paid him any attention except for a Hindu urchin in a dirty turban and dull-colored clothes. Suddenly the old man bowed his head into his knees and began to wail.

“What is the matter?” asked the boy, stepping up to him. “Have you been robbed?”

“My new disciple has left me, and I have no idea where he has gone.”

“And what sort of man was this disciple of yours?”

“It was a boy who came to me in place of the one who died, as a reward for the merit I earned when I bowed before the Law in yonder house.” He pointed toward the Museum. “He came to show me a path I had lost. He led me into the Wonder House and gave me the courage to speak to the Keeper of the Images, so that I was cheered and strengthened. When I grew faint with hunger, he begged for me just as a true disciple would for his teacher. He was sent to me suddenly, and suddenly he has gone away. I had intended to teach him the Law on the road to Benares.”

Kim stood nearby in amazement, realizing that he had overheard the talk in the Museum and knowing that the old man was speaking the absolute truth—something a native traveler rarely does when talking to a stranger.

“But I see now that he was sent for a purpose. Because of this, I know I shall find the particular river I am searching for.”

“The River of the Arrow?” Kim asked with a superior smile.

“Is this another sign?” the lama cried. “I have spoken of my search to no one except the Keeper of the Images. Who are you?”

“Your disciple,” Kim said simply, sitting down on his heels. “I have never seen anyone like you in all my life. I am going with you to Benares. Besides, I think an old man like you, who insists on telling the truth to strangers at dusk, is in desperate need of a disciple.”

“But the river—the River of the Arrow?”

“Oh, I heard about that when you were talking to the Englishman. I was lying right against the door.”

The lama sighed. “I thought you might be an appointed guide. Such things do happen sometimes—but I am not worthy. So you do not know where the river is?”

“Not I,” Kim laughed uneasily. “I am going to look for—for a bull—a Red Bull on a green field that is supposed to help me.” Being a boy, if an acquaintance had a grand plan, Kim was always ready with one of his own; and like a boy, he had actually spent twenty whole minutes thinking about his father’s prophecy.

“Look for what, child?” asked the lama.

“God knows, but that is what my father told me. I heard you talking in the Wonder House about all those strange new places in the hills, and if someone as old and small as you—so unused to telling lies—can go traveling for the sake of a mere river, it seemed to me that I ought to go traveling too. If it is our fate to find those things, we will find them—you your river, and I my bull, the strong pillars, and a few other things I’ve forgotten.”

“It is not pillars, but the Wheel, that I wish to escape,” the lama corrected him.

“It’s all the same thing. Perhaps they’ll make me a king,” Kim said, serenely ready for anything.

“I will teach you better and higher desires along the road,” the lama replied with the tone of authority. “Let us go to Benares.”

“Not at night. Thieves are everywhere. Wait until morning.”

“But there is nowhere for us to sleep.” The old man was accustomed to the orderly routine of his monastery, and although he slept on the bare ground as their Rule required, he preferred a certain decency in such matters.

“We can get good lodgings at the Kashmir Serai,” Kim said, laughing at his worry. “I have a friend there. Come along!”

The hot, crowded bazaars blazed with lights as they made their way through a throng of people from every race in Upper India. The lama drifted through it all like a man in a dream; it was his first experience of a massive manufacturing city, and the crowded tramcars with their screeching brakes frightened him. Half-pushed and half-guided, he finally reached the towering gateway of the Kashmir Serai—that huge open square opposite the railway station, surrounded by arched cloisters where camel and horse caravans put up upon returning from Central Asia. Here were northerners of every description tending tethered ponies and kneeling camels; loading and unloading heavy bales; drawing water for their evening meals from creaking well-pulleys; piling grass before wild-eyed, shrieking stallions; cursing surly caravan dogs; paying off camel-drivers; hiring new grooms; and shouting, arguing, and bargaining across the packed square. The cloisters, raised three or four masonry steps above the chaos, provided a peaceful refuge around this turbulent sea of humanity. Most of them were rented out to traders just as railway arches are rented, with the spaces between the pillars bricked or boarded off into rooms secured by heavy wooden doors and clumsy native padlocks. Locked doors indicated that the owner was away, and rude—sometimes very crude—messages written in chalk or paint showed where they had gone. For instance: “Lutuf Ullah has gone to Kurdistan.” And beneath it, in coarse verse: “O Allah, who allowest lice to live on the coat of a Kabuli, why hast thou permitted this louse Lutuf to live so long?”

Guiding the lama past excited men and frantic beasts, Kim slipped along the cloisters to the far end near the railway station, where Mahbub Ali, the horse-trader, stayed whenever he returned from the mysterious lands beyond the northern mountain passes.

Kim had dealings with Mahbub many times in his young life, especially between his tenth and thirteenth years. The burly Afghan horse-trader—whose beard was dyed bright red with henna because he was aging and wished to hide his gray hairs—knew the boy’s value as a gatherer of gossip. Sometimes Mahbub would tell Kim to watch a man who had nothing to do with horses, following him for an entire day and reporting everyone he spoke with. Kim would deliver his report by evening, and Mahbub would listen without a single word or gesture. Kim knew it was some kind of intrigue, but its true value lay in keeping absolute silence toward everyone except Mahbub, who rewarded him with hot meals from the cookshop at the head of the serai and, on one occasion, as much as eight annas in cash.

“He is here,” Kim said, giving a bad-tempered camel a tap on the nose. “Ohé, Mahbub Ali!” He stopped before a dark archway and stepped behind the bewildered lama.

The horse-trader, with his heavy, embroidered Bokharan belt unbuckled, was lounging on a pair of silk carpet saddle-bags, lazily smoking an immense silver hookah. He turned his head slightly at the call, and seeing only a tall, silent figure, chuckled deep in his chest.

“Allah! A lama! A Red Lama! It’s a long way from Lahore to the mountain passes. What are you doing here?”

The lama automatically held out his begging-bowl.

“God’s curse on all unbelievers!” Mahbub spat. “I don’t give to lousy Tibetans. Ask my Baltis over there behind the camels; they might value your blessings. Hey, horse-boys, here is a countryman of yours. See if he’s hungry.”

A shaven, crouching Balti who had traveled down with the horses—and who was nominally some sort of degraded Buddhist—fawned upon the priest and in a thick, guttural voice begged the holy man to sit by the horse-boys’ fire.

“Go on,” Kim whispered, giving him a gentle push, and the lama strode away, leaving Kim standing at the edge of the cloister.

“Go away,” Mahbub Ali said, returning to his hookah. “Little Hindu, run along. God’s curse on all unbelievers! Go beg from my men who share your faith.”

*“Maharaj,”* Kim whined, adopting the Hindu form of address and thoroughly enjoying the game, “my father is dead, my mother is dead, and my stomach is empty.”

“Beg from my men among the horses, I tell you. Surely there must be some Hindus in my camp.”

“Oh, Mahbub Ali, am I really a Hindu?” Kim asked in English.

The trader showed no sign of surprise, but looked at him keenly from beneath his shaggy eyebrows.

“Little Friend of all the World,” he said, “what is this?”

“Nothing. I am now that holy man’s disciple, and we are going on a pilgrimage together—to Benares, he says. He is completely mad, and I am tired of Lahore city. I want fresh air and water.”

“But who do you work for? Why come to me?” The trader’s voice was harsh with suspicion.

“Who else should I go to? I have no money, and it’s no good wandering about without it. You’ll be selling many horses to the officers soon—they are very fine horses, these new ones, I’ve seen them. Give me a rupee, Mahbub Ali, and when I come into my fortune I will give you a bond and pay you back.”

“Hmm!” Mahbub Ali thought rapidly. “You have never lied to me before. Call that lama back—and stand in the shadows.”

“Oh, our stories will match,” Kim laughed.

“We are going to Benares,” the lama announced as soon as he understood the drift of Mahbub Ali’s questions. “The boy and I. I am going to search for a certain river.”

“Perhaps—but what about the boy?”

“He is my disciple. He was sent, I believe, to guide me to that river. I was sitting under a cannon when he came to me suddenly. Such things happen to the fortunate when guidance is permitted. But I remember now—he said he belonged to this world, a Hindu.”

“And his name?”

“I didn’t ask. Is he not my disciple?”

“His country—his race—his village? Is he Muslim, Sikh, Hindu, Jain, low caste or high?”

“Why should I ask? There is neither high nor low on the Middle Way. If he is my disciple—does he, will he, can anyone take him from me? For look you, without him I shall never find my river.” He shook his head solemnly.

“No one will take him from you. Go sit among my Baltis,” Mahbub Ali said, and the lama drifted away, comforted by the promise.

“Isn’t he completely mad?” Kim asked, stepping back into the light. “Why would I lie to you, Hajji?”

Mahbub puffed his hookah in silence. Then he began almost in a whisper: “Ambala is on the road to Benares—if the two of you are really going there.”

“Tch! Tch! I’m telling you, he doesn’t know how to lie the way you and I do.”

“And if you carry a message for me as far as Ambala, I will give you money. It concerns a horse—a white stallion that I sold to an officer the last time I returned from the mountain passes. But the pedigree—stand closer and hold your hands out as if you’re begging—the pedigree of that white stallion was not fully settled, and the officer, who is now at Ambala, wants me to clear it up.” (Mahbub then described the horse and the officer’s appearance.) “So the message for that officer will be: ‘The pedigree of the white stallion is fully established.’ By this he will know you come from me. He will then ask, ‘What proof do you have?’ and you will answer: ‘Mahbub Ali has given me the proof.’”

“And all this for the sake of a white stallion,” Kim giggled, his eyes shining with excitement.

“I will give you that pedigree now—in my own fashion, along with a few harsh words.” A shadow passed behind Kim as a camel walked by, and Mahbub Ali raised his voice.

“Allah! Are you the only beggar in this city? Your mother is dead, your father is dead. It’s always the same story with you lot. Well, well—”

He turned as if feeling around on the floor beside him and tossed a piece of soft, greasy Muslim flatbread to the boy. “Go and lie down among my horse-boys for tonight—you and your lama. Tomorrow I may have some work for you.”

Kim slipped away, biting into the bread, and as he expected, he found a small wad of folded tissue paper wrapped in oilskin, along with three silver rupees—an enormous sum of money. He smiled and tucked both the money and the paper inside his leather amulet case. The lama, generously fed by Mahbub’s Baltis, was already asleep in the corner of one of the stalls. Kim lay down beside him and laughed to himself. He knew he had just done a favor for Mahbub Ali, and not for a single second did he believe the story about the stallion’s pedigree.

What Kim did not suspect, however, was that Mahbub Ali—known as one of the best horse-dealers in the Punjab, a wealthy and daring trader whose caravans pushed deep into the remote frontiers—was registered in the locked files of the Indian Survey Department as C25 IB. Two or three times a year, C25 would send in a short, baldly stated report that was intensely interesting and—checked against the accounts of R17 and M4—entirely accurate. These reports concerned out-of-the-way mountain principalities, foreign explorers, and the illegal arms trade. In short, they formed a small part of the vast body of “information received” upon which the Indian Government acted.

Recently, however, five allied kings who had no business forming an alliance had been quietly tipped off by a friendly Northern Power that news from their territories was leaking into British India. Consequently, the prime ministers of those kings were seriously annoyed and took stern measures in the Oriental fashion. Among others, they suspected the booming, red-bearded horse-dealer whose caravans fought their way through their snowy passes. In fact, Mahbub’s caravan had been ambushed and shot at twice during the descent that season, though his men had accounted for three strange ruffians who may or may not have been hired for the job. Therefore, Mahbub had avoided stopping at the dangerous city of Peshawar and had ridden straight through to Lahore, anticipating some very interesting developments among his own countrymen.

And Mahbub Ali was carrying something he did not wish to keep an hour longer than necessary: a wad of tightly folded tissue paper wrapped in oilskin—an unsigned, unaddressed statement with five microscopic pinholes in one corner that shockingly betrayed the five allied kings, the sympathetic Northern Power, a Hindu banker in Peshawar, a firm of gunsmiths in Belgium, and an important semi-independent Muslim ruler to the south. This last item was R17’s work, which Mahbub had picked up beyond the Dora Pass and was carrying in for R17, who, due to circumstances beyond his control, could not leave his observation post. Dynamite was mild and harmless compared to C25’s report, and even an Oriental, with his relaxed view of time, knew that the sooner it reached the proper hands, the better. Mahbub had no particular desire to die a violent death, especially since he still had two or three family blood-feuds across the border waiting to be settled, after which he intended to retire as a relatively virtuous citizen. He had not stepped outside the serai gates since arriving two days ago, but he had made a great show of sending telegrams: to Bombay, where he banked some of his money; to Delhi, where a business partner of his own clan was selling horses to a Rajputana state agent; and to Ambala, where an Englishman was anxiously demanding the pedigree of a white stallion. The public letter-writer, who knew English, had composed excellent telegrams such as: “Creighton, Laurel Bank, Ambala. Horse is Arabian as already advised. Sorrowful delayed pedigree which am translating.” And later to the same address: “Much sorrowful delay. Will forward pedigree.” To his business partner in Delhi he had wired: “Lutuf Ullah. Have wired two thousand rupees your credit Luchman Narain’s bank.” This was all standard business, but every single telegram was thoroughly discussed and analyzed by interested parties before being carried to the railway station by a foolish Balti messenger who allowed everyone along the road to read them.

When, in Mahbub’s picturesque phrase, he had muddied the waters of inquiry with the stick of caution, Kim had dropped right into his lap like a gift from heaven. Being as prompt as he was unscrupulous, and accustomed to taking bold gambles, Mahbub Ali had pressed Kim into service on the spot.

A wandering lama with a low-caste boy servant might attract a moment’s curiosity while roaming through India, the land of pilgrims, but no one would ever suspect them—or, more importantly, rob them.

Mahbub called for a fresh coal for his hookah and thought the situation over. In the worst-case scenario, if the boy came to harm, the paper would incriminate no one. And Mahbub would travel up to Ambala at his leisure and—at some risk of raising fresh suspicions—deliver his report by word of mouth to the proper authorities.

Even so, R17’s report was the absolute core of the whole affair, and it would be deeply inconvenient if it failed to arrive. Still, God was great, and Mahbub Ali felt he had done all he possibly could for the moment. Kim was the one soul in the world who had never lied to him—a fatal flaw in Kim’s character, really, except that Mahbub knew Kim could lie like a true Oriental when dealing with others for his own or Mahbub’s purposes.

Later, Mahbub Ali strolled across the serai to the Gate of the Harpies—those women who paint their eyes and trap strangers—and took the trouble to visit a certain girl whom he believed to be a close friend of a smooth-faced Kashmiri pundit who had waylaid his simple Balti messenger over the telegrams. It was a remarkably foolish thing to do, because they ended up drinking perfumed brandy in violation of the Prophet’s law. Mahbub grew wonderfully drunk, his tongue loosened completely, and he chased the Flower of Delight across the room until he collapsed heavily among the cushions. Thereupon the Flower of Delight, assisted by the smooth-faced Kashmiri pundit, searched him thoroughly from head to toe.

Around the same hour, Kim heard soft footsteps entering Mahbub’s vacant stall. Curiously enough, the horse-trader had left his door unlocked, and his men were busy celebrating their return to India with a whole sheep provided by Mahbub’s generosity. A sleek young gentleman from Delhi, armed with a bunch of keys he had unclipped from the senseless trader’s belt, went through every single box, bundle, mat, and saddlebag in Mahbub’s possession even more thoroughly than the Flower and the pundit had searched the owner.

“And I think,” the Flower said scornfully an hour later, resting one rounded elbow on the snoring carcass, “that he is nothing more than a pig of an Afghan horse-dealer with no thoughts above women and horses. Besides, he may have sent the paper away by now—if such a thing ever existed at all.”

“No—in a matter involving five kings, it would be kept right against his black heart,” the pundit replied. “Was there nothing?”

The Delhi man laughed, adjusting his turban as he re-entered. “I searched between the soles of his slippers just as carefully as you searched his clothes. This is not the right man, but someone else. I left very little unseen.”

“They didn’t say he was definitely the man,” the pundit mused. “They said, ‘See if he is the man, since our plans are troubled.’”

“That northern country is as full of horse-dealers as an old coat is of lice. There are Sikandar Khan, Nur Ali Beg, and Farrukh Shah—all caravan leaders who trade there,” said the Flower.

“They haven’t arrived yet,” the pundit said. “You’ll have to trap them later.”

*“Phew!”* the Flower said with deep disgust, shoving Mahbub’s head off her lap. “I earn my money hard. Farrukh Shah is a bear, Ali Beg is a bully, and old Sikandar Khan—ugh! Go away. I’m going to sleep now. This pig won’t stir until dawn.”

When Mahbub woke up later, the Flower lectured him severely on the sin of drunkenness. Asians do not wink when they have outmaneuvered an enemy, but as Mahbub Ali cleared his throat, tightened his belt, and staggered out beneath the early morning stars, he came very close to it.

“What a foolish trick!” he muttered to himself. “As if every girl in Peshawar doesn’t use it! But it was neatly done. Now God alone knows how many more agents are waiting along the road with orders to test me—perhaps with a knife. So it’s best that the boy goes to Ambala by train, because the writing is urgent. I’ll stay here, play along with the Flower, and drink wine like a proper Afghan horse-coper.”

He stopped at the stall two doors down from his own. His men were still fast asleep, but there was no sign of Kim or the lama.

“Wake up!” he prodded a sleeping man. “Where did those who stayed here last night go—the lama and the boy? Is anything missing?”

“No,” the man grunted sleepily. “The old madman got up at the second cockcrow saying he was going to Benares, and the young one led him away.”

“The curse of Allah on all unbelievers!” Mahbub said heartily, climbing back into his own stall and growling into his beard.

It was actually Kim who had woken the lama. Peering through a knothole in the wooden planks, Kim had witnessed the Delhi man’s search through the boxes. This was no ordinary thief looking over letters, bills, and saddles, nor a common burglar slipping a small knife into the soles of Mahbub’s slippers or expertly picking the seams of the saddlebags. At first, Kim had thought of raising the alarm—the long, drawn-out cho-or, cho-or! (thief, thief!) that sets the serai ablaze with commotion at night—but he looked closer, placed a hand on his amulet, and drew his own conclusions.

“That must be the pedigree for that fake horse-story,” he told himself, “the very thing I’m carrying to Ambala. We had better leave right now. People who search bags with knives will soon be searching bellies with knives. There’s certainly a woman behind all this. Hai! Hai!” he whispered to the sleeping old man. “Get up. It is time—time to go to Benares.”

The lama rose obediently, and together they slipped out of the serai like shadows.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.content:
And whoso will, from Pride released,
Contemning neither creed nor priest,
May feel the Soul of all the East,
About him at Kamakura.

They entered the fort-like railway station, which stood pitch dark against the dying night, while the electric lights sizzled high above the goods-yard where workers handled the heavy northern grain traffic.

“This is the work of devils!” the lama said, pulling back from the hollow, echoing darkness, the glint of steel rails between the masonry platforms, and the sprawling network of overhead girders. He stood in a gigantic stone hall paved, it seemed, with the sheeted bodies of third-class passengers who had purchased their tickets the evening before and were fast asleep in the waiting rooms. To Orientals, all hours of the day and night are alike, and their passenger traffic is arranged accordingly.

“This is where the fire-carriages come. Someone sits behind that opening”—Kim pointed to the ticket office—“who will give you a paper to take you to Ambala.”

“But we are going to Benares,” he protested irritably.

“It’s all the same. Benares, then. Hurry, it’s coming!”

“Take the purse.”

The lama, who was not nearly as accustomed to trains as he had pretended, jumped as the 3:25 a.m. southbound train roared into the station. The sleepers sprang to life instantly, and the station filled with noise and shouting: vendors calling out water and sweetmeats, native policemen yelling, and women shouting shrilly as they gathered up their baskets, their children, and their husbands.

“It is just the train—the te-rain. It won’t run us down. Wait!” Amazed at the lama’s total innocence—he had simply handed Kim a small bag stuffed with rupees—Kim went and bought a ticket to Ambala. A sleepy clerk grunted and tossed out a ticket for the very next station, just six miles away.

“No,” Kim said, inspecting it with a grin. “This might do for simple farmers, but I live in the city of Lahore. That was a clever trick, Babu. Now give me the proper ticket to Ambala.”

The Babu scowled and handed over the correct ticket.

“Now another one to Amritsar,” Kim demanded. He had no intention of spending Mahbub Ali’s money on something as straightforward as a direct ticket to Ambala. “The price is this much, and the change should be that much. I know how the te-rain works... No holy man ever needed a disciple as much as you do,” he went on cheerfully to the bewildered lama. “They would have thrown you off at Mian Mir if not for me. This way! Come along!” He returned the money, keeping back only one anna for every rupee of the Ambala ticket price as his commission—the immemorial commission of Asia.

The lama hesitated at the open door of a crowded third-class compartment. “Would it not be better to walk?” he asked weakly.

A burly Sikh artisan poked his bearded head out the door. “Is he afraid? Don’t be afraid. I remember when I was afraid of the train myself. Get in! This machine is the work of the Government.”

“I am not afraid,” the lama said. “Do you have room inside for two?”

“There is not even room for a mouse,” shrilled the wife of a well-to-do cultivator—a Hindu Jat from the rich Jullundur district. Their night trains were not as strictly regulated as the daytime ones, where men and women were kept in strictly separate carriages.

“Oh, mother of my son, we can make room,” the blue-turbaned husband said. “Pick up the child. Can’t you see he is a holy man?”

“And my lap is already full of seventy times seven bundles! Why don’t you tell him to sit on my lap, you shameless man? But men are always like this!” She looked around for approval. An Amritsar courtesan sitting near the window sniffed behind her head-covering.

“Get in! Get in!” cried a fat Hindu money-lender with his cloth-wrapped account book tucked under his arm, giving an oily smirk. “It is good to be kind to the poor.”

“Yes, especially at seven percent a month with a mortgage on an unborn calf,” a young Dogra soldier heading south on leave muttered, and everyone laughed.

“Will this thing travel to Benares?” the lama asked.

“Assuredly. Why else would we be getting on? Step inside, or we’ll be left behind!” Kim urged.

“Look!” shrilled the Amritsar girl. “He has never been on a train before. Oh, look at him!”

“Here, let me help,” the cultivator said, reaching out a large brown hand and hauling him aboard. “That’s how it’s done, father.”

“But—but—I must sit on the floor. It goes against our Rule to sit on a bench,” the lama said. “Besides, it cramps me.”

“I must say,” the money-lender began, pursing his lips, “there is hardly a rule of right living that these te-rains don’t force us to break. For instance, we have to sit side by side with all castes and kinds of people.”

“Yes, and with thoroughly shameless ones, too,” the cultivator’s wife said, glaring sourly at the Amritsar girl, who was making eyes at the young sepoy.

“I told you we should have traveled by cart along the road,” the husband remarked, “and saved ourselves some money.”

“Yes—and spent twice what we saved on food along the way. We argued about that ten thousand times.”

“Yes, by ten thousand tongues,” he grunted.

“The gods help us poor women if we aren’t even allowed to speak! Oho! He’s one of those who isn’t allowed to look at or reply to a woman.” Bound by his religious Rule, the lama was ignoring her completely. “And I suppose his disciple is just like him?”

“Not at all, mother,” Kim replied instantly, “especially when the woman is good-looking and, above all, charitable to the hungry.”

“Spoken like a true beggar!” the Sikh laughed. “You asked for that one, sister!” Kim curved his hands in supplication.

“And where are you going?” the woman asked, tossing him half a cake from a greasy bundle.

“All the way to Benares.”

“Jugglers, perhaps?” the young soldier suggested. “Do you have any tricks to pass the time? Why won’t that old man in yellow answer?”

“Because,” Kim said stoutly, “he is holy, and his mind is fixed on matters beyond your understanding.”

“That may be all very well. We of the Ludhiana Sikhs”—he pronounced it grandly—“don’t clutter our heads with doctrine. We fight.”

“My sister’s brother’s son is a corporal in that regiment,” the Sikh craftsman remarked quietly. “There are some Dogra companies stationed there, too.” The soldier glared, because a Dogras belonged to a different caste than a Sikh, and the banker snickered.

“They’re all the same to me,” the Amritsar girl said.

“We can well believe that,” the cultivator’s wife snorted viciously.

“No, but everyone who serves the Government with weapons in their hands is part of a single brotherhood. There is the brotherhood of caste, and beyond that”—she looked around timidly—“the bond of the Pulton—the Regiment—isn’t that so?”

“My brother is in a Jat regiment,” the cultivator said. “Dogras are good men.”

“Your Sikhs certainly thought so,” the soldier said, scowling at the placid old man in the corner, “when our two companies came to help them at the Pirzai Kotal against eight standards of Afridis on the ridge not three months ago.”

He proceeded to tell the story of a border skirmish in which the Dogra companies of the Ludhiana Sikhs had fought bravely. The Amritsar girl smiled, knowing the soldier was talking just to win her approval.

“Alas!” the cultivator’s wife said when he finished. “So their villages were burned and their little children left homeless?”

“They had marked our dead. They paid dearly after we Sikhs taught them a lesson. That’s how it goes. Is this Amritsar?”

“Yes, and this is where they check our tickets,” the banker said, fumbling at his belt.

The station lamps were growing pale in the dawn when the half-caste ticket collector came around. Collecting tickets is a slow process in the East, where people hide their tickets in all sorts of strange places. Kim produced his own and was promptly told to get off.

“But I am going to Ambala,” he protested. “I am traveling with this holy man.”

“You can go to hell for all I care. This ticket is only for—”

Kim burst into a flood of tears, insisting that the lama was his father and his mother, that he was the sole support of the lama’s declining years, and that the old man would die without his care. Everyone in the compartment urged the guard to show mercy—the banker was especially eloquent—but the guard hoisted Kim out onto the platform anyway. The lama blinked, completely unable to grasp the situation, while Kim raised his voice and wept loudly outside the carriage window.

“I am very poor! My father is dead, my mother is dead! O charitable ones, if I am left here, who will look after this old man?”

“What—what is this?” the lama repeated. “He must go to Benares. He must come with me. He is my disciple. If there is money to be paid—”

“Oh, be quiet,” Kim whispered to him. “Are we wealthy princes to throw away good silver when the world is so full of charity?”

The Amritsar girl stepped out onto the platform with her bundles, and Kim fixed his watchful eyes on her. Women of her profession, he knew well, could be generous.

“A ticket—just a little ticket to Ambala—O Breaker of Hearts!” he pleaded. “Have you no charity?”

“Does the holy man come from the North?”

“From far, far away in the North,” Kim cried. “From deep in the mountains.”

“There is snow among the pine trees in the North—there is snow in the hills. My mother came from Kulu. Go get your ticket. And ask him to give me a blessing.”

“Ten thousand blessings!” Kim yelled shrilly. “O Holy One, a woman has given us charity so that I may come with you—a woman with a golden heart! I am running for the ticket now!”

The girl looked up at the lama, who had automatically followed Kim onto the platform. He bowed his head so he wouldn’t have to look at her and muttered prayers in Tibetan as she walked on with the crowd.

“Easy come, easy go,” the cultivator’s wife remarked maliciously.

“She has earned spiritual merit,” the lama said. “Without a doubt, she must be a nun.”

“There are ten thousand such nuns in Amritsar alone. Get back inside, old man, or the te-rain will leave without you!” the banker shouted.

“Not only was there enough for the ticket, but for a little food as well!” Kim announced, leaping back into his seat. “Eat now, Holy One. Look, the day is breaking!”

Golden, rose, saffron, and pink, the morning mists rolled away across the flat, green plains. The entire fertile Punjab lay spread out in the splendor of the sharp morning sun. The lama flinched slightly every time a telegraph pole rushed past.

“Great is the speed of the te-rain,” the banker said with a patronizing grin. “We have traveled farther since leaving Lahore than you could walk in two days. By evening, we will be in Ambala.”

“And that is still a long way from Benares,” the lama said wearily, chewing on the cakes Kim offered him. The other passengers untied their bundles and ate their morning meals. Then the banker, the cultivator, and the soldier lit their pipes, filling the compartment with a thick, choking, acrid smoke as they spat, coughed, and enjoyed themselves. The Sikh and the cultivator’s wife chewed betel nut; the lama took snuff and fingered his prayer beads; while Kim sat cross-legged, smiling over the comfort of a full stomach.

“What rivers do you have near Benares?” the lama suddenly asked the compartment at large.

“We have the Ganges,” the banker replied after the brief laughter died down.

“What others?”

“What other is there besides the Ganges?”

“Well, I had in mind a certain River of Healing.”

“That is the Ganges. Whoever bathes in her is made clean and goes to the gods. Three times have I made the pilgrimage to the Ganges.” He looked around proudly.

“You needed to,” the young sepoy remarked dryly, and the other travelers laughed at the banker’s expense.

“Clean—only to return to the round of lives again—still bound to the Wheel,” the lama muttered, shaking his head irritably. “Yet perhaps there is a mistake. Who made the Ganges in the beginning?”

The banker looked horrified. “The gods made it. What faith do you belong to, anyway?”

“I follow the Law—the Most Excellent Law. So it was the gods who made the Ganges. What kind of gods were they?”

The passengers stared at him in utter amazement. It was unthinkable that anyone could be ignorant of the Ganges.

“What—what is your god?” the money-lender asked at last.

“Listen!” the lama said, shifting his rosary to his other hand. “Listen, for I speak of Him now! O people of India, listen!”

He began to recount the story of Lord Buddha in Urdu, but carried away by his own thoughts, he drifted into Tibetan and long-chanted verses from a Chinese text on the Buddha’s life. The gentle, tolerant people listened respectfully. All of India was full of holy men stammering gospels in strange tongues, consumed by the fire of their own devotion—dreamers, babblers, and visionaries, just as it had been from the beginning and would be to the end.

“Hmm!” said the soldier of the Ludhiana Sikhs. “There was a Muslim regiment camped next to us at the Pirzai Kotal, and a priest of theirs—a corporal, as I recall—used to preach prophecies whenever the fit took him. But madmen are all in God’s keeping; his officers overlooked a lot in that fellow.”

Remembering he was in a strange land, the lama switched back to Urdu. “Hear the tale of the arrow our Lord loosed from the bow,” he said.

This suited their tastes much better, and they listened with great curiosity as he told the story. “Now, O people of India, I am going to search for that river. Do any of you know anything that might guide me, for we are all men and women in sore distress?”

“There is the Ganges—and the Ganges alone—which washes away all sin,” murmured the voices around the compartment.

“Though, for that matter, we have very good gods around Jullundur,” the cultivator’s wife said, looking out the window. “Just look how they have blessed our crops.”

“Searching every river in the Punjab is no small task,” her husband observed. “As for me, any stream that leaves good silt on my fields is enough, and I thank Bhumia, the god of the homestead.” He shrugged a knotted, sun-bronzed shoulder.

“Do you think our Lord came this far North?” the lama asked, turning to Kim.

“Perhaps,” Kim replied soothingly, spitting red betel juice onto the floor.

“The last of the Great Ones,” the Sikh stated authoritatively, “was Sikander Julkarn [Alexander the Great]. He paved the streets of Jullundur and built a great tank near Ambala. That pavement is still there today, and the tank remains as well. I never heard of your god.”

“Let your hair grow long and start speaking Punjabi,” the young soldier teased Kim, quoting a northern proverb. “That’s all it takes to make a Sikh.” But he didn’t say it very loudly.

The lama sighed and shrank into himself, a dingy, shapeless bundle. In the pauses of their conversation, they could hear the soft, low droning—“Om mani padme hum! Om mani padme hum!”—accompanied by the steady clicking of his wooden prayer beads.

“It troubles me,” he said at last. “The speed and the noise trouble me. Moreover, my disciple, I begin to think we may have traveled past that river.”

“Peace, peace,” Kim said. “Wasn’t the river near Benares? We are still a long way from there.”

“But if our Lord came North, it might be any one of these little streams we’ve passed along the way.”

“I don’t know.”

“But you were sent to me—weren’t you sent to me?—as a reward for the merit I earned over there at Such-zen? You came to me right beside the great cannon, wearing two faces and two different sets of clothes.”

“Peace. One must not speak of such things here,” Kim whispered. “There was only one of me. Think back and you’ll remember. A boy—a Hindu boy—by the great green cannon.”

“But wasn’t there also an Englishman with a white beard—a holy man among images—who confirmed my certainty about the River of the Arrow?”

“He—we—went to the Wonder House in Lahore to pray before the gods there,” Kim explained to the deeply interested audience. “And the Sahib of the Wonder House spoke to him—yes, this is the truth—like a brother. He is a very holy man from far beyond the hills. Rest now. In a little while we will reach Ambala.”

“But my river—the River of my Healing?”

“And then, if you like, we will go hunting for that river on foot. So that we don’t miss a single thing—not even a tiny rivulet beside a field.”

“But you have a search of your own?” The lama sat straight up, very pleased with his own memory.

“Yes,” Kim said, playing along. The boy was thoroughly happy chewing betel nut and meeting new people in this vast, good-natured world.

“It was a bull—a Red Bull that was to come and help you and carry you—where? I’ve forgotten. A Red Bull on a green field, wasn't it?”

“No, it won’t carry me anywhere,” Kim said. “That was just a story I told you.”

“What is this?” The cultivator’s wife leaned forward, her silver bracelets clinking. “Do both of you dream dreams? A Red Bull on a green field that will carry you to the heavens or something? Was it a vision? Did someone make a prophecy? We have a Red Bull right in our village behind Jullundur city, and he prefers to graze in our very greenest fields!”

“Give an old woman’s tale to a weaver-bird with a leaf and thread, and they’ll weave wonders,” the Sikh remarked. “All holy men dream dreams, and by following them, their disciples catch the habit.”

“A Red Bull on a green field, was it?” the lama repeated. “In a past life you must have earned great merit, and the Bull will come to reward you.”

“No, no—it was just a story someone told me, perhaps as a joke. But I will look for the Bull around Ambala, while you look for your river and rest from the noise of the train.”

“Perhaps the Bull knows—perhaps he has been sent to guide us both,” the lama said with the hopeful innocence of a child. Then, turning to the carriage and pointing at Kim, he added, “This one was sent to me only yesterday. I don’t think he belongs to this world at all.”

“I’ve met plenty of beggars and holy men in my time, but never a yogi or a disciple quite like these two,” the woman said.

Her husband touched his forehead lightly with one finger and smiled. But the next time the lama wanted to eat, they made sure to share the very best of their own food.

At last—tired, sleepy, and covered in dust—they reached Ambala City station.

“We are stopping here for a lawsuit,” the cultivator’s wife told Kim. “We are staying with my husband’s cousin’s younger brother. There is room in the courtyard for your yogi and yourself as well. Will—will he give me a blessing?”

“O holy man! A woman with a heart of gold is giving us a place to sleep tonight. This is a kind land, this land of the South. See how we have been helped ever since the dawn!”

The lama bowed his head in blessing.

“To fill my cousin’s younger brother’s house with a pack of loafers—” the husband began, shouldering his heavy bamboo staff.

“Your cousin’s younger brother still owes my father’s cousin money from his daughter’s marriage feast,” the woman said crisply. “Let him put their food down on that account. The yogi will beg for his supper, I have no doubt.”

“Yes, I will beg for him,” Kim said, eager only to get the lama safely sheltered for the night so he could find Mahbub Ali’s Englishman and deliver the white stallion’s pedigree.

“Now,” Kim said after the lama had settled into the inner courtyard of a decent Hindu house behind the military cantonments, “I am going out for a little while—to—to buy us some food in the bazaar. Do not wander off until I come back.”

“You will return? You will surely return?” The old man caught him by the wrist. “And you will come back looking just as you do now? Is it too late to search for the river tonight?”

“Too late and too dark. Rest easy. Think how far along the road you are—a hundred kos from Lahore already.”

“Yes—and farther from my monastery. Alas! It is a great and terrible world.”

Kim slipped out into the night, looking as unremarkable as any boy carrying his own and a few thousand other people’s fates slung around his neck. Mahbub Ali’s directions left little doubt about which house the Englishman lived in, and a groom driving a dog-cart back from the Club confirmed it. It only remained to identify the man. Kim crept through the garden hedge and hid in a clump of tall grass close to the veranda. The house blazed with lights, and servants moved around tables decorated with flowers, crystal, and silver. Soon an Englishman dressed in black and white stepped out onto the veranda, humming a tune. It was too dark to see his face, so Kim tried an old beggar’s trick.

“Protector of the Poor!”

The man stepped back toward the voice.

“Mahbub Ali says—”

“Ha! What does Mahbub Ali say?” He made no effort to look for the speaker, which proved to Kim that he understood.

“The pedigree of the white stallion is fully established.”

“What proof is there?” The Englishman flicked at a rosebush beside the driveway with his riding crop.

“Mahbub Ali gave me this proof.” Kim flipped the wad of folded paper into the air, and it landed on the path beside the man, who placed his foot over it just as a gardener walked around the corner. Once the servant had passed, the Englishman picked it up, dropped a rupee—Kim heard the metallic clink—and strode into the house without turning around. Kim quickly picked up the money, but for all his street training, he was Irish enough by birth to consider silver the least important part of any game. What he really wanted to see was the actual result of his actions. Instead of sneaking away, he stayed hidden in the grass and wormed his way closer to the house.

Because Indian bungalows are completely open through and through, Kim could see the Englishman walk into a small dressing room at the corner of the veranda that served as a makeshift office, littered with papers and dispatch boxes, and sit down to read Mahbub Ali’s message. Under the bright glare of the kerosene lamp, the man’s face changed and darkened, and Kim, who as a beggar had spent his life watching faces, took careful note.

“Will! Will, dear!” a woman’s voice called out. “You ought to be in the drawing room. They’ll be here in a minute.”

The man continued reading intently.

“Will!” the voice called again five minutes later. “He’s come. I can hear the troopers in the driveway.”

The man dashed outside bareheaded just as a large carriage with four native troopers behind it pulled up to the veranda. A tall, black-haired man, as straight as an arrow, stepped out, accompanied by a young officer who was laughing pleasantly.

Kim lay flat on his stomach, almost touching the high wheels of the carriage. His Englishman and the tall stranger exchanged a couple of sentences.

“Certainly, sir,” the young officer said promptly. “Everything else can wait when a horse is concerned.”

“We won’t be more than twenty minutes,” Kim’s man said. “You can play the host—keep everyone entertained, and all that.”

“Tell one of the troopers to wait,” the tall man said, and both of them walked into the dressing room together as the carriage rolled away. Kim watched their heads bend over Mahbub Ali’s message and listened to their voices—one low and deferential, the other sharp and decisive.

“It isn’t a question of weeks. It’s a question of days—almost hours,” the older man said. “I’ve been expecting it for some time, but this”—he tapped Mahbub Ali’s paper—“settles it. Grogan’s dining here tonight, isn’t he?”

“Yes, sir, and Macklin too.”

“Very good. I’ll speak to them myself. The matter will have to go before the Council, of course, but this is a case where we are fully justified in taking immediate action. Warn the Pindi and Peshawar brigades. It’ll mess up all the summer troop rotations, but we can’t help that. This is what happens when you don’t crush them thoroughly the first time. Eight thousand men should be enough.”

“What about artillery, sir?”

“I’ll have to consult Macklin.”

“Then this means war?”

“No. Punishment. When a man is bound by the actions of his predecessor—”

“But C25 might have lied.”

“His report confirms the other intelligence. Practically speaking, they showed their hand six months ago. But Devenish insisted there was still a chance for peace. Of course, they just used that time to strengthen themselves. Send off those telegrams right away—use the new code, not the old one—mine and Wharton’s. I don’t think we need keep the ladies waiting any longer. We can settle the rest over cigars. I knew it was coming. It’s a punitive action, not a war.”

As the trooper rode off, Kim crawled around to the back of the house where, based on his experience in Lahore, he figured there would be food—and gossip. The kitchen was crowded with busy, excited scullions, one of whom gave him a kick.

*“Aie,”* Kim said, pretending to cry. “I only came to wash dishes in exchange for a meal.”

“All of Ambala is here for the exact same thing. Get out of here. They’re serving the soup right now. Do you think we who serve Creighton Sahib need stray beggar-boys to help us through a grand dinner party?”

“It must be a very big dinner,” Kim said, eyeing the silver platters.

“No wonder. The guest of honor is none other than the Commander-in-Chief himself.”

*“Ho!”* Kim muttered with the appropriate tone of wonder. He had learned what he needed to know, and by the time the scullion turned around again, Kim was gone.

“And all that trouble,” he thought to himself, translating his thoughts into Hindustani, “just for a horse’s pedigree! Mahbub Ali should have come to me if he wanted to learn proper lying. Every message I’ve carried before this was about a woman. Now it’s about men. Much better. The tall man said they are going to unleash a great army to punish someone—somewhere—and the word is going to Pindi and Peshawar. There’ll be artillery, too. I wish I had crept a bit closer. That is big news!”

When he returned to the courtyard, he found the cultivator’s cousin’s younger brother discussing his family lawsuit from every possible angle with the cultivator, his wife, and a few neighbors, while the lama dozed nearby. After the evening meal, someone handed him a water-pipe, and Kim felt very much like a grown man as he puffed on the smooth coconut-shell, sitting cross-legged in the moonlight and chiming in with remarks from time to time. His hosts were extremely polite, for the cultivator’s wife had told them all about his vision of the Red Bull and his probable descent from another world. Besides, the lama was a wonderfully venerable curiosity.

The family priest, an old and tolerant Brahman, dropped in later and naturally started a theological argument to impress the household. By belief, of course, they all sided with their own priest, but the lama was a welcome guest and a fascinating novelty. His gentle kindness and his impressive Chinese quotations—which sounded like magical spells—delighted them immensely.
