In this warm, simple atmosphere, the old man expanded like the Buddha’s own lotus, talking about his life in the grand mountains of Such-zen before, as he put it, “I set out to seek enlightenment.”

In the course of the conversation, it came out that back in his worldly days he had been an expert at casting horoscopes and natal charts. The family priest encouraged him to describe his methods, and the two men discussed planetary names the other could scarce understand while pointing up at the bright stars sailing across the dark sky. The children of the house tugged unrebuked at his rosary, and the lama completely forgot the monastic Rule forbidding monks to look at women as he talked about enduring snows, landslides, blocked mountain passes, the remote cliffs where men find sapphires and turquoise, and the wonderful upland road that finally leads all the way into Great China.

“What do you think of him?” the cultivator whispered aside to the priest.

“A holy man—truly a holy man. His gods are not our gods, but his feet are upon the Path,” the priest replied. “And his methods of casting charts—though they are beyond your understanding—are wise and sound.”

“Tell me,” Kim asked lazily, “will I find my Red Bull on a green field, just as was promised to me?”

“What do you know of the hour of your birth?” the priest asked, puffing himself up with importance.

“Between the first and second cockcrow on the first night of May.”

“Of what year?”

“I don’t know; but at the very hour I first cried out, there was a great earthquake in Srinagar, which is in Kashmir.” Kim had this from the woman who looked after him, who in turn had heard it from Kimball O’Hara. The earthquake had been felt throughout India and remained a major historical reference point in the Punjab.

“Ah!” a woman cried out excitedly. This seemed to make Kim’s supernatural origins even more certain. “Wasn't so-and-so’s daughter born right then—”

“And her mother bore her husband four sons in four years, all healthy boys,” the cultivator’s wife added from the shadows outside the circle.

“Anyone trained in the art,” the family priest declared, “never forgets how the planets stood in their houses on that night.” He began drawing symbols in the courtyard dust. “At least you have a strong claim to a share in the House of the Bull. How does your prophecy go?”

“One day,” Kim said, delighted by the sensation he was causing, “I will be made great by means of a Red Bull on a green field, but first two men will come to make everything ready.”

“Yes, that is always how a true vision opens. A thick darkness that slowly clears; then someone enters with a broom to sweep the place clean. After that, the vision begins. Two men, you say? Ah, yes. The sun leaves the House of the Bull and enters the House of the Twins—hence the two men in the prophecy. Let us consider. Bring me a twig, little one.”

He knitted his brows, scratched in the dust, smoothed it out, and drew mysterious signs all over again—to the wonder of everyone present, except the lama, who with fine intuition chose not to interfere.

At the end of half an hour, the priest tossed the twig aside with a grunt.

“Hmm! That is what the stars say. Within three days, the two men will arrive to make everything ready. After them comes the Bull; but the sign standing opposite is the sign of war and armed men.”

“There was indeed a man of the Ludhiana Sikhs in our carriage from Lahore,” the cultivator’s wife noted hopefully.

“Tch! Armed men—many hundreds of them. What business do you have with war?” the priest scolded Kim. “Yours is a red and angry sign of war that will soon be let loose upon the land.”

“None—none at all,” the lama said earnestly. “We seek only peace and our river.”

Kim smiled, remembering what he had overheard in the dressing room. Clearly, he was a favorite of the stars.

The priest brushed his foot over the crude horoscope in the dust. “I can see nothing beyond that. In three days, the boy, the Bull will come to you.”

“And my river, my river,” the lama pleaded. “I had hoped his Bull would lead us both to the river.”

“Alas for that wondrous river, my brother,” the priest answered. “Such things are not easily found.”

The next morning, though they were warmly urged to stay, the lama insisted on leaving. The family gave Kim a large bundle of good food and nearly three annas in copper coins for the road, and with many blessings, they watched the two travelers set off southward into the dawn.

“It is a pity that such people cannot be freed from—”

“If they were, only evil people would be left on earth, and who would give us food and shelter then?” Kim remarked cheerfully, adjusting his bundle and marching along.

“Yonder is a small stream. Let us go look,” the lama said, leading the way off the white road and across the fields, right into a hornets’ nest of barking pariah dogs.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
chapters.content:
Yea, voice of every Soul that clung
To life that strove from rung to rung
When Devadatta’s rule was young,
The warm wind brings Kamakura.

Behind them, an angry farmer brandished a bamboo pole. He was a market-gardener, an Arain by caste, who grew vegetables and flowers for Umballa city, and Kim knew the type well.

“Such a man,” the lama said, paying no attention to the dogs, “is impolite to strangers, foul of speech, and uncharitable. Be warned by his bad manners, my disciple.”

“Ho, shameless beggars!” shouted the farmer. “Be off! Get out of here!”

“We are going,” the lama replied with quiet dignity. “We are leaving these unblessed fields.”

“Ah,” Kim muttered, sucking in his breath. “If your next crops fail, you will only have your own tongue to blame.”

The man shifted uneasily in his slippers. “The land is full of beggars,” he began, half apologetically.

“And by what sign did you know we were going to beg from you, O Mali?” Kim asked sharply, using the term that market-gardeners dislike most. “All we wanted was to look at that river beyond the field.”

“River, indeed!” the man snorted. “What city do you come from not to know a canal cut when you see one? It runs as straight as an arrow, and I pay for the water as if it were solid silver. There is a branch of a river farther on, though. But if you need water, I can give you that—and milk.”

“No, we will go to the river,” the lama said, striding forward.

“Milk and a meal,” the man stammered, staring at the strange, tall figure. “I—I don’t want to bring bad luck on myself—or my crops. But beggars are so numerous these hard days.”

“Take note,” the lama told Kim. “He was led to speak harshly by the Red Mist of anger. Once that clears from his eyes, he becomes courteous and of a kindly heart. May his fields be blessed! Remember not to judge men too hastily, farmer.”

“I’ve met holy ones who would have cursed you from your hearthstone to your cattle-shed,” Kim said to the abashed man. “Isn’t he wise and holy? I am his disciple.”

He held his nose high in the air and stepped across the narrow field borders with great dignity.

“There is no pride,” the lama said after a pause, “there is no pride among those who follow the Middle Way.”

“But you just said he was low-caste and rude.”

“I did not say low-caste, for how can that be which has no real existence? Afterward he corrected his rudeness, and I forgot the offense. Besides, he is just like us, bound upon the Wheel of Things; he simply does not tread the way of deliverance.” He stopped at a small runlet among the fields and examined the hoof-marked bank.

“Now, how will you recognize your river?” Kim asked, squatting in the shade of some tall sugar cane.

“When I find it, enlightenment will surely be granted to me. This place, I feel, is not it. O smallest among waters, if only you could tell me where my river flows! Yet be blessed for helping the fields to bear fruit.”

“Look! Look!” Kim sprang to his side and yanked him backward. A yellow-and-brown streak glided from the rustling purple stems toward the bank, stretched its neck to the water, drank, and lay still—a large cobra with fixed, unblinking eyes.

“I don’t have a stick—I don’t have a stick,” Kim cried. “I’ll find one and break its back.”

“Why? It is upon the Wheel just as we are—a life ascending or descending—very far from deliverance. The soul that is cast into this shape must have committed great evil.”

“I hate all snakes,” Kim said. No native upbringing could ever stamp out a white man’s innate horror of serpents.

“Let it live out its life.” The coiled creature hissed and half spread its hood. “May your release come soon, brother!” the lama continued placidly. “By chance, do you know anything of my river?”

“I have never seen a man like you,” Kim whispered, completely overwhelmed. “Do snakes actually understand your talk?”

“Who knows?” The lama stepped within a foot of the cobra’s poised head. The snake flattened itself among the dusty coils.

“Come along!” the lama called over his shoulder.

“Not I,” Kim said. “I’m walking around.”

“Come. It will do no harm.”

Kim hesitated for a second. The lama reinforced his command with a droned Chinese quotation that Kim took for a magical charm. He obeyed and leaped across the streamlet, and indeed the snake made no move.

“I have never seen such a man.” Kim wiped the sweat from his forehead. “And now, where are we going?”

“That is for you to decide. I am old and a stranger—far from my own home. If the railway carriage hadn’t filled my head with the noise of devil-drums, I would have gone straight to Benares by now... Yet by traveling that way, we might miss the river. Let us find another river.”

In a region where the hard-working soil yields three or even four crops a year through patches of sugar cane, tobacco, long white radishes, and kohlrabi, they strolled on all day, turning aside at every glimpse of water, startling village dogs and sleeping hamlets at noonday. The lama answered every volley of questions with unwavering simplicity. They were searching for a river: a river of miraculous healing. Did anyone know of such a stream?

Sometimes people laughed, but more often they listened to the story to the very end and offered them a shady resting place, a drink of milk, and a meal. The women were invariably kind, and the little children—like children the world over—were alternately shy and bold.

Evening found them resting beneath the village tree of a mud-walled, mud-roofed hamlet, chatting with the headman as the cattle returned from the grazing grounds and the women prepared the evening meal. They had passed beyond the belt of market gardens surrounding hungry Umballa and were now among the mile-wide green fields of the staple crops.

The headman was a white-bearded, affable elder accustomed to entertaining strangers. He dragged out a string bedstead for the lama, set warm cooked food before him, prepared a pipe for him, and—once the evening ceremonies at the village temple were finished—sent for the village priest.

Kim told the older children tales of the size and grandeur of Lahore, of train travel, and other city wonders, while the men talked slowly, much as their cattle chewed the cud.

“I cannot make it out,” the headman said to the priest at last. “How do you interpret this talk?” The lama, his story told, sat silently turning his prayer beads.

“He is a Seeker,” the priest replied. “The land is full of them. Remember the man who came only last month—the fakir with the tortoise?”

“Yes, but that man had right and reason on his side, because Krishna Himself appeared to him in a vision, promising him Paradise without the funeral pyre if he journeyed to Prayag. This man is searching for no god known to me.”

“Peace, he is old, he comes from far away, and he is mad,” the clean-shaven priest replied. He turned to the lama. “Three kos [six miles] to the west runs the great road to Calcutta.”

“But I want to go to Benares—to Benares.”

“And you can go to Benares from there as well. It crosses all the streams on this side of India. Now, my advice to you, Holy One, is to rest here until tomorrow. Then take the road”—he meant the Grand Trunk Road—“and test every stream it crosses; for as I understand it, the virtue of your river does not lie in a single pool or place, but runs throughout its entire length. Then, if your gods will it, you may be sure you will find your freedom.”

“That is well said.” The lama was greatly impressed by the suggestion. “We will start tomorrow, and a blessing on you for showing old feet such a direct path.” A deep, sing-song Chinese half-chant concluded his sentence. Even the priest was impressed, and the headman felt a touch of superstitious fear, though no one could look into the lama’s simple, eager face and doubt him for long.

“Do you see my disciple?” the lama asked, diving into his snuff-gourd with an important sniff. It was his way of returning courtesy for courtesy.

“I see—and hear.” The headman glanced toward where Kim was chatting with a girl in blue as she laid crackling thorns on a fire.

“He also has a search of his own. Not a river, but a bull. Yes, a Red Bull on a green field that will one day raise him to honor. He is, I believe, not entirely of this world. He was sent to me quite suddenly to help me in my search, and his name is the Friend of all the World.”

The priest smiled. “Ho there, Friend of all the World,” he called across the sharp-smelling smoke, “what are you?”

“This holy man’s disciple,” Kim answered.

“He says you are a spirit.”

“Can spirits eat?” Kim asked with a twinkle in his eye. “Because I am hungry.”

“This is no joke,” the lama cried. “A certain astrologer in that city whose name I have forgotten—”

“That was only the city of Umballa where we slept last night,” Kim whispered to the priest.

“Yes, Umballa was it? He cast a horoscope and declared that my disciple would find what he seeks within two days. But what did he say about the meaning of the stars, Friend of all the World?”

Kim cleared his throat and looked around at the village elders.

“The meaning of my star is War,” he announced pompously.

Someone chuckled at the sight of the little tattered figure standing proudly on the brick platform beneath the great tree. Where a native boy might have slouched, Kim’s white blood kept him standing straight.

“Yes, War,” he repeated.

“That is a safe prophecy,” a deep voice rumbled. “For there is always war along the border—as I well know.”

It was an old, withered man who had served the Government during the Mutiny as a native officer in a newly raised cavalry regiment. The Government had granted him a good plot of land in the village, and though the financial demands of his sons—who were now grey-bearded officers in their own right—had impoverished him somewhat, he remained a man of considerable influence. English officials, even Deputy Commissioners, would occasionally turn off the main road to visit him, and on those occasions he would dress in his ancient uniform and stand as straight as a ramrod.

“But this will be a great war—a war of eight thousand,” Kim’s voice rang out clearly across the gathering crowd, surprising even himself.

“Redcoats or our own regiments?” the old man snapped sharply, as if speaking to an equal. His tone commanded the respect of everyone.

“Redcoats,” Kim guessed boldly. “Redcoats and big guns.”

“But—but the astrologer said nothing of this!” the lama cried, snuffing loudly in his excitement.

“Because I know. The news has come directly to me, who am this holy man’s disciple. There is going to be a war—a war involving eight thousand redcoats. They are being drawn from Pindi and Peshawar. This is certain.”

“The boy has simply picked up talk from the bazaar,” the priest said.

“But he was right by my side,” the lama protested. “How could he know? I certainly didn’t know.”

“He’ll make a clever conjurer once the old man is dead,” the priest muttered to the headman. “What new trick is this?”

“A sign! Give me a sign!” the old soldier suddenly thundered. “If there were a war coming, my sons would have written to tell me.”

“When everything is ready, your sons will be notified, never doubt it. But it is a long way from your sons to the man who holds the strings.” Kim warmed to the game, remembering his old letter-carrying days when, for a few copper coins, he had pretended to know far more than he actually did. But now he was playing for much higher stakes—driven by the sheer excitement and a sudden sense of power. He took a deep breath and pressed on.

“Old man, give me a sign. Do ordinary underlings direct the movements of eight thousand redcoats—with artillery?”

“No,” the old soldier answered, still treating Kim as an equal.

“Do you know the man who gives the orders?”

“I have seen him.”

“Would you know him again?”

“I have known him since he was a lieutenant in the artillery.”

“A tall man. A tall man with black hair, who walks like this?” Kim took a few paces across the platform with a stiff, wooden stride.

“Yes. But anyone might have seen that.” The crowd was breathless, completely silent throughout the exchange.

“That is true,” Kim said. “But I can tell you more. Look now. First, the great man walks this way. Then he thinks.” Kim drew a forefinger across his forehead and down to the corner of his jaw. “Next, he twitches his fingers like this. Then he shoves his hat under his left armpit.” Kim demonstrated the motion and stood like a stork.

The old man groaned, speechless with astonishment, and a shudder ran through the crowd.

“Like that—like that—like that. But what does he do right before he gives an order?”

“He rubs the back of his neck—so. Then one finger taps the table, and he makes a little sniffing sound through his nose. Then he speaks, saying: ‘Order such and such a regiment to move. Bring up such and such guns.’”

The old man rose stiffly to his feet and snapped a smart salute.

“‘For,’” Kim translated into the vernacular the decisive words he had overheard in the dressing room at Umballa, “‘For,’ says he, ‘we should have done this long ago. It is not a war—it is a chastisement. Sniff!’”

“Enough. I believe it. I have seen him like that in the smoke of battle. Seen him and heard him. It is the man!”

“I saw no smoke,” Kim shifted his voice into the hypnotic, singsong drone of a roadside fortune-teller. “I saw this in the darkness. First came a man to clear the path. Then came horsemen. Then he appeared, standing in a ring of light. The rest happened just as I described it. Old man, have I spoken the truth?”

“It is he. Beyond all doubt, it is he.”

The crowd let out a long, trembling breath, looking back and forth from the old soldier—still standing rigidly at attention—to the ragged boy standing against the purple twilight.

“Didn’t I say so—didn’t I say he came from another world?” the lama cried proudly. “He is the Friend of all the World! He is the Friend of the Stars!”

“Well, it doesn’t concern us,” another man called out. “O young soothsayer, if you have this gift at all times, I have a red-spotted cow. She might be a sister to your bull for all I know—”

“Or care,” Kim retorted. “My stars don’t concern themselves with your livestock.”

“No, but she is very sick,” a woman broke in. “My husband is a fool, or he would have chosen his words better. Can you tell me if she will recover?”

If Kim had been an ordinary boy, he would have tried to keep the game going; but you do not live in Lahore city—least of all among the fakirs around the Taksali Gate—for thirteen years without learning a great deal about human nature.

The priest looked at him sideways with a dry, bitter, and mocking smile.

“Is there no priest in this village, then? I thought I saw a great one standing right here,” Kim said.

“Yes—but—” the woman began.

“You and your husband simply hoped to get the cow cured for a handful of thanks.” The shot hit home; they were notoriously the stingiest couple in the village. “It doesn’t do to cheat the temples. Give a young calf to your own priest, and unless your gods are angry beyond repair, she’ll be giving milk within a month.”

“You are a master beggar,” the priest chuckled approvingly. “Forty years of cunning couldn’t have done better. I suppose you’ve made the old man rich with all this?”

“A little flour, a little butter, and a mouthful of cardamoms,” Kim replied, flushed with the praise but still cautious. “Does anyone grow rich on that? Besides, as you can see, he is mad. Still, it answers my purpose while I learn the road.”

He knew exactly how the fakirs of the Taksali Gate spoke among themselves and copied the cynical inflection of their degenerate disciples.

“Is his search real, then, or just a cover for something else? Could it be hidden treasure?”

“He is mad—mad in many ways. There is nothing else.”

The old soldier stumped up then and asked if Kim would accept his hospitality for the night. The priest recommended that they do so, but insisted that the honor of hosting the lama belonged to the temple—at which the lama smiled innocently. Kim glanced from one face to the other and drew his own conclusions.

“Where is the money?” he whispered, pulling the old man aside into the darkness.

“In my shirt, of course. Where else?”

“Give it to me. Quietly and quickly, give it to me.”

“Why? We don’t need to buy any tickets here.”

“Am I your disciple or am I not? Don’t I guide your old feet along the roads? Give me the money, and at dawn I’ll give it back.” He slipped his hand beneath the lama’s belt and relieved him of the purse.

“Very well—have it your own way.” The old man nodded. “This is a great and terrible world. I never knew there were so many men alive in it.”

The next morning the priest was in a foul temper, but the lama was entirely happy. Kim had spent a fascinating evening with the old soldier, who had brought out his cavalry saber, balanced it across his dry knees, and told stories of the Mutiny and of young captains who had been in their graves for thirty years, until Kim finally drifted off to sleep.

“The air in this country is certainly good,” the lama remarked. “I sleep lightly, as all old men do, but last night I slept soundly until broad daylight. Even now I feel heavy.”

“Drink some hot milk,” said Kim, who had brought plenty of such remedies to opium smokers he knew. “It’s time for us to take the road again.”

“The long road that crosses all the rivers of India,” the lama said cheerfully. “Let us go. But tell me, disciple, how shall we repay these people, and especially the priest, for their great kindness? True, they are idolaters, but perhaps in future lives they will attain enlightenment. Should we leave a rupee for the temple? The stone image inside is nothing more than stone and red paint, but we must acknowledge the goodness of men’s hearts wherever we find it.”

“Holy One, have you ever traveled the road alone?” Kim looked up sharply, much like the Indian crows that bustled about the fields.

“Certainly, child: from Kulu to Pathankot—from Kulu, where my first disciple died. When people were kind to us we made offerings, and everyone was well-disposed throughout the hills.”

“It’s different down here in India,” Kim said dryly. “Their gods have many arms and are malicious. Leave them alone.”

“I will set you part of the way on your road, Friend of all the World—you and your yellow man.” The old soldier rode up the village street in the early dawn light on a short, scissor-hocked pony. “Last night unlocked the springs of memory in my dried-up heart, and it was like a blessing to me. Truly there is war in the air. I can smell it. Look! I brought my sword.”

He sat long-legged on the small animal with the heavy sword at his side, his hand resting on the pommel as he stared fiercely across the flat fields toward the north. “Tell me again how he appeared in your vision. Come up and ride behind me; the beast can carry two.”

“I am this holy man’s disciple,” Kim replied as they passed out of the village gate. The villagers seemed almost sorry to see them go, but the priest’s farewell was cold and distant. He had wasted opium on a traveler who carried no money.

“Well spoken. I am not used to holy men, but respect is always a good thing. There is no respect nowadays—not even when a Commissioner Sahib comes to visit me. But why should a boy whose star leads him to war follow a holy man?”

“Because he is a holy man,” Kim said earnestly. “In truth, in his words, and in his actions, he is holy. He is nothing like the others. I have never seen anyone like him. We are not fortune-tellers, jugglers, or beggars.”

“You are not, I can see that. But as for the other one—he walks well, though.”

The morning freshness carried the lama forward with long, easy, camel-like strides. He was deep in meditation, mechanically clicking his prayer beads.

They followed a rutted, worn country road that wound across the flat plains between dark-green mango groves, with the snowy range of the Himalayas looming faintly to the east. All across India, people were hard at work in the fields to the creaking of well-wheels, the shouts of ploughmen behind their bullocks, and the cawing of crows. Even the old soldier’s pony felt the pleasant influence and nearly broke into a trot as Kim laid a hand on the stirrup-leather.

“I regret that I did not leave a rupee at the shrine,” the lama said on the final bead of his rosary.

The old soldier grunted in his beard, causing the lama to notice him for the first time.

“Are you searching for the river as well?” the lama asked, turning his head.

“The day is young,” the old man replied. “What need of a river except to water the horses before sundown? I’ve come to show you a short cut to the Big Road.”

“That is a kindness to be remembered, man of good will. But why the sword?”

The old soldier looked as embarrassed as a child caught playing a game.

“The sword?” he said, fumbling with the hilt. “Oh, that’s just a fancy of mine—an old man’s fancy. Strictly speaking, police orders forbid anyone from carrying weapons throughout India, but”—he cheered up and slapped the hilt—“all the constables around here know me.”

“It is a bad fancy,” the lama said. “What profit is there in killing men?”

“Very little—as I well know. But if evil men weren’t slain now and then, it wouldn’t be a safe world for weaponless dreamers. I don’t speak without experience, having seen the land from Delhi south awash with blood.”

“What madness was that?”

“Only the gods, who sent it as a plague, know. A madness seized the whole army, and they turned against their officers. That was the first evil, and it might have been remedied if they had stopped there. But they chose to murder the sahibs’ wives and children. Then the sahibs came from across the sea and called them to a terrible reckoning.”

“Some such rumor reached me long ago. They called it the Black Year, as I recall.”

“What kind of life have you led not to know about The Year? A rumor indeed! The whole earth shook and trembled!”

“Our earth shook only once—on the day the Excellent One attained Enlightenment.”

“Humph! I saw Delhi shake at least—and Delhi is the navel of the world.”

“So they turned against women and children? That was a wicked deed, and punishment for it cannot be escaped.”

“Many tried to escape it, but with very little profit. I was in a cavalry regiment then. It broke apart. Out of six hundred and eighty sabers, how many do you think remained true to their salt? Three. And I was one of them.”

“All the greater merit.”

“Merit! We didn’t consider it merit in those days. My people, my friends, my brothers fell away from me. They said, ‘The rule of the English is finished. Let everyone carve out a little estate for himself.’ But I had talked with the veterans of Sobraon, Chillianwallah, Moodkee, and Ferozeshah. I said, ‘Wait a little, and the wind will change. There is no blessing in this work.’ In those days I rode seventy miles with an English lady and her baby on my saddle-bow. (Ah, that was a horse fit for a man!) I brought them safely to shelter and rode back to my officer—the only one of our five who wasn’t killed. ‘Give me work,’ I told him, ‘for I am an outcast among my own people, and my cousin’s blood is still wet on my sword.’ ‘Be content,’ he said. ‘There is great work ahead. When this madness is over, there will be a reward.’”

“Yes, there is always a reward when the madness ends, isn’t there?” the lama muttered half to himself.

“They didn’t hand out medals in those days to everyone who merely heard a shot fired. No! I fought in nineteen pitched battles, forty-six cavalry skirmishes, and countless smaller affairs. I carry nine wounds, a medal with four clasps, and the badge of an Order. My former captains—who are generals now—remembered me when the Empress marked fifty years of her reign and the whole land rejoiced. They said, ‘Give him the Order of British India.’ I wear it around my neck to this day. I also received a grant of land from the State—a free gift to me and mine. The men of the old days, who are now high Commissioners, ride out through my crops on tall horses so that the whole village can see them, and we sit and talk over old skirmishes, one dead man’s name leading to another.”

“And afterward?” the lama asked.

“Oh, afterward they ride away, but not until my village has witnessed it.”

“And at the end, what will you do?”

“At the end, I will die.”

“And after that?”

“Let the gods decide. I have never pestered them with prayers, and I don’t expect they’ll pester me. Look you, I’ve noticed in my long life that people who constantly bother those Above with complaints, reports, wailing, and weeping are soon summoned in a hurry—just as our colonel used to summon the muddle-headed recruits who talked too much. No, I’ve never wearied the gods. They will remember that and give me a quiet place where I can drive my lance into the ground in the shade and wait to welcome my sons. I have no less than three sons who are squadron commanders in various regiments.”

“And they, too, bound upon the Wheel, pass from life to life—from despair to despair,” the lama said softly, “feverish, restless, grasping.”

“Yes,” the old soldier chuckled. “Three squadron commanders in three regiments. They like to gamble a little, but so do I. They have to keep good mounts, and you can’t just steal horses the way we took women in the old days. Still, my estate pays for all. What do you think? It’s a well-watered strip of land, though my tenants cheat me. I don’t know how to ask for things except at the point of a lance. Ugh! I lose my temper and curse them, and they pretend to be sorry, but behind my back I know they call me a toothless old ape.”

“Have you never desired anything else?”

“Yes—yes—a thousand times! A straight back and a firm knee gripping a horse once more; a quick wrist, a sharp eye, and the strength of a true man. Ah, the old days—the good days of my strength!”

“That strength is actually weakness.”

“It has turned out so; but fifty years ago I could have proved otherwise,” the old soldier retorted, digging his stirrup into the pony’s lean flank.

“Yet I know a river of great healing.”

“I’ve drunk Ganges water until I was nearly bloated. All it gave me was dysentery, not an ounce of extra strength.”

“This is not the Ganges. The river that I know washes away every trace of sin. Once you cross to the far bank, you are guaranteed Freedom. I know nothing of your life, but your face is that of an honorable and courteous man. You have stood by your path, remaining loyal when loyalty was hard to give during that Black Year of which I now hear fresh stories. Enter now upon the Middle Way, which is the path to Freedom. Listen to the Most Excellent Law, and stop chasing empty dreams.”

“Speak on, then, old man,” the soldier smiled, giving a half-salute. “We are all babblers at our age.”

静岡

The lama sat down in the shade of a mango tree, its leaves casting a checkered pattern across his face. The soldier sat stiffly on his pony, and Kim—making sure there were no snakes around—lay down in the fork of the twisted roots.

There was a drowsy buzz of insects in the hot sunshine, the cooing of doves, and the sleepy drone of distant well-wheels across the fields. Slowly and impressively, the lama began to speak. Within ten minutes, the old soldier slid down from his pony to listen better, holding the reins wrapped around his wrist. The lama’s voice softened, and his sentences grew longer. Kim was busy watching a gray squirrel. When the scolding little ball of fur pressed close against a branch finally scampered away, both preacher and listener were fast asleep—the old officer’s strong-jawed head pillowed on his arm, and the lama’s head tilted back against the tree trunk, looking like yellow ivory. A naked toddler toddled over, stared at them, and—moved by a sudden impulse of reverence—made a solemn little bow before the lama. But the child was so short and fat that it tipped over sideways, and Kim laughed out loud at the sprawling, chubby legs. Startled and indignant, the child let out a loud howl.

*“Hai! Hai!”* the soldier shouted, leaping instantly to his feet. “What is it? What are the orders? ... It’s ... a child! I thought it was an alarm. Little one—little one—don’t cry. Did I fall asleep? That was very rude indeed!”

“I’m scared! I’m afraid!” the child roared.

“What is there to be afraid of? Two old men and a boy? How will you ever make a soldier, little prince?”

The lama had woken up as well, but instead of paying direct attention to the child, he simply began clicking his prayer beads.

“What is that?” the child asked, cutting its crying short. “I’ve never seen anything like that. Give it to me.”

“Ah,” the lama smiled, trailing a loop of the beads through the grass:

This is a handful of cardamoms,
This is a lump of ghee;
This is millet and chillies and rice,
A supper for you and me!

The child shrieked with delight and grabbed at the dark, shiny beads.

*“Oho!”* the old soldier said. “Where did you learn that song, renouncer of this world?”

“I learned it in Pathankot—while sitting on a doorstep,” the lama answered shyly. “It is good to be kind to little children.”

“If I remember correctly, before we fell asleep you were telling me that marriage and raising families are hindrances to the true light and stumbling blocks on the Path. Do children drop straight from heaven in your country? Or is singing songs to them part of the Path?”

“No man is completely perfect,” the lama said gravely, winding his rosary back up. “Run along to your mother now, little one.”

“Listen to him!” the soldier told Kim. “He’s actually ashamed of making a child happy. You would have made a splendid householder, my brother. Here, child!” He tossed a copper coin to the boy. “Sweetmeats are always sweet.” And as the little figure scampered back into the sunshine, he added, “They grow up and become men. Holy One, I am sorry I fell asleep in the middle of your preaching. Forgive me.”

“We are both old men,” the lama replied. “The fault was mine. I listened to your talk about the world and its madness, and one distraction led to another.”

“Listen to him! What harm do your gods suffer from playing with a baby? And that was a very well-sung song. Let’s move on, and I’ll sing you the song of Nikal Seyn before Delhi—the old song.”

They stepped out from the shade of the mango grove, the old man’s high, thin voice ringing across the fields as verse by long-drawn verse he unfolded the story of Nikal Seyn [General John Nicholson]—the song people in the Punjab still sing to this day. Kim was delighted, and the lama listened with deep interest.

*“Ahi! Nikal Seyn is dead—he died before Delhi! Lances of the North, take vengeance for Nikal Seyn.”* He quavered it out to the very end, beating time against the pony’s rump with the flat of his sword.

“And now we have reached the Big Road,” the old man announced after accepting Kim’s compliments, for the lama remained unusually silent. “It is a long time since I traveled this way, but your boy’s talk stirred my blood. Look, Holy One—the Great Road, which is the backbone of all India. For the most part it is shaded, as it is here, by four rows of trees, while the hard center strip handles the fast traffic. Before the trains came, sahibs used to travel up and down this road by the hundreds. Now there are only country carts and the like. On the left and right are the rougher tracks for heavy transport—grain, cotton, timber, fodder, lime, and hides. A man can travel safely here because every few miles there is a police station. The police are thieves and extortioners—I would patrol the road with cavalry myself, using young recruits under a strong captain—but at least they don’t tolerate rival bandits. All castes and kinds of people pass along here.

“Look! Brahmins and chamars, bankers and tinkers, barbers and grain-merchants, pilgrims and potters—the whole world coming and going. To me, it is like a river from which I have been pulled out like a log after a flood.”

And truly, the Grand Trunk Road is a magnificent sight. It runs straight as an arrow, carrying India’s traffic for fifteen hundred miles without congestion—a river of life unlike anything else in the world. They gazed down its green-arched, shade-dappled length, its wide white surface dotted with slow-moving travelers, and the two-roomed police station standing right opposite.

“Who is carrying weapons against the law?” a constable called out laughingly when he caught sight of the old soldier’s sword. “Aren’t the police enough to keep down evil-doers?”

“It was because of the police that I bought it,” came the witty reply. “Does everything go well in India?”

“Rissaldar Sahib, everything goes well.”

“I am like an old tortoise, you see, sticking his head out of the riverbank and pulling it back in again. Yes, this is the Road of Hindustan. All men pass this way...”

“Son of a pig, is the smooth part of the road meant for you to scratch your back on? Father of all daughters of shame and husband of ten thousand worthless women, your mother was dedicated to a devil and led into it by her own mother! Your aunts haven’t had decent noses for seven generations! Your sister—what kind of fool told you to block the road with your carts? A broken wheel? Then take a broken head and mend them both at your leisure!”

This stream of abuse and venomous whip-cracking erupted from a cloud of dust fifty yards away, where a cart had broken down. A thin, high-strung Kathiawar mare, her eyes and nostrils blazing, bolted out of the traffic jam, snorting and wincing as her rider whipped her across the road in pursuit of a shouting man. The rider was tall and gray-bearded, riding the nearly wild animal as if he were part of it, and methodically lashing his target between lunges.

The old soldier’s face lit up with fierce pride. “My boy!” he said simply, trying to arch his pony’s neck into a military curve.

“Am I to be beaten in front of the police?” the carter screamed. “Justice! I demand justice—”

“Am I to be blocked by a shouting ape who dumps ten thousand sacks right under a young horse’s nose? That is no way to treat a fine mare!”

“He speaks the truth. He speaks the truth. But the lad stays close behind him,” the old man murmured proudly. The carter scurried underneath his cart and began hurling threats of vengeance.

“They are tough fellows, your sons,” the policeman remarked calmly, picking his teeth.

The horseman delivered one final, stinging cut with his whip and trotted back toward them.

“My father!” He reined in his horse ten yards away and dismounted.

The old man slid off his pony instantly, and father and son embraced, just as men do throughout the East.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
chapters.content:
Good Luck, she is never a lady,
But the cursedest quean alive,
Tricksy, wincing, and jady—
Kittle to lead or drive.
Greet her—she’s hailing a stranger!
Meet her—she’s busking to leave!
Let her alone for a shrew to the bone
And the hussy comes plucking your sleeve!
Largesse! Largesse, O Fortune!
Give or hold at your will.
If I’ve no care for Fortune,
Fortune must follow me still!

*The Wishing-Caps.*

Then, lowering their voices, they spoke together. Kim went to rest under a tree, but the lama pulled impatiently at his elbow.

“Let us go on. The River is not here.”

“Oh, my! Haven’t we walked enough for one day? Our river isn’t going to run away. Have patience, and he’ll give us a tip.”

“This man,” the old soldier said suddenly, “is the Friend of the Stars. He brought me the news yesterday, having seen the very man himself in a vision, giving orders for the war.”

“Hmm!” said his son from deep in his broad chest. “He picked up a bazaar rumor and cashed in on it.”

His father laughed. “At least he didn’t ride up to me begging for a new horse and heaven knows how many rupees. Are your brothers’ regiments also under orders?”

“I don’t know. I took leave and came straight to you in case—”

“In case they ran to you to beg first? Oh, you gamblers and spenders, every one of you! Still, you’ve never ridden in a cavalry charge yet. You’ll need a good horse for that, indeed. And a steady follower, and a pony for the march as well. Let’s see—let's see.” He drummed his fingers on his saddle-pommel.

“This is no place to settle accounts, my father. Let us go to your house.”

“At least pay the boy, then. I don’t have any small change on me, and he brought good news. Hey! Friend of all the World, a war is coming just as you said.”

“No, as I know, *the* war,” Kim replied composedly.

“Eh?” said the lama, fingering his beads, eager to be back on the road.

“My master doesn’t sell the secrets of the stars for money. We brought the news—witness that we brought the news—and now we are leaving.” Kim half-hooked his hand at his side in the traditional gesture for a tip.

The son tossed a silver coin through the sunlight, muttering something about beggars and jugglers. It was a four-anna piece, enough to feed them well for days. Seeing the flash of the metal, the lama droned a blessing.

“Go your way, Friend of all the World,” the old soldier called out, wheeling his scrawny mount. “For once in my life, I’ve met a true prophet—and he wasn’t even in the army.”

Father and son turned away together, the old man sitting as straight as the younger.

A Punjabi constable in yellow linen trousers slouched across the road. He had seen the money change hands.

“Halt!” he cried in impressive English. “Don’t you know there is a tax of two annas a head—making four annas in all—for anyone entering the road from this side-path? It’s the order of the Government, and the money is used to plant trees and beautify the pathways.”

“And to fill the bellies of the police,” Kim said, slipping well out of arm’s reach. “Think about it for a moment, you blockhead. Do you think we crawled out of the nearest pond like the frog your father-in-law? Have you ever heard the story of your brother?”

“And who was he? Leave the boy alone,” a senior constable called out, immensely amused as he squatted down to smoke his pipe on the veranda.

“He took a label off a bottle of soda water, stuck it on a bridge, and collected tolls for a month from everyone who crossed, claiming it was an order from the Government. Then an Englishman came along and cracked his head open. Ah, brother, I’m a city crow, not a village pigeon!”

The policeman drew back abashed, and Kim hooted taunts at him all down the road.

“Was there ever such a disciple as I am?” Kim cried cheerfully to the lama. “Every crow in India would have picked your bones within ten miles of Lahore if I hadn’t looked after you.”

“Sometimes I wonder in my own mind whether you are a spirit or an imp of mischief,” the lama said with a slow smile.

“I am your disciple.” Kim dropped back into step beside him—matching that tireless, rolling stride common to long-distance wanderers everywhere.

“Now let us walk,” the lama muttered, and to the rhythmic clicking of his prayer beads, they walked in silence, mile after mile. The lama was, as usual, lost in deep meditation, but Kim’s bright eyes missed nothing. This broad, smiling river of humanity, he decided, was a vast improvement over the cramped, noisy streets of Lahore. At every step there were new people and new sights—castes he recognized instantly, and others entirely outside his experience.

They passed a troop of long-haired, strong-smelling Sansis carrying baskets of lizards and other unclean foods on their backs, their lean dogs sniffing at their heels. These people stayed strictly on their own side of the road, moving at a quick, furtive trot, and all other castes gave them a wide berth because the Sansi brought ritual pollution. Behind them walked a man newly released from prison, striding stiffly with wide steps across the road, the memory of leg-irons still in his gait, his full stomach and shiny skin proving that the Government fed its prisoners better than most honest men could feed themselves. Kim knew that walk well and made loud jokes about it as they passed. Then an Akali—a wild-eyed, wild-haired Sikh devotee wearing the blue-checked clothes of his faith, with polished steel quoits gleaming from the pointed peak of his tall blue turban—strode by, returning from a visit to one of the independent Sikh states, where he had been singing the ancient glories of the Khalsa to college-educated princelings in top boots and white cord breeches. Kim took care not to provoke him, for an Akali’s temper was short and his arm was fast.

Here and there they met or were overtaken by gaily dressed crowds of villagers heading to some local fair: women with babies astride their hips walking behind the men, older boys prancing around with sugar-cane stalks for horses, dragging crude brass models of locomotives bought for a halfpenny, or flashing sunlight into the eyes of passersby with cheap toy mirrors. One could tell at a glance what each had bought, and if there was any doubt, one only had to watch the wives comparing brown arms against brown arms over newly purchased dull glass bangles from the North-West. These merrymakers walked slowly, calling out to one another and stopping to haggle with sweetmeat-sellers or offer prayers at wayside shrines—some Hindu, some Muslim—shared by the lower classes of both creeds with lovely impartiality. A solid line of blue, rising and falling like the back of a hurrying caterpillar, swung up through the shimmering dust and trotted past to a chorus of high-pitched cackling. That was a gang of *changars*—the women who maintain all the embankments of the northern railways—a flat-footed, big-bosomed, strong-limbed clan of earth-carriers in blue petticoats, hurrying north on news of road-work and wasting no time. They belonged to a caste whose men do not count, and they walked with squared elbows, swinging hips, and high-held heads, as befitted women accustomed to carrying heavy loads.

A little later, a wedding procession would turn onto the Grand Trunk Road with music, shouting, and a smell of marigold and jasmine even stronger than the dust. One could catch a glimpse of the bride’s litter—a blurred mass of red and tinsel—wobbling through the heat haze, while the bridegroom’s garlanded pony stepped aside to snatch a mouthful of hay from a passing fodder-cart. Kim would join in the chorus of good wishes and bad jokes, wishing the couple a hundred sons and no daughters, as the custom went. Even more entertaining, drawing shouts of laughter, were the strolling jugglers with half-trained monkeys, panting and feeble bears, or women who tied goat horns to their feet and danced on a tightrope, causing horses to shy and women to break into shrill, long-drawn quivers of amazement.

The lama never raised his eyes. He didn’t notice the money-lender hurrying along on a goose-rumped pony to collect cruel interest, nor the noisy, deep-voiced band of native soldiers on leave—still walking in loose military formation—rejoicing to be out of trousers and puttees and shouting outrageous comments at every respectable woman in sight. He didn’t even see the seller of Ganges water, though Kim expected he would at least stop to buy a bottle of the precious liquid. The lama stared straight at the ground, striding steadily hour after hour with his soul occupied elsewhere. But Kim was in seventh heaven. The Grand Trunk Road at this point was raised on an embankment to protect it from winter floods, so that they walked a little above the surrounding countryside along a grand elevated corridor, watching all of India spread out to their left and right. It was a wonderful sight to see the heavily laden grain and cotton wagons crawling across the side roads; one could hear their complaining axles a mile away as they drew nearer, until with shouts, curses, and whip-cracking they climbed the steep slope and rumbled onto the hard main road, teamsters hurling insults at one another. It was equally lovely to watch little clusters of travelers in red, blue, pink, white, and saffron breaking off to take the paths leading to their own villages, scattering in twos and threes across the level plains. Kim felt the beauty of these things deeply, though he lacked the words to express it, so he contented himself with buying peeled sugar-cane and spitting the fibrous pith generously along his path.

From time to time the lama took a pinch of snuff, and at last Kim could endure the silence no longer.

“This is a fine land—this land of the South!” he said. “The air is good, the water is good. Eh?”

“And they are all bound upon the Wheel,” the lama replied. “Bound from life unto life. To none of these has the Way been shown.” He shook himself back into the present.

“And now we’ve walked a weary way,” Kim said. “Surely we’ll soon reach a *parao* [resting place]. Shall we stay there? Look, the sun is getting low.”

“Who will take us in this evening?”

“That doesn’t matter. This country is full of good people. Besides,” he lowered his voice to a whisper, “we have money.”

The crowd grew thicker as they neared the resting place that marked the end of their day’s journey. A line of stalls selling basic food and tobacco, a stack of firewood, a police station, a well, a horse trough, a few shade trees, and some trampled ground dotted with the black ashes of old fires—that is all that marks a *parao* along the Grand Trunk, along with plenty of beggars and hungry crows.

By this time the sun was driving broad golden shafts through the lower branches of the mango trees. Parakeets and doves were returning home by the hundreds, while chattering, gray-backed babblers hopped back and forth almost under the travelers’ feet, gossiping about the day’s events. Rustling and scuffling in the upper branches showed that the bats were waking up for their night patrol. Swiftly, the daylight gathered itself together, painting faces, cartwheels, and bullock horns as red as blood. Then night fell, changing the feel of the air, drawing a low, even haze like a blue veil across the countryside, and bringing out the sharp, distinct scents of wood smoke, cattle dung, and wheat cakes baking on hot ashes. The evening patrol hurried out of the police station with loud coughs and shouted orders, while a glowing ember in a traveler’s hookah shone bright red as Kim watched the last flicker of sunset on his brass tweezers.

The life of the *parao* was very similar to that of the Kashmir Serai, only on a smaller scale. Kim plunged straight into the cheerful Asian disorder which, given a little time, always provides whatever a simple man requires.

His own needs were few. Since the lama had no caste restrictions, cooked food from the nearest stall would do nicely; but as a luxury, Kim bought a handful of dried dung-cakes to build a small cooking fire. All around them, men bustled about the flames calling out for oil, grain, sweetmeats, or tobacco, jostling one another while waiting at the well. Beneath the men’s voices, high-pitched giggles and whispers drifted from covered carts carrying women whose faces were hidden from public view.

Nowadays, well-educated Indians believe that when their women travel—and they do travel quite a bit—it is better to move them quickly by train in properly screened compartments, and that custom is spreading. But there are always traditionalists who cling to the old ways of their forefathers; and above all, there are elderly women—even more conservative than the men—who set out on pilgrimages toward the end of their lives. Being old and no longer concerned with strict seclusion under certain circumstances, they actually relish the bustle and excitement of the open road, the gatherings at shrines, and the endless gossip with kindred dowagers. Often, it suits a long-suffering family quite well to let a sharp-tongued, iron-willed old lady trot around India in this fashion, for pilgrimage earns great favor with the gods. Thus, across India in both remote and public places, one frequently finds a knot of grizzled servants nominally guarding an old lady curtained away inside a bullock cart. Such men are staid and discreet, setting up elaborate precautions whenever a European or high-caste native approaches, but in the rough-and-tumble of ordinary travel, those precautions often slip.

The old lady is, after all, intensely human and wants to see the world around her.

Kim’s sharp eyes picked out a brightly decorated family bullock cart (*ruth*) featuring a draped double-domed canopy resembling a two-humped camel, which had just pulled into the *parao*. An escort of eight men accompanied it, two of them carrying rusty sabers—a sure sign that they served someone of importance, since ordinary folk were not allowed to bear arms. A rising stream of complaints, orders, jokes, and what would have been considered coarse language in Europe issued from behind the curtains. Clearly, this was a woman accustomed to giving orders.

Kim inspected the retinue with a critical eye. Half of them were thin-legged, gray-bearded Ooryas from down-country; the other half were wool-clad, felt-hatted hillmen from the North. The mixture told its own story, even without the bickering between the two factions. The old lady was traveling south on a visit—probably to a rich relative, most likely a son-in-law who had sent an escort as a mark of respect. The hillmen were her own people from Kulu or Kangra. It was obvious she wasn’t taking her daughter down to be married, otherwise the curtains would have been laced tight and no strangers allowed near the cart. A merry and high-spirited dame, Kim thought, balancing a dung-cake in one hand and the cooked food in the other while guiding the lama with a gentle nudge of his shoulder. Something might come of this meeting. The lama wouldn’t offer any help, but as a dutiful disciple, Kim was more than willing to beg for two.

He built his fire as close to the cart as he dared, waiting for one of the guards to order him away. The lama dropped wearily to the ground like a heavy fruit bat and immediately went back to his rosary.

“Stand farther back, beggar!” shouted one of the hillmen in broken Hindustani.

“Huh! He’s only a hillman,” Kim muttered over his shoulder. “Since when do mountain jackasses own all of Hindustan?”

The reply was a swift and brilliant summary of Kim’s ancestry for the past three generations.

“Ah!” Kim’s voice grew sweeter than ever as he broke the dung-cake into neat pieces. “In *my* country, we call that the beginning of a love affair.”

A harsh, thin cackle from behind the curtains goaded the hillman into a second retort.

“Not bad—not bad at all,” Kim said calmly. “But be careful, brother, lest we—*we*, mind you—take it into our heads to cast a curse in return. And our curses have a nasty habit of biting home.”

The Ooryas laughed; the hillman lunged forward threateningly. Suddenly the lama raised his head, bringing his giant tam-o'-shanter hat directly into the flickering light of Kim’s newly lit fire.

“What is it?” the lama asked.

The hillman stopped dead in his tracks, as if turned to stone. “I—I—am saved from a great sin,” he stammered.

“The foreigner has finally found himself a priest,” one of the Ooryas whispered.

“Hey! Why hasn’t that beggar brat been beaten yet?” the old woman cried out.

The hillman backed away toward the cart and whispered something through the curtains. There was a dead silence, followed by a murmur of voices.

“This is going well,” Kim thought, pretending not to notice.

“When—when—he has eaten,” the hillman fawned, addressing Kim, “it—it is requested that the Holy One do us the honor of speaking with someone who wishes to address him.”

“After he has eaten, he will sleep,” Kim replied loftily. He couldn’t quite figure out the new turn events had taken, but he was determined to profit by it. “Now I will get him his food.” He spoke loudly, ending with a slight sigh as if feeling faint.

“I—I and the rest of my people will attend to that—if it is permitted.”

“It is permitted,” Kim said more grandly than ever. “Holy One, these people are going to bring us food.”

The lama muttered drowsily, “The land is good. All the country of the South is good—a great and terrible world.”

“Let him sleep,” Kim said, “but make sure we are well fed when he wakes. He is a very holy man.”

Again, one of the Ooryas muttered something contemptuously.

“He is no wandering fakir. He is no down-country beggar,” Kim declared severely to the stars. “He is the most holy of holy men. He is above all castes. I am his disciple.”

“Come here!” commanded the thin, flat voice from behind the curtain. Kim stepped closer, knowing that unseen eyes were watching him. A skinny brown finger heavy with rings rested on the edge of the cart, and the conversation began:

“Who is that?”

“An exceedingly holy one. He comes from far away. He comes from Tibet.”

“Where in Tibet?”

“From behind the snows—from a very distant place. He knows the stars, casts horoscopes, and reads destinies. But he does it for no money—only out of kindness and great charity. I am his disciple. They also call me the Friend of the Stars.”

“You are no hillman.”

“Ask him. He will tell you I was sent to him by the stars to help him reach the end of his pilgrimage.”

“Humph! Listen, brat: I am an old woman and not entirely a fool. I know lamas, and I respect them, but you are no more a lawful disciple than this finger of mine is the pole of the wagon. You are a casteless Hindu—a bold and shameless beggar attached to the Holy One merely for what you can get.”

“Don’t we all work for gain?” Kim shifted his tone instantly to match her knowing voice. “I have heard”—he took a wild shot—“I have heard—”

“What have you heard?” she snapped, tapping with her ringed finger.

“Nothing much to speak of, only some bazaar talk—which is doubtless a lie—that even Rajas—small hill Rajas—”

“Who are nevertheless of good Rajput blood.”

“Assuredly of good blood. That these men even sell the comeliest of their young women for profit. Down south they sell them—to wealthy landowners and the like all over Oudh.”

If there is one thing small hill Rajas deny most vehemently, it is precisely this accusation; yet the bazaars firmly believe it when discussing the mysterious slave traffic of India. In a tense, indignant whisper, the old lady explained to Kim exactly what kind of malicious liar he was. Had Kim hinted at such a thing when she was a girl, she told him, he would have been beaten to death by elephants that very evening. Which was probably true.

*“Ahai!”* Kim wailed in exaggerated terror. “I am only a beggar’s brat, just as the Eye of Beauty says!”

“Eye of Beauty, indeed! Who am I that you should fling cheap bazaar flattery at me?” Yet she laughed at the long-forgotten phrase. “Forty years ago that might have been said, and not without truth. Yes, thirty years ago. But such is the curse of gadding up and down India that a king’s widow must rub shoulders with all the scum of the land and become a laughingstock for beggars.”

“Great Queen,” Kim said promptly, hearing her shake with indignation, “I am indeed whatever the Great Queen says I am; but my master is holy all the same. He hasn’t yet heard the Great Queen’s command that—”

“Command? I command a Holy One—a Teacher of the Law—to come and speak to a woman? Never!”

“Forgive my stupidity. I thought it was given as an order—”

“It wasn’t. It was a petition. Is that clear now?”

A silver coin clinked against the edge of the cart. Kim caught it and bowed low. The old woman realized that as the eyes and ears of the lama, the boy had to be kept sweet.

“I am merely the Holy One’s disciple. When he has finished eating, perhaps he will come.”

“Oh, you villain, you shameless rascal!” The jewelled forefinger wagged at him in mock rebuke, but he could hear her chuckling behind the cloth.

“Now, what is it?” Kim asked, dropping into his softest, most confidential tone—the one few could resist. “Is—is there any need for a son in your family? Speak freely, for we priests—” The last phrase was a direct borrowing from a Taksali Gate fakir.

“We priests! You’re hardly old enough to—” She cut the joke short with another laugh. “Believe me, priest, we women occasionally think of matters other than sons. Besides, my daughter has already borne a son.”

“Two arrows in the quiver are better than one, and three are better still.” Kim quoted the proverb with a thoughtful cough, keeping his eyes modestly lowered.

“True—oh, true. But perhaps that will come. Those down-country Brahmins are utterly useless, though. I sent gifts, money, and more gifts, and all they did was make prophecies.”

“Ah,” Kim drawled with infinite contempt, “they prophesied!” A professional fortune-teller could not have done better.

“And my prayers weren’t answered until I remembered my own gods. I chose an auspicious hour, and—perhaps your Holy One has heard of the Abbot of the Lung-Cho monastery? I laid the matter before him, and lo and behold, everything turned out exactly as I wished. The Brahmin attached to my son-in-law’s household has since claimed it happened through *his* prayers—a minor error I intend to correct the moment we reach our destination. After that, I’m going on to Buddh Gaya to perform memorial rites for the father of my children.”

“We are going there too.”

“Doubly auspicious!” the old lady chirped. “A second grandson at least!”

“O Friend of all the World!” The lama had woken up and called for Kim with the innocent helplessness of a child lost in a strange bed.

“I’m coming! I’m coming, Holy One!” Kim dashed over to the fire, where the lama was already surrounded by dishes of food, the hillmen looking on in undisguised reverence while the Southerners glared sourly.

“Go back! Step away!” Kim cried. “Do we eat in public like dogs?” They finished their meal in silence, each turned slightly away from the other, and Kim finished his off with a hand-rolled cigarette.

“Didn’t I tell you a hundred times that the South is a good land?” Kim said. “Here we have a virtuous, high-born widow of a hill raja traveling on pilgrimage, she says, to Buddh Gaya. She is the one who sent us these dishes, and when you are rested she wishes to speak with you.”

“Was this your doing as well?” The lama dipped deep into his snuff-gourd.

“Who else has looked after you since our wonderful journey began?” Kim’s eyes danced as he blew harsh smoke through his nose and stretched out on the dusty earth. “Have I failed to look after your comforts, Holy One?”

“A blessing upon you.” The lama inclined his solemn head. “I have known many men in my long life, and more than a few disciples. But to no man—assuming you are born of woman—has my heart gone out as it has to you: thoughtful, wise, and courteous, yet something of an imp.”

“And I have never seen a priest like you.” Kim studied the kindly yellow face wrinkle by wrinkle. “It’s been less than three days since we took to the road together, and yet it feels like a hundred years.”

“Perhaps in a former life I was permitted to render you some service. Maybe,” he smiled, “I freed you from a trap, or—having caught you on a fishhook back when I was still unenlightened—threw you back into the river.”

“Maybe,” Kim said quietly. He had heard that sort of speculation often enough from men the English would never consider imaginative. “Now, regarding that woman in the bullock cart: I believe she wants a second grandson for her daughter.”

“That has nothing to do with the Way,” the lama sighed. “Still, she comes from the hills. Ah, the hills, and the snows of the hills!”

He stood up and walked over to the cart. Kim would have given his ears to follow, but the lama didn’t invite him, and the few words he caught were in an unfamiliar dialect—some common speech of the mountains. The woman seemed to be asking questions which the lama carefully weighed before answering. Every now and then, Kim heard the rhythmic cadence of a Chinese quotation. It was a strange picture framed by Kim’s half-closed eyelids. The lama, straight and tall, with the deep folds of his yellow robes slashed by black shadows from the *parao* fires—just as a knotted tree trunk is barred by shadows in the late sun—was addressing a tinsel-and-lacquered carriage that glowed like a multicolored jewel in the flickering light. The patterns on the gold-embroidered curtains shifted and shimmered in the night wind, and when the conversation grew earnest, the jewelled forefinger flashed tiny sparks of light between the threads. Behind the cart stretched a wall of darkness dotted with small fires and alive with half-seen shapes, faces, and shadows. The noise of early evening had settled into a soothing hum, its deepest note the steady chewing of the bullocks and its highest the tinkle of a Bengali dancing girl’s sitar. Most of the travelers had eaten and were pulling deeply on their gurgling, grunting hookahs, which sounded remarkably like bullfrogs.

At last the lama returned. A hillman followed him carrying a padded cotton quilt, which he carefully spread out by the fire.

“She deserves ten thousand grandchildren,” Kim thought to himself. “Though none of those dishes would have arrived if it weren’t for me.”

“A virtuous woman—and a wise one.” The lama lowered himself to the ground joint by joint, like a tired camel. “The world is full of charity for those who follow the Way.” He tossed a full half of the quilt over Kim.

“And what did she say?” Kim asked, rolling himself into his share of the bedding.

“She asked many questions and posed many problems—most of which were idle tales learned from demon-worshiping priests who pretend to follow the Way. Some I answered, and some I told her were foolish. Many wear the robe, but few keep to the Way.”

“True. That is very true.” Kim adopted the thoughtful, conciliatory tone of someone angling for confidences.

“However, by her own lights she is most right-minded. She greatly desires that we accompany her to Buddh Gaya, since her road runs alongside ours, as I understand it, for many days’ journey to the south.”

“And?”

“Patience a little. To that I replied that my search comes before all else. She had heard many foolish legends, but she had never heard this great truth of my river. Such are the priests of the lower hills! She knew the Abbot of Lung-Cho, but knew nothing of my river—nor the tale of the arrow.”

“And?”

“I spoke to her of the search, the Way, and matters of profit; while she desired only that I accompany her and offer prayers for a second grandson.”

“Aha! ‘We women’ think of nothing except children,” Kim chuckled sleepily.

“Now, since our paths lie together for a time, I see no reason why we should depart from our search if we travel with her—at least as far as—I have forgotten the name of the town.”

“Hey!” Kim turned and whispered sharply to an Oorya standing a few yards away. “Where is your master’s house?”

“A little past Saharunpore, among the fruit gardens.” He named the village.

“That was the place,” the lama said. “So far, at least, we can travel in her company.”

“Flies go to a carcass,” the Oorya muttered abstractedly.

“For a sick cow, a crow; for a sick man, a Brahmin,” Kim murmured impersonally to the treetops overhead.

The Oorya grunted and said nothing more.

“So we travel with her, Holy One?”

“Is there any reason not to? I can still step aside at any time to test the rivers crossed by the road. She wishes me to come. She desires it very greatly.”

Kim muffled a laugh inside the quilt. Once that imperious old lady got over her initial awe of a lama, he figured she would prove thoroughly entertaining.

He was nearly asleep when the lama softly quoted a proverb: “The husbands of the talkative reap a rich reward hereafter.” Then Kim heard him take three pinches of snuff and drifted off, still smiling.

The diamond-bright dawn woke men, crows, and bullocks all at once. Kim sat up, yawned, stretched himself, and felt a thrill of pure delight. This was seeing the world in earnest; this was life just as he liked it—bustling and shouting, buckling belts, beating bullocks, creaking wheels, lighting fires, cooking food, and finding fresh sights at every turn. The morning mist vanished in a whorl of silver, parakeets shrieked off in green clouds toward some distant river, and every well-wheel within earshot went to work. India was wide awake, and Kim was right in the middle of it, more alert and excited than anyone. He chewed on a twig that he would soon use as a toothbrush, borrowing freely from the customs of every community he knew and loved. There was no need to worry about food, no need to spend a single cowrie at the crowded stalls. He was the disciple of a holy man adopted by a strong-willed old lady; everything would be provided, and when respectfully invited, they would sit down and eat. As for the rest—Kim giggled as he scrubbed his teeth—his hostess would add plenty of spice to the journey. He inspected her bullocks critically as they came up grunting and blowing under their yokes. If they moved too slowly—which was unlikely—there would be a comfortable seat for him across the cart-pole, while the lama rode beside the driver. The escort would walk, of course. And the old lady would certainly talk a great deal; judging by what he’d already heard, her conversation wouldn't be dull. Already she was barking orders, scolding, rebuking, and cursing her servants for delays.

“Fetch her pipe! In the name of the gods, get her pipe and shut her ill-omened mouth!” cried an Oorya, tying up shapeless bundles of bedding. “She and the parrots are cut from the same cloth. They both screech at dawn.”

“The lead bullocks! Hey! Watch the lead bullocks!” They were backing and spinning around as a grain cart’s axle caught them by the horns. “Son of an owl, where are you driving?” shouted someone to the grinning carter.

“Hey! Yay! Yay! That person inside is the Queen of Delhi going off to pray for a son!” the carter yelled back from atop his high load. “Clear the way for the Queen of Delhi and her prime minister, the gray monkey climbing his own sword!” Another cart loaded with tree bark for a down-country tannery rumbled close behind, and its driver added a few choice compliments as the cart bullocks backed and collided again.

From behind the shaking curtains came a single volley of curses. It didn’t last long, but in variety, venom, and blistering accuracy, it surpassed anything Kim had ever heard. The carter’s bare chest visibly collapsed in shock as he salaamed reverently toward the voice, leaped down from the pole, and helped the escort haul their wheeled volcano back onto the main road. Once clear, the voice informed him precisely what kind of wife he’d married and what she was up to in his absence.

*“Oh, shabash!”* Kim muttered, unable to contain his admiration as the man slunk away.

“Well done, indeed? It’s a disgrace and a scandal that a poor woman can’t go off to pray to her gods without being shoved and insulted by every scrap of refuse in Hindustan—that she has to swallow abuse the way men swallow ghee! But I still have a sharp tongue left—a well-placed word or two for the occasion. And *still* I don’t have my tobacco! Where is the one-eyed, luckless son of shame who hasn’t prepared my pipe yet?”

It was hastily handed in by a hillman, and thin tendrils of gray smoke curling from both corners of the curtain signaled that peace had been restored.

If Kim had walked proudly the day before as a holy man’s disciple, today he marched with tenfold pride in the train of a semi-royal procession, holding an established place under the patronage of an old lady of charming manners and infinite resource. The escort, their heads tied up in native fashion, trudged along on either side of the cart, kicking up massive clouds of dust.

The lama and Kim walked slightly to one side, Kim chewing his sugar-cane and yielding the path to no one beneath the rank of a priest. They could hear the old lady’s tongue clacking as steadily as a rice husker. She instructed the escort to report everything happening along the road, and as soon as they cleared the *parao*, she threw back the curtains to peer out with her veil drawn only a third across her face. Her men never looked directly at her when she spoke, thus preserving proper decorum.

A dark, sallow English District Superintendent of Police, faultlessly uniformed and riding a tired horse, trotted past; seeing her entourage, he decided to tease her.

“O mother,” he called out, “do they do this in the zenanas? Suppose an Englishman came by and saw that you had no nose?”

“What?” she shrilled right back. “Does *your* mother have no nose? Why shout about it on the public highway, then?”

It was a neat parry. The Englishman threw up a hand in the gesture of a swordsman acknowledging a hit. She laughed and nodded.

“Is this a face to tempt virtue astray?” She threw back her veil entirely and stared at him.

It was hardly a lovely face, but as the man gathered up his reins, he called her a Moon of Paradise, a Disturber of Virtue, and several other extravagant titles that doubled her up with mirth.

“He’s a rogue,” she declared. “All police constables are rogues, but the officer chaps are the worst. Hey, my son, you never learned all that talk since you came from Europe. Who nursed you?”

“A hillwoman from Dalhousie, my mother. Keep your beauty shaded, O Dispenser of Delights,” and he trotted on.

“Those are the sort,” she assumed a judicial tone and popped a piece of betel nut into her mouth, “who understand how to keep justice. They know the land and its customs. The others, straight from Europe and nursed by white women, learning our languages from books, are worse than the plague. They do great harm to rulers.” Then she launched into a long, rambling tale for the benefit of all within earshot about an ignorant young policeman who had harassed a small hill raja—a ninth cousin of her own—over a minor land dispute, concluding with a proverb that was by no means religious.

After a while her mood shifted, and she had one of the escorts ask if the lama would walk beside the cart and discuss matters of religion. Kim dropped back into the dust, content to keep chewing his sugar-cane. For an hour or more the lama’s tam-o'-shanter bobbed like a moon through the haze, and from snatches of conversation Kim gathered that the old woman was weeping. One of the Ooryas half-apologized for his rudeness the previous night, remarking that he had never known his mistress to be in such a mild temper, attributing it entirely to the presence of the strange priest. Personally, he believed in Brahmins, though like all natives he was well aware of their greed and cunning. Still, when Brahmins irritated the master’s mother-in-law with constant demands for alms—sending them away so angry that they cursed the entire escort (which was the real reason the second off-side bullock had gone lame and the cart pole had snapped the night before)—he was quite willing to accept any priest of any other faith, in or out of India. Kim nodded wisely and pointed out that the lama took no money, and that the cost of their food would be repaid a hundredfold by the good luck he brought the caravan. He also told stories of Lahore and sang a couple of songs that made the escort laugh. As a city boy familiar with the latest tunes by fashionable composers—mostly women—Kim held a distinct advantage over men from a fruit-growing village behind Saharunpore, though he let them infer it modestly.

At noon they stepped aside to eat. The meal was plentiful, well-cooked, and served on clean leaf plates out of the dust. They gave the leftovers to local beggars to fulfill all religious duties, then settled down for a long, luxurious smoke. The old lady had retreated behind her curtains, but she joined freely in the conversation, her servants arguing and contradicting her just as servants do throughout the East. She contrasted the cool pines of the Kangra and Kulu hills with the heat and mangoes of the South; she told tales of local deities near her husband’s territory; she roundly cursed the tobacco she was smoking, berated all Brahmins without mercy, and speculated openly about her coming grandsons.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
chapters.content:
Here come I to my own again Fed, forgiven, and known again Claimed by bone of my bone again, And sib to flesh of my flesh! The fatted calf is dressed for me, But the husks have greater zest for me ... I think my pigs will be best for me, So I’m off to the styes afresh.

The Prodigal Son.

Once more the lazy, string-tied, shuffling procession got under way, and she slept until they reached the next stopping place. It was a very short march, and an hour remained before sundown, so Kim looked around for some amusement.

“Why not sit and rest?” said one of the escort. “Only devils and Englishmen walk back and forth for no reason.”

“Never make friends with the Devil, a Monkey, or a Boy. No one ever knows what they will do next,” said his companion.

Kim turned a scornful back—he did not want to hear the old story about how the Devil played with some boys, regretted it, and wandered aimlessly across the countryside.

The lama strode after him. All that day, whenever they passed a stream, he had turned aside to inspect it, but in no case had he received any sign that he had found his River. Unconsciously, too, the comfort of speaking to someone in a sensible language, and of being properly regarded and respected as a spiritual advisor by a well-born woman, had slightly weaned his thoughts from the Search. Moreover, he was prepared to spend peaceful years on his quest, possessing none of the white man’s impatience, but instead a profound faith.

“Where are you going?” he called after Kim.

“Nowhere—it was a short march, and all this”—Kim waved his hands broadly—“is new to me.”

“She is unquestionably a wise and discerning woman. But it is difficult to meditate when—”

“All women are like that.” Kim spoke as though he were Solomon.

“In front of the monastery there was a broad stone platform,” the lama muttered, looping his well-worn prayer beads. “I left the marks of my feet there—pacing back and forth with these.”

He clicked the beads and began his devotion of “Om mani padme hum,” grateful for the coolness, the quiet, and the absence of dust.

One thing after another caught Kim’s idle eye across the plain. There was no purpose to his wandering, except that the style of the nearby huts seemed new, and he wished to investigate.

They came out upon a broad grazing area, brown and purple in the afternoon light, with a dense clump of mango trees in the center. It struck Kim as strange that no shrine stood in such a favorable spot; the boy was as observant as any priest in these matters.
