Far across the plain walked four men side by side, made tiny by the distance. He looked intently under his curved palms and caught the glint of brass.

“Soldiers. White soldiers!” he said. “Let’s go see.”

“It’s always soldiers when you and I go out alone together. But I have never seen the white soldiers.”

“They never cause trouble unless they’re drunk. Stay behind this tree.”

They stepped behind the thick trunks into the cool shade of the mango grove. Two of the little figures halted; the other two advanced uncertainly. They were the advance party of a regiment on the march, sent out as usual to mark the campsite. They carried five-foot sticks with fluttering flags and shouted to one another as they spread across the flat ground.

At last they entered the mango grove, walking heavily.

“It’s here or hereabouts—officers’ tents under the trees, I reckon, and the rest of us can stay outside. Have they marked out the baggage wagons in the rear?”

They shouted again to their comrades in the distance, and a gruff answer came back, faint and mellow.

“Stick the flag in here, then,” said one.

“What are they preparing?” the lama asked, struck with wonder. “This is a great and terrible world. What is the design on the flag?”

A soldier thrust a pole within a few feet of them, grunted with dissatisfaction, pulled it up again, consulted with his companion—who looked up and down the shaded green arbor—and stuck it back in the ground.

Kim stared with all his might, his breath coming in short, sharp gasps between his teeth. The soldiers stamped off into the sunshine.

“O Holy One!” he gasped. “My horoscope! The drawing in the dust by the priest in Umballa! Remember what he said. First come two scouts—to make everything ready—in a dark place, just as it always is at the beginning of a vision.”

“But this is no vision,” said the lama. “It is merely the world’s Illusion.”

“And after them comes the Bull—the Red Bull on the green field. Look! It is him!”

He pointed to the flag snapping sharply in the evening breeze not ten feet away. It was nothing more than an ordinary camp marker, but the regiment, always punctilious about military details, had emblazoned it with the regimental emblem: the Red Bull, which is the crest of the Mavericks—the great Red Bull against a background of Irish green.

“I see, and now I remember,” said the lama. “Certainly it is your Bull. And certainly the two men came to make everything ready.”

“They are soldiers—white soldiers. What did the priest say? ‘The sign opposite the Bull is the sign of War and armed men.’ Holy One, this touches my Search.”

“True. It is true.” The lama stared fixedly at the emblem flaming like a ruby in the dusk. “The priest in Umballa said yours was the sign of War.”

“What do we do now?”

“Wait. Let us wait.”

“Even now the darkness clears,” Kim said. It was only natural that the descending sun should finally pierce the tree trunks and sweep across the grove, filling it with a dusty golden light for a few minutes; but to Kim it was the fulfillment of the Umballa Brahmin’s prophecy.

“Hark!” said the lama. “Someone is beating a drum—far off!”

At first the sound, carrying faintly through the still air, resembled the throbbing of a vein in the head. Soon a sharper beat was added.

“Ah! The music,” Kim explained. He knew the sound of a regimental band, but it amazed the lama.

At the far end of the plain, a heavy, dusty column came into view. Then the wind carried the tune:

We crave your condescension To tell you what we know Of marching in the Mulligan Guards To Sligo Port below!

Here the shrill fifes broke in:

We shouldered arms, We marched—we marched away. From Phoenix Park We marched to Dublin Bay. The drums and the fifes, Oh, sweetly they did play, As we marched—marched—marched—with the Mulligan Guards!

It was the band of the Mavericks playing the regiment into camp, for the men were route-marching with their baggage. The rippling column swung onto level ground—carts behind it split left and right, scurried about like an anthill, and...

“But this is sorcery!” said the lama.

The plain dotted itself with tents that seemed to rise fully pitched straight from the carts. Another rush of men invaded the grove, erected a huge tent in silence, put up eight or nine more beside it, and uncovered cooking pots, pans, and bundles that were quickly seized by a crowd of native servants. Behold, the mango grove had turned into an orderly town right before their eyes!

“Let us go,” said the lama, shrinking back in fear as the fires flickered and white officers with jingling swords strode into the mess tent.

“Stand back in the shadow. No one can see past the light of a fire,” Kim said, his eyes still fixed on the flag. He had never before watched the routine of an experienced regiment pitching camp in thirty minutes.

“Look! Look! Look!” clucked the lama. “Yonder comes a priest.” It was Bennett, the Church of England chaplain of the regiment, limping along in dusty black. One of the soldiers had made a crude remark about the chaplain’s stamina, and to put him to shame, Bennett had marched step for step with the men that day. His black clerical garb, the gold cross on his watch chain, his clean-shaven face, and his soft black wide-brimmed hat would have marked him as a holy man anywhere in India. He dropped into a camp chair by the door of the mess tent and pulled off his boots. Three or four officers gathered around him, laughing and joking about his feat.

“The talk of white men is entirely lacking in dignity,” observed the lama, judging solely by their tone. “Yet I observed the countenance of that priest, and I believe he is learned. Is it likely he will understand our talk? I would speak with him concerning my Search.”

“Never speak to a white man until he has eaten,” Kim said, quoting a well-known proverb. “They will eat now, and—and I don’t think they’re good people to beg from. Let’s go back to our resting place. After we have eaten, we will return. It certainly was a Red Bull—my Red Bull.”

Both of them were noticeably distracted when the old lady’s retinue set their meal before them; out of respect, no one broke their silence, for it is considered unlucky to annoy guests.

“Now,” Kim said, picking his teeth, “we will return to that place; but you, O Holy One, must wait a little way off, because your steps are heavier than mine and I am anxious to see more of that Red Bull.”

“But how can you understand their speech? Walk slowly. The road is dark,” the lama replied uneasily.

Kim brushed the objection aside. “I found a spot near the trees,” he said, “where you can sit until I call you.” No, as the lama began to protest, “remember this is my Search—the search for my Red Bull. The sign in the stars was not meant for you. I know a little of the customs of white soldiers, and I always like to see new things.”

“What is there in this world that you do not know?” The lama squatted obediently in a small hollow not a hundred yards from the mound of mango trees silhouetted against the star-powdered sky.

“Wait until I call.” Kim slipped into the dusk. He knew there would likely be sentries posted around the camp, and he smiled to himself as he heard the heavy tread of one. A boy who could dodge across the rooftops of Lahore on a moonlit night, utilizing every patch of shadow to elude pursuers, was hardly going to be stopped by a line of ordinary soldiers. He paid them the compliment of crawling between two of them, and—running and halting, crouching and dropping flat—he worked his way toward the lighted mess tent. There, pressing close behind a mango tree, he waited until some chance remark might give him a useful opening.

His mind was now entirely occupied with gathering more information about the Red Bull. For all he knew—and Kim’s knowledge had strange, sudden gaps—the men, those nine hundred absolute devils his father had prophesied, might worship the beast after the sun went down, just as Hindus worship the sacred cow. That at least would make complete sense, and the padre with the gold cross would be the proper person to consult. On the other hand, remembering the stern-faced padres he had avoided in Lahore, this priest might simply be an inquisitive nuisance who would order him back to school. But hadn’t it been proven in Umballa that his sign in the heavens foretold War and armed men? Wasn’t he the Friend of the Stars as well as of All the World, bursting with terrible secrets? Most importantly—forming the deep undercurrent of all his rapid thoughts—this adventure, though he didn’t know the English word for it, was a stupendous lark, a delightful continuation of his old rooftop escapades, as well as the fulfillment of a sublime prophecy. He lay flat on his stomach and wriggled toward the door of the mess tent, keeping a hand on the amulet around his neck.

It was just as he had suspected. The Englishmen prayed to their god; for in the center of the mess table—its only ornament while on the march—stood a golden bull fashioned from ancient loot taken from the Summer Palace in Peking—a red-gold bull with lowered head, charging across a field of Irish green. To this figure the Englishmen raised their glasses and shouted in confusion.

Now, the Reverend Arthur Bennett always left the mess after that toast, and being rather tired from his march, his movements were quicker than usual. Kim, with his head slightly raised, was still staring at his totem on the table when the chaplain stepped squarely on his right shoulder blade. Kim winced under the heavy boot and, rolling sideways, tripped the chaplain, who—being a man of action—grabbed him by the throat and nearly choked the life out of him. Kim instantly kicked him hard in the stomach. Mr. Bennett gasped and doubled over, but without letting go, he rolled across the ground and silently dragged Kim into his own tent. The Mavericks were inveterate practical jokers, and the Englishman thought it best to say nothing until he had investigated fully.

“Why, it’s a boy!” he exclaimed as he pulled his prize into the light of the tent-pole lantern, then shook him roughly. “What were you doing? You’re a thief. Choor? Mallum?” His Hindustanee was very limited, and the ruffled and disgusted Kim decided to stick to the persona mapped out for him. As he caught his breath, he quickly invented a plausible story about his connection to some camp follower, keeping a sharp eye on the chaplain’s left armpit. The chance came; he ducked toward the doorway, but a long arm shot out and grabbed his neck, snapping the amulet string and closing around the charm.

“Give it to me. Oh, give it to me. Is it lost? Give me the papers.”

The words were spoken in English—the thin, clipped English of a native-born youth—and the chaplain jumped in surprise.

“A scapular,” he said, opening his hand. “No, some sort of heathen charm. Why—why, do you speak English? Little boys who steal get beaten. You know that?”

“I don’t—I didn’t steal anything.” Kim danced in agony like a terrier facing a raised stick. “Oh, give it to me. It’s my charm. Don’t steal it from me.”

The chaplain paid no attention, but went to the tent door and called out. A plump, clean-shaven man appeared.

“I want your advice, Father Victor,” Bennett said. “I found this boy lurking in the dark outside the mess tent. Ordinarily, I’d have punished him and let him go, because I suspect he’s a thief. But he speaks English, and he places some sort of value on a charm around his neck. I thought perhaps you could help me.”

Between the Church of England chaplain and the Roman Catholic chaplain of the Irish contingent lay, as Bennett believed, an unbridgeable gulf. Yet it was remarkable that whenever the Church of England faced a human problem, it was very likely to call upon the Church of Rome. Bennett’s official horror of the Scarlet Woman and all her ways was matched only by his private respect for Father Victor.

“A thief speaking English, is it? Let’s look at his charm. No, it’s not a scapular, Bennett.” He held out his hand.

“But do we have any right to open it? A sound whipping—”

“I did not steal,” Kim protested. “You kicked me all over my body. Now give me my charm and I’ll go away.”

“Not so fast. Let’s look first,” Father Victor said, leisurely unfolding poor Kimball O’Hara’s water-resistant parchment, his discharge papers, and Kim’s baptismal certificate. On the back of the latter, O’Hara—with some vague notion that he was doing something wonderful for his son—had scrawled over and over: “Please look after the boy. Please look after the boy”—signing his name and full regimental number.

“Powers of darkness below!” Father Victor said, handing the papers over to Mr. Bennett. “Do you know what these things are?”

“Yes,” Kim said. “They’re mine, and I want to go.”

“I don’t quite understand,” Mr. Bennett said. “He probably brought them on purpose. It might be some kind of begging trick.”

“I’ve never seen a beggar less anxious to stay with his regiment, then. There’s the makings of a jolly mystery here. Do you believe in Providence, Bennett?”

“I hope so.”

“Well, I believe in miracles, so it amounts to the same thing. Powers of darkness! Kimball O’Hara! And his son! But then he’s a native, and I saw Kimball marry Annie Shott myself. How long have you had these things, boy?”

“Ever since I was a tiny baby.”

Father Victor stepped forward quickly and pulled open the front of Kim’s tunic. “You see, Bennett, he isn’t very dark. What’s your name?”

“Kim.”

“Or Kimball?”

“Maybe. Will you let me go now?”

“What else?”

“They call me Kim Rishti ke. That’s Kim of the Rishti.”

“What is that—‘Rishti’?”

“Irish—that was the regiment, my father’s.”

“Irish—oh, I see.”

“Yes. That’s what my father told me. My father, he’s lived.”

“Lived where?”

“Lived. Of course he’s dead—gone.”

“Oh! That’s your abrupt way of putting it, is it?”

Bennett interrupted. “It’s possible I’ve done the boy an injustice. He’s certainly white, though clearly neglected. I’m sure I must have bruised him. I don’t think spirits—”

“Get him a glass of sherry, then, and let him sit on the cot. Now, Kim,” Father Victor continued, “no one is going to hurt you. Drink that down and tell us about yourself. The truth, if you don’t mind.”

Kim coughed slightly as he set down the empty glass and thought things over. This seemed like a time for caution and imagination. Small boys caught prowling around camps were usually kicked out after a whipping. But he hadn’t received any lashes; the amulet was clearly working in his favor, and the Umballa horoscope, combined with the few phrases he remembered of his father’s rambling talk, fit together miraculously. Otherwise, why did the fat padre look so impressed, and why the glass of hot yellow drink from the skinny one?

“My father died in Lahore city when I was very little. The woman kept a second-hand shop near where the horse-drawn cabs park.” Kim plunged into his story, unsure how far the truth would help him.

“Your mother?”

“No!”—with a gesture of disgust. “She died when I was born. My father got these papers from the Wonder House—what do you call that?” (Bennett nodded) “because he was in good standing. What do you call that?” (Bennett nodded again). “My father told me that. He said, and the Brahmin who drew the picture in the dust at Umballa two days ago also said, that I would find a Red Bull on a green field and that the Bull would help me.”

“A phenomenal little liar,” Bennett muttered.

“Powers of darkness below, what a country!” murmured Father Victor. “Go on, Kim.”

“I did not steal. Besides, I am right now the disciple of a very holy man. He’s sitting outside. We saw two men come with flags to get the place ready. That always happens in a dream, or because of a—a—prophecy. So I knew it had come true. I saw the Red Bull on the green field, and my father said, ‘Nine hundred thorough-going devils and the Colonel riding a horse will look after you when you find the Red Bull!’ I didn’t know what to do when I saw the Bull, but I went away and came back when it was dark. I wanted to see the Bull again, and I saw it again with the—the Englishmen praying to it. I think the Bull will help me. The holy man said so too. He’s sitting outside. Will you hurt him if I call out to him now? He’s very holy. He can verify everything I say, and he knows I’m not a thief.”

“‘Englishmen praying to a bull!’ What on earth do you make of that?” Bennett said. “‘Disciple of a holy man!’ Is the boy mad?”

“It’s O’Hara’s boy, sure enough. O’Hara’s boy mixed up with all the powers of darkness. It’s very much what his father would have done if he were drunk. We’d better invite the holy man in. He might know something.”

“He doesn’t know anything,” Kim said. “I’ll show him to you if you come. He’s my master. Then afterward we can leave.”

“Powers of darkness!” was all Father Victor could say as Bennett marched off with a firm grip on Kim’s shoulder.

They found the lama right where he had been left.

“The Search is at an end for me!” Kim shouted in the vernacular. “I have found the Bull, but God knows what comes next. They won’t hurt you. Come to the fat priest’s tent with this skinny man and see how it ends. It’s all new, and they can’t speak Hindi. They’re just uncurried donkeys.”

“Then it is not wise to mock their ignorance,” the lama replied. “I am glad if you are happy, disciple.”

Dignified and unsuspecting, he strode into the small tent, saluted the clergymen as a fellow churchman, and sat down beside the open charcoal brazier. The yellow tent lining reflected the lamplight, turning his face a reddish gold.

Bennett looked at him with the triple-layered indifference of a creed that lumps nine-tenths of the world under the title of “heathen.”

“And what was the end of the Search? What gift has the Red Bull brought?” The lama addressed Kim directly.

“He asks, ‘What are you going to do?’” Bennett was staring uneasily at Father Victor, and Kim, for his own purposes, took over the role of interpreter.

“I don’t see what business this beggar has with the boy, who is probably his dupe or accomplice,” Bennett began. “We can’t allow an English boy—Assuming he’s the son of a Mason, the sooner he goes to the Masonic Orphanage, the better.”

“Ah! That’s your opinion as secretary of the regimental lodge,” Father Victor said. “But we might as well tell the old man what we’re going to do. He doesn’t look like a villain.”

“My experience is that one can never fathom the Oriental mind. Now, Kimball, I want you to tell this man what I say, word for word.”

Kim gathered the drift of the next few sentences and translated them thus:

“Holy One, the skinny fool who looks like a camel says I am an Englishman’s son.”

“But how?”

“Oh, it’s true. I’ve known it since birth, but he could only figure it out by ripping the amulet from my neck and reading all the papers. He thinks once a Englishman, always an Englishman, and between the two of them, they plan to keep me in this regiment or send me to a school. It’s happened before. I’ve always managed to avoid it. The fat fool wants one thing and the camel-like one wants another. But it doesn’t matter. I may spend tonight here and perhaps tomorrow night. It’s happened before. Then I’ll run away and come back to you.”

“But tell them you are my disciple. Tell them how you came to me when I was weak and bewildered. Tell them of our Search, and surely they will let you go now.”

“I’ve already told them. They laughed and talked about the police.”

“What are you saying?” Mr. Bennett demanded.

“Oh. He only says that if you don’t let me go, it will disrupt his business—his urgent private affairs.” This last phrase was borrowed from a Eurasian clerk in the Canal Department, but it only drew a smile that irritated Kim. “And if you knew what his business was, you wouldn’t be in such a bloody hurry to interfere.”

“What is it, then?” Father Victor asked, not without sympathy as he watched the lama’s face.

“There is a River in this country that he wants to find very, very much. It was marked by an Arrow that—” Kim tapped his foot impatiently as he translated from the vernacular into his clumsy English. “Oh, it was created by our Lord God Buddha, you know, and if you bathe in it, all your sins are washed away and you become as white as cotton wool.” (Kim had heard missionary talk in his time.) “I am his disciple, and we must find that River. It’s very important to us.”

“Say that again,” Bennett said. Kim obeyed, adding a few embellishments.

“Why, this is gross blasphemy!” cried the Church of England clergyman.

“Tck! Tck!” Father Victor said sympathetically. “I’d give a lot to be able to speak the native tongue. A river that washes away sin! And how long have you two been looking for it?”

“Oh, many days. Now we want to go away and look for it again. It’s not here, you see.”

“I see,” Father Victor said gravely. “But he can’t go on traveling with that old man. It would be different, Kim, if you weren’t a soldier’s son. Tell him the regiment will take care of you and make as good a man of you as—as good a man as possible. Tell him that if he believes in miracles, he must believe that—”

“There’s no need to pander to his credulity,” Bennett interrupted.

“I’m doing no such thing. He has to believe that the boy’s arrival here—at his very own regiment—in search of his Red Bull is practically a miracle. Consider the odds against it, Bennett. This one boy in all of India, and our regiment of all regiments on the line of march for him to stumble upon! It’s predestined on the face of it. Yes, tell him it’s Kismet. Kismet, mallum? (Do you understand?)”

He turned toward the lama, who might as well have been listening to talk about Mesopotamia.

“They say,”—the old man’s eyes lit up at Kim’s words—“they say the meaning of my horoscope is now fulfilled, and that having been led back—though as you know I went out of curiosity—to these people and their Red Bull, I must go to a school and be turned into an Englishman. Now I’m pretending to agree, because at worst it will only mean a few meals eaten away from you. Then I’ll slip away and follow the road to Saharunpore. Therefore, Holy One, stay with that Kulu woman—don’t stray far from her cart until I return. Without a doubt, my sign is of War and armed men. Look how they’ve given me wine to drink and set me upon a seat of honor! My father must have been an important person. So if they raise me to honor among them, fine. If not, fine. Whatever happens, I’ll run back to you when I’m tired. But stay with the Rajput woman, or I won’t be able to find you... Oh yes,” the boy added, “I’ve told him everything you told me to say.”

“And I see no reason why he should linger,” Bennett said, reaching into his trouser pocket. “We can look into the details later—and I’ll give him a ru—”

“Give him time. Maybe he’s fond of the lad,” Father Victor said, half-stopping the clergyman’s movement.

The lama pulled out his rosary and dragged the wide brim of his hat down over his eyes.

“What can he want now?”

“He says”—Kim raised a hand. “He says, ‘Be quiet.’ He wants to speak to me alone. You see, you don’t understand a single word of what he’s saying, and I think if you keep talking he might place a very heavy curse on you. When he handles his beads like that, you see, he always wants silence.”

The two Englishmen sat dumbfounded, though a look in Bennett’s eye promised trouble for Kim once he fell under the chaplain’s religious authority.

“An Englishman and the son of an Englishman—” The lama’s voice was harsh with pain. “Yet no white man knows this land and its customs as you do. How can this be true?”

“What does it matter, Holy One? Remember it’s only for a night or two. Remember, I can change my appearance quickly. It will all be just as it was when I first spoke to you beneath Zam-Zammah, the great gun—”

“Like a boy in white men’s clothes—when I first went to the Wonder House. And a second time you were a Hindu. What will the third incarnation be?” He chuckled bleakly. “Ah, disciple, you have wronged an old man because my heart went out to you.”

“And mine to you. But how could I know the Red Bull would lead me into this mess?”

The lama covered his face again and nervously rattled his prayer beads. Kim squatted beside him and clutched a fold of his robe.

“Now it is understood that the boy is an Englishman?” he continued in a muffled tone. “Such an Englishman as the one who kept the images in the Wonder House.” The lama’s experience with white men was limited; he seemed to be repeating a lesson. “So then it isn’t proper for him to do other than what Englishmen do. He must return to his own people.”

“For a day and a night and a day,” Kim pleaded.

“No, you don’t!” Father Victor saw Kim edging toward the door and blocked him with a sturdy leg.

“I don’t understand the customs of white men. The Priest of the Images in the Wonder House in Lahore was more courteous than this skinny one here. This boy will be taken from me. They will turn my disciple into an Englishman? Woe is me! How shall I find my River? Do they have no disciples? Ask them.”

“He says he’s very sorry that he can’t look for the River right now. He asks why you don’t have disciples and why you keep bothering him. He wants to wash away his sins.”

Neither Bennett nor Father Victor had a ready reply.

Kim said in English, distressed by the lama’s anguish: “I think if you let me go now, we can walk away quietly and not steal anything. We’ll look for that River just like before I was caught. I wish I’d never come here to find the Red Bull and all that nonsense. I don’t want it.”

“It’s the very best day’s work you ever did for yourself, young man,” said Bennett.

“Good heavens, I don’t know how to comfort him,” Father Victor muttered, watching the lama intently. “He can’t take the boy with him, and yet he’s a good man—I’m sure he’s a good man. Bennett, if you give him that rupee, he’ll curse you from root to branch!”

They listened to each other breathe for three, five full minutes. Then the lama raised his head and gazed past them into empty space.

“And I am a Follower of the Way,” he said bitterly. “The sin is mine, and the punishment is mine. I made myself believe—for I see now it was only pretense—that you were sent to me to help in the Search. So my heart went out to you for your charity, your courtesy, and the wisdom of your tender years. But those who follow the Way must harbor no fire of desire or attachment, for all of that is Illusion. As it says...” He quoted an ancient Chinese text, backed it up with another, and reinforced both with a third. “I strayed from the Way, my disciple. It was no fault of yours. I took delight in the spectacle of life, the new people along the roads, and your joy in seeing such things. I was pleased with you when I should have focused on my Search and my Search alone. Now I am sorrowful because you are taken from me and my River is far away. It is the Law that I have broken!”

“Powers of darkness below!” whispered Father Victor, who, experienced in the confessional, heard the heartbreak in every word.

“I see now that the sign of the Red Bull was meant for me as well as for you. All Desire is red—and evil. I will perform penance and find my River alone.”

“At least go back to the Kulu woman,” Kim urged, “otherwise you’ll be lost on the roads. She’ll feed you until I can run back to you.”

The lama waved a hand to show the matter was settled in his mind.

“Now,”—his tone shifted as he turned to Kim—“what will they do with you? At least by helping you, I may gain merit to wipe out past wrongs.”

“They’ll make an Englishman of me—so they think. The day after tomorrow I’ll return. Don’t grieve.”

“Of what sort? Like this man or that one?” He pointed to Father Victor. “Like the ones I saw this evening, men wearing swords and treading heavily?”

“Maybe.”

“That is not good. Those men follow desire and end in emptiness. You must not be like them.”

The Umballa priest said my star was War,” Kim chimed in. “I’ll ask these fools—though there’s truly no need. I’ll run away tonight, for all I wanted was to see new things.”

Kim asked Father Victor two or three questions in English and translated the answers for the lama.

Then: “He says, ‘You take him from me and you can’t say what you’ll make of him.’ He says, ‘Tell me before I go, for shaping a child is no small thing.’”

“You’ll be sent to a school. Later on, we’ll see. Kimball, I suppose you’d like to be a soldier?”

“Gorah-log [white folk]. No! No!” Kim shook his head violently. There was nothing in his nature that responded to drill and routine. “I won’t be a soldier.”

“You’ll be what you’re told to be,” Bennett said; “and you should be grateful we’re going to help you.”

Kim smiled sympathetically. If these men labored under the illusion that he would do anything against his will, so much the better.

Another long silence followed. Bennett fidgeted with impatience and suggested calling a sentry to remove the beggar.

“Do they give or sell education among the Englishmen? Ask them,” said the lama, and Kim translated.

“They say money is paid to the teacher—but the regiment will provide that money... What’s the need? It’s only for a night.”

“And—the more money paid, the better the education given?” The lama ignored Kim’s plans for an early escape. “There is no wrong in paying for learning. Helping the ignorant attain wisdom is always a merit.” His prayer beads clicked furiously like an abacus. Then he turned to face his opponents.

“Ask them how much money is required for wise and proper instruction? And in which city is that teaching given?”

“Well,” Father Victor said in English once Kim translated, “that depends. The regiment would pay for you the whole time you’re at the Military Orphanage, or you might go on the Punjab Masonic Orphanage list (not that either you or he would understand what that means); but the best schooling a boy can get in India is, of course, at St. Xavier’s in Partibus in Lucknow.” This took some time to translate, as Bennett tried to cut it short.

“He wants to know how much?” Kim asked placidly.

“Two or three hundred rupees a year.” Father Victor was well past any sense of shock. Bennett, impatient, didn’t understand.

“He says: ‘Write that name and the money on a piece of paper and give it to him.’ And he says you must sign your name at the bottom, because in a few days he’s going to write you a letter. He says you’re a good man. He says the other man is a fool. He’s leaving.”

The lama rose abruptly. “I continue my Search,” he cried, and walked out.

“He’ll walk straight into the sentries!” Father Victor cried, jumping up as the lama strode away. “And I can’t leave the boy.” Kim made a swift move to follow, but checked himself. There was no sound of a challenge outside. The lama had vanished.

Kim settled himself comfortably on the chaplain’s cot. At least the lama had promised to stay with the Rajput woman from Kulu, and the rest was of minor importance. He was amused that the two padres were so visibly excited. They talked for a long time in low tones, Father Victor urging some plan on Mr. Bennett, who looked skeptical. All this was very new and fascinating, but Kim was feeling sleepy. They called men into the tent—one of them was certainly the Colonel, just as his father had prophesied—and they asked him endless questions, mostly about the woman who looked after him, all of which Kim answered truthfully. They didn’t seem to think the woman made a good guardian.

After all, this was his newest experience yet. Sooner or later, if he chose, he could slip away into the vast, gray, formless expanse of India, far beyond tents, padres, and colonels. Meanwhile, if the Sahibs were to be impressed, he would do his best to impress them. He, too, was a white man.

After much discussion that he couldn’t follow, they handed him over to a sergeant with strict orders not to let him escape. The regiment would march on to Umballa, and Kim would be sent north—partly at the lodge’s expense and partly through subscriptions—to a place called Sanawar.

“It’s past all belief, Colonel,” Father Victor said after talking nonstop for ten minutes. “His Buddhist friend has vanished after taking my name and address. I can’t quite figure out if he intends to pay for the boy’s education or if he’s cooking up some witchcraft of his own.” Then, turning to Kim: “You’ll live to be grateful to your friend the Red Bull yet. We’ll make a man of you at Sanawar—even if it costs making a Protestant out of you.”

“Certainly—most certainly,” Bennett said.

“But you won’t go to Sanawar,” Kim said.

“Oh, but we will go to Sanawar, little man. That’s the order of the Commander-in-Chief, who is a trifle more important than O’Hara’s son.”

“You won’t go to Sanawar. You’re going to the War.”

There was a roar of laughter from inside the crowded tent.

“When you know your own regiment a bit better, Kim, you won’t confuse the line of march with the line of battle. We hope to go to ‘the War’ sometime.”

“Oh, I know all about that.” Kim took another wild guess. If they weren’t going to the war, at least they didn’t know what he knew from the gossip on the veranda in Umballa.

“I know you aren’t at the war now; but I tell you that as soon as you reach Umballa, you’ll be sent to the war—the new war. It’s a war involving eight thousand men, besides the artillery.”

“That’s very specific. Do you add prophecy to your other talents? Take him along, sergeant. Get him a set of clothes from the drums, and make sure he doesn’t slip through your fingers. Who says the age of miracles is past? I think I’ll go to bed. My poor mind is weakening.”

An hour later, sitting quietly as a wild animal at the far end of the camp, Kim was newly washed and dressed in a horribly stiff uniform that scratched his arms and legs.

“A most amazin’ young bird,” the sergeant remarked. “He shows up accompanied by a yellow-headed pagan priest, with his father’s lodge certificates hanging round his neck, talkin’ God knows what about a red bull. The pagan priest vanishes without a word, and the bhoy sits cross-legged on the chaplain’s cot prophesyin’ bloody war to the rank and file. India’s a wild country for a God-fearing man. I’ll just tie his leg to the tent pole in case he tries to climb the roof. What was that you said about the war?”

“Eight thousand men, besides the guns,” Kim said. “You’ll see very soon.”

“You’re a comfortin’ little imp. Lie down between the drums and go to bye-bye. Those two boys will watch over your slumbers.”

chapters.title: Chapter 6
chapters.content:
Now I remember comrades— Old playmates on new seas— Whenas we traded orpiment Among the savages. Ten thousand leagues to southward, And thirty years removed— They knew not noble Valdez, But me they knew and loved.

Song of Diego Valdez.

Very early in the morning, the white tents were struck and vanished as the Mavericks took a side road toward Umballa. The route did not pass the resting place, and Kim, trudging beside a baggage cart under a barrage of remarks from soldiers’ wives, was not as confident as he had been the night before. He discovered that he was closely watched—Father Victor on one side and Mr. Bennett on the other.

In the morning, the column halted. A camel-post rider handed the Colonel a letter. He read it and spoke to a major. Half a mile to the rear, Kim heard a hoarse and joyful roar rolling down through the thick dust. Then someone slapped him on the back, crying: “Tell us how you knew, you little limb of Satan! Father dear, see if you can make him tell.”

A pony pulled alongside, and he was hauled up onto the priest’s saddlebow.

“Now, my son, your prophecy from last night has come true. Our orders are to entrain at Umballa for the Front tomorrow.”

“What is that?” Kim asked, for “front” and “entrain” were relatively new words to him.

“We are going to ‘the War,’ as you called it.”

“Of course you are going to the War. I said so last night.”

“You did; but, Powers of Darkness, how did you know?”

Kim’s eyes sparkled. He clamped his lips shut, nodded his head, and looked unspeakable things. The chaplain moved on through the dust, and privates, sergeants, and subalterns drew each other’s attention to the boy. The Colonel, at the head of the column, stared at him curiously. “It was probably just some bazaar rumor,” he said, “but even so—” He checked the paper in his hand. “Hang it all, the decision was only made within the last forty-eight hours.”

“Are there many more like you in India,” Father Victor asked, “or are you some sort of lusus naturae?”

“Now that I’ve told you,” the boy said, “will you let me go back to my old man? If he hasn’t stayed with that woman from Kulu, I’m afraid he’ll die.”

“From what I saw of him, he’s just as able to look after himself as you are. No. You’ve brought us luck, and we’re going to make a man of you. I’ll take you back to your baggage cart, and you’ll come see me this evening.”

For the rest of the day, Kim found himself treated with marked respect by a few hundred white men. The story of his appearance in camp, the discovery of his parentage, and his prophecy had lost nothing in the retelling. A big, shapeless white woman sitting on a pile of bedding asked him mysteriously whether he thought her husband would return from the war. Kim reflected gravely and said that he would, whereupon the woman gave him food. In many ways, this massive procession that played music at intervals—this crowd that talked and laughed so easily—resembled a festival in Lahore city. So far, there was no sign of hard labor, and he decided to grant the spectacle his patronage. By evening, musical bands came out to meet them and played the Mavericks into camp near the Umballa railway station. That was an interesting night. Men from other regiments came to visit the Mavericks. The Mavericks went visiting on their own account. Their pickets hurried out to round them up, only to meet pickets from strange regiments on the same errand; and after a while, bugles blew frantically for more pickets with officers to control the uproar. The Mavericks had a reputation for liveliness to maintain. Yet they fell in on the platform the next morning in perfect shape and condition; and Kim, left behind with the sick, women, and boys, shouted excited farewells as the trains pulled away. Life as an Englishman was amusing enough so far, but he approached it with caution. Then they marched him back under the guard of a drummer boy into empty, whitewashed barracks whose floors were littered with rubbish, string, and paper, and whose ceilings echoed his lonely footsteps. True to native fashion, he curled up on a bare cot and went to sleep. An angry man stomped down the veranda, woke him up, and announced that he was a schoolmaster. That was enough for Kim, who instantly retreated into his shell. He could just barely puzzle out the English police notices in Lahore city because they affected his comfort; and among the many guests of the woman who looked after him had been a strange German who painted scenery for the Parsi traveling theater. The German told Kim he had been “on the barricades in '48,” and therefore—or so it seemed to Kim—he would teach the boy to write in exchange for food. Kim had been beaten as far as learning individual letters, but he didn’t think much of them.

“I don’t know anything. Go away!” Kim said, sensing trouble. At that, the man grabbed him by the ear, dragged him to a room in a distant wing where a dozen drummer boys sat on benches, and told him to sit still if he could do nothing else. Kim managed this very successfully. The man spent at least half an hour explaining something or other with white lines on a blackboard while Kim resumed his interrupted nap. He thoroughly disapproved of the current turn of events, for this was the exact school and discipline he had spent two-thirds of his young life avoiding. Suddenly, a brilliant idea struck him, and he wondered why he hadn’t thought of it sooner.

The schoolmaster dismissed them, and the first to leap through the veranda into the open sunshine was Kim.

“’Ere, you! ’Alt! Stop!” a high voice called from behind. “I’ve got to look after you. My orders are not to let you out of my sight. Where are you goin’?”

It was the drummer boy who had been hanging around him all morning—a fat, freckled fellow of about fourteen whom Kim loathed from the soles of his boots to his cap ribbons.

“To the bazaar—to buy sweets—for you,” Kim said after a moment’s thought.

“Well, the bazaar’s out of bounds. If we go there, we’ll catch it. You come back.”

“How near can we go?” Kim didn’t know what “out of bounds” meant, but he wanted to be polite—for the time being.

“’Ow near? ’Ow far, you mean! We can go as far as that tree down the road.”

“Then I will go there.”

“All right. I ain’t goin’. It’s too ’ot. I can watch you from ’ere. It’s no good your runnin’ away. If you did, they’d spot you by your clothes. That’s regimental gear you’re wearin’. There ain’t a picket in Umballa that wouldn’t haul you back quicker than you started out.”

This didn’t impress Kim as much as the realization that his stiff clothing would exhaust him if he tried to run. He slouched over to the tree at the corner of a bare road leading toward the bazaar and watched the natives passing by. Most of them were low-caste barrack servants. Kim hailed a sweeper, who promptly replied with unnecessary insolence, assuming the European boy couldn’t understand. Kim’s low, sharp retort undeceived him. Putting his whole soul into it and grateful for the chance to abuse someone in his native tongue, Kim snapped: “And now, go to the nearest letter writer in the bazaar and tell him to come here. I need to write a letter.”

“But—but what kind of white man’s son are you to need a bazaar letter writer? Isn’t there a schoolmaster in the barracks?”

“Yes; and hell is full of his kind. Do as I say, you—you dog! Your mother was married under a basket! Servant of Lal Beg” (Kim knew the god of the sweepers), “hurry on my business, or we’ll speak further.”

The sweeper hurried off in a fright. “There’s a white boy by the barracks waiting under a tree who isn’t really a white boy,” he stammered to the first bazaar letter writer he encountered. “He needs you.”

“Will he pay?” asked the dapper scribe, gathering up his desk, pens, and sealing wax.

“I don’t know. He isn’t like other boys. Go and see. It’s well worth your time.”

Kim danced with impatience when the slim young Kayastha came into view. As soon as he was within earshot, Kim cursed him fluently.

“First I’ll take my pay,” the letter writer said. “Bad language makes the price higher. But who are you, dressed like that, to talk like this?”

“Aha! That will be in the letter you’re going to write. There never was such a tale. But I’m in no rush. Another writer will serve me. Umballa city is as full of them as Lahore.”

“Four annas,” said the writer, sitting down and spreading his cloth in the shade of a deserted barrack wing.

Instinctively, Kim squatted beside him—squatting the way only natives can—despite the abominable, clinging trousers.

The writer eyed him sideways.

“That’s the price to charge Englishmen,” Kim said. “Now give me a fair rate.”

“An anna and a half. How do I know, once I’ve written the letter, that you won’t run away?”

“I’m not allowed to go past that tree, and there’s the cost of the stamp to consider, besides.”

“I don’t make a commission on the stamp. Once more, what kind of white boy are you?”

“That will be explained in the letter, which is addressed to Mahbub Ali, the horse dealer in the Kashmir Serai at Lahore. He is my friend.”

“Wonders never cease!” murmured the letter writer, dipping a reed pen into his inkstand. “To be written in Hindi?”

“Assuredly. To Mahbub Ali then. Begin! I have come down with the old man as far as Umballa by train. At Umballa I brought news of the bay mare’s pedigree.” After what he had witnessed in the garden, he wasn’t going to mention white stallions.

“Slower a little. What does a bay mare have to do with... Is it Mahbub Ali, the great dealer?”

“Who else? I have been in his service. Take more ink. Again. As ordered, so I did it. We then traveled on foot toward Benares, but on the third day we found a certain regiment. Is that down?”

“Yes, regiment,” muttered the writer, all ears.

“I entered their camp and was caught, and by means of the charm around my neck, which you know, it was proved that I was the son of some man in the regiment—just as the prophecy of the Red Bull foretold, which you know was common talk in our bazaar.” Kim paused to let this sink into the writer’s heart, cleared his throat, and continued: “A priest dressed me in new clothes and gave me a new name... One priest, however, was a fool. These clothes are very heavy, but I am an Englishman and my heart is heavy too. They are sending me to school and beating me. I don’t like the air and water here. Come and help me, Mahbub Ali, or send me some money, because I don’t have enough to pay the writer who is writing this.”

“‘Who is writing this.’ It’s my own fault for letting myself be tricked. You’re as clever as Husain Bux, who forged treasury stamps in Lucknow. But what a story! What a story! Is it true by any chance?”

“It does no good to lie to Mahbub Ali. It’s better to help his friends by lending them a stamp. When the money arrives, I will repay you.”

The writer grunted doubtfully, but pulled a stamp from his desk, sealed the envelope, handed it to Kim, and left. Mahbub Ali’s name carried weight in Umballa.

“That’s the way to earn merit with the gods,” Kim shouted after him.

“Pay me double when the money comes,” the man called back over his shoulder.

“What were you yapping to that native about?” the drummer boy asked when Kim returned to the veranda. “I was watchin’ you.”

“I was only talking to him.”

“You talk just like a native, don’t you?”

“No! No! I only speak a little. What shall we do now?”

“The bugles’ll sound for dinner in a minute. My Gawd! I wish I’d gone to the Front with the regiment. It’s awful doin’ nothin’ but school down ’ere. Don’t you ’ate it?”

“Oh yes!”

“I’d run away if I knew where to go, but as the men say, in this bloomin’ India you’re just a prisoner at large. You can’t desert without bein’ hauled right back. I’m fair sick of it.”

“Have you been in Eng—England?”

“Why, I only came out last trooping season with my mother. I should think I’ve been in England. What an ignorant little beggar you are! You were brought up in the gutter, weren’t you?”

“Oh yes. Tell me something about England. My father came from there.”

Though he wouldn’t admit it, Kim naturally disbelieved every word the drummer boy uttered about the Liverpool suburb that was his England. It helped pass the weary hours until dinner—a thoroughly unappetizing meal served to the boys and a few invalids in a corner of the barrack room. If he hadn’t written to Mahbub Ali, Kim would have felt utterly depressed. He was accustomed to the indifference of native crowds, but this stark isolation among white men weighed heavily on him. He felt grateful when, during the afternoon, a big soldier led him over to Father Victor, who lived in another wing across a dusty parade ground. The priest was reading an English letter written in purple ink. He looked at Kim with more curiosity than ever.

“And how do you like it so far, my son? Not much, eh? It must be hard—very hard on a wild creature. Listen to this. I’ve received an astonishing letter from your friend.”

“Where is he? Is he well? Oh! If he knows how to write letters to me, that’s all right.”

“You’re fond of him, then?”

“Of course I’m fond of him. He was fond of me.”

“It seems so, judging by this. He can’t write English, can he?”

“Oh no. Not that I know of, but of course he found a letter writer who can write English very well, and so he wrote. I hope you understand.”

“That explains it. Do you know anything about his financial affairs?” Kim’s expression showed he did not.

“How should I know?”

“That’s what I’m asking. Now listen and see if you can make head or tail of this. We’ll skip the first part... It’s written from Jagadhri Road... ‘Sitting on wayside in grave meditation, trusting to be favoured with your Honour’s applause of present step, which recommend your Honour to execute for Almighty God’s sake. Education is greatest blessing if of best sorts. Otherwise no earthly use.’ Faith, the old man hit the bull’s-eye that time! ‘If your Honour condescending giving my boy best educations Xavier’ (I suppose that’s St. Xavier’s in Partibus) ‘in terms of our conversation dated in your tent 15th instant’ (a businesslike touch there!) ‘then Almighty God blessing your Honour’s succeedings to third an’ fourth generation and’—now listen!—‘confide in your Honour’s humble servant for adequate remuneration per hundi per annum three hundred rupees a year to one expensive education St. Xavier, Lucknow, and allow small time to forward same per hundi sent to any part of India as your Honour shall address yourself. This servant of your Honour has presently no place to lay crown of his head, but going to Benares by train on account of persecution of old woman talking so much and unanxious residing Saharunpore in any domestic capacity.’ Now what in the world does all that mean?”

“She asked him to be her priest—her clergyman—at Saharunpore, I think. He wouldn’t do it because of his River. She certainly did talk a lot.”

“It’s clear to you, is it? It completely baffles me. ‘So going to Benares, where will find address and forward rupees for boy who is apple of eye, and for Almighty God’s sake execute this education, and your petitioner as in duty bound shall ever awfully pray. Written by Sobrao Satai, Failed Entrance Allahabad University, for Venerable Teshoo Lama the priest of Such-zen looking for a River, address care of Tirthankars’ Temple, Benares. P.S.—Please note boy is apple of eye, and rupees shall be sent per hundi three hundred per annum. For God Almighty’s sake.’ Now, is that raving lunacy or a business proposition? I’m asking you, because I’m fairly at my wit’s end.”

“He says he’ll give me three hundred rupees a year? So he will give them to me.”

“Oh, is that how you see it?”

“Of course. If he says so!”

The priest whistled, then addressed Kim as an equal. “I don’t believe it; but we’ll see. You were supposed to go off today to the Military Orphanage at Sanawar, where the regiment would keep you until you were old enough to enlist. You’d have been raised in the Church of England. Bennett arranged that. On the other hand, if you go to St. Xavier’s, you’ll get a better education and—and you can keep your own religion. Do you see my dilemma?” Kim saw nothing except a vision of the lama heading south on a train with no one to beg for him.

“Like most people, I’m going to stall. If your friend sends the money from Benares—Powers of Darkness below, where is a street beggar going to raise three hundred rupees?—you’ll go down to Lucknow and I’ll pay your fare, because I can’t touch the subscription money if I intend, as I do, to make you a Catholic. If he doesn’t pay, you’ll go to the Military Orphanage at the regiment’s expense. I’ll give him three days’ grace, though I don’t believe it for a second. Even then, if he fails to keep up the payments later on... but it’s beyond me. We can only take one step at a time in this world, praise God! And they sent Bennett to the Front and left me behind. Bennett can’t expect everything.”

“Oh yes,” Kim said vaguely.

The priest leaned forward. “I’d give a month’s pay to know what’s going on inside that little round head of yours.”

“There is nothing,” Kim said, scratching it. He wondered whether Mahbub Ali would send him as much as a whole rupee. Then he could pay the letter writer and send letters to the lama in Benares. Perhaps Mahbub Ali would visit him the next time he traveled south with horses. Surely Mahbub must know that Kim’s delivery of the message to the officer in Umballa had triggered the great war the men and boys had been arguing about so loudly over dinner. But if Mahbub Ali didn’t know that, it would be very dangerous to tell him. Mahbub Ali was harsh with boys who knew, or thought they knew, too much.

“Well, until I get further news,” Father Victor’s voice broke into his reverie, “you can run along now and play with the other boys. They’ll teach you something—though I don’t think you’ll like it.”

The day dragged to its weary close. When he wanted to sleep, he was instructed how to fold his clothes and arrange his boots, to the mockery of the other boys. Bugles woke him at dawn; the schoolmaster caught him after breakfast, thrust a page of meaningless characters under his nose, gave them absurd names, and beat him for no reason. Kim considered poisoning him with opium borrowed from a barrack sweeper, but realized that since they all ate together at a public table (which Kim found uniquely repulsive, preferring to turn his back on the world during meals), the attempt could be dangerous. Then he tried running away to the village where the priest had attempted to drug the lama—the village where the old soldier lived. But sharp-eyed sentries at every exit turned the little scarlet-clad figure back. The trousers and jacket crippled both body and mind alike, so he abandoned the plan and fell back, in true Oriental fashion, on time and chance.

Three days of torment passed within the massive, echoing white rooms. He walked out afternoons under the escort of the drummer boy, and all he heard from his companions were the few useless curse words that seemed to comprise two-thirds of the white man’s vocabulary. Kim had known and despised them all long ago. The drummer boy resented Kim’s silence and indifference by beating him, which was only natural. Kim cared nothing for the bazaars that were within bounds. He labeled all natives “niggers,” yet servants and sweepers called him vile names to his face; misled by their polite tone, he never understood, which somewhat consoled him for the beatings.

On the morning of the fourth day, retribution caught up with the drummer boy. They had gone out together toward the Umballa racecourse. The boy returned alone, weeping, with the news that young O’Hara—while doing nothing in particular—had hailed a scarlet-bearded native on horseback; that the native had promptly lashed him with a peculiarly stinging riding crop, scooped up young O’Hara, and galloped off. This news reached Father Victor, who drew down his long upper lip. He was already sufficiently rattled by a letter from the Temple of the Tirthankars in Benares enclosing a native banker’s promissory note for three hundred rupees along with a startling prayer to “Almighty God.” The lama would have been far more annoyed than the priest had he known how the bazaar letter writer had translated his phrase “to acquire merit.”

“Powers of Darkness below!” Father Victor fumbled with the note. “And now he’s run off with another of his dawn-riding friends. I don’t know whether it’s a greater relief to get him back or to have him stay lost. He’s beyond my comprehension. How the divil—yes, he’s the man I mean—can a street beggar raise enough money to educate white boys?”

Three miles away, on the Umballa racecourse, Mahbub Ali, reining in a gray Kabuli stallion with Kim perched in front of him, was saying:

“But, Little Friend of all पेड-the-World, I have my honor and reputation to consider. Every officer-Sahib in every regiment, and all of Umballa, knows Mahbub Ali. People saw me pick you up and thrash that boy. We are visible across this entire plain now. How can I take you away, or explain your disappearance if I drop you off and let you run into the crops? They would throw me in jail. Be patient. Once an Englishman, always an Englishman. When you grow up—who knows?—you will be grateful to Mahbub Ali.”

“Take me past their sentries where I can change this red uniform. Give me money and I will go to Benares and be with my lama again. I don’t want to be an Englishman, and remember, I did deliver that message.”

The stallion bolted wildly. Mahbub Ali had accidentally driven home his sharp-edged stirrup. (He wasn’t the modern sort of smooth horse dealer who wears English boots and spurs.) Kim drew his own conclusions from that slip.

“That was a minor matter. It lay straight on the road to Benares. The Sahib and I have forgotten it by now. I send so many letters and messages to men who ask about horses that I can hardly tell one from another. Was it something about a bay mare that Captain Peters wanted the pedigree of?”

Kim spotted the trap instantly. If he had said “bay mare,” Mahbub would have known from his eagerness to agree that the boy suspected something. Kim replied instead:

“Bay mare? No. I don’t forget my messages like that. It was a white stallion.”

“Ah, yes, so it was. A white Arab stallion. But you wrote ‘bay mare’ to me.”

“Who cares about telling the truth to a letter writer?” Kim retorted, feeling Mahbub’s palm rest against his heart.

“Hey! Mahbub, you old rogue, pull up!” shouted a voice, as an Englishman raced alongside on a small polo pony. “I’ve been chasing you half over the country. That Kabuli of yours can move. For sale, I suppose?”

“I have some young stock coming along, bred by Heaven for the delicate and difficult polo game. He has no equal. He—”

“Plays polo and waits at table. Yes, we know all that. What on earth do you have there?”

“A boy,” Mahbub said gravely. “He was being beaten by another boy. His father was once a white soldier in the big war. The boy was a child in Lahore city. He played with my horses when he was a baby. Now I think they want to make a soldier of him. He was recently caught by his father’s regiment, which went up to the front last week. But I don’t think he wants to be a soldier. I’m taking him for a ride. Tell me where your barracks are and I will drop him off.”

“Let me go. I can find the barracks myself.”

“And if you run away, who will say it wasn’t my fault?”

“He’ll run back for his dinner. Where else does he have to go?” the Englishman asked.

“He was born in this land. He has friends. He goes wherever he pleases. He is a sharp lad. It would take only a change of clothes, and in the blink of an eye he’d look like a low-caste Hindu boy.”

“The deuce he would!” The Englishman looked critically at the boy as Mahbub steered toward the barracks. Kim ground his teeth. Mahbub was mocking him, the way faithless Afghans do, for he went on:

“They will send him to school, put heavy boots on his feet, and smother him in these clothes. Then he will forget everything he knows. Now, which of these barracks is yours?”

Kim pointed—he couldn’t speak—toward Father Victor’s wing, which stood out starkly white nearby.

“Perhaps he’ll make a good soldier,” Mahbub said thoughtfully.

“He’d make a good orderly at least. I sent him to deliver a message from Lahore once. A message regarding the pedigree of a white stallion.”

This was a deadly insult heaped upon an even deadlier injury—and the Englishman to whom he had so cunningly handed that war-instigating letter heard every word of it. Kim imagined Mahbub Ali frying in hellfire for his treachery, while for himself he saw only a long, gray vista of barracks, schools, and more barracks. He gazed imploringly at the chiseled face, which showed not a flicker of recognition; yet even in this extremity, it never crossed his mind to throw himself on the white man’s mercy or to expose the Afghan. Mahbub stared deliberately at the Englishman, who stared just as deliberately at Kim, who sat trembling and tongue-tied.

“My horse is well trained,” the dealer remarked. “Others would have kicked, Sahib.”

“Ah,” the Englishman said at last, rubbing his pony’s damp shoulders with the butt of his whip. “Who’s making the boy a soldier?”

“He says the regiment that found him, and especially the padre of that regiment.”

“There’s the padre!” Kim choked as Father Victor, bareheaded, marched out from the veranda.

“Powers of Darkness below, O’Hara! How many more mixed-up friends do you keep in Asia?” the priest cried as Kim slid down and stood helplessly before him.

“Good morning, padre,” the Englishman said cheerfully. “I know you well enough by reputation. I meant to come over and call sooner. I’m Creighton.”

“Of the Ethnological Survey?” Father Victor asked. The Englishman nodded. “Faith, I’m glad to meet you then; and I owe you thanks for bringing the boy back.”

“No thanks due to me, padre. Besides, the boy wasn’t running away. You don’t know old Mahbub Ali.” The horse dealer sat impassive in the sunlight. “You will once you’ve been stationed here a month. He sells us all our cast-offs. That boy is quite a curiosity. Can you tell me anything about him?”

“Can I tell you?” Father Victor puffed. “You’re the exact man who can help me out of my dilemmas. Tell you! Powers of Darkness, I’m bursting to tell someone who understands natives!”

A groom rounded the corner. Colonel Creighton raised his voice and spoke in Urdu: “Very well, Mahbub Ali, but what is the use of telling me all those stories about the pony? I won’t give a single pice more than three hundred and fifty rupees.”

“The Sahib is a little hot and bothered after his ride,” the horse dealer replied with the grin of a privileged jester. “Presently he will see the points of my horse more clearly. I will wait until he finishes talking with the padre. I’ll wait under that tree.”

“Confound you!” The Colonel laughed. “That’s what happens when you look at one of Mahbub’s horses. He’s a regular old leech, padre. Wait then, if you have so much time to waste, Mahbub. Now I’m at your service, padre. Where is the boy? Ah, he’s gone off to palaver with Mahbub. Odd sort of boy. Might I ask you to have my mare led around under cover?”

He dropped into a chair that commanded a clear view of Kim and Mahbub Ali conferring beneath the tree. The padre went indoors for cheroots.

Creighton overheard Kim say bitterly: “Trust a Brahmin before a snake, a snake before a harlot, and a harlot before a Pathan, Mahbub Ali.”

“That is all as it should be.” The great red beard wagged solemnly. “Children should not look at a carpet on the loom until the pattern is clear. Believe me, Friend of all the World, I am doing you a great service. They will not turn you into a soldier.”

“You crafty old sinner!” Creighton thought. “Still, you aren’t far wrong. That boy mustn’t be wasted if he’s as good as advertised.”

“Excuse me half a minute,” the padre called from inside, “I’m just getting the case documents.”

“If through me the favor of this bold and wise Colonel Sahib comes to you, and you are raised to honor, what thanks will you give Mahbub Ali when you are a man?”

“No, no! I begged you to let me take the road again, where I would have been safe; and you’ve sold me back to the English. What are they paying you for blood money?”

“A spirited young demon!” The Colonel bit his cigar and turned politely to Father Victor.

“What are those letters the fat priest is waving at the Colonel? Stand behind the stallion as if you’re looking at my bridle!” Mahbub Ali instructed.

“A letter from my lama written from Jagadhri Road, saying he will pay three hundred rupees a year for my schooling.”

“Oho! Is old Red Hat of that sort? At which school?”

“God knows. I think in Lucknow.”

“Yes. There’s a big school there for the sons of Englishmen and half-castes. I’ve seen it when selling horses there. So the lama also loved the Friend of all the World?”

“Yes; and he didn’t lie to me or hand me back into captivity.”

“Small wonder the padre doesn’t know how to untangle this thread. How fast he’s talking to the Colonel Sahib!” Mahbub Ali chuckled. “By Allah!”—his sharp eyes swept the veranda for a fraction of a second—“your lama has sent what looks to me like a promissory note. I’ve had a few dealings with hundis. The Colonel Sahib is examining it.”

“What good is all this to me?” Kim said wearily. “You’ll go away, and they’ll send me back to those empty rooms where there’s nowhere decent to sleep and the boys beat me.”

“I don’t think so. Have patience, child. All Pathans aren’t faithless—except when dealing in horseflesh.”

Five, ten, fifteen minutes passed while Father Victor talked energetically or asked questions that the Colonel answered.

“Now I’ve told you everything I know about the boy from start to finish; and it’s a blessed relief. Did you ever hear the like?”

“At any rate, the old man has sent the money. Gobind Sahai’s promissory notes are good from here to China,” the Colonel observed. “The more one learns about natives, the less one can predict what they will or won’t do.”

“That’s reassuring—coming from the head of the Ethnological Survey. But it’s this mix of red bulls, rivers of healing (poor heathen, God help him!), promissory notes, and Masonic certificates. Are you a Mason by any chance?”

“By Jove, I am, now that I think of it. That’s an extra reason,” the Colonel said abstractedly.

“I’m glad you see some reason in it. But as I said, it’s this hodgepodge of things that gets past me. And his prophesying to our Colonel, sitting on my bed with his little shirt ripped open showing his white skin; and the prophecy coming true! They’ll cure all that nonsense at St. Xavier’s, won’t they?”

“Sprinkle him with holy water,” the Colonel laughed.

“On my word, I sometimes think I should. But I’m hoping he’ll be raised a good Catholic. My only worry is what happens if the old beggar man—”

“Lama, lama, my dear sir; and some of them are gentlemen of standing in their own country.”

“The lama, then, fails to pay next year. He’s got a sharp business head to hatch a plan on the spur of the moment, but he’s bound to die someday. And taking a heathen’s money to give a child a Christian education—”

“But he stated explicitly what he wanted. As soon as he realized the boy was white, he seems to have made his arrangements accordingly. I’d give a month’s pay to know how he explained it all at the Tirthankars’ Temple in Benares. Look here, padre, I don’t pretend to understand natives, but if he says he’ll pay, he’ll pay—dead or alive. Meaning his heirs will honor the debt. My advice to you is to send the boy down to Lucknow. If your Anglican chaplain thinks you’ve stolen a march on him—”

“Bad luck to Bennett! He was sent to the Front instead of me. Doughty declared me medically unfit. I’ll excommunicate Doughty if he makes it back alive! Surely Bennett ought to be satisfied with—”

“Glory, leaving you the religion. Quite so! As a matter of fact, I don’t think Bennett will mind. Pin the blame on me. I—er—strongly recommend sending the boy to St. Xavier’s. He can travel down on a pass as a soldier’s orphan, so the rail fare is covered. You can buy him an outfit using the regimental subscription fund. The lodge will be spared the cost of his education, which will keep the lodge in a good humor. It’s perfectly straightforward. I have to go down to Lucknow next week anyway. I’ll look after the boy on the journey—place him in the care of my servants, and so forth.”

“You’re a good man.”

“Not in the least. Don’t make that mistake. The lama has sent us money for a specific purpose. We can hardly return it. We have no choice but to follow his instructions. Well, that’s settled, isn’t it? Shall we say that on Tuesday next you’ll hand him over to me at the night train south? That’s only three days away. He can’t cause too much trouble in three days.”

“It’s a weight off my mind, but—what about this thing here?”—he waved the promissory note—“I don’t know Gobind Sahai, or his bank, which might just be a hole in the wall.”

“You’ve clearly never been a subaltern in debt. I’ll cash it for you if you like and forward the vouchers properly.”

“But with all your own work on top of that! It’s asking—”

“It’s no trouble at all, truly. You see, as an ethnologist, I find the whole thing fascinating. I’d like to make a note of it for some government work I’m doing. The transformation of a regimental badge like your Red Bull into a sort of fetish that the boy follows is quite remarkable.”

“Well, I can’t thank you enough.”

“There is one thing you can do. We ethnologists are as jealous as jackdaws of each other’s discoveries. They’re of no interest to anyone else, of course, but you know how collectors are. Just don’t breathe a word, directly or indirectly, about the Asiatic side of the boy’s background—his adventures, his prophecy, and all that. I’ll worm those details out of the boy myself later, and—you understand?”

“I do. I’ll never say a single word to anyone until I see it in print.”

“Thank you. That goes straight to an ethnologist’s heart. Well, I must get back to breakfast. Good heavens! Old Mahbub is still here?” He raised his voice, and the horse dealer stepped out from the tree’s shadow. “Well, what is it?”

“Regarding that young horse,” Mahbub said, “I maintain that when a colt is born to be a polo pony, following the ball instinctively without training—when such a colt understands the game by sheer intuition—then it is a terrible wrong to break that colt to a heavy cart, Sahib!”

“So say I too, Mahbub. The colt will be entered strictly for polo. (These fellows think of nothing in the world but horses, padre.) I’ll see you tomorrow, Mahbub, if you have anything promising for sale.”

The dealer saluted in horseman fashion with a sweep of his offhand. “Be patient a little, Friend of all the World,” he whispered to the distraught Kim. “Your fortune is made. In a short while you are going to Lucknow, and—here is some money to pay the letter writer. I will see you again, I think, many times,” and he cantered off down the road.

“Listen to me,” the Colonel said from the veranda, speaking in the vernacular. “In three days you will travel with me to Lucknow, seeing and hearing new things all the way. Therefore, sit quietly for three days and do not run away. You are going to school in Lucknow.”

“Shall I meet my Holy One there?” Kim whimpered.

“At the very least, Lucknow is closer to Benares than Umballa is. It may be that you will travel under my protection. Mahbub Ali knows this, and he will be angry if you return to the road now. Remember—much has been told me which I do not forget.”

“I will wait,” Kim said, “but the boys will beat me.”

Then the bugles blew for dinner.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
chapters.content:
Unto whose use the pregnant suns are poised With idiot moons and stars retracing stars? Creep thou betweene—thy coming’s all unnoised. Heaven hath her high, as Earth her baser, wars. Heir to these tumults, this affright, that fraye (By Adam’s, fathers’, own, sin bound alway); Peer up, draw out thy horoscope and say Which planet mends thy threadbare fate or mars!

Sir John Christie.

In the afternoon, the red-faced schoolmaster told Kim that he had been “struck off the strength,” which meant nothing to him until he was ordered to go away and play. Then he ran to the bazaar and found the young letter writer to whom he owed for a stamp.

“Now I am paying,” said Kim regally, “and now I need another letter written.”

“Mahbub Ali is in Umballa,” the writer said airily. By virtue of his profession, he served as a clearinghouse for general misinformation.

“This is not for Mahbub, but for a priest. Take your pen and write quickly. To Teshoo Lama, the Holy One from Bhotiyal seeking a River, who is now in the Temple of the Tirthankars at Benares. Take more ink! In three days I am to go down to Lucknow to the school in Lucknow. The name of the school is Xavier. I do not know where that school is, but it is in Lucknow.”

“But I know Lucknow,” the writer interrupted. “I know the school.”

“Tell him where it is, and I’ll give you half an anna.”

The reed pen scratched busily. “He cannot make a mistake.” The man raised his head. “Who is watching us across the street?”

Kim looked up quickly and saw Colonel Creighton in tennis flannels.

“Oh, that’s just some Sahib who knows the fat priest at the barracks. He’s beckoning to me.”

“What are you doing?” the Colonel asked when Kim trotted up.

“I—I’m not running away. I’m sending a letter to my Holy One in Benares.”

“I hadn’t thought of that. Did you mention that I am taking you to Lucknow?”

“No, I didn’t. Read the letter if you have any doubts.”

“Then why did you leave my name out when writing to that Holy One?” The Colonel wore a curious smile. Kim gathered his courage.

“It was once told to me that it is unwise to write the names of strangers involved in any matter, because naming names often brings good plans to confusion.”

“You have been well taught,” the Colonel replied, and Kim flushed. “I left my cheroot case on the padre’s veranda. Bring it to my house this evening.”

“Where is the house?” Kim asked. His sharp wit told him he was being tested in some way, and he kept his guard up.

“Ask anyone in the big bazaar.” The Colonel walked on.

“He forgot his cheroot case,” Kim said upon returning. “I must take it to him this evening. That is the end of my letter, except for three times over: Come to me! Come to me! Come to me! Now I’ll pay for a stamp and mail it.” He stood up to leave, and as an afterthought asked, “Who is that sour-faced Sahib who lost the cheroot case?”

“Oh, he is just Creighton Sahib—a very foolish Sahib who is a Colonel without a regiment.”

“What does he do?”

“God knows. He is always buying horses he can’t ride and asking riddles about the works of God—like plants and stones and people’s customs. The dealers call him the father of fools because he is so easily cheated on a horse. Mahbub Ali says he is madder than most Sahibs.”

“Oh!” said Kim, and left. His upbringing had given him a fair judge of character, and he reasoned that fools are not entrusted with information leading to the mobilization of eight thousand men plus artillery. The Commander-in-Chief of all India did not converse, as Kim had heard him converse, with fools. Nor would Mahbub Ali’s tone have shifted—as it did every time he mentioned the Colonel’s name—if the Colonel were truly a fool. Therefore—and this realization made Kim want to skip—there was a mystery afoot, and Mahbub Ali probably spied for the Colonel much as Kim had spied for Mahbub. And, like the horse dealer, the Colonel evidently respected people who didn’t try to look too clever.

He was glad he hadn’t let slip that he knew where the Colonel lived; and when he got back to the barracks and found that no cheroot case had been left behind at all, he beamed with delight. Here was a man after his own heart—a devious, indirect person playing a hidden game. Well, if the Colonel could play the fool, so could Kim.

He showed no trace of his thoughts during the next three mornings while Father Victor lectured him on an entirely new pantheon of gods and goddesses—notably a goddess named Mary, who, he gathered, was identical to Bibi Miriam in Mahbub Ali’s theology. He betrayed no emotion when Father Victor dragged him from shop to shop afterward to buy his outfit, nor did he complain when envious drummer boys kicked him for going to a fancy school; instead, he awaited the turn of events with a deeply interested soul. Father Victor, good man, took him to the station, settled him in an empty second-class compartment right next to Colonel Creighton’s first-class one, and said goodbye with genuine emotion.

“They’ll make a man of you, O’Hara, at St. Xavier’s—a white man, and, I hope, a good man. They know all about your coming, and the Colonel will see that you aren’t lost or misplaced anywhere along the road. I’ve given you some notion of religious matters—at least I hope so—and you’ll remember, when they ask your religion, that you’re a Catholic. Better say Roman Catholic, though I’m not fond of the word.”

Kim lit a harsh cigarette—he had carefully bought a supply in the bazaar—and lay down to think. This solitary journey was vastly different from that joyous trip down-country in third class with the lama. “Sahibs get very little pleasure out of traveling,” he reflected. “Alas! I move from place to place like a kicked football. It is my fate. No man can escape his fate. But I am supposed to pray to Bibi Miriam, and I am a Sahib.” He looked down at his boots ruefully. “No; I am Kim. This is the great world, and I am only Kim. Who is Kim?” He pondered his own identity—something he had never done before—until his head swam. He was merely one insignificant person amid this roaring torrent of India, heading south toward an unknown fate.

Before long, the Colonel summoned him and talked at length. As far as Kim could gather, he was expected to study diligently and eventually join the Survey of India as a chainman. If he worked very hard and passed the required exams, he would be earning thirty rupees a month by the time he was seventeen, and Colonel Creighton would make sure he found proper employment.

At first, Kim pretended to understand perhaps one word in every three. Then the Colonel, realizing his mistake, switched to fluent, picturesque Urdu, and Kim felt at ease. No man could be a fool who knew the language that intimately, moved with such quiet grace, and possessed eyes so utterly different from the dull, heavy gaze of other Sahibs.

“Yes, and you must learn how to sketch roads, mountains, and rivers—to hold those pictures in your mind until the right time comes to put them down on paper. Perhaps someday, when you are a chainman, I might say to you while we are working together: ‘Go across those hills and see what lies beyond.’ Then someone might warn: ‘There are dangerous people living in those hills who will kill a chainman if he looks like a Sahib.’ What then?”

Kim thought. Would it be safe to follow the Colonel’s lead?

“I would tell the other man what he wanted to hear.”

“But what if I replied: ‘I will give you a hundred rupees for knowledge of what is behind those hills—for a sketch of a river and a bit of news about what the villagers are saying there’?”

“How can I tell? I am only a boy. Wait until I am a man.” Then, seeing the Colonel’s brow darken, he added, “Though I think I could earn the hundred rupees in a few days.”

“By what method?”

Kim shook his head firmly. “If I told you how I’d earn it, someone else might overhear and beat me to it. It’s not wise to sell knowledge for nothing.”

“Take this as a gift, then,” Creighton said, tossing over a coin. Kim’s hand reached out halfway, then stopped.

“No, Sahib, no. I know the price that would be paid for the answer, but I don’t know why the question is asked.”

“Keep it as a gift, then,” said Creighton, tossing it across. “You have a good spirit in you. Don’t let St. Xavier’s grind it out of you. There are many boys there who look down on natives.”

“Their mothers were bazaar women,” Kim said. He knew well enough that there is no hatred quite like that of the half-caste for his native relatives.

“True; but you are a Sahib and an Englishman’s son. Therefore, never allow yourself to despise natives. I’ve known young men just entering government service who pretended not to understand the language or customs of the natives. Their pay was docked for sheer ignorance. There is no sin greater than ignorance. Remember that.”

Several times during the long twenty-four-hour journey south, the Colonel sent for him, always expanding upon this theme.

“We’re all pulling on the same towrope, then,” Kim said finally. “The Colonel, Mahbub Ali, and me—once I become a chainman. He’ll use me the way Mahbub Ali did, I suppose. That’s fine, as long as it lets me get back on the road. These clothes don’t get any more comfortable with wear.”
