When they arrived at the crowded Lucknow station, there was no sign of the lama. Kim swallowed his disappointment while the Colonel bundled him and his neat belongings into a hired carriage and dispatched him alone to St. Xavier’s.

“I won’t say goodbye, because we will meet again,” the Colonel called out. “Again, and many times, if you prove to have the right spirit. But you haven’t been tested yet.”

“Wasn’t I tested when I brought you”—Kim actually dared use the familiar tum reserved for equals—“the pedigree of that white stallion that night?”

“Much is gained by forgetting, little brother,” the Colonel said with a look that drilled right through Kim’s shoulder blades as he scrambled into the carriage.

It took him nearly five minutes to recover. Then he sniffed the new air appreciatively. “A wealthy city,” he murmured. “Richer than Lahore. How wonderful the bazaars must be! Coachman, drive me through the bazaars for a bit.”

“My orders are to take you straight to the school.” The driver used the disrespectful “thou” form usually reserved for natives. In the clearest and most fluent vernacular, Kim corrected his grammar, climbed up onto the box seat, and—once perfect mutual understanding was established—spent a couple of hours driving up and down, observing, comparing, and enjoying. There is no city—except Bombay, the queen of them all—more dazzling in her gaudy style than Lucknow, whether viewed from the river bridge or from the top of the Imambara looking down upon the gilded umbrellas of the Chutter Munzil and the lush trees cradling the town. Kings have adorned her with fantastic architecture, endowed her with charities, crammed her with pensioners, and soaked her in blood. She is the very capital of idleness, intrigue, and luxury, sharing with Delhi the claim to speak the only pure Urdu.

“A fine city—a beautiful city.” The driver, a Lucknow native, was pleased by the compliment and told Kim many astonishing tales where an English guide would merely have chattered about the Mutiny.

“Now we’ll go to the school,” Kim said at last. The ancient campus of St. Xavier’s in Partibus—block upon block of low white buildings—stands in vast grounds facing the Gomti River, some distance from the city proper.

“What kind of folk are inside?” Kim asked.

“Young Sahibs—all little devils. But to tell the truth, and I drive plenty of them back and forth from the station, I’ve never seen one who had the makings of a more complete devil than you—this young Sahib I’m driving right now.”

Naturally—since he had never been taught to consider such things improper—Kim had exchanged pleasantries with a few frivolous ladies sitting at upper windows in a certain street, and naturally, in that exchange of banter, he had acquitted himself well. He was just about to acknowledge the driver’s parting insolence when his eye—the light was fading—caught sight of a figure sitting against one of the white plaster gate pillars along the sweeping wall.

“Stop!” he cried. “Wait here. I’m not going into the school just yet.”

“And who’s going to pay me for all this running around?” the driver grumbled petulantly. “Is the boy mad? Last time it was a dancing girl. This time it’s a priest.”

Kim leaped headlong from the carriage, patting the dusty feet tucked beneath the dirty yellow robe.

“I have waited here a day and a half,” the lama’s level voice began. “No, I had a companion with me. The friend who helped me at the Tirthankars’ Temple provided a guide for the journey. I came from Benares on the train when your letter reached me. Yes, I am well fed. I need nothing.”

“But why didn’t you stay with the Kulu woman, O Holy One? How did you manage to get to Benares? My heart has been heavy since we parted.”

“The woman wore me out with her endless chatter and her demands for charms to protect children. I parted company with her, allowing her to gain merit through gifts. She is at least a woman of generous hands, and I made a promise to return to her house if need ever arose. Then, finding myself alone in this vast and terrible world, I thought of the train to Benares, knowing someone lived in the Tirthankars’ Temple there who was a Seeker, just like me.”

“Ah! Your River,” Kim said. “I had forgotten the River.”

“So soon, my disciple? I have never forgotten it. But after I left you, it seemed best to go to the Temple and seek counsel; for, you see, India is very large, and it is possible that wise men before us—some two or three—have left a record of where our River lies. There is debate on this matter in the Tirthankars’ Temple; some say one thing, some another. They are courteous folk.”

“Very well; but what are you doing here now?”

“I am gaining merit by helping you, my disciple, toward wisdom. The priest of those men who serve the Red Bull wrote to me that everything would be arranged as I desired for you. I sent funds to cover one full year, and then I came, as you see me now, to watch you enter the Gates of Learning. I have waited a day and a half—not out of any affection for you, for that has no place on the Way, but because, as they explained at the Tirthankars’ Temple, since money had been paid for your education, it was proper for me to oversee the end of the matter. They resolved my doubts quite clearly. I feared at first that I came because I wished to see you—misled by the Red Mist of affection. It is not so... Besides, I am troubled by a dream.”

“But surely, Holy One, you haven’t forgotten the Road and all that happened along it? Surely you came at least a little bit to see me?”

“The horses are cold, and it’s past their feeding time,” the driver whined.

“Go to hell and stay there with your disreputable aunt!” Kim snarled over his shoulder. “I am all alone in this place; I don’t know where I’m going or what will happen to me. My heart was in that letter I sent you. Except for Mahbub Ali, and he’s a Pathan, I have no friend in the world except you, Holy One. Don’t just walk away.”

“I have considered that as well,” the lama replied with a shaking voice. “It is clear that from time to time I shall gain merit—if I have not found my River before then—by assuring myself that your feet are set firmly on the path of wisdom. What they will teach you I cannot say, but the priest wrote that no son of an Englishman in all India will be better taught than you. Therefore, from time to time I will return. Perhaps you will grow up to be a Sahib like the one who gave me these spectacles”—the lama wiped them meticulously—“in the Wonder House at Lahore. That is my hope, for he was a Fountain of Wisdom—wiser than many abbots... Then again, perhaps you will forget me and our meetings.”

“If I eat your bread,” Kim cried passionately, “how could I ever forget you?”

“No—no.” He gently pushed the boy away. “I must return to Benares. Now that I understand the ways of letter writers in this land, I will send you a letter from time to time, and from time to time I will come to see you.”

“But where shall I send my letters?” wailed Kim, clutching at the robe, completely forgetting he was an Englishman now.

“To the Tirthankars’ Temple in Benares. That is the home I have chosen until I find my River. Do not weep; for look you, all Desire is Illusion and binds us tighter to the Wheel. Go up to the Gates of Learning. Let me watch you enter... Do you love me? Then go, or my heart will break... I will return. Assuredly I will return.”

The lama watched the carriage rumble into the compound and then strode away, sniffing between every long stride.

The “Gates of Learning” swung shut with a clang.

A boy born and raised in the country has manners and customs all his own, entirely unlike those of any other place, and his teachers reach him through methods an English schoolmaster would never grasp. Therefore, you would hardly be interested in Kim’s experiences as a St. Xavier’s boy among two or three hundred precocious youths, most of whom had never even seen the ocean. He suffered the usual punishments for sneaking out of town when there was a cholera outbreak—which happened before he had learned to write decent English, forcing him to rely once more on a bazaar letter writer. He was formally reprimanded, naturally, for smoking and for using curses far more colorful than St. Xavier’s had ever heard. He learned to scrub himself with the Levitical scrupulosity of the native-born, who in his heart considers Englishmen rather dirty. He played the standard pranks on the exhausted coolies pulling the punkah fans in the dormitories where the boys argued through the sweltering nights until dawn, quietly sizing himself up against his self-reliant peers.

They were the sons of subordinate officials in the railway, telegraph, and canal services; of warrant officers, sometimes retired and sometimes serving as commanders-in-chief for a feudatory prince’s army; of Indian Marine captains, government pensioners, planters, presidency shopkeepers, and missionaries. A few were scions of old Eurasian families that had put down deep roots in Dhurrumtollah—Pereiras, De Souzas, and D’Silvas. Their parents could easily have afforded to educate them in England, but they loved the school that had shaped their own youth, and sallow generation followed sallow generation through St. Xavier’s. Their homes ranged from Howrah among the railway folk to abandoned military stations like Monghyr and Chunar; remote tea gardens up toward Shillong; villages where their fathers were large landowners in Oudh or the Deccan; mission stations a week away from the nearest rail line; southern seaports facing the booming Indian surf; and cinchona plantations even further south. The mere casual stories of their journeys to and from school—adventures they regarded as entirely ordinary—would have made a Western boy’s hair stand on end. They were accustomed to setting off alone across a hundred miles of jungle, where a delay caused by tigers was simply an anticipated inconvenience; yet they would no more have swum in the English Channel in August than their overseas cousins would have lain still while a leopard sniffed at their palanquin. There were fifteen-year-olds who had spent a day and a night stranded on an islet in the middle of a flooded river, taking charge as a matter of course of a camp of panicked pilgrims returning from a shrine. There were seniors who had commandeered a passing Rajah’s elephant in the name of St. Francis Xavier when the monsoon washed out the dirt road to their father’s estate, nearly losing the massive beast in a quicksand. There was one boy who claimed—and nobody doubted it—that he had helped his father beat off a raid of Akas from the veranda with rifles back when those headhunters still dared attack isolated plantations.

Every story was told in the even, uninflected voice of the native-born, sprinkled with quaint reflections unconsciously borrowed from native foster mothers and turns of phrase that revealed they had been translated straight from the vernacular on the spot. Kim watched, listened, and approved. This wasn’t the insipid, monosyllabic chatter of drummer boys. It dealt with a life he knew and partly understood. The atmosphere suited him, and he thrived inch by inch. They dressed him in a white drill suit as the weather warmed, and he reveled in the physical comfort just as he enjoyed sharpening his mind against their academic tasks. His quickness would have delighted an English schoolmaster, but at St. Xavier’s they well knew the initial burst of brilliance shown by minds quickened by sun and climate, just as they knew the sudden exhaustion that sets in around twenty-two or twenty-three.

Even so, he remembered to keep a modest profile. When tall tales were swapped on sweltering nights, Kim didn’t try to dominate the room with his own exploits; St. Xavier’s looked down on boys who “went native altogether.” One must never forget one’s status as an Englishman, and that someday, once exams were passed, one would command natives. Kim made a mental note of this, as he began to grasp where those examinations ultimately led.

Then came the long recess from August to October—the extended holiday forced by the heat and the monsoon rains. Kim was informed he would travel north to some hill station behind Umballa, where Father Victor would look after him.

“A barrack school?” asked Kim, who had asked many questions and thought about even more.

“Yes, I suppose so,” the master replied. “It won’t do you any harm, and it keeps you out of mischief. You can travel up as far as Delhi with young De Castro.”

Kim weighed the options carefully. He had worked hard, exactly as the Colonel advised. A boy’s holiday was his own property—his schoolmates had made that abundantly clear—and a barrack school would be pure torture after St. Xavier’s. Moreover—and this was magic beyond price—he could write. In three months he had learned how men could communicate across distances without a third party, for the mere cost of half an anna and a bit of literacy. Not a word had arrived from the lama, but the Road was still there. Kim’s soul yearred for the feel of soft mud squishing between his toes, while his mouth watered for mutton stewed with butter and cabbage, rice spiced with fragrant cardamom, saffron-tinted rice with garlic and onions, and the rich, greasy sweets of the bazaars banned at school. At the barrack school they would feed him raw beef off a platter, and he’d have to sneak his smokes. But then again, he was an Englishman and a St. Xavier’s boy, and that scoundrel Mahbub Ali... No, he wouldn’t test Mahbub’s hospitality—and yet... He turned it over in his mind alone in the dormitory and concluded he had been unfair to Mahbub.

The school was nearly deserted; most of the masters had left. Colonel Creighton’s railway pass rested in his pocket, and Kim congratulated himself on not having squandered Creighton’s or Mahbub’s money on high living. He still commanded two rupees and seven annas. His new bullock trunk, stenciled “K. O’H.”, and his bedding roll sat in the empty dormitory.

“Sahibs are always chained to their luggage,” Kim muttered, nodding at them. “You can stay right here.” He stepped out into the warm rain with a wicked smile and sought out a particular house whose location he had noted down some time before...

“Hey! Do you even know what kind of women live in this quarter? Oh, the shame of it!”

“Was I born yesterday?” Kim squatted native-fashion on the cushions of that upstairs room. “Just a little dye and three yards of cloth to pull off a joke. Is that too much to ask?”

“Who is she? You’re awfully young, for a Sahib, to be getting into this kind of mischief.”

“Oh, her? She’s the daughter of a regiment’s schoolmaster in the cantonments. He’s beaten me twice already for sneaking over their wall in these clothes. Now I want to go disguised as a gardener’s boy. Old men are fiercely jealous.”

“That’s the truth. Hold your face still while I dab this juice on.”

“Not too dark, Naikan. I don’t want to look like a black man to her.”

“Oh, love ignores such things. And how old is she?”

“Twelve, I think,” said the shameless Kim. “Spread some on my chest, too. Her father might rip my clothes off, and if I’m piebald—” he laughed.

The girl worked briskly, dabbing a rag into a saucer of brown dye that lasted longer than ordinary walnut juice.

“Now send out and get me a cloth for a turban. Woe is me, my head is completely unshaved! And he’s sure to knock my turban off.”

“I’m no barber, but I’ll make do. You were born to be a heartbreaker! All this disguise for a single evening? Remember, this stuff doesn’t wash out.” She shook with laughter until her bracelets and anklets chimed. “And who is going to pay me for this? Even Huneefa couldn’t have given you better work.”

“Trust in the gods, my sister,” Kim said solemnly, twisting his face as the stain dried. “Besides, have you ever helped paint a Sahib like this before?”

“Never, truly. But a joke isn’t money.”

“It’s worth much more.”

“Child, you are beyond all question the most shameless son of Satan I’ve ever met—wasting a poor girl’s time with this nonsense and then saying, ‘Isn’t the joke enough?’ You’ll go far in this world.” She gave him the mocking salute of a dancing girl.

“All the same, hurry up and rough-cut my hair.” Kim shifted restlessly from foot to foot, his eyes sparkling with mischief as he anticipated the grand days ahead. He tossed the girl four annas and scampered down the stairs transformed into a low-caste Hindu boy—flawless in every detail. His next stop was a cookshop, where he feasted on extravagant and greasy luxuries.

At the Lucknow station platform, he watched young De Castro, sweltering in prickly heat, board a second-class compartment. Kim patronized third class and became the life and soul of the carriage. He informed his fellow passengers that he was an assistant to a conjuror who had abandoned him behind sick with fever, and that he planned to rejoin his master in Umballa. As the occupants of the carriage shifted at various stops, he adapted the story or embellished it with the blossoms of a budding imagination, all the more rampant for having been starved of native speech for so long. On that particular night, there was no happier human being in all of India than Kim.

At Umballa he got off and headed east, splashing across the sodden fields to the village where the old soldier lived.

Around this time, Colonel Creighton in Simla received a telegram from Lucknow stating that young O’Hara had vanished. Mahbub Ali was in town selling horses, and the Colonel confided the news to him one morning while cantering around the Annandale racecourse.

“Oh, that’s nothing,” the horse dealer said. “Men are like horses. At certain times they need salt, and if that salt isn’t in the mangers, they’ll lick it straight off the ground. He’s gone back to the road for a bit. The school bored him. I knew it would. Next time, I’ll take him out on the road myself. Don’t be troubled, Creighton Sahib. It’s simply like a polo pony breaking loose to learn the game on its own.”

“Then you don’t think he’s dead?”

“Fever might get him, I suppose. Otherwise, I don’t worry for the boy. A monkey doesn’t fall out of trees.”

The next morning, on the same track, Mahbub’s stallion pulled alongside the Colonel’s mount.

“It is as I suspected,” said the horse dealer. “He has passed through Umballa at least, and left a letter for me there, having learned in the bazaar that I was here.”

“Read it,” the Colonel said with a sigh of relief. It was absurd for a man in his position to care so much about a stray country-bred vagabond, but the Colonel kept recalling their train conversation and had caught himself thinking about the queer, silent, self-assured boy repeatedly over the past few months. His running away was, of course, the height of insolence, but it also showed resourcefulness and nerve.

Mahbub’s eyes twinkled as he reined his horse out into the center of the cramped little plain where no one could approach unseen.

“‘The Friend of the Stars, who is the Friend of all the World—’”

“What is this?”

“A nickname we have for him in Lahore city. ‘The Friend of all the World takes leave to go his own way. He will return on the appointed day. Let his trunk and bedding roll be sent for; and if a fault has been committed, may the Hand of Friendship turn aside the Whip of Calamity.’ There is a little more, but—”

“Never mind, read the rest.”

“‘Certain things remain unknown to those who eat with forks. It is wiser to eat with both hands for a while. Speak softly to those who do not understand this, so that the return may be auspicious.’ Now, the phrasing of that is clearly the work of a bazaar letter writer, but look how cleverly the boy arranged it so no hint is dropped except to those who know!”

“Is this the Hand of Friendship averting the Whip of Calamity?” the Colonel laughed.

“See how smart the boy is. He wanted to return to the Road, as I said. Since he doesn’t know your trade yet—”

“I’m not entirely sure of that,” the Colonel muttered.

“He turns to me to make peace with you. Isn’t he clever? He says he’ll come back. He’s just sharpening his skills. Think of it, Sahib! He spent three months at that school. But he isn’t broken to the bit yet. For my part, I’m glad. The pony is learning the game.”

“Yes, but next time he must not go off alone.”

“Why not? He went alone before he came under the Colonel Sahib’s protection. When he enters the Great Game, he must travel alone—alone, risking his very neck. If he so much as spits, sneezes, or sits differently from the people he is watching, he could be killed. Why hold him back now? Remember the Persian saying: The jackal of the Mazanderan wilds can only be caught by the hounds of Mazanderan.”

“True. That’s true, Mahbub Ali. And if he comes to no harm, I want nothing better. Still, it’s a tremendous piece of insolence on his part.”

“He didn’t even tell me where he was heading,” Mahbub remarked. “He’s no fool. When his time is up, he’ll come to me. It’s time the pearl merchant took him in hand. He’s ripening too fast—at least by Sahib standards.”

This prediction came true down to the last detail a month later. Mahbub had traveled down to Umballa to pick up a fresh batch of horses, and Kim met him on the Kalka road at dusk, riding alone, begged an alms of him, was cursed at in return, and answered in English. There was no one within earshot to hear Mahbub’s gasp of astonishment.

“Oho! And where have you been?”

“Up and down—down and up.”

“Come under a tree out of the rain and tell me.”

“I stayed for a while with an old man near Umballa; then with some acquaintances in Umballa itself. With one of them I traveled as far south as Delhi. That is a wondrous city. After that, I drove an oilman’s bullock northward; but hearing of a great festival in Patiala, I went there with a firework maker. It was a magnificent festival” (Kim rubbed his belly). “I saw Rajahs, and elephants with gold and silver trappings; and they set off all the fireworks at once, killing eleven men—my firework maker among them—and I was blown right across a tent but came away unhurt. Then I rode back to the railway with a Sikh horseman, serving as his groom for my bread; and so here I am.”

“Well done!” said Mahbub Ali.

“But what does the Colonel Sahib say? I hope I won’t get beaten.”

“The Hand of Friendship has turned aside the Whip of Calamity; but next time you hit the Road, you go with me. This was much too soon.”

“Late enough for me. I’ve learned to read and write a little English at the school. I’ll soon be a full Sahib.”

“Just listen to him!” Mahbub laughed, watching the little drenched figure dancing in the rain. “Salaam, Sahib,” and he saluted mockingly.

“Well, are you sick of the Road, or will you come on to Umballa with me and help drive the horses back?”

“I’m coming with you, Mahbub Ali.”

chapters.title: Chapter 8
chapters.content:
Something I owe to the soil that grew—
More to the life that fed—
But most to Allah Who gave me two
Separate sides to my head.

I would go without shirts or shoes,
Friends, tobacco or bread
Sooner than for an instant lose
Either side of my head.”

“Then in God’s name take blue for red,” said Mahbub, referring to the Hindu color of Kim’s disreputable turban.

Kim countered with the old proverb, “I will change my faith and my bedding, but thou must pay for it.”

The dealer laughed until he nearly fell from his horse. At a shop on the edge of the city the change was made, and Kim stood up—outwardly, at least—as a Mohammedan.

Mahbub rented a room right across from the railway station, and sent for a finely cooked meal complete with almond-curd sweets (which we call balushai) and finely chopped Lucknow tobacco.

“This is better than some of the food I ate with the Sikh,” said Kim, grinning as he squatted, “and certainly they provide no such victuals at my madrissah.”

“I have a desire to hear about that same madrissah.” Mahbub stuffed himself with large mouthfuls of spiced mutton fried in fat with cabbage and golden-brown onions. “But tell me first, completely and truthfully, how you managed to escape. For, O Friend of all the World,”—he loosened his creaking belt—“I don’t think it happens very often that a Sahib and the son of a Sahib runs away from a place like that.”

“How could they? They don’t know the country. It was nothing,” said Kim, and began his story. When he reached the part about his disguise and his conversation with the girl in the bazaar, Mahbub Ali lost all his seriousness. He laughed out loud and slapped his thigh.

“Shabash! Shabash! Well done, little one! What will the dealer in turquoises say to this? Now, slowly, let us hear what happened afterward—step by step, leaving nothing out.”

Step by step, then, Kim told his adventures, pausing between coughs as the strong tobacco hit his lungs.

“I said,” muttered Mahbub Ali to himself, “I said it was just the pony breaking out to play polo. The fruit is already ripe—except that he still needs to learn distances, pacings, rods, and compasses. Listen now. I deflected the Colonel’s whip from your skin, and that is no small favor.”

“True.” Kim puffed serenely. “That is true.”

“But you must not think that running in and out like this is a good thing.”

“It was my holiday, Hajji. I was a slave for many weeks. Why shouldn't I run away when school was closed? Besides, look how I—living off my friends or working for my bread, as I did with the Sikh—saved Colonel Sahib a great deal of money.”

Mahbub’s lips twitched beneath his neatly trimmed Mohammedan mustache.

“What are a few rupees,”—the Pathan waved an open hand carelessly—“to Colonel Sahib? He spends money for a purpose, not out of any love for you.”

“That,” said Kim slowly, “I knew a very long time ago.”

“Who told you?”

“Colonel Sahib himself. Not in those exact words, but plainly enough for anyone who isn’t completely thick-headed. Yes, he told me on the te-rain when we went down to Lucknow.”

“Very well. Then I will tell you more, Friend of all the World, even though telling it puts my head at risk.”

“It was already forfeit to me,” said Kim with great relish, “in Umballa, when you picked me up on your horse after the drummer-boy beat me.”

“Speak a little more plainly. Everyone in the world may lie except you and me. Your life is just as forfeit to me if I choose to raise my finger right here.”

“I know that too,” said Kim, adjusting the burning charcoal on his pipe. “It is a very strong bond between us. In fact, your hold on me is surer than mine on you; for who would miss a boy beaten to death, or perhaps thrown into a well by the roadside? On the other hand, most people here, in Simla, and across the passes behind the Hills would ask, ‘What has happened to Mahbub Ali?’ if he were found dead among his horses. And Colonel Sahib would certainly make inquiries. But again,”—Kim’s face puckered with cunning,—“he wouldn’t inquire for too long, for fear people would ask, ‘What does this Colonel Sahib have to do with that horse-dealer?’ But as for me—if I lived—”

“As you certainly would die—”

“Perhaps; but I say if I lived, I and I alone would know that someone had come by night, like a common thief, to Mahbub Ali’s compartment in the serai, and had slain him there, either before or after searching his saddlebags and between the soles of his slippers. Is that news to tell the Colonel, or would he ask me—(I haven’t forgotten when he sent me back for a cigar-case he hadn’t left behind)—‘What is Mahbub Ali to me?’?”

A thick puff of smoke rose into the air. There was a long pause, and then Mahbub Ali spoke in admiration: “And with all these thoughts in your mind, do you lie down and rise again among all the little Sahib sons at the madrissah and quietly take instruction from your teachers?”

“It is an order,” said Kim smoothly. “Who am I to dispute an order?”

“You are a thoroughly finished Son of Eblis,” said Mahbub Ali. “But what is this story about a thief and a search?”

“What I saw,” said Kim, “the night my lama and I stayed right next to your place in the Kashmir Serai. The door was left unlocked, which I don’t think is your custom, Mahbub. He came in as someone who was sure you wouldn't return anytime soon. My eye was pressed against a knot-hole in the plank. He was searching for something—not a rug, not stirrups, not a bridle, or brass pots—something small and very carefully hidden. Why else would he poke with an iron rod between the soles of your slippers?”

“Ha!” Mahbub Ali smiled gently. “And seeing all this, what story did you invent for yourself, Well of the Truth?”

“None. I put my hand on my amulet, which always rests against my skin, and remembering the pedigree of a white stallion that I had bitten out of a piece of Mussalmani bread, I went away to Umballa, realizing that a heavy responsibility had been placed on me. At that moment, if I had chosen, your head was forfeit. I only needed to say to that man, ‘I have a paper here about a horse that I cannot read.’ And then?” Kim peered at Mahbub from beneath his eyebrows.

“Then you would have drunk water twice—perhaps three times afterward. I don’t think more than three times,” said Mahbub simply.

“It is true. I thought about that a little, but mostly I thought that I loved you, Mahbub. Therefore I went to Umballa, as you know, but (and this you do not know) I hid in the garden grass to see what Colonel Creighton Sahib would do upon reading the white stallion’s pedigree.”

“And what did he do?”—for Kim had cut off the conversation.

“Do you give news for love, or do you sell it?” Kim asked.

“I sell and I buy.” Mahbub took a four-anna coin from his belt and held it up.

“Eight!” said Kim, instinctively falling into the bargaining habits of the East.

Mahbub laughed and put the coin away. “It’s too easy to do business with you, Friend of all the World. Tell me for love. Our lives are in each other’s hands.”

“Very well. I saw the Jang-i-Lat Sahib [the Commander-in-Chief] come to a big dinner. I saw him in Creighton Sahib’s office. I saw the two of them read the white stallion’s pedigree. I heard the exact orders given to start a great war.”

“Hah!” Mahbub nodded, his deep eyes glowing. “The game was well played. That war is over now, and the disaster was nipped in the bud—thanks to me and you. What did you do afterward?”

“I used the news as a hook to catch food and respect from the villagers where a priest had drugged my lama. But I took the old man’s purse, and the Brahmin found nothing. So he was angry the next morning! Ho! Ho! And I used the news again when I fell into the hands of that white Regiment with their Bull!”

“That was foolish.” Mahbub scowled. “News isn’t meant to be thrown around like cow-dung cakes; it should be used sparingly, like bhang.”

“I think so now too, and besides, it didn't do me any good. But that was a very long time ago,”—he brushed the thought away with a thin brown hand—“and since then, especially during the hot nights under the punkah at the madrissah, I have done a great deal of thinking.”

“May I be permitted to ask where the Heaven-born’s thoughts have led him?” said Mahbub with elaborate sarcasm, stroking his scarlet beard.

“You are permitted,” said Kim, throwing back the exact same tone. “They say in Lucknow that no Sahib must ever tell a native that he has made a mistake.”

Mahbub’s hand shot straight to his chest, for calling a Pathan a “black man” (kala admi) is a mortal insult. Then he remembered and laughed. “Speak, Sahib. Your native hears you.”

“But,” said Kim, “I am not a Sahib, and I admit I made a mistake by cursing you, Mahbub Ali, that day in Umballa when I thought I was betrayed by a Pathan. I wasn't thinking straight; I had just been caught, and I wanted to kill that low-caste drummer-boy. I say now, Hajji, that it was handled well, and I see my path clearly ahead of me toward good service. I will stay in the madrissah until I am ready.”

“Well said. Especially since distances, numbers, and how to use compasses must be learned in that game. Someone is waiting in the Hills above to show you.”

“I will accept their teaching on one condition—that my time is entirely my own when the madrissah is closed. Ask the Colonel for that on my behalf.”

“Why not ask the Colonel yourself in the Sahibs’ language?”

“The Colonel is a servant of the Government. He is sent here and there at a moment's notice and must look out for his own advancement. (See how much I've already learned in Lucknow!) Besides, I have only known the Colonel for three months. I have known Mahbub Ali for six years. So! I will go to the madrissah. I will study at the madrissah. I will act like a Sahib at the madrissah. But when the madrissah closes, I must be free to go among my own people. Otherwise I will die!”

“And who are your people, Friend of all the World?”

“This great and beautiful land,” said Kim, gesturing widely around the small clay-walled room where the oil-lamp in its niche burned dimly through the tobacco smoke. “And besides, I want to see my lama again. And furthermore, I need money.”

“That is everyone’s need,” said Mahbub ruefully. “I will give you eight annas, because money isn't picked up from horses' hooves, and it has to last for many days. As for the rest, I am well pleased, and no more needs to be said. Learn quickly, and in three years, or perhaps less, you will be a help—even to me.”

“Have I been such a hindrance until now?” said Kim with a boyish giggle.

“Don’t talk back,” Mahbub grunted. “You are my new horse-boy. Go and sleep among my men. They are near the north end of the station with the horses.”

“They will beat me all the way to the south end of the station if I go without proof.”

Mahbub reached into his belt, wetted his thumb on a block of Chinese ink, and pressed his thumbprint onto a piece of soft native paper. From Balkh to Bombay, men knew that rough-ridged print with the old scar running diagonally across it.

“That is enough to show my headman. I will come in the morning.”

“Which road?” said Kim.

“The road from the city. There is only one, and then we return to Creighton Sahib. I have saved you a beating.”

“Allah! What is a beating when my head is barely secure on my shoulders?”

Kim slipped quietly out into the night, walked halfway around the house keeping close to the walls, and headed away from the station for a mile or so. Then, making a wide circle, he worked his way back at a leisurely pace, needing time to invent a story in case any of Mahbub’s men asked questions.

They were camped on a piece of wasteland beside the railway. Being natives, they hadn’t unloaded the two freight cars where Mahbub’s animals were stabled alongside a shipment of local horses bought by the Bombay tram company. The headman, a run-down, consumptive-looking Mohammedan, immediately challenged Kim, but was pacified at the sight of Mahbub’s seal.

“The Hajji has graciously given me employment,” Kim said irritably. “If you doubt it, wait until he arrives in the morning. In the meantime, give me a place by the fire.”

Then followed the usual pointless chatter that every low-caste native stirs up on every occasion. Eventually it died down, and Kim lay down behind the small group of Mahbub’s followers, almost beneath the wheels of a horse-truck, pulling a borrowed blanket over himself. Now, sleeping among bricks and ballast-gravel on a damp night, surrounded by overcrowded horses and unwashed Baltis, wouldn't appeal to many white boys; but Kim was completely happy. Change of scene, employment, and surroundings were the breath of life to him, and thinking of the neat white cots at St. Xavier’s lined up neatly under the punkah gave him as much joy as reciting his English multiplication tables.

“I am very old,” he thought sleepily. “Every month I grow a year older. I was very young, and a fool besides, when I carried Mahbub’s message to Umballa. Even when I was with that white Regiment I was very young and small and had no wisdom. But now I learn something every day, and in three years the Colonel will take me out of the madrissah and let me hit the Road with Mahbub to hunt for horse pedigrees, or perhaps I will go by myself, or perhaps I will find the lama and go with him. Yes, that is best. To walk again as a chela with my lama when he returns to Benares.”

His thoughts grew slower and more disconnected. He was drifting into a pleasant dreamland when his ears caught a whisper, thin and sharp, cutting through the monotonous murmuring around the fire. It came from behind the iron-sheathed horse truck.

“He isn't here, then?”

“Where else would he be but carousing in the city? Who looks for a rat in a frog-pond? Let’s go. He isn't our man.”

“He must not go back beyond the Passes a second time. That is the order.”

“Hire some woman to drug him. It only costs a few rupees, and there’ll be no evidence.”

“Except the woman. It has to be more certain; and remember the bounty on his head.”

“True, but the police have a long reach, and we are far from the Border. If it were in Peshawar, now!”

“Yes—in Peshawar,” the second voice sneered. “Peshawar, full of his blood-relatives—full of escape routes and women behind whose clothes he can hide. Yes, Peshawar or Hell would suit us equally well.”

“So what is the plan?”

“You fool, haven’t I told you a hundred times? Wait until he lies down, and then one sure shot. The trucks are between us and any pursuit. We just have to run back across the tracks and go our way. They won't see where the shot came from. Wait here at least until dawn. What kind of faquir are you, trembling at a little waiting?”

“Oho!” thought Kim with his eyes tightly shut. “It’s Mahbub again. Clearly, a white stallion’s pedigree is a dangerous thing to peddle to Sahibs! Or perhaps Mahbub has been selling other news. Now what are you going to do, Kim? I don’t know where Mahbub is staying, and if he comes here before dawn, they will shoot him. That won't do you any good, Kim. And this isn't a matter for the police—that wouldn't do Mahbub any good either; and”—he giggled almost aloud—“I don’t remember learning anything at Lucknow that will help me out of this. Allah! Here is Kim, and there are they. First, Kim must wake up and leave so they won't suspect. A bad dream wakes a man up like this—”

He threw the blanket off his face and suddenly sat up, letting out the terrifying, bubbling, meaningless shriek of an Asian startled by a nightmare.

“Urr-urr-urr-urr! Ya-la-la-la-la! Narain! The churel! The churel!”

A churel is the especially malicious ghost of a woman who died in childbirth. She haunts lonely roads, her feet are turned backward at the ankles, and she lures men to their doom.

Kim’s trembling howl grew louder until he finally leaped to his feet and staggered off sleepily, while the camp cursed him for waking them. About twenty yards further up the tracks he lay down again, taking care that the whisperers could hear his grunts and groans as he settled back in. After a few minutes, he rolled toward the road and slipped away into the thick darkness.

He hurried along swiftly until he reached a drainage culvert, dropping down behind it with his chin level with the stone coping. From here he could watch all the night traffic while remaining completely hidden.

Two or three carts passed by, jingling toward the suburbs, followed by a coughing policeman and a couple of hurrying pedestrians singing to ward off evil spirits. Then came the sound of a horse’s iron-shod hooves.

“Ah! This sounds more like Mahbub,” thought Kim as the animal shied at the small head visible above the culvert.

“Ho, Mahbub Ali,” he whispered, “watch out!”

The horse was pulled back almost onto its haunches and forced toward the culvert.

“Never again,” said Mahbub, “will I ride a shod horse for night work. They pick up every bone and nail in the city.” He bent down to lift its front hoof, which brought his head within a foot of Kim’s.

“Down—keep down,” he muttered. “The night is full of eyes.”

“Two men are waiting for you behind the horse trucks. They plan to shoot you when you lie down because there is a bounty on your head. I heard them while sleeping near the horses.”

“Did you see them? ... Stand still, spawn of the devil!” This last was said furiously to the horse.

“No.”

“Was one dressed perhaps like a faquir?”

“One said to the other, ‘What kind of faquir are you, trembling at a little waiting?’”

“Good. Go back to the camp and lie down. I am not going to die tonight.”

Mahbub wheeled his horse around and vanished. Kim scrambled back down the ditch until he reached a point opposite his second resting spot, slipped across the road like a weasel, and wrapped himself back up in the blanket.

“At least Mahbub knows,” he thought contentedly. “And he certainly spoke like a man who expected it. I don’t think those two men will profit much from tonight’s watch.”

An hour passed, and despite his best intentions to stay awake all night, he fell into a deep sleep. Every now and then a night train roared along the tracks within twenty feet of him; but he possessed all the Eastern indifference to mere noise, and it didn't even disturb his dreams.

Mahbub was anything but asleep. He was extremely annoyed that people outside his tribe, unaffected by his casual romances, were hunting him for his life. His first, natural impulse was to cross the tracks further down, circle around, and catch his well-wishers from behind to swiftly slaughter them. But he reflected with sorrow that another branch of the Government, completely unconnected with Colonel Creighton, might demand explanations that would be hard to provide; and he knew that south of the Border people made a ridiculous fuss over a corpse or two. He hadn't been troubled this way since he sent Kim to Umballa with the message, and he had hoped that suspicion had been permanently diverted.

Then a brilliant idea struck him.

“The English are forever telling the truth,” he said, “and therefore we of this country are forever made to look foolish. By Allah, I’ll tell the truth to an Englishman! Of what use are the Government police if a poor Kabuli can have his horses stolen right out of their own railcars? This is as bad as Peshawar! I should lodge a complaint at the station. Better yet, some young Sahib on the Railway! They are eager, and if they catch thieves, it brings them honor.”

He tied up his horse outside the station and strode onto the platform.

“Hello, Mahbub Ali,” said a young Assistant District Traffic Superintendent who was waiting to travel down the line—a tall, tow-haired, horsey young man dressed in dingy white linen. “What are you doing here? Selling tobacco—eh?”

“No; I’m not worried about my horses. I came to look for Lutuf Ullah. I have a carload of them up the line. Could anyone take them out without the Railway knowing?”

“Hardly think so, Mahbub. You can file a claim against us if they do.”

“I saw two men crouching under the wheels of one of the cars for nearly the whole night. Faquirs don’t steal horses, so I didn't give them another thought. I wanted to find Lutuf Ullah, my partner.”

The deuce you did? And you didn't bother your head about it? Upon my word, it’s a lucky thing I ran into you. What did they look like, eh?”

“They were only faquirs. They probably just wanted to steal a little grain from one of the cars. There are many such men up the line. The State will never miss the grain. I came here looking for my partner, Lutuf Ullah.”

“Never mind your partner. Where are your horse cars?”

“A little this side of the farthest place where they make train lights—”

“The signal-box! Yes.”

“And on the track closest to the road on the right-hand side—looking up the line this way. But about Lutuf Ullah—a tall man with a broken nose, and a Persian greyhound. Aie!”

The young man hurried off to wake an enthusiastic young policeman because, as he said, the Railway had suffered heavily from thefts in the goods yard. Mahbub Ali chuckled into his dyed beard.

“They’ll walk in their heavy boots making a racket, and then they'll wonder why there are no faquirs in sight. They are very clever boys—Barton Sahib and Young Sahib.”

He waited idly for a few minutes, expecting to see them rush up the line ready for action. A light engine slipped through the station, and he caught a glimpse of young Barton sitting in the cab.

“I did that boy an injustice. He isn't completely a fool,” said Mahbub Ali. “Using a fire-engine to catch a thief is a new game!”

When Mahbub Ali returned to his camp at dawn, no one thought it worth his while to share any news of the night. No one, that is, except one small horse-boy recently promoted to the great man’s service, whom Mahbub called into his tiny tent to help with some packing.

“I know all about it,” whispered Kim, leaning over the saddlebags. “Two Sahibs came up on a te-train. I was running back and forth in the dark on this side of the cars as the te-train moved slowly up and down. They fell upon two men sitting beneath this car—Hajji, what should I do with this lump of tobacco? Wrap it in paper and put it under the salt bag? Yes—and struck them down. But one man struck at a Sahib with a faquir’s buck-horn” (Kim meant the joined black-buck horns that serve as a faquir’s only earthly weapon)—“and blood was drawn. So the other Sahib, after knocking his own man senseless, struck the stabber with a short gun that had slipped from the first man’s hand. They all fought like madmen.”

Mahbub smiled with heavenly resignation. “No! That isn't dewanee [madness, or a civil case—the word has a double meaning], but nizamut [a criminal case]. A gun, you say? Ten good years in jail.”

“Then they both lay still, but I think they were nearly dead when they were loaded onto the te-train. Their heads were rolling like this. And there is a lot of blood on the tracks. Come and see?”

“I have seen blood before. Prison is the proper place—and they will certainly give false names, and no one will find them for a long time. They were enemies of mine. Your fate and mine seem tied to the same string. What a story for the dealer in pearls! Now, hurry with the saddlebags and the cooking utensils. We’ll take out the horses and head to Simla.”

Quickly—as Orientals understand speed—with long explanations, insults, and windy talk, casually pausing amidst a hundred delays for forgotten items, the messy camp broke up and led half a dozen stiff, irritable horses along the Kalka road in the fresh, rain-swept dawn. Kim, regarded as Mahbub Ali’s favorite by everyone trying to stay on the Pathan’s good side, wasn't asked to do any hard labor. They strolled along at a very easy pace, stopping every few hours at a roadside shelter. Many Sahibs travel along the Kalka road; and, as Mahbub Ali noted, every young Sahib considers himself an expert on horseflesh and, even if he is head over heels in debt to the moneylender, feels obliged to pretend he might buy. That was why Sahib after Sahib, rolling past in a carriage, would stop and start a conversation. Some would even climb out of their vehicles to feel the horses' legs, asking foolish questions or, through pure ignorance of the local language, grossly insulting the imperturbable trader.

“When I first did business with Sahibs—back when Colonel Soady Sahib was Governor of Fort Abazai and flooded the Commissioner’s camping ground just to be spiteful,” Mahbub confided to Kim while the boy filled his pipe under a tree, “I didn't realize how terribly foolish they were, and it used to make me furious. For instance—” and he told Kim a story about an innocent phrase used incorrectly that made Kim double over with laughter. “Now, however,”—he exhaled smoke slowly—“I see it’s the same with them as with all men: in some matters they are wise, and in others completely foolish. It’s very foolish to use the wrong word to a stranger; for even if your heart is free of bad intentions, how is the stranger to know that? He’s more likely to look for the truth with a dagger.”

“True. True words,” said Kim solemnly. “Fools talk about a cat when a woman is giving birth, for instance. I’ve heard them.”

“Therefore, someone in your position needs to remember how to wear two faces. Among Sahibs, never forget you are a Sahib; among the people of Hind, always remember you are—” He paused with a puzzled smile.

“What am I? Muslim, Hindu, Jain, or Buddhist? That is a hard knot to untie.”

“You are undoubtedly an unbeliever, and therefore you will be damned. At least, that’s what my religion says—or I think it does. But you are also my Little Friend of all the World, and I love you. That’s what my heart says. This whole matter of creeds is just like horses. A wise man knows horses are good—that there is a profit to be made from all of them; and for myself—except that I am a good Sunni and hate the men of Tirah—I could believe the same of all the Faiths. Clearly, a Kathiawar mare taken from the sands of her birthplace and brought to western Bengal will fail—nor is even a Balkh stallion (and there are no better horses than those from Balkh, even if they are a bit heavy in the shoulder) of any use in the great northern deserts compared to the snow-camels I have seen. Therefore I say in my heart that the Faiths are like horses. Each has its own merit in its own country.”

“But my lama said something completely different.”

“Oh, he is just an old dreamer of dreams from Bhotiyal. My heart feels a little angry, Friend of all the World, that you see such value in a man so insignificant.”

“It’s true, Hajji; but I do see that value, and my heart is drawn to him.”

“And his to yours, I hear. Hearts are like horses. They pull against the bit or respond to the spur whether you like it or not. Tell Gul Sher Khan over there to hammer the pickets for that bay stallion in more securely. We don’t want a horse-fight at every resting place, and the dun and the black are already acting up... Now listen to me. Is it essential to your happiness to see that lama?”

“It is part of my agreement,” said Kim. “If I don’t see him, and if he is taken away from me, I will walk right out of that madrissah in Lucknow and—once I’m gone, who will ever find me again?”

“It’s true. A colt was never held by a lighter tether than you.” Mahbub nodded his head.

“Don’t worry.” Kim spoke as though he could vanish into thin air at any moment. “My lama said he would come to visit me at the madrissah—”

“A beggar with his bowl in front of those young Sa—”

“Not all of them!” Kim interrupted with a snort. “Their eyes are bruised and their fingernails are stained with low-caste blood, many of them. Sons of sweepers’ wives—brothers-in-law to the garbage collectors.”

We don’t need to follow the rest of the lineage; but Kim made his point clearly and calmly while chewing on a piece of sugar-cane.

“Friend of all the World,” said Mahbub, pushing the pipe across for the boy to clean, “I have met many men, women, and boys, and quite a few Sahibs. I have never in all my days met such a rascal as you.”

“Why? When I always tell you the truth.”

“Perhaps that’s the very reason, for this is a dangerous world for honest men.” Mahbub Ali hauled himself up from the ground, tightened his belt, and walked over to the horses.

“Or sell it?”

There was something in the tone that made Mahbub stop and turn around. “What new devilry?”

“Eight annas, and I’ll tell you,” said Kim, grinning. “It concerns your safety.”

“O Satan!” Mahbub handed over the money.

“Do you remember that little business with the thieves in the dark down there in Umballa?”

“Considering they tried to take my life, I haven't entirely forgotten. Why?”

“Do you remember the Kashmir Serai?”

“I’ll twist your ears in a second, Sahib.”

“No need, Pathan. Only, the second faquir—the one the Sahibs beat senseless—was the very man who came to search your compartment in Lahore. I saw his face when they helped him onto the engine. It was the exact same man.”

“Why didn't you tell me before?”

“Oh, he’s going to prison and will be out of the way for a few years. There’s no need to tell more than is necessary at any given time. Besides, I didn't need money for sweets back then.”

“Allah kerim!” said Mahbub Ali. “Will you sell my head for a few sweets one of these days if the mood strikes you?”

Kim would remember until his dying day that long, lazy journey from Umballa, through Kalka and the nearby Pinjore Gardens, all the way up to Simla. A sudden flood in the Ghaggar River swept away one horse (the most valuable one, naturally) and nearly drowned Kim among the tumbling boulders. Further up the road, the horses were stampeded by a Government elephant, and since they were high-spirited from grazing, it took a day and a half to round them up again. Then they ran into Sikandar Khan coming down the mountain with a few unsalable nags—the leftovers of his string—and Mahbub, who had more horse-trading skill in his little fingernail than Sikandar Khan had in all his tents, insisted on buying two of the worst ones, which meant eight hours of exhausting diplomacy and endless tobacco. But it was all pure delight—the wandering road, climbing, dipping, and winding around the growing mountain spurs; the morning light stretching across the distant snows; the tiered cacti on the stony hillsides; the music of a thousand water channels; the chattering of the monkeys; the solemn deodar trees climbing one after another with drooping branches; the grand view of the Plains spread out far below; the constant honking of tonga horns and the wild rush of the led horses whenever a tonga swung around a curve; the stops for prayer (Mahbub was very religious about ritual washings and chanting when time permitted); the evening gatherings at the halting places where camels and bullocks chewed quietly together and stolid drivers shared the news of the Road—all these things made Kim’s heart sing within him.

“But when the singing and dancing are over,” said Mahbub Ali, “comes the business with Colonel Sahib, and that isn't nearly so sweet.”

“A fair land—a most beautiful land is this Hind—and the land of the Five Rivers is fairer than all,” Kim half-chanted. “I’ll go back there if Mahbub Ali or the Colonel ever raise a hand or foot against me. Once I’m gone, who can find me? Tell me, Hajji, is that the city of Simla over there? Allah, what a city!”

“My father’s brother—and he was an old man when Mackerson Sahib’s well was new at Peshawar—could remember when there were only two houses here.”

He led the horses below the main road into the lower Simla bazaar—the crowded rabbit warren that climbs up from the valley to the Town Hall at a forty-five-degree angle. Anyone who knows their way around there can defy all the police of India’s summer capital, so cleverly do verandas connect with verandas, alleyways with alleyways, and escape routes with escape routes. Here live the people who serve the pleasures of the wealthy city—the jhampanis who pull the pretty ladies’ rickshaws by night and gamble until dawn; grocers, oil-sellers, antique dealers, firewood merchants, priests, pickpockets, and native government clerks. Here, courtesans discuss what are thought to be the deepest secrets of the India Council, and here gather all the sub-agents of half the Native States. Here, too, Mahbub Ali rented a room, much more securely locked than his compartment in Lahore, inside the house of a Mohammedan cattle dealer. It was a place of miracles as well, for a Mohammedan horse-boy went in at twilight, and an hour later a Eurasian lad emerged—the Lucknow girl’s dye was of the highest quality—wearing poorly fitting shop clothes.

“I have spoken with Creighton Sahib,” declared Mahbub Ali, “and for a second time the Hand of Friendship has turned away the Whip of Calamity. He says you have completely wasted sixty days on the Road, and it is therefore too late to send you to any school in the Hills.”

“I told you my holidays are my own. I won't go to school twice over. That is part of our agreement.”

The Colonel Sahib isn't yet aware of that contract. You are to stay at Lurgan Sahib’s house until it’s time to return to Lucknow.”

“I’d rather stay with you, Mahbub.”

“You don’t realize the honor. Lurgan Sahib himself asked for you. You will go up the hill and along the upper road, and once there, you must forget for a while that you ever saw or spoke to me—Mahbub Ali, who sells horses to Creighton Sahib, whom you do not know. Remember this order.”

Kim nodded. “Good,” he said, “and who is Lurgan Sahib? No”—he caught Mahbub’s sword-sharp glance—“truly, I’ve never heard his name. Is he perhaps—” he lowered his voice—“one of us?”

“What kind of talk is this about us, Sahib?” Mahbub Ali replied, using the formal tone he reserved for Europeans. “I am a Pathan; you are a Sahib and the son of a Sahib. Lurgan Sahib has a shop among the European shops. All Simla knows it. Ask there... and, Friend of all the World, he is a man to be obeyed to the very blinking of his eyelashes. People say he does magic, but that shouldn't bother you. Go up the hill and ask. Here begins the Great Game.”

chapters.title: Chapter 9
chapters.content:
S’ doaks was son of Yelth the wise—
Chief of the Raven clan.
Itswoot the Bear had him in care
To make him a medicine-man.

He was quick and quicker to learn—
Bold and bolder to dare:
He danced the dread Kloo-Kwallie Dance
To tickle Itswoot the Bear!

_Oregon Legend._

Kim threw himself wholeheartedly into the next turn of the wheel. He would be a Sahib again for a while. With that in mind, as soon as he reached the broad road below the Simla Town Hall, he looked around for someone to impress. A Hindu boy of about ten years old was sitting under a lamp-post.

“Where is Mr. Lurgan’s house?” Kim demanded.

“I do not understand English,” the boy replied, so Kim switched his language accordingly.

“I will show you.”

Together they set off through the mysterious dusk, filled with the sounds of the city below the hillside and the breath of a cool wind in the deodar-crowned Jakko, which brushed against the stars. The scattered house-lights on every level created a double firmament. Some were stationary, while others belonged to the rickshaws of careless, outspoken English people heading out to dinner.

“It is here,” said Kim’s guide, stopping at a veranda level with the main road. There was no door, only a curtain of beaded reeds that filtered the lamplight from within.

“He has come,” said the boy in a voice little louder than a sigh, and vanished. Kim was certain the boy had been stationed to guide him from the start, but putting on a bold face, he pushed the curtain aside. A black-bearded man wearing a green eyeshade sat at a table. With short, white hands, he picked up drops of light one by one from a tray before him, threaded them onto a gleaming silk string, and hummed softly to himself. Kim sensed that beyond the circle of light, the room was filled with things smelling like every temple in the East. A whiff of musk, a puff of sandalwood, and a breath of sickly jasmine oil struck his open nostrils.

“I am here,” Kim said at last, speaking in the native tongue—the smells made him forget he was supposed to be a Sahib.

“Seventy-nine, eighty, eighty-one,” the man counted to himself, stringing pearl after pearl so fast Kim could barely follow his fingers. He slid the green shade up and stared fixedly at Kim for a full half-minute. The pupils of his eyes dilated and contracted down to pin-pricks, seemingly at will. There was a faquir by the Taksali Gate who had this exact gift and made money from it, especially when cursing foolish women. Kim stared with interest. His disreputable friend could also twitch his ears almost like a goat, and Kim was slightly disappointed that this new man couldn't do that.

“Do not be afraid,” Lurgan Sahib said suddenly.

“Why should I be afraid?”

“You will sleep here tonight, and stay with me until it is time to return to Lucknow. It is an order.”

“It is an order,” Kim repeated. “But where shall I sleep?”

“Here, in this room.” Lurgan Sahib waved his hand toward the darkness behind him.

“Very well,” Kim said calmly. “Now?”

He nodded and held the lamp above his head. As the light swept across the room, Tibetan devil-dance masks leaped out from the walls, hanging above fiend-embroidered draperies from those ghastly ceremonies—horned masks, scowling masks, and masks of idiotic terror. In the corner, a Japanese warrior in armor and plumes threatened him with a halberd, and a score of lances, khandas, and kuttars reflected the unsteady gleam. But what interested Kim more than anything else—he had seen devil-dance masks at the Lahore Museum—was a glimpse of the soft-eyed Hindu boy who had left him at the doorway, sitting cross-legged under the table of pearls with a faint smile on his scarlet lips.

“I think Lurgan Sahib wants to frighten me. And I’m sure that devil’s brat under the table wants to see me frightened.”

“This place,” he said aloud, “is like a Wonder House. Where is my bed?”

Lurgan Sahib pointed to a native quilt in a corner near the horrifying masks, picked up the lamp, and left the room in pitch darkness.

“Was that Lurgan Sahib?” Kim asked as he settled down. There was no answer. However, he could hear the Hindu boy breathing, and guided by the sound, he crawled across the floor, lashed out into the darkness, and called out, “Answer me, you little devil! Is this the way to treat a Sahib?”

From the darkness, he thought he heard the echo of a chuckle. It couldn't have been his soft-fleshed companion, because the boy was quietly weeping. So Kim raised his voice and called out loudly:

“Lurgan Sahib! O Lurgan Sahib! Is it an order that your servant is not allowed to speak to me?”

“It is an order.” The voice came from right behind him, and he jumped.

“Very well. But remember,” he muttered as he crawled back to his quilt, “I’m going to beat you in the morning. I don’t like Hindus.”

It was not a restful night; the room seemed crowded with voices and music. Kim was woken twice by someone calling his name. The second time, he got up to search and ended up bruising his nose against a box that certainly spoke with a human tongue, though with no recognizable human accent. It seemed to end in a tin trumpet and was connected by wires to a smaller box on the floor—at least, that’s what he could tell by touch. The voice, harsh and whirring, poured out of the trumpet. Kim rubbed his nose and grew furious, thinking as usual in Hindi:

“This might work on a beggar from the bazaar, but—I am a Sahib and the son of a Sahib, and what’s twice as important, a student from Lucknow. Yes” (here he switched to English), “a boy from St. Xavier’s. Damn Mr. Lurgan’s eyes! It’s just some kind of sewing-machine machinery. Oh, he has a lot of nerve—we aren’t scared by things like that in Lucknow—No!” Then in Hindi: “But what does he gain by it? He’s only a shopkeeper—and I’m in his shop. But Colonel Creighton is a Colonel—and I think Colonel Creighton gave orders for this to be done. How I’m going to thrash that Hindu boy in the morning! What is this?”

The trumpet-box was now pouring out the most elaborate string of insults Kim had ever heard, delivered in a high, emotionless voice that made the short hairs on the back of his neck stand up. When the vile contraption paused for breath, Kim was reassured by the soft, sewing-machine-like whirr.

“Chûp! (Be quiet),” he yelled, and once more he heard a chuckle that made up his mind. “Chûp—or I’ll break your head.”

The box took no notice. Kim wrenched at the tin trumpet, and something lifted with a click. He had evidently raised a lid. If there was a devil inside, now was its chance, for—he sniffed—it smelled just like the sewing-machines in the bazaar. He would clean that shaitan out. He slipped off his jacket and shoved it straight into the box’s mouth. Something long and round bent under the pressure, there was a whirr, and the voice stopped—as voices naturally must when you jam a folded coat onto the wax cylinder and straight into the works of an expensive phonograph. Kim finished his night’s sleep with a peaceful mind.

In the morning, he woke to find Lurgan Sahib looking down at him.

“Oah!” said Kim, determined to maintain his Sahib status. “There was a box last night that talked nonsense to me. So I stopped it. Was it your box?”

The man held out his hand.

“Shake hands, O’Hara,” he said. “Yes, it was my box. I keep such things because my friends the Rajahs like them. That one is broken, but it was cheap at the price. Yes, my friends the Kings are very fond of toys—and so am I sometimes.”

Kim eyed him cautiously from the corners of his eyes. While he was a Sahib in the sense that he wore European clothes, his Urdu accent and the intonation of his English showed he was anything but a true Sahib. He seemed to understand what was passing through Kim’s mind before the boy even spoke, and he didn't bother offering long explanations the way Father Victor or the Lucknow teachers did. Best of all, he treated Kim as an equal on the Asian level.

“I’m sorry you can’t beat my boy this morning. He says he wants to kill you with a knife or with poison. He’s jealous, so I’ve put him in the corner and won’t speak to him today. He just tried to kill me, too. You must help me with breakfast. He’s almost too jealous to trust right now.”

A proper imported Sahib from England would have made a huge fuss over a story like that. Lurgan Sahib stated it as simply as Mahbub Ali used to report his little affairs in the North.

The back veranda of the shop was built out over the sheer hillside, allowing them to look right down into their neighbors’ chimney-pots, as is the custom in Simla. But even more than the thoroughly Persian meal that Lurgan Sahib cooked with his own hands, the shop itself fascinated Kim. The Lahore Museum was larger, but this place held more wonders—ghost-daggers and prayer-wheels from Tibet; necklaces of turquoise and raw amber; green jade bangles; jars of incense sticks encrusted with raw garnets; the devil-masks from the night before and a wall covered in peacock-blue draperies; gilded figures of Buddha and tiny portable lacquer altars; Russian samovars with turquoises set into their lids; eggshell china tea-sets packed in quaint octagonal cane boxes; yellow ivory crucifixes—from Japan, of all places in the world, as Lurgan Sahib claimed; dusty bales of carpets smelling terribly, pushed behind torn and rotten wooden screens of geometric patterns; Persian water-jugs for washing hands after meals; dull copper incense burners, neither Chinese nor Persian, decorated with friezes of fantastic demons; tarnished silver belts that knotted like raw hide; hairpins made of jade, ivory, and plasma; weapons of all kinds; and a thousand other odd things were cased, piled, or simply tossed into the room, leaving just enough clear space around the rickety deal table where Lurgan Sahib worked.

“Those things are nothing,” said his host, following Kim’s gaze. “I buy them because they are pretty, and sometimes I sell them—if I like the look of the buyer. My real work is on the table—some of it.”

It flashed in the morning light—all red, blue, and green glints, accented here and there by the vicious blue-white sparkle of a diamond. Kim opened his eyes wide.

“Oh, those stones are quite healthy. It won't hurt them to catch the sun. Besides, they’re cheap. But sick stones are completely different.” He piled Kim’s plate again. “There is no one except me who can doctor a sick pearl and restore the blue to turquoises. Opals I’ll grant you—any fool can cure an opal—but for a sick pearl, there is only me. Suppose I were to die! Then there would be no one... Oh no! You can’t do anything with precious stones. It will be quite enough if you understand a little about turquoises—some day.”

He walked over to the end of the veranda to refill the heavy, porous clay water-jar from the filter.

“Do you want a drink?”

Kim nodded. Lurgan Sahib, standing fifteen feet away, placed one hand on the jar. The next instant, the jar was sitting right beside Kim’s elbow, filled to within half an inch of the brim—the white tablecloth showing only a tiny wrinkle where the jar had slid into place.

“Wah!” cried Kim in sheer amazement. “That is magic.” Lurgan Sahib’s smile showed that the compliment had hit its mark.

“Throw it back.”

“It will break.”

“I said, throw it back.”

Kim tossed it carelessly. It fell short and smashed into fifty pieces, the water dripping through the rough wooden boards of the veranda.

“I told you it would break.”

“All the same. Look at it. Look at the largest piece.”

It lay there with a sparkle of water in its curve, gleaming like a star on the floor. Kim stared intently. Lurgan Sahib placed one hand gently on the back of Kim’s neck, stroked it two or three times, and whispered: “Look! It is coming back to life, piece by piece. First, the big piece will join itself to two others on the right and the left—on the right and the left. Look!”

To save his life, Kim couldn't have turned his head. The light touch held him like a vise, and a pleasant tingling sensation ran through his body. There was now one large piece of the jar where there had been three, and above them appeared the shadowy outline of the entire vessel. He could see the veranda through it, but it was growing thicker and darker with every beat of his pulse. Yet the jar—how slowly his thoughts came!—the jar had been smashed right before his eyes. Another wave of prickly warmth raced down his neck as Lurgan Sahib moved his hand.

“Look! It is taking shape,” said Lurgan Sahib.

Up to this point, Kim had been thinking in Hindi, but a tremor seized him, and with an effort like a swimmer fighting off sharks who hurls himself half out of the water, his mind dragged itself up from the darkness trying to swallow it and took refuge in—the English multiplication table!

“Look! It is taking shape,” whispered Lurgan Sahib.

The jar had been smashed—yes, smashed—not the native word, he refused to think in that—but smashed—into fifty pieces, and twice three is six, and thrice three is nine, and four times three is twelve. He clung desperately to the recitation. The shadowy outline of the jar cleared like mist after rubbing one’s eyes. There were the broken shards; there was the spilled water drying in the sun; and through the cracks of the veranda floorboards he could see the white wall of the house below—and thrice twelve is thirty-six!

“Look! Is it taking shape?” asked Lurgan Sahib.

“But it’s smashed—smashed,” he gasped—Lurgan Sahib had been murmuring softly for the last half-minute. Kim violently jerked his head aside. “Look! Dekho! It’s there just like it was.”

“It is there just like it was,” said Lurgan, watching Kim closely as the boy rubbed the back of his neck. “But you are the first of many who has ever seen it that way.” He wiped his broad forehead.

“Was that more magic?” Kim asked suspiciously. The tingling had left his veins; he felt unusually wide awake.

“No, that wasn't magic. It was only to check if there was a flaw in a jewel. Sometimes very fine gems will shatter into pieces if someone holds them in their hand and knows the proper method. That is why one must be extremely careful before setting them. Tell me, did you actually see the shape of the pot?”

“For a little while. It started growing up from the floor like a flower.”

“And then what did you do? I mean, what were you thinking?”

“Oah! I knew it was broken, and so, I suppose, that’s what I kept thinking—and it stayed broken.”

“Hmm! Has anyone ever tried that kind of magic on you before?”

“If they had,” said Kim, “do you think I’d let them do it again? I’d run away.”

“And now you aren't afraid—eh?”

“Not now.”

Lurgan Sahib looked at him more closely than ever. “I’ll ask Mahbub Ali—not now, but some day later,” he muttered. “I am pleased with you—yes; and I am pleased with you—no. You are the first person who ever saved himself. I wish I knew what it was that... But you’re right. You shouldn't tell—not even to me.”

He turned away into the dim gloom of the shop and sat down at the table, rubbing his hands softly together. A small, muffled sob came from behind a stack of carpets. It was the Hindu boy, obediently facing the wall, his thin shoulders shaking with grief.

“Ah! He is jealous, so jealous. I wonder if he’ll try to poison my breakfast again and make me cook it twice.”

“Kubbee—kubbee nahin,” came the broken reply.

“And whether he’ll try to kill this other boy?”

“Kubbee—kubbee nahin.” (Never—never. No!)

“What do you think he will do?” He turned suddenly on Kim.

“Oah! I don’t know. Let him go, perhaps. Why did he want to poison you anyway?”

“Because he is so fond of me. Suppose you were fond of someone, and you saw a newcomer arrive, and the man you cared for seemed more pleased with him than with you—what would you do?”

Kim thought about it. Lurgan repeated the question slowly in the vernacular.

“I wouldn't poison the man,” Kim said thoughtfully, “but I’d beat the boy—if that boy cared about my man. But first, I’d ask the boy if it were true.”

“Ah! He thinks everyone must be devoted to me.”

“Then I think he’s a fool.”

“Do you hear that?” Lurgan Sahib said to the shaking shoulders. “The Sahib’s son thinks you’re a little fool. Come out here, and next time your heart is troubled, don’t try using white arsenic quite so openly. Surely the demon Dasim was running our tablecloth that day! It could have made me sick, child, and then a stranger would have been guarding the jewels. Come!”

The child, heavy-eyed from crying, crept out from behind the carpet bale and threw himself passionately at Lurgan Sahib’s feet with an extravagance of remorse that impressed even Kim.

“I will look into the ink-pools—I will faithfully guard the jewels! Oh, my Father and my Mother, send him away!” He gestured toward Kim with a backward jerk of his bare heel.

“Not yet—not yet. In a little while he will leave again. But now he is at school—at a new madrissah—and you shall be his teacher. Play the Game of the Jewels against him. I will keep score.”

The child dried his tears instantly and dashed to the back of the shop, returning with a copper tray.

“Give them to me!” he told Lurgan Sahib. “Let them come from your hand, so he can’t claim I knew them beforehand.”

“Gently, gently,” the man replied, and from a drawer beneath the table he dealt a handful of clattering trifles onto the tray.

“Now,” said the child, waving an old newspaper. “Look at them as long as you like, stranger. Count them and, if you need to, handle them. One look is enough for me.” He turned his back proudly.

“But what is the game?”

“When you’ve counted and handled them and are sure you remember them all, I’ll cover them with this paper, and you must recite the list to Lurgan Sahib. I will write mine down.”

“Oah!” The competitive instinct flared in Kim’s chest. He bent over the tray. There were only fifteen stones on it. “That’s easy,” he said after a minute. The child slid the paper over the winking jewels and began scribbling in a native account book.

“Under that paper there are five blue stones—one big, one smaller, and three small,” Kim said hurriedly. “There are four green stones, and one with a hole in it; there is one yellow stone that I can see through, and one shaped like a pipe stem. There are two red stones, and—and—I counted fifteen, but I’ve forgotten two. No! Give me time. One was made of ivory, small and brownish; and—and—give me time...”

“One—two—” Lurgan Sahib counted up to ten. Kim shook his head.

“Hear my count!” the child burst out, laughing with delight. “First, two flawed sapphires—one of two ruttees and one of four, as I judge. The four-ruttee sapphire is chipped on the edge. There is one Turkestan turquoise, plain with black veins, and two inscribed ones—one with a Name of God in gold leaf, and the other cracked across because it came from an old ring; I can’t read it. That makes all five blue stones. There are four flawed emeralds, but one is drilled in two places, and one is slightly carved—”

“Their weights?” Lurgan Sahib asked impassively.

“Three, five, five, and four ruttees, as I judge. There is one piece of old greenish pipe amber, and a cut European topaz. There is one Burmese ruby of two ruttees without a flaw, and a flawed balas-ruby of two ruttees. There is a carved ivory from China showing a rat sucking an egg; and finally—ah ha!—a crystal ball the size of a bean set on a leaf of gold.”

He clapped his hands in triumph.

“He is your master,” said Lurgan Sahib, smiling.

“Huh! He knew the names of the stones,” Kim flushed. “Try again! With everyday things that both he and I know.”

They piled the tray high with odds and ends gathered from the shop and even the kitchen, and every single time the child won, leaving Kim amazed.

“Blindfold my eyes—let me feel them just once with my fingers, and even then I’ll leave you behind,” Kim challenged.

Kim stamped his foot with frustration when the boy proved his boast true.

“If it were men—or horses,” he said, “I could do better. Playing with tweezers, knives, and scissors is too small.”

“Learn first—teach later,” said Lurgan Sahib. “Is he your master?”

“Truly. But how is it done?”

“By doing it over and over until it is done perfectly—because it is worth doing.”

The Hindu boy, in high spirits, actually patted Kim on the back.

“Don’t despair,” he said. “I will teach you myself.”

“And I’ll see that you’re well taught,” Lurgan Sahib added, still speaking in the vernacular, “because except for my boy here—though it was foolish of him to buy so much white arsenic when I could have given it to him if he’d asked—except for my boy here, I haven’t met anyone worth teaching in a long time. And you have ten more days before you must go back to Lucknow, where they teach nothing—at great expense. I think we shall be friends.”

They were a completely crazy ten days, but Kim enjoyed himself far too much to reflect on their madness. In the mornings they played the Jewel Game—sometimes with actual gems, sometimes with piles of swords and daggers, and sometimes with photographs of natives. Throughout the afternoons, he and the Hindu boy stood guard in the shop, sitting silently behind a carpet bale or screen to watch Mr. Lurgan’s many and very peculiar visitors. There were minor Rajahs whose escorts coughed out on the veranda, coming to buy curiosities like phonographs and mechanical toys. There were ladies looking for necklaces, and men—or so it seemed to Kim, though his mind may have been corrupted by his early training—looking for the ladies; natives from independent and feudatory states whose official business was the repair of broken necklaces—rivers of light poured out upon the table—but whose real purpose seemed to be raising money for angry Maharanees or young Rajahs. There were Babus with whom Lurgan Sahib spoke with strict authority, yet at the end of each meeting he handed them silver coins and paper currency. Occasionally, groups of long-coated theatrical natives gathered to discuss metaphysics in English and Bengali, to Mr. Lurgan’s great delight—he was always fascinated by religion. At the end of the day, Kim and the Hindu boy—whose name changed at Lurgan’s whim—were expected to give a detailed account of everything they had seen and heard: their reading of each man’s character based on his face, speech, and manner, and their guesses about his true mission. After dinner, Lurgan Sahib’s interests turned toward what might be called dressing up, a game he took very seriously. He could paint faces remarkably well, changing them beyond recognition with a dab of a brush here and a line there.
