The shop was filled with all sorts of clothing and turbans, and Kim was dressed up variously as a well-to-do young Mohammedan, an oil-merchant, and once—which was a most joyful evening—as the son of an Oudh landowner in his absolute Sunday best. Lurgan Sahib had a hawk’s eye for the slightest flaw in a disguise; lying on a worn teakwood couch, he would spend half an hour explaining how a certain caste talked, walked, coughed, spat, or sneezed, and—since the “hows” matter little in this world—the “why” of everything. The Hindu child played this game poorly. His mind, sharp as an icicle when counting jewels, couldn't stretch itself to inhabit another person’s soul; but a demon inside Kim woke up and sang with joy whenever he put on different clothes, matching his speech and gestures to them.

Carried away by enthusiasm, he volunteered to show Lurgan Sahib one evening how the disciples of a certain sect of faquirs—old acquaintances from Lahore—begged for alms by the roadside, and what kind of language they used toward an Englishman, a Punjabi farmer heading to a fair, and an unveiled woman. Lurgan Sahib laughed uproariously and begged Kim to stay just as he was, completely still for half an hour—cross-legged, ash-smeared, and wild-eyed—in the back room. At the end of that time, in walked a bulky, obese Babu whose stockinged legs shook with fat, and Kim immediately hit him with a stream of roadside banter. Lurgan Sahib—much to Kim’s annoyance—watched the Babu instead of the performance.

“I think,” said the Babu heavily, lighting a cigarette, “that it is a most extraordinary and efficient performance. If you hadn’t told me beforehand, I would have sworn that—that—that you were pulling my leg. How soon can he become an approximately efficient chain-man? Because then I’ll requisition him.”

“That is what he has to learn at Lucknow.”

“Then order him to be quick about it. Good-night, Lurgan.” The Babu swung out of the room with the gait of a bogged cow.

When they were reviewing the day’s list of visitors afterward, Lurgan Sahib asked Kim who he thought the man was.

“God knows!” Kim said cheerfully. That tone might have fooled Mahbub Ali, but it completely failed with the healer of sick pearls.

“That’s true. God knows; but I want to know what you think.”

Kim glanced sideways at his companion, whose eyes had a way of compelling the truth.

“I—I think he’ll want me when I come back from school, but”—he added confidentially as Lurgan Sahib nodded in approval—“I don’t understand how he can wear so many costumes and speak so many languages.”

“You’ll understand many things later on. He writes reports and stories for a certain Colonel. His reputation is great only in Simla, and it’s notable that he has no name, but only a number and a letter—that is our custom.”

“And is there a bounty on his head too—like on Mah—all the others?”

“Not yet; but if a boy who is sitting here right now got up and went—look, the door is open!—as far as a certain house with a red-painted veranda behind the old theater in the Lower Bazaar, and whispered through the shutters, ‘Hurree Chunder Mookerjee brought bad news last month,’ that boy could walk away with a belt full of rupees.”

“How many?” Kim asked instantly.

“Five hundred—a thousand—as many as he asked for.”

“Good. And how long would such a boy live after telling that news?” He smiled merrily right into Lurgan Sahib’s beard.

“Ah! That requires some thought. Perhaps if he were very clever, he might survive the day—but not the night. By no means the night.”

“Then why does the Babu work for such low pay if there’s a bounty like that on his head?”

“Eighty—perhaps a hundred—maybe a hundred and fifty rupees; but the pay is the least part of it. From time to time, God creates men—and you are one of them—who have a craving to travel abroad at the risk of their lives to gather news. Today it might be about faraway places, tomorrow about a hidden mountain, and the next day about locals who have done something foolish against the State. Such souls are very rare; and of those few, no more than ten are truly elite. I count the Babu among those ten, which is remarkable. Just think how grand and desirable a business it must be to harden the heart of a Bengali!”

“True. But the days pass slowly for me. I’m still just a boy, and it was only two months ago that I learned to write English. Even now I can’t read it very well. And there are still years and years and long years before I can even become a chain-man.”

“Have patience, Friend of all the World”—Kim started at the title. “I wish I had some of the years that weigh on you so heavily. I have tested you in several small ways. That won’t be forgotten when I make my report to Colonel Sahib.” Then, switching abruptly to English with a deep laugh:

“By Jove! O’Hara, I think there’s a lot of potential in you; but you mustn't become proud, and you mustn't talk. You must go back to Lucknow, be a good little boy, mind your books as the English say, and perhaps, next holidays, if you like, you can come back to me!” Kim’s face fell. “Oh, I mean if you want to. I know where you’d rather go.”

Four days later, a seat was booked for Kim and his small trunk at the back of a Kalka tonga. His traveling companion was the whale-like Babu, who, with a fringed shawl wrapped around his head and his fat, openwork-stockinged left leg tucked beneath him, shivered and grunted in the morning chill.

“How is it that this man is one of us?” Kim thought to himself as they jolted down the road; the reflection put him into a very pleasant daydream. Lurgan Sahib had given him five rupees—a magnificent sum—along with the promise of his protection if he worked hard. Unlike Mahbub, Lurgan Sahib had spoken very explicitly about the rewards of obedience, and Kim was satisfied. If only he could achieve the dignity of a letter and a number like the Babu—and a price on his head! Someday he would be all that and more. Someday he might be almost as great as Mahbub Ali! His hunting grounds would cover half of India; he would track down Kings and Ministers just as he used to follow lawyers’ touts and agents across Lahore city for Mahbub Ali’s sake. In the meantime, there was the immediate, and quite pleasant, reality of St. Xavier’s waiting for him. There would be new boys to lord it over, and holiday adventures to boast about. Young Martin, son of the tea planter at Manipur, had bragged that he was going to war with a rifle against head-hunters.

That might be true, but young Martin certainly hadn't been blown halfway across the courtyard of a Patiala palace by a fireworks explosion, nor had he... Kim began recounting his own adventures from the past three months in his head. He could have stunned St. Xavier’s—even the biggest boys who shaved—with the tale, if it had been allowed. But of course, that was out of the question. A bounty would be placed on his head in good time, as Lurgan Sahib had promised; and if he talked foolishly now, not only would that bounty never happen, but Colonel Creighton would cast him off—leaving him to the mercy of Lurgan Sahib and Mahbub Ali for whatever short span of life remained to him.

“So I shouldn't lose Delhi just for the sake of a fish,” ran his proverbial philosophy. It was his duty to forget his holidays (though he could always invent imaginary adventures) and, as Lurgan Sahib had said, to work. Of all the boys hurrying back to St. Xavier’s—from the sands of Sukkur to the palms of Galle—none was filled with more virtue than Kimball O’Hara as he bounced down toward Umballa behind Hurree Chunder Mookerjee, whose official name in one branch of the Ethnological Survey was R.17.

And if he needed any extra motivation, the Babu provided it. After eating a massive meal at Kalka, he talked nonstop. Was Kim going to school? Then he, an M.A. from Calcutta University, would explain the immense benefits of education. There were marks to be earned by paying proper attention to Latin and Wordsworth’s Excursion (all of which sounded like Greek to Kim). French was also vital, and the best place to pick it up was Chandernagore, a few miles from Calcutta. A man could also go far, as he himself had done, by paying strict attention to plays like King Lear and Julius Caesar, both heavily favored by examiners. Lear wasn't packed with as many historical allusions as Julius Caesar; the book cost four annas, but could be bought secondhand in Bow Bazaar for two. Even more important than Wordsworth or the eminent authors Burke and Hare were the arts and sciences of mensuration. A boy who passed his examinations in those subjects—for which, by the way, there were no cram-books—could, merely by marching across a country with a compass, a level, and a straight eye, bring back a picture of that landscape that could be sold for large sums of silver coin. But since carrying measuring chains around wasn't always practical, a boy would do well to know the exact length of his own pace, so that when he was deprived of what Hurree Chunder called adventitious aids, he could still measure distances accurately. To keep count of thousands of paces, Hurree Chunder had found nothing more useful than a rosary of eighty-one or one hundred and eight beads, because “it is easily divided and subdivided into many multiples.” Through the flood of English words, Kim caught the general drift of the talk, and it interested him deeply. Here was a new skill a man could tuck away inside his head, and looking at the vast world unfolding before him, it seemed the more a man knew, the better off he would be.

When the Babu had talked for an hour and a half, he said, “I hope some day to enjoy your official acquaintance. Ad interim, if I may be pardoned the expression, I shall present you with this betel-box, which is a highly valuable item and cost me two rupees only four years ago.” It was a cheap, heart-shaped brass trinket with three compartments for carrying the eternal betel nut, lime, and pan leaf, but it was filled with tiny sample bottles.

“That is a reward of merit for your performance as that holy man. You see, you’re so young you think you’ll live forever and never need to take care of your body. It’s a great nuisance to fall sick in the middle of business. I am fond of drugs myself, and they come in handy for treating poor people too. These are good departmental medicines—quinine and so on. I give it to you as a souvenir. Now, goodbye. I have urgent private business right here by the roadside.”

He slipped out as silently as a cat onto the Umballa road, hailed a passing cart, and jingled away, while Kim sat speechless, turning the brass betel-box over in his hands.

Records of a boy’s education rarely interest anyone except his parents, and, as you know, Kim was an orphan. The books of St. Xavier’s note that a report of Kim’s progress was sent at the end of each term to Colonel Creighton and Father Victor, who regularly provided the funds for his schooling. The same records show that he displayed a great talent for mathematics and map-making, winning a prize (The Life of Lord Lawrence, tree calf, two volumes, nine rupees, eight annas) for his proficiency; and that same term he played in the St. Xavier’s eleven against Aligarh Mohammedan College at the age of fourteen years and ten months. He was also re-vaccinated (suggesting another smallpox outbreak in Lucknow) around the same time. Pencil notes scribbled in the margin of an old muster roll record that he was punished several times for “conversing with improper persons,” and it seems he was once given a heavy punishment for “absenting himself for a day in the company of a street beggar.” That was the time he scaled the school wall and spent the whole day pleading with the lama along the banks of the Gomti River to let him go on the Road during the next holidays—just for one month, just for a single week—while the lama set his face like flint against it, insisting the time had not yet come. Kim’s duty, the old man told him as they shared cakes together, was to master all the wisdom of the Sahibs, and then they would see. The Hand of Friendship must have successfully averted the Whip of Calamity, because six weeks later Kim apparently passed an examination in elementary surveying “with great credit” at the age of fifteen years and eight months. From that point on, the school record goes silent. His name doesn't appear among the year’s graduates entering the subordinate Survey of India, but next to it are simply the words “removed on appointment.”

Several times during those three years, the lama turned up at the Temple of the Tirthankars in Benares—a little thinner and a shade yellower, if possible, but as gentle and untainted as ever. Sometimes he arrived from the South—from south of Tuticorin, where the wonderful fire-boats sail to Ceylon, home to priests who know Pali; sometimes from the wet green West and the thousands of cotton-mill chimneys surrounding Bombay; and once from the North, having doubled back eight hundred miles just to talk for a day with the Keeper of the Images in the Wonder House. He would stride to his cell in the cool, polished marble—the temple priests were always kind to the old man—wash off the dust of travel, offer his prayers, and set off for Lucknow in a third-class railway carriage, perfectly accustomed to train travel by now. Upon his return, as his friend the Seeker pointed out to the head priest, it was noticeable that he temporarily stopped mourning the loss of his River or drawing wondrous pictures of the Wheel of Life, preferring instead to talk about the beauty and wisdom of a certain mysterious chela whom no one at the temple had ever laid eyes on. Yes, he had followed the traces of the Blessed Feet all across India. (The Curator still preserves a most marvelous record of those wanderings and meditations.) Nothing else mattered in life except finding the River of the Arrow. Yet it had been revealed to him in dreams that the task could not be undertaken with any hope of success unless the seeker was accompanied by the one chela appointed to bring the event to a happy conclusion—someone well-versed in profound wisdom, such as white-haired Keepers of Images possess. For example (here came out the snuff-gourd, and the kindly Jain priests hurried to keep silent):

“Long, long ago, when Devadatta was King of Benares—let all listen to the Jâtaka!—an elephant was captured for a time by the king’s hunters, and before he broke free, a cruel iron ring was clamped around his leg. He tried to tear it off with intense rage and frustration, rushing back and forth through the forest and begging his fellow elephants to wrench it apart. One by one, using their strong trunks, they tried and failed. Finally, they concluded that the ring could not be broken by any brute force. Meanwhile, in a thicket, newly born and wet with the fluids of birth, lay a day-old calf whose mother had died. The shackled elephant, forgetting his own agony, thought: ‘If I do not help this little one, it will be trampled underfoot by the herd.’ So he stood guard over the newborn, using his legs as buttresses against the restless herd; he begged milk for it from a gentle cow, and the calf thrived, with the chained elephant acting as its guide and protector. Now, the lifespan of an elephant—let all listen to the Jâtaka!—reaches its full strength at thirty-five years, and for thirty-five rains the fettered elephant protected the younger one while the iron shackle slowly ate into his flesh.

“Then one day the younger elephant noticed the half-buried iron, and turning to the elder, asked, ‘What is this?’ ‘It is my sorrow,’ replied the one who had befriended him. Then the younger elephant reached out his trunk and, in the twinkling of an eye, shattered the iron ring, saying, ‘The appointed time has come.’ Thus, the virtuous elephant who had waited with patience and done good deeds was freed, at the appointed hour, by the very calf he had paused to cherish—let all listen to the Jâtaka!—for the Elephant was Ananda, and the Calf that broke the ring was none other than The Lord Himself...”

Then he would shake his head benignly, and, fingering his ever-clicking rosary, point out how free that elephant-calf was from the sin of pride. He was as humble as a chela who, seeing his master sitting in the dust outside the Gates of Learning, jumped straight over the gates (even though they were locked) and took his master to his heart in the middle of that proud city. Rich indeed would be the reward of such a master and such a chela when the time came for them to seek freedom together!

Thus the lama spoke, moving quietly across India like a bat in the night. A sharp-tongued old woman living among the fruit trees behind Saharanpur honored him the way a woman honors a prophet, though his quarters were far from being upon the wall. In a room overlooking cooing doves, he would sit while she laid aside her useless veil and chattered about spirits and demons in Kulu, about grandchildren yet unborn, and about the outspoken brat who had spoken to her at the resting place. Once, too, he wandered alone from the Grand Trunk Road below Umballa to the very village whose priest had tried to drug him; but the kindly Heaven that watches over lamas guided him safely at twilight through the crops, lost in thought, straight to the Rissaldar’s door. A serious misunderstanding nearly occurred there when the old soldier asked him why the Friend of the Stars had passed by that way only six days earlier.

“That cannot be,” said the lama. “He has returned to his own people.”

“He sat in that very corner telling a hundred merry tales five nights ago,” his host insisted. “True, he vanished rather suddenly at dawn after talking nonsense with my granddaughter. He’s growing fast, but he’s the same Friend of the Stars who brought me true word about the war. Have you parted company?”

“Yes—and no,” the lama replied. “We—we haven't completely parted, but the time isn't right for us to take the Road together. He is learning wisdom elsewhere. We must wait.”

“As you say—but if it wasn't the boy, how did he come to speak of you so constantly?”

“And what did he say?” the lama asked eagerly.

“Sweet words—a hundred thousand of them—that you are his father and mother and all that. It’s a pity he doesn't join the Queen’s service. He has no fear.”

This news astonished the lama, who didn't yet realize how religiously Kim kept to the agreement made with Mahbub Ali and sanctioned by Colonel Creighton...

“You can’t keep a young pony away from the game,” the horse-dealer remarked when the Colonel pointed out that wandering across India during the holidays was absurd. “If you refuse him permission to come and go as he pleases, he’ll just ignore the refusal. And then who’s going to catch him? Colonel Sahib, once in a thousand years is a horse born as perfectly suited for this game as our colt. And we need men.”

chapters.title: Chapter 10
chapters.content:
Your tiercel’s too long at hack, Sire. He’s no eyass
But a passage-hawk that footed ere we caught him,
Dangerously free o’ the air. Faith! were he mine
(As mine’s the glove he binds to for his tirings)
I’d fly him with a make-hawk. He’s in yarak
Plumed to the very point—so manned, so weathered...
Give him the firmament God made him for,
And what shall take the air of him?—Old Play.

Lurgan Sahib did not speak quite as directly, but his advice matched Mahbub’s, and the outcome was good for Kim. He knew better now than to leave Lucknow in native dress, and whenever Mahbub was within reach of a letter, he headed straight for the Pathan’s camp to make his disguise under the dealer’s watchful eye. If the small Survey paint-box he used for tinting maps during the school term could have spoken about his holiday activities, Kim might have been expelled. Once, Mahbub and Kim traveled all the way to the beautiful city of Bombay with three carloads of tram-horses, and Mahbub nearly melted when Kim suggested sailing in a dhow across the Indian Ocean to buy Gulf Arabs, which he understood—from a hanger-on of the dealer Abdul Rahman—fetched higher prices than ordinary Kabulis.

He dipped his hand into the same dish as that great merchant when Mahbub and a few fellow Muslims were invited to a grand Eid feast. They returned by sea via Karachi, during which Kim experienced his first bout of seasickness while sitting on the forward hatch of a coasting steamer, thoroughly convinced he had been poisoned. The Babu’s famous medicine-box proved useless, even though Kim had restocked it in Bombay. Mahbub had business in Quetta, and there Kim—as Mahbub admitted—earned his keep and a little extra by spending four strange days as a scullion in the house of a fat Commissariat sergeant. During an opportune moment, Kim slipped a vellum ledger from the sergeant’s desk and copied it all through one hot night, lying behind an outhouse by moonlight; it seemed to deal entirely with cattle and camel sales. Then he put the ledger back where he found it and, at Mahbub’s signal, left that job unpaid, rejoining him six miles down the road with the clean copy tucked inside his shirt.

“That soldier is a small fish,” Mahbub Ali explained, “but in time we’ll catch a bigger one. He only sells oxen at two prices—one for himself and one for the Government—which I don’t think is much of a sin.”

“Why couldn’t I just take the little book and be done with it?”

“Then he would have panicked and told his master. And we might have missed a large shipment of new rifles being smuggled up from Quetta to the North. The Game is so vast that one can only see a small piece of it at a time.”

“Oho!” said Kim, and kept his mouth shut. That was during the monsoon holidays, after he had won the mathematics prize. He spent the Christmas holidays—minus ten days for private amusements—with Lurgan Sahib, sitting mostly in front of a roaring wood fire (Jakko Road was four feet deep in snow that year). Since the young Hindu boy had left to get married, Kim helped Lurgan thread pearls. He made Kim memorize entire chapters of the Koran until he could recite them with the exact rhythm and cadence of a mullah. Furthermore, he taught Kim the names and properties of numerous native drugs, along with the incantations needed when administering them. In the evenings, he had Kim write magical charms on parchment—elaborate pentagrams crowned with the names of devils like Murra and Awan, the Companion of Kings, scrawled fantastically in the corners. More practically, he advised Kim on how to take care of his health, treat fever, and use simple roadside remedies. A week before it was time to return to school, Colonel Creighton Sahib—which Kim thought was quite unfair—sent him a written examination paper dealing entirely with rods, chains, links, and angles.

During the next holidays, he was out with Mahbub, and during this trip he nearly died of thirst while plodding through the sand on a camel to the mysterious city of Bikaner, where the wells are four hundred feet deep and entirely lined with camel bones. It wasn’t a very amusing trip from Kim’s perspective because—contrary to their agreement—the Colonel ordered him to map that wild, walled city; and since Mohammedan horse-boys and pipe-tenders aren’t expected to drag survey chains around the capital of an independent Native State, Kim was forced to measure all his distances by counting beads on a rosary. He used his compass for bearings whenever he could—mostly after dark once the camels were fed—and with his little six-cake watercolor paint-box and three brushes, he produced something not entirely unlike the city of Jaisalmer. Mahbub laughed heartily and advised him to write a detailed report as well; so Kim set to work in the back of the large account book tucked under the flap of Mahbub’s favorite saddle.

“It must include everything you have seen, touched, or thought about. Write as though the Commander-in-Chief himself had slipped out with a massive army to start a war.”

“How large an army?”

“Oh, fifty thousand men.”

“Folly! Remember how few and terrible the wells are in the sand. Not even a thousand thirsty men could survive near here.”

“Then write that down—along with every break in the walls, where they cut their firewood, and the mood and loyalty of the King. I’ll stay here until all my horses are sold. I’ll rent a room by the gateway, and you can be my accountant. There’s a good lock on the door.”

That report, written in Kim’s unmistakable St. Xavier’s cursive script along with the brown, yellow, and lake-tinted map, could be found until a few years ago (a careless clerk filed it alongside the rough notes of the Second Seistan Survey), though by now the pencil marks are likely almost illegible. Kim translated it for Mahbub, sweating under the light of an oil lamp, on the second day of their return journey.

The Pathan stood up and reached into his dappled saddlebags.

“I knew it would be worthy of a robe of honor, so I prepared one,” he smiled. “If I were the Amir of Afghanistan—and someday we may see him—I’d fill your mouth with gold.” He laid the garments formally at Kim’s feet. There was a gold-embroidered Peshawar turban-cap rising to a point, and a large turban cloth ending in a broad gold fringe. There was a Delhi-embroidered vest to wear over a milk-white, flowing shirt that buttoned on the right; green pajamas with a twisted silk drawstring; and, so that nothing would be missing, wonderfully fragrant Russian leather slippers with aggressively curled toes.

“To put on new clothes on a Wednesday morning is auspicious,” Mahbub said solemnly. “But we mustn’t forget the wicked people in the world. So!”

He topped off the magnificent outfit—which had left Kim breathless with delight—with a mother-of-pearl, nickel-plated, self-extracting .450 revolver.

“I considered a smaller caliber, but realized this takes Government ammunition. A man can always get his hands on that—especially across the Border. Stand up and let me have a look at you.” He clapped Kim on the shoulder. “May you never grow tired, Pathan! Oh, the hearts you’re going to break! Oh, those eyes glancing sideways from under their eyelashes!”

Kim spun around, pointed his toes, stretched, and automatically felt for the mustache that was just beginning to grow. Then he bowed down toward Mahbub’s feet, making quick, fluttering gestures of respect with his hands, his heart too full for words. Mahbub stopped him and pulled him into an embrace.

“My son,” he said, “what need is there for words between us? But isn’t that little gun a delight? All six cartridges pop out with a single twist. Carry it against your skin in your shirt, which keeps it naturally oiled. Never put it anywhere else, and please God, someday you’ll kill a man with it.”

“Hai mai!” Kim said ruefully. “If a Sahib kills a man, he gets hanged in jail.”

“True: but one step beyond the Border, men are wiser. Put it away, but load it first. What good is an unfed gun?”

“When I go back to the madrissah, I have to return it. They don’t allow small guns there. Will you keep it for me?”

“Son, I’m getting tired of that madrissah, where they waste the best years of a man teaching him things he can only truly learn on the Road. The foolishness of the Sahibs has no beginning or end. No matter. Perhaps your written report will save you from further bondage; and God knows we need men more and more in the Game.”

They marched across the salt desert toward Jodhpur, their jaws clamped shut against the blowing sand, and there Mahbub and his handsome nephew Habib Ullah did a brisk trade. Afterward, dressed uncomfortably in European clothes that he was quickly outgrowing, Kim traveled second-class back to St. Xavier’s. Three weeks later, Colonel Creighton was examining Tibetan ghost-daggers at Lurgan’s shop, standing before Mahbub Ali in open defiance. Lurgan Sahib acted as their reserve support.

“The pony is trained—finished—broken and paced, Sahib! From now on, day by day, he’ll lose his good habits if you keep him tied up with tricks. Drop the reins on his back and let him go,” urged the horse-dealer. “We need him.”

“But he’s so young, Mahbub—not more than sixteen, is he?”

“When I was fifteen, Sahib, I had shot my first man and fathered my first child.”

“You incorrigible old heathen!” Creighton turned to Lurgan. The black-bearded man nodded in agreement with the dyed-red Pathan’s wisdom.

“I should have used him long ago,” Lurgan said. “The younger the better. That’s why I always have my truly valuable jewels watched by a child. You sent him to me to be tested. I tested him every possible way: he’s the only boy I couldn't influence to see things.”

“In the crystal—in the ink-pool?” demanded Mahbub.

“No. Under my own touch, as I told you. That’s never happened before. It means he’s strong enough—though you think it’s nonsense, Colonel Creighton—to make anyone do whatever he wants. And that was three years ago. I’ve taught him a great deal since then, Colonel Creighton. I think you’re wasting him now.”

“Hmm! Maybe you’re right. But as you know, there’s no Survey work for him right at the moment.”

“Let him out—let him go,” Mahbub interrupted. “Who expects any young colt to carry a heavy load right away? Let him run with the caravans—like our white camel colts—for luck. I’d take him myself, but—”

“There is a delicate piece of business where he would be extremely useful—down in the South,” said Lurgan with peculiar smoothness, lowering his heavy, blue-lidded eyes.

“E.23 has that handled,” Creighton replied quickly. “He must not go down there. Besides, he doesn’t know a word of Turki.”

“Just tell him the shape and smell of the letters we need, and he’ll bring them back,” Lurgan insisted.

“No. That’s a man’s job,” said Creighton.

It was a thorny affair involving unauthorized and inflammatory correspondence between a man claiming supreme authority over all matters of the Mohammedan religion worldwide, and a junior member of a royal house who had been disciplined for abducting women within British territory. The Muslim Archbishop had been forceful and overbearing; the young prince was merely sulking over the reduction of his privileges, but there was no reason for him to continue a correspondence that might eventually compromise him. One letter had indeed been recovered, but the agent who found it was later discovered dead by the roadside dressed as an Arab trader, as E.23 duly reported when he took over the assignment.

These facts, alongside a few other unpublishable details, caused both Mahbub and Creighton to shake their heads.

“Let him go out with his Red Lama,” the horse-dealer said with visible effort. “He is fond of the old man. At least he can practice pacing his distances by counting his rosary.”

“I’ve had some dealings with the old man—by letter,” Colonel Creighton said, smiling to himself. “Where is he heading?”

“Up and down the country, just as he’s done these past three years. He’s searching for a River of Healing. God’s curse upon all—” Mahbub caught himself. “He sleeps at the Temple of the Tirthankars or at Buddh Gaya whenever he comes in from the Road. Then he goes to see the boy at the madrissah, as we know, since the boy was punished for it two or three times. He’s completely mad, but a peaceful man. I’ve met him. The Babu has had dealings with him too. We’ve kept an eye on him for three years. Red Lamas aren’t so common in Hind that one loses track of them.”

“Babus are very peculiar,” Lurgan remarked thoughtfully. “Do you know what Hurree Babu actually wants? He wants to be elected a member of the Royal Society by gathering ethnological notes. I tell him—I tell him everything about the lama that Mahbub and the boy have told me. Hurree Babu goes down to Benares—at his own expense, I believe.”

“I don’t think so,” Creighton said briefly. He had paid Hurree’s travel expenses himself out of a sharp curiosity to find out what the lama was really about.

“And he approaches the lama for details on Lamaism, devil dances, spells, and charms several times over these past few years. Holy Virgin! I could have told him all of that years ago. I think Hurree Babu is getting too old for the Road. He prefers collecting information on manners and customs now. Yes, he wants to be an F.R.S.”

“Hurree thinks well of the boy, doesn’t he?”

“Oh, very much so—we’ve spent some pleasant evenings at my place—but I think it would be a waste to throw him away with Hurree on the ethnological side.”

“Not for a first assignment. How does that sound to you, Mahbub? Let the boy run with the lama for six months. After that, we’ll see. He’ll gain experience.”

“He has experience already, Sahib—as a fish controls the water it swims in. But for every reason, it will be good to release him from the school.”

“Very well, then,” Creighton said, half to himself. “He can go with the lama, and if Hurree Babu wants to keep an eye on them, so much the better. He won’t lead the boy into danger the way Mahbub would. It’s curious—that wish of his to be an F.R.S. Very human, too. He really is best suited for the ethnological side, Hurree is.”

No amount of money or promotion could have lured Creighton away from his work on the Indian Survey, but deep in his heart he also harbored the ambition to place the letters “F.R.S.” after his name. He knew certain honors could be gained through cleverness and friends, but he believed only hard work—papers representing a lifetime of research—could earn a man entry into the Society, which he had pelted for years with monographs on strange Asian cults and obscure customs. Nine men out of ten would flee a Royal Society soirée out of sheer boredom; but Creighton was the tenth, and at times his soul yearned for those crowded London rooms where silver-haired, bald gentlemen who knew nothing of the military moved among spectroscopic exhibits, tundra plants, electric flight-measuring machines, and precision instruments for slicing the left eye of a female mosquito into fractions of a millimeter. By all rights, it should have been the Royal Geographical Society that attracted him, but men are as fickle as children when choosing their playthings. So Creighton smiled and thought all the better of Hurree Babu for sharing a similar ambition.

He dropped the ghost-dagger and looked up at Mahbub.

“How soon can we get the colt out of the stable?” the horse-dealer asked, reading his eyes.

“Hmm! If I pull him out by official order now—what do you think he’ll do? I’ve never helped train someone quite like this before.”

“He’ll come straight to me,” Mahbub replied promptly. “Lurgan Sahib and I will prepare him for the Road.”

“So be it then. For six months he can run as he pleases. But who will sponsor him?”

Lurgan tilted his head slightly. “He won’t give anything away, if that’s what you’re worried about, Colonel Creighton.”

“He’s only a boy, after all.”

“Yes; but first, he has nothing to tell; and second, he knows what the consequences would be. Besides, he’s very fond of Mahbub, and somewhat fond of me.”

“Will he draw a salary?” the practical horse-dealer demanded.

“Food and travel allowance only. Twenty rupees a month.”

One great advantage of the Secret Service is that it has no troublesome audits. The service is pitifully starved for funds, of course, but the money is managed by a few men who never ask for receipts or itemized accounts. Mahbub’s eyes lit up with almost a Sikh’s love for money. Even Lurgan’s impassive face shifted. He pictured the years ahead when Kim would be fully initiated into the Great Game that never stops day or night across all of India. He foresaw honor and praise coming to him from his pupil through the mouths of a chosen few. Lurgan Sahib had shaped E.23 out of a bewildered, insolent, lying little man from the North-West Province.

Yet the joy of these masters was pale and smoky compared to the joy Kim felt when the head of St. Xavier’s called him aside to announce that Colonel Creighton had sent for him.

“I understand, O’Hara, that he has found you a position as an assistant chain-man in the Canal Department: that’s what comes of studying mathematics. It’s tremendous luck for you, seeing you’re only sixteen; though of course you understand you won’t become pukka [permanent] until you pass the autumn examinations. So you mustn’t think you’re being sent out into the world to enjoy yourself, or that your fortune is made. There’s a great deal of hard work ahead of you. Still, if you succeed in becoming pukka, you can rise, as you know, to four hundred and fifty a month.” With that, the Principal offered him plenty of good advice regarding his conduct, manners, and morals; while other older students, who hadn’t been handed jobs so easily, grumbled the way only Anglo-Indian lads can about favoritism and corruption. Indeed, young Cazalet, whose father was a pensioner at Chunar, hinted broadly that Colonel Creighton’s interest in Kim was directly paternal; and Kim, instead of fighting back, didn’t even bother to curse. He was too busy thinking about the immense fun awaiting him, and Mahbub’s letter from the day before, neatly written in English, setting an appointment for that afternoon at a house whose very name would have made the Principal’s hair stand on end...

Kim said to Mahbub at the Lucknow railway station that evening beside the luggage scales: “I was afraid that at the very last moment the roof would cave in and cheat me. Is it truly all finished, O my father?”

Mahbub snapped his fingers to show how completely it was over, and his eyes blazed like red coals.

“Then where is the pistol so I can wear it?”

“Softly! A half-year to run free without a tether. I begged that much from Colonel Creighton Sahib. At twenty rupees a month. Old Red Hat knows you are coming.”

“I will pay you dustoorie [commission] on my wages for three months,” Kim said gravely. “Yes, two rupees a month. But first we must get rid of these.” He tugged at his thin linen trousers and pulled at his collar. “I brought everything I need for the Road with me. My trunk has already gone up to Lurgan Sahib’s.”

“Who sends his regards to you—Sahib.”

“Lurgan Sahib is a very clever man. But what are you going to do?”

“I’m heading North again, back to the Great Game. What else? Is your mind still set on following old Red Hat?”

“Don’t forget he made me what I am—even if he didn’t realize it. Year after year, he sent the money that paid for my schooling.”

“I would have done just as much—if it had occurred to my thick head,” Mahbub grumbled. “Come along. The lamps are lit now, and no one will notice you in the bazaar. We’re going to Huneefa’s house.”

On the way there, Mahbub gave him advice much like a mother’s warning to her son, and oddly enough, Mahbub made a point of showing how Huneefa and her kind could destroy kings.

“And I remember,” he quoted maliciously, “someone who said, ‘Trust a snake before a harlot, and a harlot before a Pathan, Mahbub Ali.’ Now, except for Pathans—being one myself—all of that is true. It is truest of all in the Great Game, because it is always through women that plans fall apart and we end up lying out in the dawn with our throats cut. That’s what happened to such a man.” He provided the bloodiest details.

“Then why—?” Kim stopped before a filthy staircase climbing into the warm darkness of an upper room in the district behind Azim Ullah’s tobacco shop. Those who knew it called it The Birdcage—it was so full of whispers, whistles, and chirping sounds.

The room, filled with dirty cushions and half-smoked hookahs, smelled horribly of stale tobacco. In one corner lay a huge, shapeless woman dressed in greenish gauzes and weighed down with heavy native jewelry on her brow, nose, ears, neck, wrists, arms, waist, and ankles. When she shifted, it sounded like clashing copper pots. A skinny cat on the balcony outside mewed hungrily. Kim hesitated, bewildered, at the doorway curtain.

“Is that the new material, Mahbub?” Huneefa asked lazily, barely bothering to take the mouthpiece from her lips. “O Buktanoos!”—like most of her kind, she swore by the Djinns—“O Buktanoos! He is very pleasant to look upon.”

“That’s part of selling the horse,” Mahbub explained to Kim, who laughed.

“I’ve heard that line since I was six days old,” Kim replied, squatting near the lamp. “Where does it lead?”

“To protection. Tonight we’ll change your skin color. Living under roofs has bleached you like an almond. But Huneefa holds the secret of a dye that really sticks—not just paint that washes off in a day or two. Also, we’ll fortify you against the hazards of the Road. That is my gift to you, my son. Take off all metal objects and lay them here. Get ready, Huneefa.”

Kim pulled out his compass, watercolor paint box, and the newly refilled medicine chest. They had accompanied him on all his travels, and like a true boy, he valued them immensely.

The woman rose slowly, moving with her hands held slightly out in front of her. Then Kim saw that she was blind. “No, no,” she muttered, “the Pathan speaks the truth—my dye doesn’t fade in a week or a month, and those under my protection are heavily guarded.”

“When a man is far away and alone, it wouldn’t do for him to suddenly turn blotched and leprous,” Mahbub said. “When you were with me, I could keep an eye on things. Besides, a Pathan has fair skin. Strip to the waist now and see how pale you’ve become.” Huneefa felt her way back from an inner room. “It doesn’t matter, she can’t see.” He took a pewter bowl from her ringed hand.

The dye mixture looked blue and gummy. Kim tested it on the back of his wrist with a cotton ball, but Huneefa heard him.

“No, no,” she cried, “it isn’t done that way—it requires proper ceremonies. The coloring is the least of it. I am giving you the full protection of the Road.”

“Jadoo [magic]?” Kim asked with a slight start. He didn’t like her white, sightless eyes. Mahbub’s hand forced his neck down until his nose was an inch from the floorboards.

“Be still. No harm will come to you, my son. I am your sacrifice!”

He couldn’t see what the woman was doing, but he heard the clinking of her jewelry for many minutes. A match flared in the darkness, and he caught the familiar hiss and scent of burning incense. Then the room filled with heavy, aromatic, stupefying smoke. Through a growing drowsiness, he heard the names of demons invoked—Zulbazan, Son of Eblis, who haunts bazaars and caravanserais, stirring up sudden lewd wickedness at roadside stops; Dulhan, invisible around mosques, dwelling among the sandals of the faithful to distract them from prayer; and Musboot, Lord of lies and panic. Huneefa touched him with horribly soft fingers, sometimes whispering directly into his ear, sometimes seeming to speak from far away, until Mahbub’s grip finally relaxed and the boy lost consciousness with a sigh.

“Allah! How he fought! We never could have managed it without the drugs. Must be his white blood, I suppose,” Mahbub muttered irritably. “Carry on with the dawut [invocation]. Give him full protection.”

“O Hearer! You who hear with ears, be present. Listen, O Hearer!” Huneefa moaned, her dead eyes turned toward the west. The dark room filled with groans and unearthly whistlings.

From the outer balcony, a heavy figure raised a round, bullet-shaped head and coughed nervously.

“Don’t interrupt these ventriloquial necromantics, my friend,” it said in English. “I reckon it’s quite disturbing to you, but an enlightened observer isn’t the least bit upset.”

“...I will lay a plot for their destruction! O Prophet, bear with the unbelievers. Leave them alone awhile!” Huneefa’s face, turned toward the north, twisted horribly, and voices seemed to answer her from the ceiling.

Hurree Babu went back to his notebook balanced on the windowsill, though his hand was shaking. Huneefa, caught in some drugged ecstasy, rocked back and forth as she sat cross-legged by Kim’s motionless head, calling upon demon after demon in the ancient order of the ritual to shield the boy from harm in all his actions.

“With Him are the keys of the Secret Things! None knoweth them besides Himself! He knoweth that which is in the dry land and in the sea!” The unearthly whistling replies broke out again.

“I—I assume this isn’t actually malignant in its operation?” Hurree Babu asked, watching the muscles in Huneefa’s throat twitch and jerk as she spoke in multiple voices. “It—it’s not likely she’s killed the boy, is it? Because if so, I refuse to testify at the trial... What was that last hypothetical devil named?”

“Babuji,” Mahbub said in the vernacular. “I don’t care much for the demons of Hind, but the Sons of Eblis are quite different; and whether they are jumalee [benign] or jullalee [terrifying], they certainly don’t love infidels.”

“Then you think I’d better leave?” Hurree Babu asked, half rising. “They are, naturally, dematerialized phenomena, as Spencer points out.”

Huneefa’s trance ended, as these things always did, in a paroxysm of howling accompanied by foaming at the mouth. She collapsed, exhausted and motionless, beside Kim, and the eerie voices stopped.

“Wah! The work is done. Let’s hope the boy benefits from it; Huneefa is certainly a master of the dawut. Help me pull her aside, Babu. Don’t be afraid.”

“How could I fear something that is entirely non-existent?” Hurree Babu said, speaking English to reassure himself. It is a dreadful thing to still dread the very magic you view with contempt—to collect folklore for the Royal Society while harboring a lively belief in all the Powers of Darkness.

Mahbub chuckled. He had traveled the Road with Hurree before. “Let’s finish the coloring,” he said. “The boy is well protected—if the Lords of the Air have ears to hear. I am a sufi [free-thinker], but when you can get the better of a woman, a stallion, or a devil, why go out of your way to invite a kick? Set him on his way, Babu, and make sure old Red Hat doesn’t lead him beyond our reach. I have to get back to my horses.”

“All right,” Hurree Babu said. “He is quite a curious spectacle at present.”

Around the third cockcrow, Kim woke up after sleeping for what felt like a thousand years. Huneefa was snoring loudly in her corner, but Mahbub was gone.

“I hope you weren’t frightened,” an oily voice said beside his elbow. “I supervised the entire operation, which was deeply interesting from an ethnological perspective. It was a top-class dawut.”

“Huh!” Kim muttered, recognizing Hurree Babu, who smiled ingratiatingly.

“And I also had the honor of bringing your new costume down from Lurgan’s. It’s not officially my job to carry such finery to subordinates, but”—he giggled—“your case is marked as exceptional in the records. I trust Mr. Lurgan will note my efforts.”

Kim yawned and stretched. It felt good to move inside loose clothing once again.

“What is this?” He looked curiously at the heavy duffle fabric scented with the fragrances of the far North.

“Oho! That is the unassuming dress of a chela attached to the service of a lamaistic lama. Complete in every detail,” Hurree Babu said, waddling out onto the balcony to clean his teeth with a water jug. Then he recited an Arya-Samaj prayer in English and stuffed his mouth with pan and betel nut.

“Oh yes. I’ve met him several times in Benares and also at Buddh Gaya to question him on religious points and devil worship. He’s a pure agnostic—just like me.”

Inside, Huneefa stirred in her sleep, and Hurree Babu jumped nervously toward the copper incense burner—blackened and tarnished by the morning light—dipped a finger into the accumulated soot, and smeared it diagonally across his face.

“Who died in your house?” Kim asked in the vernacular.

“No one. But that sorceress might have the Evil Eye,” the Babu replied.

“What are you doing now, then?”

“I’m going to set you on your way to Benares, if that’s where you’re heading, and tell you what must be known by Us.”

“I’m going. What time does the te-rain leave?” He stood up, looking around the dreary room and at Huneefa’s yellow waxen face as the morning sun crept across the floorboards. “Is there money to be paid to that witch?”

“No. She has charmed you against all devils and dangers in the name of her spirits. It was Mahbub’s wish.” Then in English: “He is terribly old-fashioned, I think, to indulge in such superstition. Why, it’s all ventriloquism. Belly-talking—eh?”

Kim instinctively snapped his fingers to ward off any evil—though he knew Mahbub meant no harm—that might have hitched a ride through Huneefa’s rituals; and Hurree giggled again. But as he crossed the room, he was careful not to step on Huneefa’s blotched, squat shadow on the floor. Witches—when their powers are active—can grab hold of the heels of a man’s soul if he steps on their shadow.

“Now you must listen closely,” the Babu said once they were out in the fresh air. “Part of the ceremonies we just witnessed includes providing an efficient amulet for members of our Department. If you feel at your neck, you’ll find a small silver amulet—very cheap. That is ours. Do you understand?”

“Oh yes, a hawa-dilli [heart-lifter],” Kim said, touching his neck.

“Huneefa makes them for two rupees and twelve annas with—well, all sorts of exorcisms. They’re quite common, except they have a bit of black enamel on them, and there’s a paper inside each one filled with the names of local saints and such things. That is Huneefa’s contribution, you see? Huneefa makes them exclusively for us, but just in case she hasn’t, when we receive them, we insert a small piece of turquoise before handing them out. Mr. Lurgan supplies those. There’s no other source; but I invented the whole scheme myself. It’s strictly unofficial, of course, but very handy for subordinates. Colonel Creighton doesn’t know about it. He’s a European. The turquoise is wrapped inside the paper... Yes, that’s the road to the railway station... Now, suppose you’re traveling with the lama, or with me someday, or with Mahbub. Suppose we get into a tight spot. I’m a fearful man—most fearful—but I can tell you I’ve been in tighter spots than there are hairs on my head. You just say: ‘I am Son of the Charm.’ Very good.”

“I don’t quite understand. We shouldn’t be speaking English here.”

“That’s quite all right. I’m just a Babu showing off my English to you. All of us Babus speak English to show off,” Hurree said, giving his shoulder cloth a jaunty toss. “As I was saying, ‘Son of the Charm’ means you might be a member of the Sat Bhai—the Seven Brothers—which is both Hindi and Tantric. It’s popularly believed to be an extinct society, but I’ve written papers proving it’s still active. You see, I invented all of that too. Very good. The Sat Bhai has many members, and perhaps before they cheerfully cut your throat, they’ll give you a fighting chance at life. That’s useful to know. Besides, these foolish natives—if they aren’t too worked up—always pause to think before killing a man who claims membership in any specific organization. You see? So when you’re in a tight spot, you say, ‘I am Son of the Charm,’ and you might just—ah—get your second wind. That’s only for extreme emergencies, or to open negotiations with a stranger. Do you follow? Very good. But suppose now that I, or someone else from the Department, approach you dressed completely differently. You wouldn’t recognize me at all unless I wanted you to, I bet. Someday I’ll prove it to you. I might show up as a Ladakhi trader—or anything—and say to you: ‘Do you want to buy precious stones?’ You reply: ‘Do I look like a man who buys precious stones?’ Then I say: ‘Even a very poor man can buy a turquoise or tarkeean.’”

“That’s kichree—vegetable curry,” Kim noted.

“Of course it is. You say: ‘Let me see the tarkeean.’ Then I reply: ‘It was cooked by a woman, and perhaps it isn’t good for your caste.’ Then you say: ‘There is no caste when men go to—look for tarkeean.’ You pause slightly between those words: ‘to—look’. That’s the entire secret. That little pause before those words.”

Kim repeated the test sentence.

“That’s correct. Then I’ll show you my turquoise if there’s time, and you’ll know who I am, and we can exchange views, documents, and everything else. It’s the same with any of our other men. We talk sometimes about turquoises and sometimes about tarkeean, but always with that little pause in the words. It’s very simple. First, ‘Son of the Charm’ if you’re in a tight spot. That might help you—perhaps not. Second, what I told you about the tarkeean if you want to conduct official business with a stranger. Of course, right now you have no official business. You’re—ah, yes—a supernumerary on probation. Quite a unique specimen. If you were born Asian, you’d be put straight to work; but this six-month leave is meant to de-Englishize you, you see? The lama is expecting you, because I semi-officially informed him that you’ve passed all your examinations and will soon receive a Government appointment. Oh ho! You’re drawing acting-allowance, you see; so if you’re ever called upon to help the Sons of the Charm, make sure you jolly well try. Now I’ll say goodbye, my dear fellow, and I hope you—ah—come out on top alright.”

Hurree Babu stepped back into the crowd near the entrance of the Lucknow station and vanished. Kim took a deep breath and hugged himself in delight. He could feel the nickel-plated revolver tucked against his chest inside his drab robe; the amulet rested on his neck; his begging bowl, rosary, and ghost-dagger (Mr. Lurgan had forgotten nothing) were all ready at hand, alongside his medicine box, paint box, and compass; and tucked into an old, worn purse-belt embroidered with porcupine quills lay a month’s wages. Kings couldn’t be richer. He bought sweets wrapped in a leaf cup from a Hindu merchant and ate them with joyous rapture until a policeman ordered him off the steps.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
chapters.content:
Give the man who is not made
To his trade
Swords to fling and catch again,
Coins to ring and snatch again,
Men to harm and cure again,
Snakes to charm and lure again—
He’ll be hurt by his own blade,
By his serpents disobeyed,
By his clumsiness bewrayed,
By the people mocked to scorn—
So ’tis not with juggler born!
Pinch of dust or withered flower,
Chance-flung fruit or borrowed staff,
Serve his need and shore his power,
Bind the spell, or loose the laugh!

_But a man who, etc._, Op. 15

Followed a sudden natural reaction.

“Now am I alone—all alone,” he thought. “In all India is no one so alone as I! If I die today, who shall bring the news—and to whom? If I live and God is good, there will be a price upon my head, for I am a Son of the Charm—I, Kim.”

A very few white people, but many Asiatics, can throw themselves into a trance-like state simply by repeating their own names over and over again to themselves, letting the mind wander freely into speculation about what is called personal identity. As people grow older, this ability usually disappears, but while it lasts, it can descend upon a man at any moment.

“Who is Kim—Kim—Kim?”

He squatted in a corner of the noisy waiting-room, completely absorbed, with his hands folded in his lap and his pupils shrunk to pin-points. In a minute—in another half-second—he felt he would arrive at the solution of this tremendous puzzle; but here, as always happens, his mind dropped away from those heights with the rush of a wounded bird, and passing his hand before his eyes, he shook his head.

A long-haired Hindu bairagi (holy man), who had just bought a ticket, stopped before him at that moment and stared intently.

“I also have lost it,” he said sadly. “It is one of the Gates to the Way, but for me it has been shut for many years.”

“What are you talking about?” said Kim, feeling abashed.

“You were wondering there in your spirit what manner of thing your soul might be. The seizure came suddenly. I know. Who should know better than I? Where are you going?”

“Toward Kashi [Benares].”

“There are no Gods there. I have proved them. I go to Prayag [Allahabad] for the fifth time—seeking the Road to Enlightenment. Of what faith are you?”

“I too am a Seeker,” said Kim, using one of the lama’s favorite words. “Though”—he forgot his Northern dress for the moment—“though Allah alone knows what I seek.”

The old man slipped the bairagi’s crutch under his armpit and sat down on a patch of reddish leopard skin as Kim rose when the Benares train was called.

“Go in hope, little brother,” he said. “It is a long road to the feet of the One; but thither do we all travel.”

Kim did not feel quite so lonely after this, and before he had spent twenty minutes in the crowded compartment, he was cheering his neighbors with a string of wonderful tales about his own and his master’s magical powers.

Benares struck him as a particularly filthy city, though it was pleasant to see how much his clothes were respected. At least one-third of the population prays constantly to various groups among the millions of deities, and thus reveres every sort of holy man. Kim was guided to the Temple of the Tirthankars, about a mile outside the city near Sarnath, by a Punjabi farmer he met by chance—a Kamboh from the Jullundur area who had appealed in vain to every God of his homestead to cure his small son, and was trying Benares as a last resort.

“Are you from the North?” he asked, pushing his way through the dense, foul-smelling streets much like his own pet bull at home.

“Yes, I know the Punjab. My mother was a hill-woman, but my father came from Amritsar—near Jandiala,” said Kim, oiling his ready tongue for the needs of the Road.

“Jandiala—Jullundur? Oh! Then we are neighbors of a sort.” He nodded tenderly to the wailing child in his arms. “Whom do you serve?”

“A most holy man at the Temple of the Tirthankars.”

“They are all most holy and—most greedy,” said the Jat with bitterness. “I have walked the pillars and trodden the temples until my feet are raw, and the child is no better. And his mother is sick too... Hush now, little one... We changed his name when the fever came. We put him in a girl’s clothes. There was nothing we did not do, except—I told his mother when she hurried me off to Benares—she should have come with me—I said Sakhi Sarwar Sultan would serve us best. We know His generosity, but these down-country Gods are strangers.”

The child turned on the cushion of the huge corded arms and looked at Kim through heavy eyelids.

“And was it all useless?” Kim asked with casual interest.

“All useless—all useless,” said the child, his lips cracking with fever.

“The Gods have given him a good mind, at least,” said the father proudly. “To think he should have listened so cleverly! Yonder is your temple. Now I am a poor man—many priests have dealt with me—but my son is my son, and if a gift to your master can cure him—I am at my wits’ end.”

Kim considered for a moment, tingling with pride. Three years ago he would have made a quick profit from the situation and gone his way without a thought; but now, the very respect the Jat showed him proved that he was a man. Moreover, he had suffered from fever himself once or twice already, and knew enough to recognize starvation when he saw it.

“Call him forth and I will give him a bond on my best yoke of oxen, provided the child is cured.”

Kim stopped at the carved outer door of the temple. A white-clad Oswal banker from Ajmer, whose sins of usury had just been wiped clean, asked him what he wanted.

“I am a disciple to Teshoo Lama, a Holy Man from Tibet—inside there. He told me to come. I am waiting. Tell him.”

“Do not forget the child,” cried the persistent Jat over his shoulder, and then bellowed in Punjabi: “O Holy One—O disciple of the Holy One—O Gods above all the Worlds—behold affliction sitting at the gate!” That cry is so common in Benares that passers-by never turned their heads.

The Oswal banker, at peace with mankind, carried the message into the darkness within, and the easy, uncounted Eastern minutes passed by; for the lama was asleep in his cell, and no priest would wake him. When the click of his rosary once more broke the silence of the inner court where the calm images of the Arhats stand, a novice whispered, “Your disciple is here,” and the old man strode out, forgetting the end of that prayer.

Scarcely had the tall figure appeared in the doorway than the Jat ran up to him, lifted the child, and cried: “Look upon this, Holy One! And if the Gods will, he lives—he lives!”

He fumbled in his waist-belt and drew out a small silver coin.

“What is it now?” The lama’s eyes turned to Kim. It was noticeable that he spoke much clearer Urdu than he had long ago under the Zam-Zammah cannon; but his father would allow no private conversation.

“It is nothing more than a fever,” said Kim. “The child is not well fed.”

“He gets sick at everything, and his mother is not here.”

“If it is permitted, I can cure him, Holy One.”

“What! Have they made you a healer? Wait here,” said the lama, and he sat down by the Jat on the lowest step of the temple, while Kim, looking out of the corner of his eye, slowly opened the small betel-box. He had dreamed dreams at school of returning to the lama as a Sahib—of teasing the old man before revealing his identity—pure boyish dreams. There was far more drama in this distracted, brow-furrowed search through the medicine bottles, pausing here and there to think and muttering a prayer between times. He had quinine in tablets and dark brown meat lozenges—beef most probably, but that was none of his business. The little boy would not eat, but he sucked greedily at a lozenge and said he liked the salty taste.

“Take these six, then.” Kim handed them to the man. “Praise the Gods, and boil three in milk, and the other three in water. After he has drunk the milk, give him this” (it was half a quinine pill), “and wrap him up warmly. Give him the water from the other three and the other half of this white pill when he wakes. Meanwhile, here is another brown medicine that he may suck on the way home.”

“Gods, what wisdom!” said the Kamboh, snatching them eagerly.

It was as much as Kim could remember of his own treatment during a bout of autumn malaria—aside from the patter he added to impress the lama.

“Now go! Come back in the morning.”

“But the price—the price,” said the Jat, throwing back his sturdy shoulders. “My son is my son. Now that he is going to be well again, how can I go back to his mother and say I accepted help by the roadside and did not even give a bowl of curds in return?”

“They are all alike, these Jats,” said Kim softly. “The Jat stood on his manure-pile as the King’s elephants went by. ‘O driver,’ said he, ‘what will you sell those little donkeys for?’”

The Jat burst into a roar of laughter, quickly stifled with apologies to the lama. “That is the saying of my own country—the very talk of it! That is how we Jats all are. I will come tomorrow with the child; and the blessing of the Gods of the Homesteads—who are good little Gods—be upon you both... Now, son, we are growing strong again. Do not spit it out, little prince! King of my heart, do not spit it out, and we shall be strong men, wrestlers and club-swingers, by morning.”

He walked away, humming and muttering. The lama turned to Kim, and all his loving old soul shone through his narrow eyes.

“To heal the sick is to gain merit; but first one must acquire knowledge. That was wisely done, O Friend of all the World.”

“I was made wise by you, Holy One,” said Kim, forgetting the little performance just ended; forgetting St. Xavier’s; forgetting his white blood; forgetting even the Great Game as he stooped, in the Mohammedan fashion, to touch his master’s feet in the dust of the Jain temple. “My teaching I owe to you. I have eaten your bread for three years. My time is finished. I am released from the schools. I have come to you.”

“Herein is my reward. Enter! Enter! And is all well?” They passed into the inner court, where the afternoon sun cast a golden glow across the stones. “Stand so that I may see you. There!” He peered critically. “You are no longer a child, but a man, ripened in wisdom, walking as a physician. I did well—I did well when I gave you up to the armed men on that black night. Do you remember our first day under the Zam-Zammah cannon?”

“Yes,” said Kim. “Do you remember when I leaped off the carriage the first day I went to—”

“The Gates of Learning? Truly. And the day we ate the cakes together behind the river at Lucknow. Ah! Many times have you begged for me, but that day I begged for you.”

“For good reason,” said Kim. “I was then a scholar at the Gates of Learning, and dressed as a Sahib. Do not forget, Holy One,” he continued playfully. “I am still a Sahib—by your favor.”

“True. And a Sahib held in very high esteem. Come to my cell, disciple.”

“How do you know that?”

The lama smiled. “First, through letters from the kindly priest whom we met in the camp of armed men; but he has now gone to his own country, and I sent the money to his brother.” Colonel Creighton, who had taken over the guardianship when Father Victor went to England with the Mavericks, was hardly the chaplain’s brother. “But I do not understand Sahibs’ letters very well. They have to be interpreted to me. I chose a surer way. Many times when I returned from my Search to this temple, which has always been a refuge for me, someone would come seeking Enlightenment—a man from Leh who had been, he said, a Hindu, but had grown tired of all those Gods.” The lama pointed to the Arhats.

“A fat man?” said Kim with a twinkle in his eye.

“Very fat; but I soon saw that his mind was wholly given up to useless things—such as devils and charms and the forms and fashions of our tea-drinkings in the monasteries, and the ways by which we initiate novices. A man full of questions; but he was a friend of yours, disciple. He told me you were on the road to much honor as a scribe. And I see you are a physician.”

“Yes, that I am—a scribe when I am a Sahib, but I lay that aside when I come as your disciple. I have completed the years appointed for a Sahib.”

“Like a novice?” said the lama, nodding his head. “Are you freed from the schools? I would not have you unripe.”

“I am completely free. In due time I will take service under the Government as a scribe—”

“Not as a warrior. That is well.”

“But first I come to wander with you. Therefore I am here. Who begs for your food these days?” he went on quickly. The ice was thin.

“Very often I beg for myself; but, as you know, I am seldom here except when I come to look again upon my disciple. From one end of India to the other I have traveled on foot and by the te-rain. A great and wonderful land! But here, when I return, it is as though I were in my own Tibet.”

He looked around the clean little cell with satisfaction. A low cushion provided a seat, upon which he had settled himself cross-legged like the Bodhisattva emerging from meditation; a black teak-wood table, less than twenty inches high, set with copper teacups, stood before him. In one corner was a tiny altar, also heavily carved from teak, bearing a copper-gilt image of the seated Buddha, fronted by a lamp, an incense burner, and a pair of copper flower-pots.

“The Keeper of the Images in the Museum gained merit by giving me these a year ago,” he said, following Kim’s gaze. “When one is far from one’s own land, such things bring remembrance; and we must honor the Lord for showing the Way. Look!” He pointed to a curiously shaped mound of colored rice crowned with a fantastic metal ornament. “When I was Abbot in my own place—before I attained better knowledge—I made that offering daily. It is the Sacrifice of the Universe to the Lord. Thus do we of Tibet offer the whole world daily to the Excellent Law. And I do it even now, although I know that the Excellent One is beyond all earthly offerings.” He took a pinch of snuff from his gourd.

“It is well done, Holy One,” Kim murmured, sinking comfortably onto the cushions, feeling very happy and rather tired.

“And also,” the old man chuckled, “I draw pictures of the Wheel of Life. Three days to a picture. I was busy with it—or perhaps I closed my eyes for a little while—when they brought word of you. It is good to have you here; I will show you my art—not out of pride, but because you must learn. The Sahibs do not possess all this world’s wisdom.”

He pulled from under the table a sheet of strangely scented yellow Chinese paper, along with some brushes and a slab of Indian ink. With the cleanest, strictest outlines, he had traced the Great Wheel with its six spokes, whose center is formed by the joined Hog, Snake, and Dove (representing Ignorance, Anger, and Lust), and whose compartments contain all Heavens, Hells, and human fortunes. People say that the Bodhisattva Himself first drew it with grains of rice upon the dust to teach His disciples the cause of all things. Many ages have crystallized it into a wonderful traditional design crowded with hundreds of figures, every line carrying a meaning. Few can translate this picture-parable; there are not twenty people in the entire world who can draw it accurately without a copy, and of those who can both draw and explain it, there are only three.

“I have learned a little about drawing,” said Kim. “But this is a marvel beyond marvels.”

“I have drawn it for many years,” said the lama. “There was a time when I could draw the whole thing between one lamp-lighting and the next. I will teach you the art—after proper preparation; and I will explain the meaning of the Wheel to you.”

“Are we taking to the Road, then?”

“The Road and our Search. I was only waiting for you. It was made plain to me in a hundred dreams—especially one that came on the very night the Gates of Learning first closed—that without you I would never find my River. Again and again, as you know, I pushed this thought away, fearing it was an illusion. That is why I would not take you with me that day at Lucknow when we ate the cakes. I would not take you until the time was ripe and auspicious. From the Hills to the Sea, and from the Sea to the Hills have I gone, but it was in vain. Then I remembered the Jataka story.”

He told Kim the story of the elephant with the leg-iron, just as he had told it so often to the priests of Kulu.

“No further proof is needed,” he concluded serenely. “You were sent to help me. Without that help, my Search came to nothing. Therefore we will go out together again, and our Search is certain to succeed.”

“Where are we going?”

“What does it matter, Friend of all the World? The Search, I say, is certain. If necessary, the River will burst from the ground right before us. I gained merit when I sent you to the Gates of Learning and gave you the jewel of Wisdom. You returned, as I saw just now, a follower of Sakyamuni, the Physician, whose altars are numerous in Tibet. It is enough. We are together, and all things are as they were—Friend of all the World—Friend of the Stars—my disciple!”

Then they talked of ordinary matters; but it was noticeable that the lama never asked for any details of life at St. Xavier’s, nor showed the slightest curiosity about the manners and customs of Sahibs. His mind dwelt entirely in the past, and he recalled every step of their wonderful first journey together, rubbing his hands and chuckling until he curled up for the sudden sleep of old age.

Kim watched the last dusty sunshine fade out of the courtyard, playing with his ghost-dagger and rosary. The noise of Benares—the oldest of all earth’s cities, awake before the Gods day and night—beat against the walls like the roar of the sea around a breakwater. Every now and then, a Jain priest crossed the court with a small offering for the images, sweeping the path before him so as not to accidentally kill any living creature. A lamp flickered, followed by the sound of prayer. Kim watched the stars rise one by one in the still, sticky darkness until he fell asleep at the foot of the altar. That night he dreamed entirely in Hindustani, without a single English word...

“Holy One, there is the child to whom we gave the medicine,” he said around three o’clock in the morning, when the lama, waking from his own dreams, was preparing to set out on his pilgrimage. “The Jat will be here at dawn.”

“I am rightly answered. In my haste I would have done a wrong thing.” He sat down on the cushions and returned to his rosary. “Old people are surely like children,” he said pathetically. “They set their hearts on something—and look, it must be done instantly, or they fret and weep! Many times when I was on the Road I have been ready to stamp my feet because an ox-cart blocked my way, or merely because of a cloud of dust. It was not so when I was a younger man—a long time ago. Nevertheless, it is wrong—”

“But you truly are old, Holy One.”

“The thing was done. A Cause was set in motion in the world, and whether old or young, sick or well, knowing or unknowing, who can hold back the effects of that Cause? Does the Wheel stop spinning if a child spins it—or a drunkard? Disciple, this is a great and terrible world.”

“I think it is a good world,” Kim yawned. “What is there to eat? I have not eaten since yesterday evening.”

“I forgot your need. Yonder is some good Tibetan tea and cold rice.”

“We cannot walk far on such stuff.” Kim felt all a European’s craving for meat, which was unavailable in a Jain temple. Yet, instead of rushing out immediately with his begging-bowl, he filled his stomach with slabs of cold rice until full dawn. It brought the farmer, talkative and stuttering with gratitude.

“In the night the fever broke and the sweat poured out,” he cried. “Feel here—his skin is fresh and new! He liked the salt lozenges and took his milk greedily.” He pulled the cloth from the child’s face, and the boy smiled sleepily at Kim. A small group of Jain priests, silent but observant, gathered by the temple door. They knew, and Kim knew that they knew, how the old lama had met his disciple. Being courteous men, they had not intruded the night before with their presence, words, or gestures. Therefore, Kim thanked them as the sun rose.

“Thank the Gods of the Jains, brother,” he said, not knowing the proper names of those Gods. “The fever is indeed broken.”

“Look! See!” The lama beamed in the background upon his hosts of the past three years. “Was there ever such a disciple? He follows our Lord the Healer.”

The Jains officially recognize all the Gods of the Hindu pantheon, as well as the Lingam and the Snake. They wear the Brahminical thread and adhere to every rule of Hindu caste law. But because they knew and loved the lama, because he was an old man, because he sought the Way, because he was their guest, and because he spent long nights in conversation with their head priest—as free-thinking a metaphysician as ever split a hair into seventy parts—they murmured their assent.

“Remember,” Kim bent over the child, “this trouble may return.”

“Not if you give him the proper spell,” said the father.

“But in a little while we are leaving.”

“True,” said the lama to all the Jains. “We are now going together upon the Search of which I have often spoken. I waited until my disciple was ripe. Behold him! We are going North. I shall never look upon this place of rest again, O people of good will.”

“But I am not a beggar.” The farmer rose to his feet, clutching the child.

“Be still. Do not trouble the Holy One,” a priest cried.

“Go,” Kim whispered. “Meet us again under the big railway bridge, and for the sake of all the Gods of our Punjab, bring food—curry, lentils, cakes fried in fat, and sweetmeats. Especially sweetmeats. Be quick!”

The paleness of hunger suited Kim very well as he stood, tall and slim, in his sand-colored flowing robes, one hand on his rosary and the other raised in a gesture of blessing faithfully copied from the lama. An English observer might have thought he looked like a young saint in a stained-glass window, whereas he was simply a growing boy faint with emptiness.

Long and formal were the farewells, thrice ended and thrice renewed. The Seeker—the hairless, silver-faced ascetic who had invited the lama to that haven from far-away Tibet—took no part in them, but meditated, as always, alone among the images. The others were very human, pressing small comforts upon the old man—a betel box, a fine new iron pen case, a food bag, and the like—warning him against the dangers of the outside world and prophesying a happy end to his Search. Meanwhile Kim, lonelier than ever, squatted on the steps and swore to himself in the language of St. Xavier’s.

“But it is my own fault,” he concluded. “With Mahbub, I ate Mahbub’s bread, or Lurgan Sahib’s. At St. Xavier’s, three meals a day. Here I must jolly well look out for myself. Besides, I am not in good training. How I could eat a plate of beef right now!... Are you finished, Holy One?”

The lama, raising both hands, intoned a final blessing in ornate Chinese. “I must lean on your shoulder,” he said as the temple gates closed behind them. “We grow stiff, I think.”

The weight of a six-foot man is not light to steady through miles of crowded streets, and Kim, loaded down with bundles and packages for the journey, was glad to reach the shadow of the railway bridge.

“Here we eat,” he said decisively as the Kamboh, dressed in blue and smiling broadly, came into view with a basket in one hand and the child in the other.

“Fall to, Holy Ones!” he cried from fifty yards away. (They were near the shallow water under the first bridge span, out of sight of hungry priests.) “Rice and good curry, cakes all warm and well-scented with asafetida, curds, and sugar. King of my fields,”—this to his small son—“let us show these holy men that we Jats of Jullundur know how to show gratitude... I had heard the Jains would eat nothing they had not cooked themselves, but truly”—he looked away politely across the broad river—“where there is no eye, there is no caste.”

“And we,” said Kim, turning his back and piling a leaf-platter high for the lama, “are beyond all castes.”

They gorged themselves on the good food in silence. Not until he had licked the last sticky sweetness from his little finger did Kim notice that the Kamboh was also dressed for travel.

“If our roads lie together,” he said roughly, “I am going with you. One does not often find a worker of miracles, and the child is still weak. But I am not entirely defenseless.” He picked up his lathi—a five-foot male-bamboo staff ringed with bands of polished iron—and flourished it in the air. “Jats are called quarrelsome, but that is not true. Except when we are provoked, we are like our own buffaloes.”

“So be it,” said Kim. “A good stick is a good argument.”

The lama gazed placidly upstream, where long, hazy columns of smoke rose ceaselessly from the cremation grounds along the riverbank. Every now and then, despite all municipal regulations, fragments of half-burned bodies bobbed by on the swift current.

“But for you,” said the Kamboh to Kim, pulling the child against his hairy chest, “I might have gone down there today—with this one. The priests tell us that Benares is holy—which nobody doubts—and a desirable place to die in. But I do not know their Gods, and they ask for money; and when you finish one worship, a shaved-head priest declares it is worthless unless you pay for another. Wash here! Wash there! Pour, drink, bathe, and scatter flowers—always paying the priests. No, give me the Punjab and the soil of the Jullundur doab as the best soil of all.”

“I have said many times—in the temple, I think—that if necessary, the River will open at our feet.
