We will therefore go North,” said the lama, rising. “I remember a pleasant place surrounded by fruit-trees where one can walk in meditation—and the air is cooler there. It comes from the Hills and the mountain snows.”

“What is the name of it?” asked Kim.

“How should I know? Did you not—no, that was after the army rose out of the earth and took you away. I lived there in meditation in a room near the dovecot—except when that woman talked endlessly.”

“Ah! The woman from Kulu. That is near Saharanpur,” Kim laughed.

“How does the spirit move your master? Does he travel on foot for the sake of past sins?” the Jat asked cautiously. “It is a long way to Delhi.”

“No,” said Kim. “I will beg a ticket for the train.” One never admits to having money in India.

“Then, in the name of the Gods, let us take the fire-carriage! My son travels best in his mother’s arms. The Government has brought many taxes upon us, but it gives us one good thing—the train that joins friends and unites the anxious. A wonderful thing is the train.”

A couple of hours later, they all piled into a carriage and slept through the heat of the day. The Kamboh plied Kim with ten thousand questions about the lama’s life and work, receiving some curious answers in return. Kim was content simply to be where he was, to look out at the flat North-Western landscape, and to talk to the shifting crowd of fellow-passengers. Even today, tickets and ticket-punchers remain a dark oppression to Indian peasants. They do not understand why, after they have paid for a magic piece of paper, strangers should punch great holes out of their charm. As a result, long and furious arguments frequently break out between travelers and Eurasian ticket-collectors. Kim assisted at two or three such disputes with solemn advice meant to confuse the issue and show off his wisdom before the lama and the admiring Kamboh. But at Somna Road, fate provided him with something else to think about.

Just as the train was pulling out, a mean, thin little man tumbled into the compartment—a Mahratta, judging by the tilt of his tight turban. His face was cut, his muslin upper garment badly torn, and one leg was bandaged. He told them that a farm cart had overturned and nearly killed him; he was on his way to Delhi, where his son lived. Kim watched him closely. If he had really been rolled over and over on the ground as he claimed, there should have been gravel rashes on his skin. But all his injuries were clean cuts, and a simple fall from a cart could not throw a man into such an extreme state of terror. As he nervously retied the torn cloth around his neck with shaking fingers, he exposed an amulet of the type known as a heart-keeper. Now, amulets are common enough, but they are not usually strung on square-plaited copper wire, and even fewer bear black enamel on silver. Only the Kamboh and the lama were in the compartment with him, which fortunately was an old-style carriage with solid ends. Kim pretended to scratch his chest, thereby lifting his own amulet. The Mahratta’s face changed completely at the sight, and he quickly tucked his own amulet back out of sight upon his breast.

“Yes,” he continued to the Kamboh, “I was in a hurry, and the cart, driven by a fool, caught its wheel in an irrigation ditch, and besides the harm done to me, a whole dish of curry was lost. I was not a Son of the Charm [a lucky man] that day.”

“That was a great loss,” said the Kamboh, losing interest. His experience in Benares had made him suspicious.

“Who cooked it?” asked Kim.

“A woman.” The Mahratta raised his eyes.

“But all women can cook curry,” said the Kamboh. “It is a good dish, as I know.”

“Oh yes, it is a good curry,” said the Mahratta.

“And cheap,” said Kim. “But what about caste?”

“Oh, there is no caste where men go to—look for curry,” the Mahratta replied in the prescribed rhythmic cadence. “Whose service are you in?”

“In the service of this Holy One.” Kim pointed to the happy, drowsy lama, who jerked awake at the beloved word.

“Ah, he was sent from Heaven to help me. He is called the Friend of all the World. He is also called the Friend of the Stars. He walks as a physician—his time having come. Great is his wisdom.”

“And a Son of the Charm,” Kim muttered under his breath as the Kamboh hurriedly prepared a pipe to prevent the Mahratta from begging.

“And who is that?” the Mahratta asked, glancing sideways nervously.

“Someone whose child we—I have cured, who owes us a great debt. Sit by the window, man from Jullundur. Here is a sick man.”

“Humph! I have no desire to mix with chance-met vagrants. My ears are not long. I am no woman looking to overhear secrets.” The Jat slid himself heavily into a far corner.

“Are you any sort of healer? I am deep in trouble,” cried the Mahratta, picking up the cue.

“This man is cut and bruised all over. I go about curing him,” Kim retorted. “No one interfered between your baby and me.”

“I am rebuked,” said the Kamboh meekly. “I am your debtor for the life of my son. You are a miracle-worker—I know it.”

“Show me the cuts.” Kim bent over the Mahratta’s neck, his heart nearly choking him; for this was the Great Game in earnest now. “Now, tell your story quickly, brother, while I pretend to say a charm.”

“I come from the South, where my work lay. One of our men was slain by the roadside. Have you heard?” Kim shook his head. He naturally knew nothing of E23’s predecessor, killed down South while disguised as an Arab trader. “Having found a certain letter I was sent to seek, I got away. I escaped from the city and ran to Mhow. I was so sure no one knew that I did not even change my appearance. At Mhow, a woman accused me of stealing jewelry in the very city I had left. Then I knew the hunt was out against me. I fled Mhow by night, bribing the police, who had already been paid to hand me over quietly to my enemies in the South. Then I hid in the old city of Chittor for a week as a penitent in a temple, but I could not get rid of the letter I was carrying. I buried it under the Queen’s Stone at Chittor, in a place known to us all.”

Kim did not know the place, but for worlds he would not have broken the thread.

“At Chittor, you see, I was surrounded by native states; for Kotah to the east is beyond British law, and east of that lie Jaipur and Gwalior. None of them love spies, and there is no justice there. I was hunted like a wet jackal; but I broke through to Bandikui, where I heard there was an arrest warrant out against me for murder in the city I had left—the murder of a boy. They have both the corpse and the witnesses waiting.”

“But cannot the Government protect you?”

“We of the Game are beyond protection. If we die, we die. Our names are simply erased from the books. That is all. At Bandikui, where one of Us lives, I thought to throw them off the scent by changing my appearance, so I disguised myself as a Mahratta. Then I came to Agra and intended to go back to Chittor to recover the letter, so sure was I that I had eluded them. Therefore I did not send a telegram to anyone saying where the letter was hidden. I wanted the credit for it myself.”

Kim nodded. He understood that feeling well.

“But at Agra, while walking in the street, a man accused me of a debt and, approaching with numerous witnesses, tried to drag me straight to the courts. Oh, they are clever in the South! He recognized me as his cotton agent. May he burn in Hell for it!”

“And were you?”

“You fool! I was the very man they wanted for the matter of the letter! I ran into the Butcher’s Ward and came out by the House of the Jew, who feared a riot and pushed me out. I walked on foot to Somna Road—I only had enough money for a train ticket to Delhi—and there, while I lay in a ditch with a fever, someone sprang out of the bushes, beat me, cut me, and searched me from head to foot. And all within earshot of the train!”

“Why didn’t they kill you outright?”

“They are not so foolish. If I am caught in Delhi at the lawyers’ request on a proven murder charge, my body is handed over to the state that wants it. I go back under guard, and then—I die slowly as an example to the rest of Us. The South is not my country. I run in circles—like a one-eyed goat. I have not eaten for two days. I am marked”—he touched the filthy bandage on his leg—“so they will recognize me in Delhi.”

“You are safe in the train, at least.”

“Live for a year at the Great Game and tell me that again! The telegraph wires will be out against me in Delhi, describing every tear and rag on my body. Twenty—a hundred witnesses, if need be—will have seen me murder that boy. And you are useless!”

Kim knew enough of native methods of attack not to doubt that the case would be airtight—complete even to the corpse. The Mahratta twitched his fingers in pain from time to time. The Kamboh glared sullenly from his corner; the lama was busy with his beads; and Kim, fumbling like a doctor at the man’s neck, plotted his plan between muttered prayers.

“Do you have a charm to change my shape? Otherwise I am a dead man. If I had been given five or ten minutes alone, without this rush, I might have—”

“Is he cured yet, miracle-worker?” asked the Kamboh jealously. “You have been chanting long enough.”

“No. There is no cure for his injuries that I can see, unless he sits for three days in the habit of a bairagi.” This was a common penance often imposed on wealthy traders by their spiritual teachers.

“One priest always tries to make another priest,” the Kamboh muttered. Like most deeply superstitious people, he could not resist mocking his own religion.

“Will your son be a priest, then? It is time he took another dose of my quinine.”

“We Jats are all stubborn as buffaloes,” said the Kamboh, softening once more.

Kim rubbed a fingertip dipped in bitter medicine onto the child’s trusting little lips. “I have asked for nothing,” he said sternly to the father, “except food. Do you begrudge me that? I am going to heal another man. Do I have your permission—Prince?”

The man’s huge hands flew up in supplication. “No—no. Do not mock me like that.”

“It pleases me to cure this sick man. You will gain merit by helping. What color of ash is in your pipe bowl? White. That is auspicious. Was there raw turmeric among your provisions?”

“I—I—”

“Open your bundle!”

It was the usual collection of small oddments: scraps of cloth, quack medicines, cheap trinkets, a bundle of coarse grayish native flour, twists of country tobacco, cheap pipe stems, and a packet of curry powder, all wrapped in a quilt. Kim turned them over with the air of a wise sorcerer, muttering a Mohammedan prayer.

“This is wisdom I learned from the Sahibs,” he whispered to the lama; and here, considering his training under Lurgan Sahib, he spoke nothing less than the truth. “There is a great evil in this man’s fortune, as shown by the stars, which—which troubles him. Shall I take it away?”

“Friend of the Stars, you have done well in all things. Let it be as you wish. Is this another healing?”

“Quick! Be quick!” gasped the Mahratta. “The train might stop.”

“A healing against the shadow of death,” said Kim, mixing the Kamboh’s flour with the charred tobacco ash in the red clay bowl of the pipe. E23, without a word, slipped off his turban and shook down his long black hair.

“That is my food—priest,” the Jat growled.

“A buffalo in the temple! Did you dare to look even this far?” said Kim. “I must perform mysteries before fools; but watch out for your eyes. Is there a film forming over them already? I save your baby, and in return you—how shameless!” The man flinched under Kim’s direct, earnest gaze.

“Shall I curse you, or shall I—” He picked up the outer cloth of the bundle and threw it over the Jat’s bowed head. “Just dare to think of peeking, and—and even I cannot save you. Sit! Keep quiet!”

“I am blind—dumb. Do not curse me! Co—come, child, let us play a hide-and-seek game. For my sake, do not look out from under the cloth.”

“I see hope,” said E23. “What is your plan?”

“This comes next,” said Kim, grabbing the man’s thin undershirt. E23 hesitated, showing all a North-Westerner’s aversion to stripping his upper body.

“What is caste to a cutthroat?” said Kim, tearing the shirt down to the waist. “We must turn you into a yellow-smeared Sadhu completely. Strip—strip quickly, and shake your hair over your eyes while I scatter the ash. Now, a caste-mark on your forehead.” He pulled his little Survey paint box and a cake of crimson lake from his tunic.

“Are you only a beginner?” asked E23, fighting literally for his dear life as he shed his remaining wraps and stood in a loincloth while Kim boldly splashed a caste-mark across his ash-smeared brow.

“I entered the Game only two days ago, brother,” Kim replied. “Smear more ash on your chest.”

“Have you met—the physician of sick pearls?” E23 whipped out his long, tightly wound turban cloth and, with lightning-fast hands, wrapped it around his loins into the intricate style of a Sadhu’s waist-cloth.

“Ha! Do you know his touch, then? He was my teacher for a while. We must cover your legs. Ash heals wounds. Smear it on again.”

“I was once his pride, but you are almost better. The Gods are good to us! Give me that.”

It was a small tin box of opium pills from the rubbish in the Jat’s bundle. E23 gulped down half a handful. “They are good against hunger, fear, and cold. And they make the eyes red, too,” he explained. “Now I will have the heart to play the Game. We only lack a Sadhu’s iron tongs. What about my old clothes?”

Kim rolled them into a tight bundle and stuffed them into the loose folds of his tunic. With a yellow-ochre paint cake, he smeared the man’s legs and chest with broad streaks over the background of flour, ash, and turmeric.

“The blood on them is enough to hang you, brother.”

“Maybe; but there is no need to throw them out the window... It is finished.” His voice thrilled with a boy’s pure delight in the Game. “Turn around and look, O Jat!”

“May the Gods protect us,” said the hooded Kamboh, emerging like a buffalo from the reeds. “But—where did the Mahratta go? What have you done?”

Kim had been trained by Lurgan Sahib, and E23, by the nature of his profession, was no bad actor. In place of the trembling, cringing trader, there now leaned against the corner an almost naked, ash-smeared, ochre-striped, dusty-haired Sadhu. His swollen eyes—opium takes effect quickly on an empty stomach—shone with insolence and wild lust, his legs crossed beneath him, Kim’s brown rosary around his neck, and a scant yard of worn, flowered chintz thrown over his shoulders. The child buried his face in his astonished father’s arms.

“Look up, little prince! We are traveling with wizards, but they will not hurt you. Oh, do not cry... What is the sense of curing a child one day only to frighten him half to death the next?”

“The child will be fortunate all his life. He has witnessed a great healing. When I was a child I used to make clay men and horses.”

“I made them too. Sir Banas comes in the night and brings them to life behind our kitchen rubbish heap,” piped the child.

“So you aren’t frightened of anything now, eh, Prince?”

“I was only frightened because my father was frightened. I felt his arms shaking.”

“Oh, you chicken-hearted man!” said Kim, and even the abashed Jat laughed. “I have performed a healing on this poor trader. He must abandon his profits and account books and sit by the roadside for three nights to overcome the malice of his enemies. The stars are against him.”

“The fewer moneylenders the better, I say; but Sadhu or no Sadhu, he ought to pay for my provisions he’s carrying.”

“Is that so? But that is your child on your shoulder—handed over to the cremation grounds not two days ago. There is one more thing. I performed this magic in your presence because the need was great. I changed his shape and his soul. Nevertheless, if by any chance, man from Jullundur, you ever mention what you have seen—either among the elders sitting under the village tree, in your own house, or with your priest when he blesses your cattle—a murrain will strike your buffaloes, fire will consume your thatch, rats will infest your grain bins, and the curse of our Gods will make your fields barren before your feet and behind your plow.” This was part of an old curse picked up from a faqir near the Taksali Gate back in Kim’s innocent days. It lost none of its power through repetition.

“Stop, Holy One! Have mercy, stop!” cried the Jat. “Do not curse my household! I saw nothing! I heard nothing! I am your cow!” And he lunged to grab Kim’s bare foot as it beat rhythmically against the carriage floor. “Since you allowed me to help you with a pinch of flour, a little opium, and such trifles as I honored by letting you use in your art, may the Gods return the blessing—” And he recited a long blessing he had learned from Lurgan Sahib.

The lama stared through his spectacles in a way he had not stared at the disguise process. “Friend of the Stars,” he said at last, “you have acquired great wisdom. Beware that it does not breed pride. No man who has the Law before his eyes speaks hastily of any matter he has witnessed or experienced.”

“No—no—no, indeed,” cried the farmer, terrified lest the master should try to improve upon the pupil. E23, his mouth slack, surrendered himself entirely to the opium that served him as meat, tobacco, and medicine.

And so, in an atmosphere of awed incomprehension, they slid into Delhi right around lamp-lighting time.

chapters.title: Chapter 12
chapters.content:
Who hath desired the Sea—the sight of salt-water unbounded?
The heave and the halt and the hurl and the crash of the comber wind-hounded?
The sleek-barrelled swell before storm—grey, foamless, enormous, and growing?
Stark calm on the lap of the Line—or the crazy-eyed hurricane blowing?
His Sea in no showing the same—his Sea and the same ’neath all showing—
His Sea that his being fulfils?
So and no otherwise—so and no otherwise
Hill-men desire their Hills!

The Sea and the Hills.

“I have found my heart again,” said E23, under cover of the platform’s tumult. “Hunger and fear make men dazed, or I might have thought of this escape before. I was right. They come to hunt for me. You have saved my head.”

A group of yellow-trousered Punjab policemen, led by a hot and perspiring young Englishman, parted the crowd around the carriages. Behind them, inconspicuous as a cat, ambled a small, fat person who looked like a lawyer’s tout.

“See the young Sahib reading from a paper. My description is in his hand,” said E23. “They go carriage by carriage, like fisher-folk netting a pool.”

When the procession reached their compartment, E23 was counting his beads with a steady jerk of his wrist, while Kim jeered at him for being so drugged as to have lost the ringed fire-tongs that are a Sadhu’s distinguishing mark. The lama, deep in meditation, stared straight ahead; and the farmer, glancing furtively, gathered up his belongings.

“Nothing here but a parcel of holy-bolies,” said the Englishman aloud, and passed on amid a ripple of uneasiness; for native police mean extortion to ordinary Indians all over the country.

“The trouble now,” whispered E23, “lies in sending a telegram about the place where I hid that letter I was sent to find. I cannot go to the telegraph office in this disguise.”

“Is it not enough that I saved your neck?”

“Not if the work is left unfinished. Did the healer of sick pearls never tell you that? Here comes another Sahib! Ah!”

This was a tall, sallow District Superintendent of Police—complete with belt, helmet, polished spurs, and all—strutting and twirling his dark moustache.

“What fools these police Sahibs are!” said Kim cheerfully.

E23 glanced up from under his eyelids. “It is well said,” he muttered in a changed voice. “I am going to drink water. Keep my place.”

He blundered out, almost running into the Englishman’s arms, and was cursed in clumsy Urdu.

“Tum mut? Are you drunk? You mustn’t barge about as though Delhi station belonged to you, my friend.”

E23, not moving a single muscle of his face, answered with a stream of the filthiest abuse, at which Kim naturally rejoiced. It reminded him of the drummer-boys and barrack-sweepers at Ambala during the terrible days of his first schooling.

“My good fool,” the Englishman drawled. “Nickle-jao! Go back to your carriage.”

Step by step, withdrawing deferentially and lowering his voice, the yellow Sadhu climbed back to the carriage, cursing the D.S.P. to the remotest posterity by—here Kim almost jumped—by the curse of the Queen’s Stone, by the writing under the Queen’s Stone, and by an assortment of Gods with entirely new names.

“I don’t know what you’re saying,” the Englishman flushed angrily, “but it’s some piece of blasted impertinence. Get out of here!”

E23, pretending to misunderstand, solemnly produced his ticket, which the Englishman wrenched angrily from his hand.

“Oh, zoolum! What oppression!” growled the Jat from his corner. “All for the sake of a joke, too.” He had been grinning at the freedom of the Sadhu’s tongue. “Your charms do not work well today, Holy One!”

The Sadhu followed the policeman, fawning and supplicating. The crowd of passengers, busy with their babies and bundles, had not noticed the affair. Kim slipped out behind him, for it flashed through his mind that he had heard this angry, stupid Sahib shouting personal remarks at an old lady near Ambala three years ago.

“It is well,” the Sadhu whispered, wedged in the calling, shouting, bewildered press—with a Persian greyhound between his feet and a cageful of yelling hawks under the charge of a Rajput falconer pressed against his lower back. “He has gone now to send word about the letter I hid. They told me he was in Peshawar. I might have known he is like the crocodile—always at the other ford. He has saved me from immediate danger, but I owe my life to you.”

“Is he also one of Us?” Kim ducked under a Mewar camel-driver’s greasy armpit and bumped into a flock of jabbering Sikh matrons.

“Not less than the greatest. We are both fortunate! I will report to him what you have done. I am safe under his protection.”

He pushed through the edge of the crowd besieging the carriages and squatted by the bench near the telegraph office.

“Go back, or someone will take your place! Have no fear for the work, brother—or for my life. You have given me breathing space, and Strickland Sahib has pulled me ashore. We may work together at the Game yet. Farewell!”

Kim hurried back to his carriage, elated, bewildered, but a little annoyed that he had no key to the secrets around him.

“I am only a beginner at the Game, that is certain. I could not have leaped into safety as the Sadhu did. He knew it was darkest right under the lamp. I would never have thought to pass on news under the pretense of cursing... and how clever the Sahib was! No matter, I saved a man’s life... Where has the Kamboh gone, Holy One?” he whispered as he took his seat in the now crowded compartment.

“Fear gripped him,” the lama replied with a touch of gentle malice. “He saw you change the Mahratta into a Sadhu in the twinkling of an eye as a protection against evil. That shook him. Then he saw the Sadhu fall straight into the hands of the police—all the result of your art. So he gathered up his son and fled; for he said that you turned a quiet trader into an impudent brawler with the Sahibs, and he feared a like fate. Where is the Sadhu?”

“With the police,” said Kim... “Yet I saved the Kamboh’s child.”

The lama took a pinch of snuff placidly.

“Ah, disciple, see how you are caught! You cured the Kamboh’s child solely to gain merit. But you cast a spell on the Mahratta out of pride—I watched you—and with sidelong glances to bewilder an old man and a foolish farmer, bringing calamity and suspicion in your wake.”

Kim controlled himself with an effort beyond his years. Like any other youngster, he did not like to swallow dirt or be misjudged, but he saw he was trapped. The train rolled out of Delhi into the night.

“It is true,” he murmured. “Where I have offended you, I have done wrong.”

“It is more than that, disciple. You have set an Act loose upon the world, and like a stone thrown into a pool, its consequences spread far beyond your knowing.”

This ignorance was fortunate both for Kim’s vanity and for the lama’s peace of mind, considering that at that very moment a coded telegram was being handed in at Simla reporting the arrival of E23 at Delhi and, more importantly, the location of the letter he had been ordered to abstract. Incidentally, an overzealous policeman had arrested—on a charge of murder committed in a far southern state—a horribly indignant Ajmer cotton-broker who was loudly explaining himself to Mr. Strickland on the Delhi platform, while E23 was slipping through back alleys into the locked heart of Delhi city. Within two hours, several telegrams had reached the angry minister of that southern state reporting that all trace of a somewhat bruised Mahratta had been lost; and by the time the leisurely train halted at Saharanpur, the final ripple of the stone Kim had helped to throw was lapping against the steps of a mosque in far-off Rome—where it disturbed a pious man at his prayers.

The lama performed his devotions with full ceremony near the dewy bougainvillea trellis beside the platform, cheered by the bright sunshine and the presence of his disciple.

“We will put these things behind us,” he said, pointing to the brass engine and the gleaming tracks. “The jolting of the train—though a wonderful thing—has turned my bones to water. We will use clean air from now on.”

“Let us go to the Kulu woman’s house,” said Kim, stepping out cheerfully under the weight of the bundles. Early morning around Saharanpur is clean and fragrant. He thought of other mornings at St. Xavier’s, which topped his already overflowing contentment.

“Where does this sudden haste come from? Wise men do not run about like chickens in the sun. We have come hundreds upon hundreds of miles already, and until now I have scarcely been alone with you for an instant. How can you receive instruction when jostled by crowds? How can I, overwhelmed by a flood of talk, meditate upon the Way?”

“Her tongue doesn’t grow any shorter with the years, then?” the disciple smiled.

“Nor her desire for charms. I remember once when I spoke of the Wheel of Life”—the lama fumbled in his tunic for his latest copy—“she was only curious about the devils that plague children. She shall gain merit by entertaining us—after a little while—on another occasion—softly, softly. Now we will wander freely, waiting upon the Chain of Things. The Search is sure.”

So they traveled very easily across and among the broad, blossoming fruit gardens—by way of Aminabad, Sahaigunge, Akrola of the Ford, and little Phulesa—with the line of the Siwalik Hills always to the north, and behind them the snow-capped mountains. After long, sweet sleep under the dry stars came the lordly, leisurely passage through a waking village—the begging bowl held forth in silence, but Kim’s eyes roving in defiance of the Rule from one edge of the sky to the other. Then Kim would return light-footed through the soft dust to his master resting under the shadow of a mango tree or the lighter shade of a white Doon siris tree, to eat and drink at leisure. At midday, after conversation and a short walk, they slept, meeting the world refreshed when the evening air grew cooler. Night found them venturing into new territory—some chosen village sighted three hours before across the fertile land and thoroughly discussed along the road.

There they told their stories—a new one every evening as far as Kim was concerned—and there they were made welcome, by either priest or headman, following the custom of the kindly East.

When the shadows shortened and the lama leaned more heavily upon Kim, there was always the Wheel of Life to pull out, lay flat beneath weighed stones, and explain cycle by cycle with a long straw. Here sat the Gods on high—mere dreams of dreams. Here was our Heaven and the world of the demi-Gods—horsemen fighting among the hills. Here were the agonies inflicted on beasts, souls ascending or descending the ladder and therefore not to be interfered with. Here were the Hells, hot and cold, and the abodes of tormented ghosts. The disciple would study the troubles arising from overeating—the bloated stomach and burning bowels—just as the lama directed. Obediently, with bowed head and a brown finger ready to follow the pointer, the disciple studied; but when they reached the Human World, busy and profitless, sitting just above the Hells, his mind would wander; for right by the roadside trundled the very Wheel itself—eating, drinking, trading, marrying, and quarreling, all vibrantly alive. Often the lama used these living pictures to illustrate his teachings, telling Kim—who was all too ready to listen—how the flesh assumes a thousand shapes, desirable or detestable as men reckon them, but in truth of no account either way; and how the foolish spirit, enslaved by the Hog, the Dove, and the Serpent—lusting after betel nut, a new yoke of oxen, women, or the favor of kings—is forced to follow the body through all the Heavens and Hells, right back around again. Sometimes a woman or a poor man, watching the ritual—for it was nothing less—as the great yellow chart was unfolded, would toss a few flowers or a handful of cowries upon its edge. It satisfied these humble souls simply to have met a Holy One who might remember them in his prayers.

“Cure them if they are sick,” the lama said when Kim’s adventurous instincts stirred. “Cure them if they have fever, but on no account work magic. Remember what befell the Mahratta.”

“Then all action is evil?” Kim replied, lying out under a big tree at the fork of the Doon road, watching tiny ants scurry across his hand.

“To abstain from action is good—except to acquire merit.”

“At the Gates of Learning we were taught that abstaining from action is unbefitting a Sahib. And I am a Sahib.”

“Friend of all the World,” the lama looked directly at Kim, “I am an old man—pleased by shows just as children are. To those who follow the Way, there is neither black nor white, Indian nor Tibetan. We are all souls seeking escape. No matter what wisdom you learned among the Sahibs, when we reach my River you will be freed from all illusion—at my side. Ah! My bones ache for that River, just as they ached in the train; but my spirit sits high above my bones, waiting. The Search is sure!”

“I am answered. Am I permitted to ask a question?”

The lama inclined his stately head.

“I ate your bread for three years—as you know. Holy One, where did it come from—?”

“There is much wealth, as men count it, in Tibet,” the lama replied calmly. “In my own place I hold the illusion of honor. I ask for what I need. I am not troubled by the accounts. That is for my monastery. Ah! The black high seats in the monastery, and the novices all in order!”

And he told stories, tracing patterns in the dust with his finger, about the immense and lavish rituals of cathedrals guarded by avalanches; of processions and devil-dances; of monks and nuns transformed into swine; of holy cities fifteen thousand feet in the air; of political intrigue between monasteries; of voices echoing among the hills; and of the mysterious mirage that dances across dry snow. He spoke even of Lhasa and of the Dalai Lama, whom he had seen and adored.

Each long, perfect day became another barrier behind Kim, cutting him off from his race and his mother tongue. He slipped back into thinking and dreaming in the vernacular, and mechanically followed the lama’s ceremonial customs regarding eating, drinking, and the like. The old man’s thoughts turned more and more toward his monastery as his eyes turned toward the steadfast snows. His River troubled him very little now. Occasionally, indeed, he would gaze long and intently at a tuft of grass or a twig, expecting, he said, the earth to split open and grant its blessing; but he was content just to be with his disciple, resting easily in the temperate breeze blowing down from the Doon valley. This was not Ceylon, nor Buddh Gaya, nor Bombay, nor some grass-tangled ruins he seemed to have stumbled upon two years ago. He spoke of those places like a scholar free of vanity, like a Seeker walking in humility, like a wise and temperate old man illuminating knowledge with brilliant insight. Bit by bit, disjointedly, each tale prompted by something along the roadside, he spoke of all his wanderings up and down India; until Kim, who had loved him without reason, now loved him for fifty good reasons. So they enjoyed themselves in high happiness, abstaining—as the Rule requires—from evil words and covetous desires; not overeating, not sleeping on high beds, nor wearing rich clothes. Their stomachs told them the time, and the people brought them their food, as the saying goes. They were lords of the villages of Aminabad, Sahaigunge, Akrola of the Ford, and little Phulesa, where Kim bestowed a blessing on the soulless woman.

But news travels fast in India, and all too soon a tall, white-whiskered servant—a lean, dry Oorya—shuffled across the fields carrying a basket of fruit, a box of Kabul grapes, and gilt oranges, begging them on behalf of his mistress to honor her with their presence; she was distressed in her mind that the lama had neglected her for so long.

“Now I remember,” the lama spoke as though it were a completely new thought. “She is virtuous, but an inordinate talker.”

Kim was sitting on the edge of a cow’s manger, telling stories to the village blacksmith’s children.

“She will only ask for another son for her daughter. I haven’t forgotten her,” he said. “Let her gain merit. Send word that we will come.”

They covered eleven miles through the fields in two days, and were overwhelmed with attention upon arrival; for the old lady maintained a grand tradition of hospitality, forcing it upon her son-in-law, who was dominated by his womenfolk and bought peace by borrowing from the moneylender. Age had neither weakened her tongue nor her memory, and from a discreetly barred upper window, within earshot of at least a dozen servants, she paid Kim compliments that would have sent a European audience into shocked dismay.

“But you are still the shameless beggar-brat of the traveler’s rest-house,” she shrilled. “I have not forgotten you. Wash yourselves and eat. The father of my daughter’s son has gone away for a while, leaving us poor women useless and silenced.”

To prove it, she scolded the entire household without mercy until food and drink were brought out; and in the evening—the smoke-scented evening, copper-brown and turquoise across the fields—she had her palanquin carried out into the untidy courtyard by smoky torchlight, where, behind curtains that were not drawn too closely, she gossiped away.

“Had the Holy One come alone, I would have received him differently; but with this rascal here, who can be too careful?”

“Maharanee,” said Kim, choosing his grandest title as usual, “is it my fault that none other than a Sahib—a police Sahib—called the Maharanee—whose face he—”

“Hush! That was on the pilgrimage. When we travel—you know the proverb.”

“—called the Maharanee a Breaker of Hearts and a Dispenser of Delights?”

“He actually remembered that! It was true, too. He certainly did. That was back when my beauty was in full bloom.” She chuckled like a contented parrot over a lump of sugar. “Now tell me of your comings and goings—as much as you can without shame. How many maidservants and whose wives are hanging upon your eyelashes? You hail from Benares? I would have gone there again this year, but my daughter—we only have two sons. Phew! Such is the effect of these low plains. Now up in Kulu the men are like elephants. But I want to ask your Holy One—step aside, rascal—for a charm against the most lamentable windy colic that attacks my daughter’s eldest every mango season. Two years ago he gave me a powerful spell.”

“Oh, Holy One!” said Kim, bubbling with laughter at the lama’s rueful face.

“It is true. I gave her one against wind.”

“Teeth—teeth—teeth!” snapped the old woman.

“‘Cure them if they are sick,’” Kim quoted with relish, “‘but on no account work magic. Remember what befell the Mahratta.’”

“That was two monsoons ago; she wore me out with her endless demands.” The lama groaned much like the unjust judge of scripture. “Thus it happens—take note, my disciple—that even those who strive to follow the Way are sidetracked by foolish women. For three whole days, while the child was sick, she talked to me.”

“Arre! And who else was I to talk to? The boy’s mother knew nothing, and the father—during the cold winter nights—‘Pray to the Gods,’ he would say, and then just roll over and snore!”

“I gave her the charm. What is an old man to do?”

“‘To abstain from action is well—except to acquire merit.’”

“Ah, disciple, if you desert me, I am all alone.”

“He cut his milk-teeth easily enough anyway,” said the old lady. “All priests are alike, though.”

Kim coughed severely. Being young, he did not approve of her flippancy. “To pester the wise out of season is to invite disaster.”

“There is a talking mynah bird,” the retort came back with the familiar snap of her jewelled forefinger, “over by the stables that has picked up the exact tone of the family priest. Maybe I am failing in respect to my guests, but if you had seen him press both fists into his belly—which looked like a half-grown gourd—and cry out, ‘Here is the pain!’ you would forgive me. I am half tempted to try the doctor’s medicine. He sells it cheap, and it certainly made him as fat as Shiva’s own bull. He doesn’t hold back remedies, but I had my doubts about the child because of the suspicious color of his bottles.”

Under cover of this monologue, the lama had slipped away quietly into the darkness toward his prepared room.

“You have angered him perhaps,” said Kim.

“Not he. He is just tired, and I forgot myself, being a grandmother. (No one but a grandmother should ever supervise a child; mothers are only good for bearing them.) Tomorrow, when he sees how my daughter’s son has grown, he will write the charm. Then he can judge the new doctor’s drugs as well.”

“Who is this doctor, Maharanee?”

“A wanderer like yourself, but a most sober Bengali from Dacca—a master of medicine. He cured me of a stomach obstruction after a heavy meal by means of a little pill that worked like a loose demon. He travels about now selling very valuable preparations. He even carries printed papers in English telling of all the things he has done for weak-backed men and slack women. He has been here four days; but hearing that you were coming—doctors and priests are like snake and tiger the world over—he has apparently gone into hiding.”

While she paused for breath after this tirade, the old servant, sitting unrebuked on the edge of the torchlight, muttered: “This house is like a cattle pound for all sorts of charlatans and priests. Let the boy stop eating mangoes... but who can argue with a grandmother?” Then he raised his respectful voice: “Sahiba, the doctor is sleeping after his meal. He is staying in the quarters behind the dovecot.”

Kim bristled like an eager terrier. To outface and outtalk a Calcutta-educated Bengali, a voluble Dacca drug-vendor, would be fine sport. It was not right that the lama, and by extension himself, should be pushed aside for such a man. He knew those bizarre, bastard English advertisements on the backs of native newspapers. St. Xavier’s boys sometimes smuggled them in to snigger over with their mates, for the language in which grateful patients recounted their symptoms was delightfully simple and revealing. The Oorya, not entirely unwilling to pit one parasite against the other, slunk off toward the dovecot.

“Yes,” said Kim with measured scorn. “Their entire stock-in-trade is a little colored water and a great deal of shamelessness. Their prey is broken-down kings and overfed Bengalis. Their profit comes from children who were never born.”

The old lady chuckled. “Don’t be envious. Charms are better, eh? I’ve never denied it. Just make sure your Holy One writes me a good amulet by morning.”

“None but the ignorant deny—” a thick, heavy voice boomed through the darkness as a figure stepped forward and sat down cross-legged—“none but the ignorant deny the value of charms. And none but the ignorant deny the value of medicines.”

“A rat found a piece of turmeric and said, ‘I’ll open a grocery store,’” Kim retorted.

Battle was fairly joined now, and they heard the old lady stiffen with attention.

“The priest’s boy knows the names of his nurse and three Gods. He says, ‘Listen to me, or I’ll curse you by the three million Great Ones.’” Clearly this invisible opponent had a few arrows in his quiver. He continued: “I am merely a teacher of the alphabet. I have mastered all the wisdom of the Sahibs.”

“The Sahibs never grow old. They dance and play like children even when they are grandfathers. A strong-backed breed,” piped the voice from inside the palanquin.

“I also carry remedies that clear the humors of the head in hot-tempered men. Sena leaves well compounded when the moon is in the proper House; I have yellow earths—arplan from China that makes a man renew his youth and astonish his household; saffron from Kashmir, and the finest salep from Kabul. Many people have died before—”

“That I can easily believe,” said Kim.

“They knew the value of my medicines. I do not offer my patients the mere ink in which a charm is written, but hot, powerful drugs that go down and wrestle with the evil.”

“Very mightily they do so,” sighed the old lady.

The voice launched into an immense tale of misfortune and bankruptcy, studded with numerous petitions to the Government. “But for my ill fate, which overrules everything, I would have been in Government service by now. I hold a degree from the great college at Calcutta—whither the son of this house will perhaps go one day.”

“He certainly will! If our neighbor’s brat can be made an F.A. after only a few years” (she used the English term she had heard so often), “how much more so will children as clever as those I know carry off prizes in rich Calcutta.”

“Never,” declared the voice, “have I seen such a child! Born under an auspicious star, and—except for that colic which, alas! if it turns to black bile, might carry him off like a pigeon—he is destined for many years. He is truly enviable.”

“Hai mai!” said the old lady. “It is unlucky to praise children, or I could listen to this talk. But the back of the house is unguarded, and even in this soft air men think themselves brave, and women, well, we know... The child’s father is away too, and I must act as watchman in my old age. Up! Up! Lift the palanquin! Let the doctor and the young priest settle between them whether charms or medicine are better. Ho, worthless people! Bring tobacco for the guests, and—I must go make my rounds of the homestead!”

The palanquin swung away, followed by scattering torches and a pack of barking dogs. Twenty villages knew the Sahiba—her failings, her sharp tongue, and her great charity. Twenty villages cheated her according to ancient custom, but no man would have dared to rob or steal within her jurisdiction for any prize under heaven. Nevertheless, she made a great show of her formal inspections, the noise of which could be heard halfway to Mussoorie.

Kim relaxed, as one expert does upon meeting another. The doctor, still squatting, slid his hookah over with a friendly foot, and Kim took a pull at the good weed. The hangers-on expected a grand professional debate and perhaps a little free medical advice.

“To discuss medicine before the ignorant is like teaching a peacock to sing,” remarked the doctor.

Kim echoed, “True courtesy is very often just inattention.”

These, it should be understood, were formal company manners designed to impress the crowd.

“Hi! I have an ulcer on my leg,” cried a kitchen scullion. “Look at it!”

“Get away! Begone!” said the doctor. “Is it the custom here to pester honored guests? You crowd around like buffaloes.”

“If the Sahiba knew—” Kim began.

“Ai! Ai! Come away. They are food for our mistress. When her young Shaitan’s colic is cured, perhaps we poor people will be allowed to—”

“The mistress fed your wife when you were in jail for cracking the moneylender’s head. Who are you to speak against her?” The old servant curled his white mustache fiercely in the young moonlight. “I am responsible for the honor of this house. Go!” And he drove the underlings before him.

Said the doctor, scarcely moving his lips: “How do you do, Mister O’Hara? I am jolly glad to see you again.”

Kim’s hand clenched around the pipe stem. On the open road anywhere else, he might not have been surprised; but here, in this quiet backwater of life, he was completely unprepared for Hurree Babu.

“Ah ha! I told you at Lucknow—resurgam—I shall rise again and you will not know me. How much did you bet—eh?”

He chewed leisurely on a few cardamom seeds, though he breathed rather uneasily.

“But why come here, Babuji?”

“Ah! That is the question, as Shakespeare has it. I came to congratulate you on your extraordinarily efficient performance at Delhi. Oh! I tell you, we are all proud of you. It was very neat and handy. Our mutual friend is an old friend of mine. He has been in some dangerously tight places. Now he’ll be in a few more. He told me; I told Mr. Lurgan; and he is pleased you graduated so nicely. The whole Department is pleased.”

For the first time in his life, Kim thrilled to the clean pride (which can nonetheless be a deadly pitfall) of departmental praise—praise from an equal for work appreciated by fellow workers. Earth holds nothing quite comparable to it. But, reminded the Oriental within him, Babus do not travel far just to hand out compliments.

“Tell your tale, Babu,” Kim said authoritatively.

“Oh, it is nothing. Only I was at Simla when the telegram came in about what our mutual friend said he had hidden, and old Creighton—” He glanced to see how Kim would take this piece of boldness.

“The Colonel Sahib,” the boy from St. Xavier’s corrected.

“Of course. He found me at a loose end, and I had to go down to Chittor to find that beastly letter. I do not like the South—too much railway travel—but I drew a good traveling allowance. Ha, ha! I met our mutual friend at Delhi on his way back. He is lying quiet just now and says the Sadhu disguise suits him down to the ground. Well, there I heard what you did so well, so quickly, upon the spur of the moment. I told our mutual you took the bally bun, by Jove! It was splendid. I came to tell you so.”

“Umm!”

The frogs were busy in the ditches, and the moon was sliding toward the horizon. Some happy servant had gone outside to commune with the night and beat upon a drum. Kim’s next sentence was in the vernacular.

“How did you follow us?”

“Oh! That was nothing. I knew from our mutual friend that you were going to Saharanpur. So I came on. Red Lamas are not inconspicuous people. I bought my drug box, and I really make a very good doctor. I went to Akrola of the Ford, heard all about you, and talked here and there. All the common people know what you did. I knew when the hospitable old lady sent the palanquin. They have great recollections of the old lama’s visits here. I knew old ladies couldn’t keep their hands off medicines. So I became a doctor, and—did you hear my talk? I think it was very good. My word, Mister O’Hara, the common people know about you and the lama for fifty miles around. So I came. Do you mind?”

“Babuji,” said Kim, looking up at the broad, grinning face, “I am a Sahib.”

“My dear Mister O’Hara—”

“And I hope to play the Great Game.”

“You are subordinate to me departmentally at present.”

“Then why talk like a monkey in a tree? Men don’t chase after someone from Simla and change their clothes just for a few sweet words. I am not a child. Talk Hindi and let’s get to the yolk of the egg. You are here—not speaking one word of truth in ten. Why are you here? Give me a straight answer.”

“That is so very disconcerting of the Europeans, Mister O’Hara. You should know a heap better at your time of life.”

“But I want to know,” Kim laughed. “If it’s the Game, I might be able to help. How can I do anything if you babble all over the place?”

Hurree Babu reached for the pipe and sucked it until it gurgled.

“Now I will speak vernacular. You sit tight, Mister O’Hara... It concerns the pedigree of a white stallion.”

“Still? That was finished long ago.”

“When everyone is dead, the Great Game is finished. Not before. Listen to me until the end. There were Five Kings who prepared a sudden war three years ago, when you were given the stallion’s pedigree by Mahbub Ali. Because of that news, and before they were ready, our Army fell upon them.”

“Yes—eight thousand men with guns. I remember that night.”

“But the war wasn’t pushed. That is the Government’s custom. The troops were recalled because the Government believed the Five Kings were frightened into submission, and it isn’t cheap to feed men among the high mountain passes. Hilas and Bunar—Rajas with guns—contracted for a price to guard the passes against anyone coming from the North. They professed both fear and friendship.” He broke off with an English giggle: “Of course, I tell you this unofficially to elucidate the political situation, Mister O’Hara. Officially, I am debarred from criticizing the actions of my superiors. Now I continue.—This pleased the Government, which was anxious to avoid expenses, and a bond was made for so many rupees a month stipulating that Hilas and Bunar should guard the passes as soon as the state’s troops were withdrawn. At that time—after you and I met—I, who had been selling tea in Leh, became an accounts clerk in the Army. When the troops pulled back, I was left behind to pay the coolies building new roads in the Hills. That road-making was part of the agreement between Bunar, Hilas, and the Government.”

“So? And then?”

“I tell you, it was jolly bloody cold up there after summer,” Hurree Babu said confidentially. “I was afraid these Bunar men would cut my throat every night for the pay chest. My native sepoy guard just laughed at me! By Jove, I was such a cowardly fellow. Never mind that. I’ll go on colloquially... I sent word many times that these two Kings were sold to the North; and Mahbub Ali, who was even farther North, fully confirmed it. Nothing was done. Only my toes froze and one dropped off. I sent word that the roads I was paying coolies to dig were actually being built for the feet of strangers and enemies.”

“For whom?”

“For the Russians. It was an open joke among the coolies. Then I was called down to report what I knew in person. Mahbub came South too. And see the outcome! Over the passes this year after the snow melted”—he shivered again—“two strangers came disguised as hunters shooting wild goats. They carry guns, but they also carry chains, leveling instruments, and compasses.”

“Aha! Things are getting clearer.”

“They were well received by Hilas and Bunar. They made grand promises, speaking as the mouthpiece of an Emperor bearing gifts. Up the valleys and down the valleys they went, saying, ‘Here is a place to build a breastwork; here you can pitch a fort. Here you can hold the road against an army’—the very roads for which I was paying out rupees every month. The Government knows, but does nothing. The other three Kings, who were not paid to guard the passes, sent word by runners about the bad faith of Bunar and Hilas. When all the damage is done, mind you—when these two strangers with their levels and compasses convince the Five Kings that a massive army will sweep through the passes tomorrow or the next day (mountain people are all fools)—the order finally comes to me, Hurree Babu: ‘Go North and see what those strangers are doing.’ I told Creighton Sahib, ‘This isn’t a lawsuit where we go around collecting evidence.’ ” Hurree slipped back into English: “ ‘By Jove,’ I said, ‘why the deuce don’t you issue semi-official orders to some brave man to poison them as an example? It is, if you’ll pardon the observation, most reprehensible laxity on your part.’ And Colonel Creighton just laughed at me! That is all your beastly English pride. You think nobody would ever dare to conspire! It’s all utter nonsense.”

Kim smoked slowly, turning the whole business over in his sharp mind.

“Then you are going out to follow the strangers?”

“No. To meet them. They are coming down to Simla to send their hunting trophies to be mounted in Calcutta. They are strictly sporting gentlemen, and they are granted special facilities by the Government. Naturally, we always do that. It is our British pride.”

“Then what is there to fear from them?”

“By Jove, they aren’t black people. I can handle all sorts of things with black people, of course. These are Russians, and highly unscrupulous individuals. I—I don’t want to consort with them without a witness.”

“Will they kill you?”

“Oh, that’s nothing. I’m enough of a Herbert Spencerian, I trust, to face a little thing like death, which is simply part of my fate, you know. But—but they might beat me.”

“Why?”

Hurree Babu snapped his fingers in irritation. “Of course I shall attach myself to their camp in a supernumerary capacity—perhaps as an interpreter, or a simple-minded, starving fellow, or something of the sort. Then I’ll pick up what I can, I suppose. That’s as easy for me as playing doctor to the old lady. Only—only, you see, Mister O’Hara, I am unfortunately an Asian, which is a serious disadvantage in certain respects. And also I am a Bengali—a cowardly fellow.”

“God made the hare and the Bengali. Where is the shame in that?” said Kim, quoting the proverb.

“It was a process of evolution, I think, from Primal Necessity, but the fact remains when you consider cui bono. I am, oh, awfully frightened! I remember once they wanted to cut off my head on the road to Lhasa. (No, I never actually reached Lhasa.) I sat down and cried, Mister O’Hara, imagining all sorts of Chinese tortures. I don’t suppose these two gentlemen will torture me, but I like to provide for possible contingencies with European assistance in an emergency.” He coughed and spat out the cardamom seeds. “It’s a purely unofficial request, to which you can say ‘No, Babu.’ If you have no pressing business with your old man—perhaps you could divert him; perhaps I can capture his fancy—I would like you to stay in departmental touch with me until I find those sporting coves. I have a great opinion of you since I met my friend at Delhi. Furthermore, I will include your name in my official report when the matter is finally settled. It will be a great feather in your cap. That’s why I really came here.”

“Hmm! The end of the story is true enough, I think, but what about the beginning?”

“About the Five Kings? Oh, there is ever so much truth in it. A lot more than you’d suppose,” Hurree said earnestly. “You’ll come—eh? I’m going straight from here into the Doon. It is very green and full of pleasant meadows. I’ll go to Mussoorie—good old Mussoorie Pahar, as the gentry say. Then via Rampur into Chini. That’s the only route they can take. I don’t like waiting in the cold, but we must wait for them. I want to walk alongside them to Simla. You see, one of the Russians is a Frenchman, and I know my French pretty well. I have friends in Chandernagore.”

“He would certainly rejoice to see the Hills again,” Kim said thoughtfully. “All his talk these past ten days has been of little else. If we go together—”

“Oh! We can be complete strangers on the road if your lama prefers. I’ll just stay four or five miles ahead. There’s no hurry for Hurree—that’s a European pun, ha, ha!—and you can follow after. There’s plenty of time; they’ll be plotting, surveying, and mapping, of course. I’ll leave tomorrow, and you can start the next day if you choose. Eh? Think it over until morning. By Jove, it’s almost morning now.” He yawned heavily and lumbered off toward his sleeping place without another polite word. But Kim slept very little, and his thoughts ran in Hindustani:

“Well is the Game called great! I was a scullion at Quetta for four days, waiting on the wife of the man whose book I stole. And that was part of the Great Game! From the South—God knows how far—the Mahratta came up playing the Great Game in fear of his life. Now I will go far, far into the North playing the Great Game. Truly, it runs like a shuttle through the whole fabric of India. And my share and my joy”—he smiled into the darkness—“I owe to the lama here. Also to Mahbub Ali—and to Creighton Sahib, but chiefly to the Holy One. He is right—it is a great and wonderful world—and I am Kim—Kim—Kim—alone—just one person—right in the middle of it all. But I will see these strangers with their levels and chains...”

“What was the outcome of last night’s chatter?” the lama asked after finishing his prayers.

“A strolling medicine vendor appeared—a hanger-on of the Sahiba’s. I got rid of him through arguments and logic, proving that our charms are worthier than his colored waters.”

“Alas, my charms! Is that virtuous woman still set on getting a new one?”

“Most stubbornly.”

“Then it must be written, or she will deafen me with her clamor.” He fumbled for his pen case.

“Down in the Plains,” said Kim, “there are always far too many people. In the Hills, as I understand, there are fewer.”

“Ah, the Hills, and the snow upon the Hills!” The lama tore off a tiny square of paper just large enough for an amulet. “But what do you know of the Hills?”

“They are very close.” Kim pushed open the door and looked at the long, peaceful line of the Himalayas glowing in the morning gold. “Except when dressed as a Sahib, I have never set foot among them.”

The lama sniffed the wind wistfully.

“If we go North,”—Kim put the question to the waking sunrise—“wouldn’t we avoid a lot of the midday heat by walking among the lower hills at least?... Is the charm made, Holy One?”

“I have written the names of seven silly devils—not one of whom is worth a grain of dust in the eye. That is how foolish women drag us away from the Way!”

Hurree Babu emerged from behind the dovecot, brushing his teeth with elaborate ceremony. Plump, heavy-haunched, bull-necked, and deep-voiced, he didn’t look like a “cowardly fellow” at all. Kim gave a scarcely perceptible nod to show that matters were progressing well, and when his morning toilet was finished, Hurree Babu came over with flowery speech to pay his respects to the lama. They ate apart, of course, and afterward the old lady, more or less veiled behind her window, returned to the vital matter of green-mango colics in her grandson. The lama’s knowledge of medicine was naturally only sympathetic; he believed that the dung of a black horse, mixed with sulphur and carried in a snakeskin, was a reliable remedy for cholera, but the symbolism interested him far more than the science. Hurree Babu deferred to these views with charming politeness, prompting the lama to call him a courteous physician. Hurree Babu replied that he was no more than an unskilled dabbler in the mysteries, but at least—and he thanked the Gods for it—he knew when he was sitting in the presence of a master. He himself had been trained by Sahibs who spared no expense in the lordly halls of Calcutta; but, as he was always first to acknowledge, there lay a wisdom beyond earthly wisdom—the high, lonely lore of meditation. Kim looked on with envy. The Hurree Babu of his past acquaintance—oily, effusive, and nervous—was gone; gone, too, was the brazen drug-vendor of the night before. There remained a polished, polite, attentive, sober, and learned son of experience and adversity, gathering wisdom from the lama’s lips.

The old lady confided to Kim that these elevated philosophical heights were quite beyond her. She preferred charms with plenty of ink that you could wash off in water, swallow, and be done with. Otherwise, what was the use of the Gods? She liked real men and women, and she loved to talk about them—the petty kings she had known in the past; her own youth and beauty; the depredations of leopards and the eccentricities of Asian romance; taxes, rack-renting, funeral ceremonies, her son-in-law (alluding to him in ways easily followed), the rearing of the young, and the total lack of decency in the younger generation. And Kim, just as interested in the life of this world as she was in leaving it, squatted with his feet tucked under the hem of his robe, drinking it all in, while the lama systematically demolished one medical theory after another put forward by Hurree Babu.

At noon the Babu strapped up his brass-bound medicine box, tucked his patent-leather court shoes under one arm, opened a gay blue-and-white umbrella with the other, and set off northward toward the Doon, where he said his services were in great demand among the minor chieftains of those parts.

“You are going to the Hills? And by the Kulu road? Oh, thrice happy!” shrilled the old lady. “If I weren’t so tied down with running the household, I’d take a palanquin... but that would be shameless, and my reputation would be ruined. Ho, ho! I know that road—every single march of it. You’ll find charity all along—it’s never denied to a good-looking face. I’ll give orders for provisions. Do you want a servant to start you on your way? No? Then at least I will cook you some good food.”

“What a woman the Sahiba is!” said the white-bearded Oorya when a commotion arose near the kitchen quarters. “She never forgets a friend, and she never forgets an enemy in all her years. And her cooking—wah!” He rubbed his slender stomach.

There were cakes, sweets, and cold fowl stewed to rags with rice and prunes—enough to burden Kim like a mule.

“I am old and useless,” she said. “No one loves me now, and no one respects me—yet there are few who can match me when I call upon the Gods and sit down at my cooking pots. Come back again, O people of good will. Holy One and disciple, come back. My room is always prepared; my welcome is always ready... Make sure the women don’t follow your disciple too openly. I know the women of Kulu. Take care, disciple, that he doesn’t run away when he smells his Hills again... Hey! Don’t tilt the rice bag upside down... Bless the household, Holy One, and forgive your servant her foolishness.”

She wiped her red, aged eyes on the corner of her veil and clucked in her throat.

“Women talk,” the lama said at last, “but that is a woman’s weakness. I gave her a charm. She is bound to the Wheel and wholly given over to the illusions of this life; but nevertheless, disciple, she is virtuous, kindly, hospitable—with a whole and zealous heart. Who is to say she does not gain merit?”

“Not I, Holy One,” said Kim, readjusting the generous provisions over his shoulders. “In my mind—behind my eyes—I have tried to picture someone like her completely freed from the Wheel—desiring nothing, causing nothing—a nun, as it were.”

“And, you little rogue?” The lama almost laughed aloud.

“I can’t picture it.”

“Nor can I. But there are many, many millions of lives before her. She will gain a little wisdom, perhaps, in each one.”

“And will she forget how to make saffron stews along that road?”

“Your mind dwells on unworthy things. But she has skill. I feel refreshed all over. Once we reach the lower hills I shall grow even stronger. The doctor spoke truly this morning when he said a breath from the snows blows twenty years off a man’s life. We will go up into the Hills—the high hills—up to the sound of snow-fed waters and rustling trees—for a little while. The doctor said we could return to the Plains at any time, since we are only skirting the pleasant places. He is full of learning, yet he has no pride at all. I spoke to him—while you were talking to the Sahiba—about a certain dizziness that seizes the back of my neck at night, and he said it arose from excessive heat, to be cured by cool air. Upon reflection, I marveled that I hadn’t thought of such a simple remedy myself.”

“Did you tell him of your Search?” asked Kim, a little jealously. He preferred to guide the lama himself rather than through the wiles of Hurree Babu.

“Assuredly. I told him of my dream, and how I gained merit by having you taught wisdom.”

“You didn’t tell him I was a Sahib?”

“What need? I have told you many times we are merely two souls seeking escape. He said—and he is quite right in this—that the River of Healing will break forth just as I dreamed, at my feet if need be. Once you have found the Way, you see, which frees me from the Wheel, do I need to trouble myself about the mere fields of earth, which are nothing but illusion? That would be senseless. I have my dreams, repeated night after night; I have the Jataka tales; and I have you, Friend of all the World. It was written in your horoscope that a Red Bull on a green field—I haven’t forgotten—would bring you to honor. Who but I saw that prophecy fulfilled? Indeed, I was the instrument. You are destined to find my River for me, being in return my instrument. The Search is sure!”

He turned his ivory-yellow face, serene and untroubled, toward the beckoning Hills; his shadow stretched far out before him in the dust.

chapters.title: Chapter 13
chapters.content:
Who hath desired the Sea—the immense and contemptuous surges?
The shudder, the stumble, the swerve ere the star-stabbing bowsprit merges—
The orderly clouds of the Trades and the ridged roaring sapphire thereunder—
Unheralded cliff-lurking flaws and the head-sails’ low-volleying thunder?
His Sea in no wonder the same—his Sea and the same in each wonder—
His Sea that his being fulfils?
So and no otherwise—so and no otherwise hill-men desire their hills!

The Sea and the Hills.

“Who goes to the hills goes to his mother.”

They had crossed the Siwaliks and the half-tropical Doon valley, left Mussoorie behind them, and headed north along the narrow mountain roads. Day after day they plunged deeper into the piled-up mountains, and day after day Kim watched the lama regain a man’s full strength. Among the terraces of the Doon he had leaned on the boy’s shoulder, glad to rest at every turn. Below the great slope rising to Mussoorie, however, he had pulled himself together like an old hunter facing a well-remembered bank; and where he should have sunk exhausted, he swung his long draperies about him, drew a deep double lungful of the crystal air, and walked as only a hillman can. Kim, raised on the plains and fed on the plains, sweated and panted in sheer astonishment. “This is my country,” said the lama. “Compared to Such-zen, this is flatter than a rice field”; and with steady, powerful strides from the hips, he marched upward. But it was on the steep downhill marches—dropping three thousand feet in three hours—that he completely outpaced Kim, whose back ached from holding himself back and whose big toe was nearly severed by the string of his grass sandal. Through the dappled shadows of great deodar forests; past oak trees feathered and plumed with ferns, birch, holly, rhododendron, and pine; out onto the bare, sun-baked, slippery grass of the hillsides, and back into the cool woodlands again until oak gave way to bamboo and valley palms—the lama strode on untiringly.

Glancing back in the twilight at the massive ridges behind them and the thin, faint line of the road they had traveled, he would plan out, with a hillman’s broad vision, fresh marches for the morrow; or, pausing in the notch of some high pass looking toward Spiti and Kulu, he would stretch out his hands yearningly toward the distant snow peaks. At dawn, those peaks flared a windy red against stark blue as Kedarnath and Badrinath—the kings of that wilderness—caught the first sunlight. All day long they lay like molten silver under the sun, and at evening put on their jewels again. At first they breathed gently upon the travelers, winds that were welcome when scrambling over some gigantic ridge; but after a few days, at an altitude of nine or ten thousand feet, those breezes had a sharp bite, and Kim gladly let a village of hillmen gain merit by giving him a rough blanket coat. The lama was mildly surprised that anyone could object to the knife-edged breezes that had stripped years off his shoulders.

“These are only the lower hills, disciple. There is no real cold until we reach the true Hills.”

“Air and water are good, and the people are devout enough, but the food is terrible,” Kim growled; “and we walk as if we were crazy—or English. It freezes at night, too.”

“A little, perhaps; but only enough to make old bones rejoice in the sun. We must not always crave soft beds and rich food.”

“We might at least stay on the road.”

Kim had all a plainsman’s fondness for the well-trodden track, less than six feet wide, that wound among the mountains; but the lama, being Tibetan, could not resist taking short cuts over spurs and across gravel-covered slopes. As he explained to his limping disciple, a man raised among mountains can foresee the course of a mountain road; and though low-lying clouds might trouble a stranger taking short cuts, they made no difference at all to a thoughtful man. Thus, after long hours of what would count as serious mountaineering in civilized countries, they would pant over a saddleback, sidle past a few landslips, and drop straight down through the forest at a forty-five-degree angle back onto the road. Along their path lay the villages of the hill folk—mud and earth huts with timbers occasionally carved roughly with an axe—clinging like swallows’ nests against the steep cliffs, huddled on tiny flats halfway down a three-thousand-foot slope, wedged into corners between cliffs that funneled and focused every stray gust of wind, or, for the sake of summer pasture, cowering down on a mountain neck that in winter would be buried ten feet deep in snow. And the people—the sallow, greasy, rough-clad folk with short bare legs and faces almost like Eskimos—would crowd out and worship. The Plains—kindly and gentle—had treated the lama merely as a holy man among others. But the Hills worshipped him as one possessing the confidence of all their local spirits. Their religion was an almost vanished Buddhism overlaid with a nature worship as fantastic as their own landscape and as intricate as the terracing of their tiny fields; yet they recognized the big hat, the clicking rosary, and the rare Chinese texts as marks of supreme authority, and they deeply respected the man beneath the hat.

“We saw you come down over the black Breasts of Eua,” said a Betah man who gave them cheese, sour milk, and stone-hard bread one evening. “We don’t use that path often—except when calving cows stray in the summer. There is a sudden wind among those rocks that knocks men down even on the calmest day. But what do such people care for the Devil of Eua!”

Then Kim—aching in every muscle, dizzy from looking down, and footsore from jamming his toes into inadequate cracks—felt the true joy of the march; the kind of joy a St. Xavier’s boy who had won the quarter-mile flat race might feel upon hearing the praises of his friends. The hills sweated the butter and sugar fat right out of his bones; the dry air, gasped in at the crests of cruel passes, expanded and strengthened his upper ribs; and the steep inclines built hard new muscles in his calves and thighs.

They meditated often on the Wheel of Life—all the more because, as the lama said, they were free from its visible temptations. Except for a gray eagle, an occasional distant bear grubbing and rooting on the hillside, the vision of a furious painted leopard seen at dawn devouring a goat in a quiet valley, and now and then a brightly colored bird, they were completely alone with the winds and the singing grass. The women in the smoky huts over whose roofs the two walked as they descended the mountains were unlovely and unclean, sharing many husbands and afflicted with goiter. The men were woodcutters when not farming—meek and of an incredible simplicity. But so that proper conversation should not fail, Fate sent across their path the courteous Dacca physician, who paid for his food with ointments good for goiter and advice that restored peace between husbands and wives. He seemed to know these hills as well as he knew the hill dialects, and advised the lama on the lay of the land toward Ladakh and Tibet. He remarked that they could return to the Plains at any time, but meanwhile, for those who loved mountains, that road had its amusements. This information was not given all at once, but during evening chats on stone threshing floors when, his patients tended, the doctor would smoke and the lama take snuff, while Kim watched tiny cows grazing on the housetops or let his soul follow his eyes across the deep blue gulfs between range and range. There were also private talks in the dark woods when the doctor went searching for herbs and Kim, acting as a budding physician, had to accompany him.

“You see, Mister O’Hara, I don’t know what the deuce I shall do when I finally find our sporting friends; but if you will kindly stay within sight of my umbrella, which serves as a fixed point for a cadastral survey, I shall feel much better.”

Kim looked out across the chaotic sea of peaks. “This is not my country, doctor. It would be easier, I think, to find a single louse in a bear skin.”

“Oh, that is my strong point. There is no hurry for Hurree. They were at Leh not so long ago. They said they came down from the Karakorum with their heads and horns and all. I am only afraid they may have sent back all their letters and compromising papers from Leh into Russian territory. Of course, they will travel as far east as possible—just to prove they were never in the Western States. You don’t know the Hills?” He scratched a mark in the dirt with a twig. “Look! They ought to have come in through Srinagar or Abbottabad. That is their short route—down the river through Bunji and Astor. But they’ve caused trouble in the West. So”—he drew a furrow from left to right—“they march and march all the way east to Leh (ah, it’s cold there!), down the Indus to Hanle (I know that road), and then down, you see, into the Bushahr and Chini valley. That is figured out by elimination, and also by asking questions of the people I cure so well. Our friends have spent a long time roaming around and making an impression, so they are well known from afar. You’ll see me catch them somewhere in the Chini valley. Please keep your eye on the umbrella.”

It nodded like a wind-blown harebell down the valleys and around the mountain sides, and in due time the lama and Kim—navigating by compass—would catch up to it as it vended ointments and powders at dusk. “We came by such and such a path!” the lama would gesture carelessly back toward the ridges, and the umbrella would burst into compliments.

They crossed a snowy pass in the cold moonlight when the lama, teasing Kim good-naturedly, sank up to his knees in snow like a Bactrian camel—that mountain-bred, shaggy sort seen in the Kashmir serai. They waded across patches of soft snow and shale powdered with white, taking shelter from a gale in a camp of Tibetans hurrying down small sheep laden with bags of borax. They emerged onto grassy shoulders still speckled with snow, and passed through forests out onto grassy meadows again. Despite all their marching, Kedarnath and Badrinath remained unimpressed; and it was only after days of travel that Kim, standing on some minor ten-thousand-foot mound, could see that a shoulder or horn of the two great peaks had—ever so slightly—shifted its outline.

At last they entered a world within a world—a vast valley where the towering hills seemed mere rubble and debris swept from the knees of the greater mountains. Here a day’s march seemed to take them no farther than a dreamer moves in a nightmare. They skirted a rocky spur for hours, only to find it was merely a minor outcrop on an outlying buttress of the main range! A rounded meadow, once reached, revealed itself as a massive tableland stretching far into the valley. Three days later, that same tableland was just a dim fold in the earth far to the south.

“Surely the Gods live here!” said Kim, overwhelmed by the silence and the massive sweep of cloud shadows after rain. “This is no place for men!”

“Long and long ago,” said the lama, speaking almost to himself, “the Lord was asked whether the world was everlasting. To this the Excellent One made no reply... When I was in Ceylon, a wise Seeker confirmed that from the scriptures written in Pali. Naturally, since we know the way to Freedom, such questions are unprofitable, but—look, and recognize illusion, disciple! These are the true Hills! They are like my hills near Such-zen. There never were hills like these!”

Far above them, immensely high, the earth towered toward the snow line where, stretching from east to west across hundreds of miles as straight as if drawn with a ruler, the last sturdy birches ended. Above that, in upheaved cliffs and blocks, the naked rock fought to thrust its head above the white smother. Higher still, unchanged since the world began yet shifting with every mood of sun and cloud, lay the eternal snow. They could see dark bluffs and smears across its face where storms and mountain squalls whirled about. Below them, as they stood, the forest plunged down in a sheet of blue-green for mile upon mile; below the forest lay a village sprinkled among terraced fields and steep pastures. Below the village they knew—though a thunderstorm rumbled and growled there for the moment—another fifteen-hundred-foot drop led to the moist valley where streams gather to form the young Sutlej River.

As usual, the lama had led Kim along cow paths and side trails, far from the main route where Hurree Babu, that “fearful man,” had trudged three days before through a storm that nine Englishmen out of ten would have avoided. Hurree was no hunter—the snap of a rifle made him change color—but, as he would have put it, he was a “fairly efficient stalker,” and he had scanned the huge valley with cheap binoculars to good purpose. Moreover, the white of worn canvas tents against green vegetation carries a long way. Hurree Babu had seen all he needed to see while sitting on the threshing floor of Ziglaur, twenty miles away as the eagle flies and forty by road—that is to say, two tiny dots that one day were just below the snow line and the next had drifted downward perhaps six inches on the hillside. Once his mind was made up to work, his fat, bare legs could cover a surprising amount of ground; and this was why, while Kim and the lama sheltered in a leaky hut at Ziglaur waiting out the storm, an oily, wet, but ever-smiling Bengali—speaking the best English with the most absurd phrases—was ingratiating himself with two soaked and rather rheumatic foreigners.

He had arrived, full of wild schemes, right on the heels of a lightning strike that had split a pine tree near their camp. This had so convinced a dozen or two impressed baggage coolies that the day was cursed for travel that they had dropped their loads and refused to budge. They were subjects of a hill rajah who hired out their services for private profit, and to make matters worse, the strange Sahibs had already threatened them with rifles. Most of them knew rifles and Sahibs of old—they were trackers and hunters of the northern valleys, skilled in following bear and wild goat—but they had never been treated like this before.
