So the forest swallowed them up, and despite all threats and shouting, refused to give them back. There was no need for him to pretend madness—the Babu had thought of another way to secure a warm welcome. He wrung out his wet clothes, slipped on his patent-leather shoes, opened his blue-and-white umbrella, and with a mincing gait and a heart pounding against his ribs, presented himself: “Agent for His Royal Highness, the Rajah of Rampur, gentlemen. What can I do for you, please?”

The gentlemen were delighted. One was visibly French, the other Russian, but they spoke English nearly as well as the Babu. They begged for his assistance. Their native servants had fallen sick back at Leh. They had hurried on because they wanted to bring their hunting trophies to Simla before the skins were ruined by moths. They carried a general letter of introduction (the Babu salaamed to it orientally) addressed to all Government officials. No, they hadn’t met any other hunting parties en route. They cooked for themselves, carried plenty of supplies, and only wished to push on as quickly as possible. At this, Hurree intercepted a cowering hillman among the trees, and after three minutes of talk and a little silver (one cannot be economical when on State service, though Hurree’s heart bled at the waste), the eleven coolies and three hangers-on reappeared. At the very least, the Babu would be a witness to their oppression.

“My royal master, he will be much annoyed, but these people are only common folks and grossly ignorant. If your honors will kindly overlook this unfortunate affair, I shall be very pleased. In a little while the rain will stop and we can proceed. You have been shooting, eh? That is a fine performance!”

He skipped nimbly from one kilta basket to the next, pretending to adjust each conical burden. Englishmen are not usually familiar with Asians, but this was a kind Babu who had accidentally upset a basket with a red oilcloth cover, so they wouldn’t strike him across the wrist. On the other hand, they wouldn’t offer a drink to a Babu, however friendly, nor invite him to share a meal. The strangers did none of these things, but asked many questions—mostly about women—to which Hurree returned gay and unstudied replies. They offered him a glass of whitish fluid like gin, and then another; and soon his grave demeanor vanished. He became deeply treasonous, speaking with sweeping indecency about a Government that had forced a white man’s education upon him while neglecting to provide a white man’s salary. He babbled tales of oppression and injustice until tears ran down his cheeks for the miseries of his homeland. Then he staggered off, singing love songs of Lower Bengal, and collapsed upon a wet tree trunk. Never was such an unfortunate product of British rule in India thrust so unhappily upon foreigners.

“They are all cut from that same pattern,” one sportsman remarked to the other in French. “When we get into India proper, you’ll see. I should like to visit his Rajah. We might put in a good word there. It’s possible he has heard of us and wishes to show his goodwill.”

“We haven’t time. We must reach Simla as soon as possible,” his companion replied. “For my part, I wish our reports had already been sent back from Hilas or even Leh.”

The English postal service is safer and better. Remember we are given every facility—and, by God, they give them to us! Is it unbelievable stupidity?”

“It is pride—pride that deserves and will receive punishment.”

“Yes! To fight a fellow European at our own game is something. There’s a risk attached, but these people—bah! It’s too easy.”

“Pride—all pride, my friend.”

“Now what on earth is the use of Chandernagore being so close to Calcutta,” Hurree muttered, snoring open-mouthed on the wet moss, “if I can’t understand their French? They talk so particularly fast! It would have been much better to just cut their bloody throats.”

When he presented himself again, he was racked with a headache—penitent, and volubly terrified that in his drunkenness he might have been indiscreet. He loved the British Government; it was the source of all prosperity and honor, and his master in Rampur held the exact same view. At this, the men began to mock him and throw his own words back at him, until step by step, with deprecating smirks, oily grins, and leers of infinite cunning, the poor Babu was forced out of his defenses and compelled to speak the truth. When Lurgan was told the story later, he mourned aloud that he hadn’t been in the place of those stubborn, indifferent coolies who, with grass mats over their heads and raindrops pooling in their footprints, had waited out the weather. All the Sahibs they usually knew—rough-clad men returning joyously year after year to their favorite valleys—brought servants, cooks, and orderlies, very often hillmen. These Sahibs traveled without any retinue at all. Therefore they were poor Sahibs and ignorant ones, for no Sahib in his right mind would follow a Bengali’s advice. But the Bengali, appearing from nowhere, had given them money and could make shift with their dialect. Accustomed to general abuse from their own countrymen, they suspected a trap and stood ready to bolt at the first opportunity.

Then, through the freshly washed air steaming with delicious earth smells, the Babu led the way down the slopes—walking ahead of the coolies with pride, and following behind the foreigners with humility. His thoughts were varied and numerous. The least of them would have fascinated his companions beyond words. But he was an agreeable guide, always eager to point out the beauties of his royal master’s domain. He populated the hills with whatever game they wished to hunt—thar, ibex, markhor, and bear by the grace of God. He discoursed on botany and ethnology with unimpeachable inaccuracy, and his store of local legends—remember, he had been a trusted state agent for fifteen years—was bottomless.

“Decidedly this fellow is an original,” said the taller of the foreigners. “He is like the nightmare of a Viennese courier.”

“He represents India in miniature during a period of transition—the monstrous hybridism of East and West,” the Russian replied. “It is we who know how to deal with Orientals.”

“He has lost his own country and hasn’t acquired another. But he has a most complete hatred of his conquerors. Just listen to what he confided to me last night,” said the other.

Beneath the striped umbrella, Hurree Babu was straining his ears and brain to follow the rapidly spoken French, keeping both eyes fixed on a basket full of maps and documents—an extra-large one with a double red oilcloth cover. He had no wish to steal anything; he merely wanted to know what to steal, and incidentally how to make off with it afterward. He thanked all the Gods of Hindustan and Herbert Spencer that there were still valuables left to steal.

On the second day the road climbed steeply to a grassy spur above the forest; and it was there, around sunset, that they came upon an aged lama—though they called him a bonze—sitting cross-legged over a mysterious chart held down by stones, explaining it to a young man of striking, if unwashed, beauty. The striped umbrella had been spotted half a march away, and Kim had suggested pausing until it caught up with them.

“Ha!” said Hurree Babu, resourceful as Puss in Boots. “That is an eminent local holy man. Probably a subject of my royal master.”

“What is he doing? It looks very curious.”

“He is explaining a holy picture—all hand-drawn.”

The two men stood bareheaded in the low afternoon sunlight stretching across the golden grass. The sullen coolies, glad of the halt, dropped their loads and sat down.

“Look!” said the Frenchman. “It is like a scene from the birth of a religion—the first teacher and the first disciple. Is he a Buddhist?”

“Of some debased sort,” the other answered. “There are no true Buddhists in the Hills. But look at the folds of his robes. And his eyes—how insolent! Why does looking at him make us feel like such a young people?” The speaker struck savagely at a tall weed. “We haven’t left our mark anywhere yet. Nowhere! That, you see, is what troubles me.” He scowled at the placid face and monumental calm of the pose.

“Have patience. We shall make our mark together—we and you young people. In the meantime, draw his picture.”

The Babu stepped forward grandly, his posture entirely out of keeping with his deferential words and his wink toward Kim.

“Holy One, these are Sahibs. My medicines cured one of a stomach ailment, and I am going to Simla to oversee his recovery. They wish to see your picture—”

“To heal the sick is always good. This is the Wheel of Life,” said the lama, “the very one I showed you in the hut at Ziglaur when the rain fell.”

“And to hear you explain it.”

The lama’s eyes lit up at the prospect of new listeners. “To expound the Most Excellent Way is good. Do they know any Hindi, like the Keeper of Images?”

“A little, perhaps.”

At that, simply as a child engrossed in a new game, the lama threw back his head and began the full-throated invocation of the Doctor of Divinity before launching into the full doctrine. The strangers leaned on their alpenstocks and listened. Kim, squatting humbly, watched the red sunlight on their faces and the blending and parting of their long shadows. They wore un-English leggings and curious belted coats that reminded him vaguely of the illustrations in a book in the St. Xavier’s library—The Adventures of a Young Naturalist in Mexico, it was called. Yes, they looked very much like the wonderful M. Sumichrast from that tale, and nothing at all like the “highly unscrupulous folk” of Hurree Babu’s imagination. The coolies, earth-colored and silent, crouched reverently twenty or thirty yards away, while the Babu—the loose cloth of his outfit snapping like a marker flag in the chilly breeze—stood by with an air of happy proprietorship.

“These are the men,” Hurree whispered while the ritual continued and the two white men followed the grass blade sweeping from Hell to Heaven and back again. “All their books are in that large basket with the red top—books, reports, and maps—and I’ve seen a king’s letter written by either Hilas or Bunar. They guard it most carefully. They’ve sent nothing back from Hilas or Leh. That’s certain.”

“Who is with them?”

“Only the forced-labor coolies. They have no servants. They are so secretive they cook their own food.”

“What am I supposed to do?”

“Wait and see. Only if any chance comes my way, you’ll know where to look for the papers.”

“Those would be safer in Mahbub Ali’s hands than a Bengali’s,” Kim said scornfully.

“There are more ways of winning a sweetheart than by breaking down the door.”

“See here the Hell appointed for avarice and greed, flanked on one side by Desire and on the other by Weariness.” The lama warmed to his subject, and one of the strangers sketched him quickly in the fading light.

“That’s enough,” the man said abruptly at last. “I can’t understand him, but I want that picture. He’s a better artist than I am. Ask him if he’ll sell it.”

“He says no, sir,” the Babu replied. The lama, of course, would no more have parted with his chart to a random traveler than an archbishop would pawn the sacred vessels of his cathedral. All Tibet was full of cheap reproductions of the Wheel, but the lama was an artist as well as a wealthy abbot in his own monastery.

“Perhaps in three days, or four, or ten, if I see that the Sahib is a Seeker and of good understanding, I may draw him another. But this one was used for the initiation of a novice. Tell him that, doctor.”

“He wants it right now—for money.”

The lama shook his head slowly and began to roll up the Wheel. The Russian saw nothing more than a dirty old man haggling over a filthy piece of paper. He pulled out a handful of rupees and half-jestingly snatched at the chart, which tore in the lama’s grip. A low murmur of horror rose from the coolies—some of whom were Spiti men and, by their standards, good Buddhists. The lama rose at the insult; his hand went to the heavy iron pen case that served as a priest’s weapon, and the Babu danced in agony.

“Now you see—you see why I wanted witnesses! They are highly unscrupulous people. Oh, sir! Sir! You must not hit a holy man!”

“Disciple! He has defiled the Written Word!”

It was too late. Before Kim could stop him, the Russian struck the old man square in the face. The next instant he was rolling over and over down the hill with Kim at his throat. The blow had awakened every dormant Irish devil in the boy’s blood, and the sudden fall of his enemy did the rest. The lama dropped to his knees, half-stunned; the coolies with their loads fled up the hill as fast as plainsmen run across level ground. They had witnessed unspeakable sacrilege, and it behooved them to get away before the Gods and demons of the hills took vengeance. The Frenchman rushed toward the lama, fumbling for his revolver with some vague idea of making him a hostage. A shower of sharp stones—hillmen are remarkably accurate marksmen—drove him back, and a coolie from Ao-chung swept the lama along in the stampede. Everything happened as swiftly as sudden mountain darkness.

“They’ve taken the baggage and all the guns!” yelled the Frenchman, firing blindly into the twilight.

“All right, sir! All right! Don’t shoot. I’m coming to rescue you!” and Hurree, crashing down the slope, threw his weight bodily upon the delighted and astonished Kim, who was currently banging his breathless foe’s head against a boulder.

“Go back to the coolies,” the Babu whispered in his ear. “They have the baggage. The papers are in the basket with the red top, but check everything. Take their papers, especially the king’s letter. Go! The other man is coming!”

Kim scrambled uphill. A revolver bullet sang off a rock nearby, and he ducked like a startled partridge.

“If you shoot,” Hurree shouted, “they’ll come down and wipe us out! I’ve rescued the gentleman, sir. This is particularly dangerous.”

“By Jove!” Kim thought furiously in English. “This is a damned tight spot, but I think it’s self-defense.” He felt inside his tunic for Mahbub’s gift, and uncertainly—having fired only a few practice shots in the Bikaner desert—pulled the trigger.

“What did I tell you, sir?” The Babu seemed near tears. “Come down here and help revive him. We’re all up a tree, I tell you.”

The shooting stopped. There was the sound of stumbling feet, and Kim hurried upward through the gloom, swearing like a cat—or a country-bred native.

“Were you wounded, disciple?” the lama called from above him.

“No. And you?” Kim dived into a thicket of stunted firs.

“Unhurt. Come away. We are going with these people to Shamlegh-under-the-Snow.”

“Not before we’ve done justice,” another voice cried out. “I’ve got the Sahibs’ guns—all four of them. Let’s go down.”

“He struck the Holy One—we all saw it! Our cattle will go barren—our wives will stop bearing children! The snows will slide down upon us on our way home... And on top of all their other oppression!”

The small fir clump filled with clamoring coolies—panic-stricken and capable of anything in their terror. The man from Ao-chung impatiently clicked the bolt of a rifle and made as if to head back down.

“Wait a little, Holy One; they can’t get far. Wait until I come back,” he said.

“It is this person who suffered the wrong,” said the lama, placing a hand over his brow.

“For that very reason.”

“If this person overlooks it, your hands are clean. Furthermore, you gain merit through obedience.”

“Wait, and we will all go to Shamlegh together,” the man insisted.

For a moment—just as long as it takes to shove a cartridge into a breech-loader—the lama hesitated. Then he rose to his feet and laid a hand on the man’s shoulder.

“Have you heard? I say there shall be no killing—I who was Abbot of Such-zen. Do you have any desire to be reborn as a rat, or a snake under the eaves, or a worm in the belly of the lowest beast? Is it your wish to—”

The man from Ao-chung dropped to his knees, for the voice rang out like a Tibetan devil-gong.

“Ai! Ai!” cried the Spiti men. “Don’t curse us—don’t curse him! It was only his zeal, Holy One!... Put down that rifle, fool!”

“Anger upon anger! Evil upon evil! There will be no killing. Let the priest-beaters go bound by their own acts. Just and sure is the Wheel, never swerving a hair! They will be reborn many times—in torment.” His head drooped, and he leaned heavily on Kim’s shoulder.

“I have come close to great evil, disciple,” he whispered in the dead silence beneath the pines. “I was tempted to loose the bullet; and truly, in Tibet there would have been a slow and heavy death for them... He struck me across the face... upon the flesh...” He slid to the ground, breathing heavily, and Kim could hear his overtaxed heart thumping and skipping beats.

“Have they hurt him to the death?” asked the Ao-chung man while the others stood in silence.

Kim knelt over the body in sheer terror. “No,” he cried passionately, “this is only exhaustion.” Then he remembered he was a white man, with a white man’s emergency supplies at hand. “Open the baskets! The Sahibs might have medicine.”

“Oho! Then I know it,” laughed the Ao-chung man. “I was Yankling Sahib’s hunter for five years without learning about that medicine. I’ve tasted it myself. Look!”

He pulled a bottle of cheap whisky—the kind sold to explorers at Leh—from his tunic and expertly forced a little between the lama’s teeth.

“That’s what I did when Yankling Sahib twisted his ankle beyond Astor. Aha! I’ve already looked through their baskets—but we’ll make a fair division at Shamlegh. Give him a little more. It’s good medicine. Feel! His heart is beating better now. Lay his head down and rub a little on his chest. If he’d waited quietly while I settled the Sahibs, none of this would have happened. But perhaps the Sahibs will chase us here. In that case, wouldn’t it be right to shoot them with their own guns, eh?”

“One of them has been paid back already, I think,” Kim muttered between his teeth. “I kicked him in the groin as we went downhill. I only wish I’d killed him!”

“It’s easy to be brave when you don’t live in Rampur,” remarked another man whose hut was within a few miles of the Rajah’s ramshackle palace. “If we get a bad name with the Sahibs, no one will hire us as hunters again.”

“Oh, but these aren’t English Sahibs—not jolly fellows like Fostum Sahib or Yankling Sahib. They’re foreigners—they can’t speak English like real Sahibs.”

At that moment the lama coughed and sat up, groping for his rosary.

“There shall be no killing,” he murmured. “Just is the Wheel! Evil upon evil—”

“No, Holy One. We are all here.” The Ao-chung man timidly patted the lama’s feet. “Except by your command, no one shall be harmed. Rest awhile. We’ll make a small camp here, and later, when the moon rises, we’ll move on to Shamlegh-under-the-Snow.”

“After a blow,” a Spiti man said sagely, “it is best to sleep.”

“There is, as it were, a dizziness at the back of my neck and a pinching sensation. Let me rest my head on your lap, disciple. I am an old man, yet not entirely free from passion... We must ponder the Cause of Things.”

“Give him a blanket. We dare not light a fire in case the Sahibs see it.”

“We’d better get away to Shamlegh. Nobody will follow us there.” This was the nervous Rampur man speaking.

“I have been Fostum Sahib’s hunter, and I am Yankling Sahib’s hunter. I should be with Yankling Sahib right now if not for this cursed forced labor. Let two men watch below with the guns in case the Sahibs try any more foolishness. I am staying right here with this Holy One.”

They sat down a little apart from the lama and, after listening intently for a while, passed around a water pipe made from an old Day and Martin blacking bottle. The glow of the red charcoal as it was passed from hand to hand illuminated their narrow, blinking eyes, high Chinese cheekbones, and thick bull necks melting into the dark woolen folds around their shoulders. They looked like goblins from some magical mine—mountain gnomes in council. While they talked, the sound of the surrounding snow-fed streams began to fade as the night frost choked and clogged the trickling channels.

“How he stood up to us!” a Spiti man said admiringly. “I remember an old ibex near Ladakh that Dupont Sahib missed on a shoulder shot seven seasons ago, standing just like him. Dupont Sahib was a good hunter.”

“Not as good as Yankling Sahib.” The Ao-chung man took a pull from the whisky bottle and passed it on. “Now listen to me—unless anyone else thinks he knows better.”

Nobody took up the challenge.

“We go to Shamlegh when the moon rises. There we will divide the baggage fairly among us. I am satisfied with this new little rifle and all its cartridges.”

“Are the bears the only trouble on your land?” asked another companion, puffing at the pipe.

“No; but musk pods are worth six rupees apiece now, and your women can use the tent canvas and some of the cooking gear. We’ll sort it all out at Shamlegh before dawn. Then we all go our separate ways, remembering that we never saw or worked for these Sahibs, who might otherwise claim we stole their baggage.”

“That’s fine for you, but what will our Rajah say?”

“Who is going to tell him? Those Sahibs who can’t speak our language, or the Babu who gave us money for his own purposes? Is he going to lead an army against us? What evidence is left? Whatever we don’t need we’ll throw onto the Shamlegh garbage heap, where no man has ever set foot.”

“Who is at Shamlegh this summer?” The place consisted of merely three or four grazing huts.

“The Woman of Shamlegh. She has no love for Sahibs, as we well know. The others can be bought off with small presents; and there’s more than enough here for all of us.” He patted the rounded side of the nearest basket.

“But—but—”

“I told you they aren’t real Sahibs. All their skins and heads were bought in the bazaar at Leh. I recognize the marks. I pointed them out to you last march.”

“True. They were all store-bought skins and heads. Some of them even had moths in them.”

That was a convincing argument, and the Ao-chung man knew his audience.

“If worst comes to worst, I’ll tell Yankling Sahib, who has a merry disposition, and he’ll just laugh. We aren’t doing any wrong to any Sahibs we know. They are priest-beaters. They frightened us, and we fled! Who knows where we dropped the baggage? Do you think Yankling Sahib will let down-country police wander all over the hills disrupting his game? It’s a long way from Simla to Chini, and even farther from Shamlegh to the Shamlegh garbage heap.”

“So be it, but I’m carrying the big basket. The one with the red top that the Sahibs packed themselves every morning.”

“That proves it,” the Shamlegh man argued craftily. “That they are Sahibs of no consequence. Who ever heard of Fostum Sahib, or Yankling Sahib, or even little Peel Sahib who sits up nights to shoot serow—I ask you, who ever heard of such Sahibs coming into the hills without a down-country cook, a bearer, and all manner of well-paid, high-handed, oppressive followers? How can they make trouble? What about the basket?”

“Nothing, except that it’s full of the Written Word—books and papers they wrote in, and strange instruments like those used for worship.”

The Shamlegh garbage heap can take them all.

“True! But what if we offend the Sahibs’ Gods by doing that? I don’t like handling the Written Word that way. And their brass idols are beyond my understanding. It’s no plunder for simple hill folk.”

“The old man is still sleeping. Quiet! Let’s ask his disciple.” The Ao-chung man refreshed himself again, swelling with the pride of leadership.

“We have here,” he whispered, “a basket whose contents we don’t know.”

“But I do,” Kim said cautiously. The lama was breathing in deep, easy slumber, and Kim had been thinking of Hurree’s final instructions. As a player of the Great Game, he felt a sudden surge of respect for the Babu. “It’s a basket with a red top full of very wonderful things, not to be handled by fools.”

“I said so; I said so!” cried the bearer of that burden. “Do you think it will bring bad luck upon us?”

“Not if it is given to me. I know how to control its magic. Otherwise it will cause great harm.”

“A priest always wants his share.” The whisky was loosening the Ao-chung man’s judgment.

“It makes no difference to me,” Kim answered with the native craft of his upbringing. “Share it among yourselves and see what happens!”

“Not I. I was only joking. Give the command. There’s more than enough for everyone. We’ll be on our way from Shamlegh at dawn.”

They discussed and re-discussed their simple plans for another hour while Kim shivered with cold and excitement. The humor of the situation tickled both the Irish and the Oriental sides of his soul. Here were the agents of the dreaded Northern Power—very likely as important in their own country as Mahbub Ali or Colonel Creighton—suddenly left helpless. One of them, he knew privately, would limp for a while. They had made grand promises to kings. Tonight they were stranded somewhere below him, without charts, food, tents, or guns—and, apart from Hurree Babu, without a guide. And this collapse of their Great Game (Kim wondered who they would eventually report to), this panicky flight into the night, had come about through no clever trick of Hurree’s or scheming of Kim’s, but simply, beautifully, and inevitably, much like the capture of Mahbub’s fakir friends by the zealous young policeman at Ambala.

“They are down there with nothing; and by Jove, it’s cold! I’m up here with all their gear. Oh, they’re going to be furious! I almost feel sorry for Hurree Babu.”

Kim could have saved his pity, for though at that exact moment the Bengali was suffering acutely in the flesh, his spirit was puffed up and lofty. A mile down the hill on the edge of the pine forest, two half-frozen men—one violently sick at intervals—were alternating between mutual recriminations and the most vitriolic abuse of the Babu, who seemed nearly paralyzed with terror. They demanded a plan of action. He explained that they were extremely lucky to be alive; that their coolies, if not currently hunting them down, had vanished beyond recall; that his master the Rajah was ninety miles away and, far from lending them money and an escort for the journey to Simla, would certainly clap them in prison if he heard they had struck a priest. He enlarged upon this sin and its dreadful consequences until they ordered him to change the subject. Their only hope, he said, was an unostentatious flight from village to village until they reached civilization; and, dissolving in tears for the hundredth time, he asked the high stars why the Sahibs “had beaten holy man.”

Ten steps would have taken Hurree into the rustling gloom completely out of their reach—toward the shelter and food of the nearest village, where glib-tongued doctors were scarce. Yet he preferred to endure the cold, the hunger, the harsh words, and the occasional blows in the company of his esteemed employers. Crouched against a tree trunk, he sniffed dolefully.

“And have you considered,” asked the uninjured man angrily, “what kind of spectacle we will present wandering through these hills among these savages?”

Hurree Babu had been thinking of little else for hours, but the remark wasn’t directed at him.

“We can’t wander! I can hardly walk,” groaned Kim’s victim.

“Perhaps the holy man will show mercy in his loving-kindness, sir, otherwise—”

“I promise myself a special pleasure in emptying my revolver into that young bonze the next time we meet,” came the unchristian reply.

“Revolvers! Vengeance! Bonzes!” Hurree crouched lower. The war was flaring up again. “Have you no regard for our loss? The baggage! The baggage!” He could hear the speaker literally dancing on the grass. “Everything we carried! Everything we secured! Our gains! Eight months of work! Do you know what that means? ‘Decidedly it is we who can deal with Orientals!’ Oh, you’ve done brilliantly.”

They launched into a fresh argument in several languages, and Hurree smiled in the dark. Kim was with the baskets, and inside those baskets lay eight months of fine diplomacy. There was no way to communicate with the boy, but Kim could be trusted. For the rest, Hurree could manage the journey through the hills so that Hilas, Bunar, and four hundred miles of mountain roads would tell the story for a generation. Men who cannot control their own coolies are held in low regard in the Hills, and the hillman possesses a very sharp sense of humor.

“If I had done it myself,” Hurree thought, “it couldn’t have turned out better; and, by Jove, now that I think of it, of course I arranged the whole thing myself. How quick-witted I am! I thought of it the moment I ran downhill! The outrage was accidental, but only I could have worked it—ah—for all it was damn well worth. Just consider the moral effect on these ignorant people! No treaties—no papers—no written documents at all—and me interpreting the whole thing for them. How I’ll laugh with the Colonel! I wish I had their papers too; but you can’t occupy two places in space simultaneously. That is axiomatic.”

chapters.title: Chapter 14
chapters.content:
My brother kneels (so saith Kabir) To stone and brass in heathen wise, But in my brother’s voice I hear My own unanswered agonies. His God is as his Fates assign— His prayer is all the world’s—and mine.

KABIR.

At moonrise the cautious coolies set off. The lama, refreshed by his sleep and the alcohol, needed only Kim’s shoulder to guide him—a silent, swift-striding man. They held the grass-covered, shale-sprinkled slope for an hour, swept around the shoulder of an eternal cliff, and climbed into a new region entirely cut off from any view of the Chini valley. A massive pasture climbed upward in a fan shape toward the permanent snows. At its base lay perhaps half an acre of flat land holding a few dirt and timber huts. Behind them—perched on the edge of the abyss, as hill dwellings often are—the ground dropped straight down two thousand feet to the Shamlegh rubbish heap, where no human foot had ever trod.

The men made no move to divide the plunder until they had settled the lama in the best room of the place, with Kim massaging his feet in the Muslim fashion.

“We will send food,” said the man from Ao-chung, “and the red-topped carrying basket. By dawn there will be no one left to give evidence either way. If anything in the basket is not needed—look here!”

He pointed through the window—which opened into empty space filled with moonlight reflected off the snow—and threw out an empty whisky bottle.

“No need to listen for it to land. This is the edge of the world,” he said, and went out. The lama looked out, with a hand on each window frame, his eyes shining like yellow opals. From the vast pit before him, white peaks rose up, yearning toward the moonlight. Everything else was as dark as interstellar space.

“These,” he said slowly, “are truly my Hills. This is how a man should live, perched above the world, far from worldly pleasures, contemplating vast matters.”

“Yes; if he has a disciple to prepare his tea, fold a blanket for his head, and chase away wandering cows.”

A smoky lamp burned in a wall niche, but the full moonlight overpowered it; and in this mixed light, bending over the food bag and cups, Kim moved like a tall ghost.

“Ah! But now that the adrenaline has worn off, my head still throbs and pounds, and there is a tight band around the back of my neck.”

“No wonder. It was a heavy blow. May he who struck it—”

“If not for my own passions, there would have been no evil.”

“What evil? You saved the Englishmen from the death they deserved a hundred times over.”

The lesson is not well learned, disciple.” The lama settled onto a folded blanket as Kim went forward with his evening routine. “The blow was merely a shadow upon a shadow. Evil in itself—my legs grow weary quickly these latter days!—it encountered evil within me: anger, rage, and a desire to return evil. These stirred in my blood, raised a tumult in my stomach, and blurred my hearing.” Here he drank scalding black tea ceremonially, taking the hot cup from Kim’s hand. “Had I been free of passion, the evil blow would have caused only bodily harm—a scar or a bruise—which is an illusion. But my mind was not at peace, for a desire immediately rushed in to let the Spiti men kill. In fighting that desire, my soul was torn and wrenched beyond a thousand blows. Not until I repeated the Blessings” (he meant the Buddhist Beatitudes) “did I achieve calm. But the evil planted in me by that moment’s carelessness must run its course. Just is the Wheel, never swerving a hair! Learn the lesson, disciple.”

“It is too deep for me,” Kim muttered. “I am still entirely shaken. I am glad I hurt the man.”

“I felt that, sleeping upon your knees in the woods below. It disturbed me in my dreams—the evil in your soul reaching into mine. Yet on the other hand”—he loosened his prayer beads—“I have gained merit by saving two lives—the lives of those who wronged me. Now I must look into the Cause of Things. The boat of my soul is staggering.”

“Sleep, and regain your strength. That is the wisest course.”

“I am meditating. There is a need greater than you know.”

Until dawn, hour after hour, as the moonlight faded on the high peaks and the once-black hillsides turned into soft green forests, the lama stared fixedly at the wall. From time to time he groaned. Outside the barred door, where confused cows came to look for their old stable, Shamlegh and the coolies surrendered themselves to plunder and wild living. The man from Ao-chung was their leader, and once they opened the Englishmen’s tinned food and found it very good, they knew they could not turn back. The Shamlegh kitchen rubbish heap took the baggage.

When Kim, after a night of bad dreams, crept out to brush his teeth in the morning chill, a fair-skinned woman wearing turquoise-studded headgear drew him aside.

“The others have gone. They left you this carrying basket, as promised. I do not like Englishmen, but you will make us an amulet in return for it. We do not want little Shamlegh to get a bad reputation because of the—accident. I am the Woman of Shamlegh.” She looked him over with bold, bright eyes, unlike the usual shy glances of mountain women.

“Certainly. But it must be done in secret.”

She lifted the heavy carrying basket as if it were a toy and hauled it into her own hut.

“Go out and bar the door! Let no one come near until it is finished,” Kim said.

“But afterward—may we talk?”

Kim tipped the carrying basket onto the floor, sending out a cascade of surveying instruments, books, diaries, letters, maps, and strangely scented native correspondence. At the very bottom lay an embroidered bag containing a sealed, gilded, and illuminated document, the kind one king sends to another. Kim caught his breath with delight and assessed the situation from an Englishman's point of view.

“I don’t want the books. Besides, they are logarithms—surveying, I suppose.” He laid them aside. “I don’t understand the letters, but Colonel Creighton will. They must all be kept. The maps—they draw better maps than I do—of course. All the native letters—oho!—and especially the official missive.” He sniffed the embroidered bag. “That must be from Hilás or Bunár, and Hurree Babu spoke the truth. By Jove! It is a fine haul. I wish Hurree could know... The rest must go out the window.” He fingered a superb prismatic compass and the shiny top of a theodolite. But after all, an Englishman cannot easily steal, and these items might become inconvenient evidence later. He sorted out every scrap of manuscript, every map, and the native letters. They formed one soft bundle. The three locked, leather-backed books, along with five worn pocketbooks, he set aside.

“The letters and the missive I must carry inside my coat and under my belt, and the handwritten books I must put in the food bag. It will be very heavy. No, I don’t think there is anything else. If there is, the coolies threw it down the ravine, so that is all right. Now you go too.” He repacked the basket with everything he intended to throw away and heaved it up onto the windowsill. A thousand feet below lay a long, lazy, rounded bank of mist, untouched as yet by the morning sun. A thousand feet below that was a hundred-year-old pine forest. He could see the green treetops looking like a bed of moss when a breeze thinned the clouds.

“No! I don’t think anyone will go after you!”

The spinning basket spilled its contents as it fell. The theodolite struck a jutting cliff ledge and shattered like a shell; the books, inkstands, paintboxes, compasses, and rulers flashed like a swarm of bees for a few seconds. Then they vanished; and though Kim leaned halfway out the window and strained his young ears, not a single sound rose from the abyss.

“Five hundred—a thousand rupees couldn’t buy them,” he thought sorrowfully. “It was very wasteful, but I have all their other stuff—everything they did, I hope. Now how on earth am I to tell Hurree Babu, and what on earth am I to do? And my old man is sick. I must tie up the letters in oilskin. That is something to do first, otherwise they will get soaked with sweat... And I am all alone!” He bound them into a neat packet, pressing down the stiff, sticky oilskin at the corners, for his roaming life had made him as methodical as an old hunter on the trail. Then, with extra care, he packed the books away at the bottom of the food bag.

The woman knocked at the door.

“But you haven't made any amulet,” she said, looking around.

“There is no need.” Kim had completely forgotten the need for a little charm-talk. The woman laughed irreverently at his confusion.

“None—for you. You can cast a spell with just the wink of an eye. But think of us poor people when you are gone. They were all too drunk last night to listen to a woman. You aren’t drunk, are you?”

“I am a priest.” Kim had recovered his composure, and since the woman was far from unattractive, he decided to maintain his professional dignity.

“I warned them that the Englishmen will be angry and will launch an investigation and report it to the Rajah. The Babu is with them too. Clerks have long tongues.”

“Is that all your trouble?” The plan formed completely in Kim’s mind, and he smiled dazzlingly.

“Not all,” said the woman, holding out a hard, brown hand covered with turquoises set in silver.

“I can finish that in a breath,” he went on quickly. “The Babu is the very doctor (you’ve heard of him?) who was wandering through the hills near Ziglaur. I know him.”

“He will tell for the sake of a reward. Englishmen can’t tell one hillman from another, but Babus have an eye for men—and women.”

“Carry a message to him from me.”

“There is nothing I wouldn't do for you.”

He accepted the compliment calmly, as men must in lands where women make the advances, tore a leaf from a notebook, and with an indelible copying pencil wrote in rough Shikast—the script bad little boys use to write rude words on walls: “I have everything they wrote: their pictures of the country, and many letters. Especially the missive. Tell me what to do. I am at Shamlegh-under-the-Snow. The old man is sick.”

“Take this to him. It will completely shut his mouth. He can’t have gone far.”

“Indeed no. They are still in the forest across the ridge. Our children went to watch them when the light came and shouted the news as they moved.”

Kim looked astonished; but from the edge of the sheep pasture floated a shrill, kite-like trill. A child tending cattle had picked it up from a brother or sister on the far side of the slope overlooking the Chini valley.

“My husbands are also out there gathering wood.” She drew a handful of walnuts from her bodice, cracked one neatly, and began to eat. Kim feigned absolute ignorance.

“Don’t you know the meaning of the walnut, priest?” she asked coyly, handing him the half-shells.

“Well thought of.” He quickly slipped the scrap of paper between them. “Do you have a little wax to seal this letter shut?”

The woman sighed deeply, and Kim softened.

“There is no payment until service is rendered. Carry this to the Babu, and say it was sent by the Son of the Charm.”

“Ah! Truly! Truly! By a magician—who is like an Englishman.”

“No, a Son of the Charm: and ask if there is any answer.”

“But what if he is rude? I—I am afraid.”

Kim laughed. “He is, no doubt, very tired and very hungry. The hills make cold bedfellows. Ah, my”—it was on the tip of his tongue to say Mother, but he changed it to Sister—“you are a wise and witty woman. By now all the villages know what happened to the Englishmen—eh?”

“True. The news reached Ziglaur by midnight, and by tomorrow it should reach Kotgarh. The villages are both afraid and angry.”

“No need to be. Tell the villages to feed the Englishmen and pass them along in peace. We must get them quietly out of our valleys. To steal is one thing—to kill another. The Babu will understand, and there will be no later complaints. Be quick. I must tend to my master when he wakes.”

“So be it. After service—as you said?—comes the reward. I am the Woman of Shamlegh, and I hold my land from the Rajah. I am no common bearer of children. Shamlegh is yours: hoof and horn and hide, milk and butter. Take it or leave it.”

She turned resolutely uphill, her silver necklaces clicking against her broad breast to meet the morning sun fifteen hundred feet above them. This time Kim thought in the local dialect as he sealed the edges of the oilskin packets with wax.

“How can a man follow the Way or the Great Game when he is constantly pestered by women? There was that girl at Akrola of the Ford; and the scullion’s wife behind the dovecot—not to mention the others—and now this one! When I was a child it was fine enough, but now I am a man and they still won't treat me like one. Walnuts, indeed! Ho, ho! It’s almonds down in the Plains!”

He went out to levy supplies from the village—not with a begging bowl, which might work down-country, but with the air of a prince. Shamlegh’s summer population consisted of only three families—four women and eight or nine men. They were all full of tinned meats and mixed drinks, ranging from ammoniated quinine to white vodka, for they had taken a full share in the previous night’s loot. The neat continental tents had been cut up and shared long ago, and patent aluminum saucepans were everywhere.

Yet they considered the lama’s presence a perfect shield against any consequences, and unrepentantly brought Kim the best they had—even a drink of chang, the barley beer from the direction of Ladakh. Then they thawed out in the sun, sitting with their legs dangling over endless drops, chatting, laughing, and smoking. They judged India and its government solely by their experiences with wandering Englishmen who had employed them or their friends as hunting guides. Kim heard tales of missed shots at ibex, serow, or markhor by Englishmen twenty years in their graves—every detail lit up from behind like twigs on treetops against lightning. They told him of their minor ailments and, more importantly, the diseases of their tiny, sure-footed cattle; of trips as far as Kotgarh, where the strange missionaries lived, and even beyond to marvelous Simla, where the streets are paved with silver and anyone, mind you, can find work with the Englishmen, who ride around in two-wheeled carts and spend money lavishly. Presently, grave and aloof, walking with a heavy tread, the lama joined the chatter under the eaves, and they made plenty of room for him. The thin air revived him, and he sat on the edge of the precipices with the best of them, occasionally tossing pebbles into the void when conversation lagged. Thirty miles away as the crow flies lay the next mountain range, furrowed and channeled and dotted with patches of brushwood forests, each a day’s dark march away. Behind the village, the Shamlegh hill blocked all view to the south. It felt like sitting in a swallow’s nest beneath the eaves of the roof of the world.

From time to time the lama stretched out his hand and, with quiet prompting, pointed out the road to Spiti and northward across the Parungla pass.

“Beyond, where the mountains crowd together, lies De-ch’en” (he meant Han-lé), “the great Monastery. s’Tag-stan-ras-ch’en built it, and this legend is told of him.” Whereupon he told it: a fantastic, winding tale of witchcraft and miracles that left Shamlegh gasping. Turning slightly west, he pointed toward the green hills of Kulu and sought Kailung beneath the glaciers. “For I went there in the long, long ago. I came from Leh, over the Baralachi pass.”

“Yes, yes; we know it,” said the widely traveled people of Shamlegh.

“And I spent two nights with the priests of Kailung. These are the Hills of my delight! Shadows blessed above all other shadows! There my eyes first opened to this world; there my eyes were opened to the true world; there I found Enlightenment; and there I prepared myself for my Search. Out of the Hills I came—the high Hills and the strong winds. Oh, just is the Wheel!” He blessed them one by one—the great glaciers, the bare rocks, the piles of moraine and tumbled shale; the dry uplands, hidden salt lakes, ancient timber, and fertile, well-watered valleys, just as a dying man blesses his family; and Kim marveled at his intense emotion.

“Yes—yes. There is no place like our Hills,” said the people of Shamlegh. And they wondered how anyone could live in the hot, terrible Plains where cattle grow as big as elephants and are useless for plowing a hillside; where village touches village for a hundred miles, they had heard; and where people go about stealing in gangs, leaving whatever the robbers spare to be entirely carried off by the police.

So the quiet morning passed, and just as it ended, Kim’s messenger dropped down from the steep pasture as fresh as when she had started.

“I sent a message to the doctor,” Kim explained while she paid her respects.

“Did he join himself to the idolaters? Ah, I remember he healed one of them. He has gained merit, even though the healed man used his strength for evil. Just is the Wheel! What of the doctor?”

“I feared that you had been bruised and—and I knew he was wise.” Kim took the waxed walnut shell and read the English message written on the back of his note: Your favor received. Cannot get away from present company at present, but shall take them into Simla. After which, hope to rejoin you. Inexpedient to follow angry gentlemen. Return by same road you came, and will overtake. Highly gratified about correspondence due to my forethought. “He says, Holy One, that he will slip away from the idolaters and return to us. Shall we wait here at Shamlegh for a while, then?”

The lama looked long and lovingly at the hills and shook his head.

“That cannot be, disciple. From the marrow of my bones I desire it, but it is forbidden. I have seen the Cause of Things.”

“Why? When the Hills give you back your strength day by day? Remember how weak and fainting we were down below in the Doon valley.”

“I grew strong to do evil and to forget. I was a brawler and a ruffian upon the mountainsides.” Kim bit back a smile. “Just and perfect is the Wheel, never swerving a hair. When I was a man—a long time ago—I made a pilgrimage to Guru Ch’wan among the poplars” (he pointed toward Bhutan), “where they keep the Sacred Horse.”

“Quiet, be quiet!” Shamlegh murmured in unison. “He is speaking of Jam-lin-nin-k’or, the Horse That Can Go Round The World in a Day.”

“I speak only to my disciple,” the lama said in gentle reproof, and they scattered like frost on a southern rooftop in the morning sun. “I did not seek truth in those days, but theological debates. All illusion! I drank the beer and ate the bread of Guru Ch’wan. The next day someone said: ‘We are going out to fight Sangor Gutok down the valley to discover’ (notice once again how Desire is tied to Anger!) ‘which Abbot shall rule the valley and take the profits from the prayers printed at Sangor Gutok.’ I went, and we fought for a day.”

“But how, Holy One?”

“With our long pen-cases, as I could have shown you... I tell you, we fought beneath the poplars, Abbots and monks alike, and someone split my forehead to the bone. Look!” He pushed back his cap and showed a puckered, silvery scar. “Just and perfect is the Wheel! Yesterday the scar itched, and after fifty years I remembered how it was inflicted and the face of the man who did it, lingering a little in illusion. That led to what you saw—strife and foolishness. Just is the Wheel! The idolater’s blow fell right upon the scar. Then my soul was shaken: my soul grew dark, and the boat of my soul rocked upon the waters of illusion. Not until I reached Shamlegh could I meditate upon the Cause of Things or trace the creeping roots of Evil. I struggled all through the long night.”

“But, Holy One, you are innocent of all evil. May I be your sacrifice!”

Kim was genuinely distressed by the old man’s grief, and Mahbub Ali’s phrase slipped out unconsciously.

“At dawn,” the lama continued more gravely, his prayer beads clicking between his slow sentences, “enlightenment came. It is here... I am an old man... bred in the hills, nourished by the hills, yet never allowed to rest among my Hills. For three years I traveled through Hindustan, but—can any place be stronger than Mother Earth? My foolish body longed for the Hills and the mountain snows from down below. I told myself—and thought it true—that my Search was secure. So, at the Kulu woman’s house, persuaded by my own desires, I turned back toward the hills. The doctor is not to blame. He—following Desire—predicted that the Hills would make me strong. They strengthened me to do evil, to forget my Search. I took delight in life and the lust of living. I wanted steep slopes to climb. I cast about to find them. I tested the strength of my sinful body against the high Hills. I mocked you when your breath grew short below Jamnotri. I teased you when you refused to face the snow on the pass.”

“But what harm was there? I was afraid. It was fair. I am no hillman; and I loved you for your renewed strength.”

“More than once I remember”—he rested his cheek sorrowfully on his hand—“I sought your praise and the doctor’s simply for the physical strength in my legs. Thus evil led to evil until the cup was full. Just is the Wheel! For three years all Hindustan honored me. From the Fountain of Wisdom in the Wonder House to”—he smiled—“a little child playing by a great cannon—the world paved my road. And why?”

“Because we loved you. It is merely the fever from the blow. I myself am still sick and shaken.”

“No! It was because I was upon the Way—tuned like cymbals to the purpose of the Law. I strayed from that ordinance. The tune was broken; the punishment followed. In my own Hills, on the edge of my own country, right in the place of my evil desire, the blow fell—here!” (He touched his brow.) “Just as a novice is punished when he misplaces the cups, so am I punished, who once was Abbot of Such-zen. No words, mind you, but a blow, disciple.”

“But the Englishmen didn’t know who you were, Holy One?”

“We were well matched. Ignorance and Desire met Ignorance and Desire upon the road, and they gave birth to Anger. The blow was a sign to me, who am no better than a strayed yak, that my place is not here. Whoever can understand the Cause of an act is halfway to Freedom! ‘Return to the path,’ says the Blow. ‘The Hills are not for you. You cannot choose Freedom and remain a slave to the pleasures of life.’”

“I wish we had never met that cursed Russian!”

“Our Lord Himself cannot make the Wheel spin backward. And because of the merit I have gained, I am given yet another sign.” He put his hand inside his tunic and drew out the Wheel of Life. “Look! I examined this after my meditation. There is no more than the width of my fingernail left untorn by the idolater.”

“I see.”

“That much, then, is the remaining span of my life in this body. I have served the Wheel all my days. Now the Wheel serves me. But for the merit I earned by guiding you upon the Way, yet another life would have been added to me before I found my River. Is it clear, disciple?”

Kim stared at the brutally torn chart. The tear ran diagonally from left to right—from the Eleventh House where Desire gives birth to the Child (as drawn by Tibetans)—across the human and animal realms, to the Fifth House—the empty House of the Senses. The logic was undeniable.

“Before our Lord won Enlightenment”—the lama reverently folded the chart away—“He was tempted. I too have been tempted, but it is over. The Arrow fell in the Plains—not in the Hills. Therefore, what are we doing here?”

“Shall we at least wait for the doctor?”

“I know how long I shall live in this body. What can a doctor do?”

“But you are sick and shaken. You cannot walk.”

“How can I be sick if I see Freedom?” He stood up unsteadily.

“Then I must get food from the village. Oh, what a weary Road!” Kim felt that he needed rest too.

“That is right. Let us eat and go. The Arrow fell in the Plains... but I yielded to Desire. Prepare yourself, disciple.”

Kim turned to the woman with the turquoise headgear, who was idly tossing pebbles over the cliff. She smiled very kindly.

“I found him like a strayed buffalo in a cornfield—the Babu; snorting and sneezing from the cold. He was so hungry that he forgot his dignity and spoke sweetly to me. The Englishmen have nothing.” She held out an empty palm. “One is very sick in his stomach. Your doing?”

Kim nodded, his eyes bright.

“I spoke to the Bengali first—and then to the people of a nearby village. The Englishmen will be given food as they need it—and the people won't ask for money. The plunder is already divided up. The Babu is telling lies to the Englishmen. Why doesn’t he leave them?”

“Out of the goodness of his heart.”

“There never was a Bengali with a heart bigger than a dried walnut. But it doesn't matter... Now about walnuts. After service comes reward. I told you the village is yours.”

“It is my loss,” Kim began. “Even now I had planned wonderful things in my heart which—” (there is no need to repeat the formal compliments usual on such occasions). He sighed deeply... “But my master, led by a vision—”

“Hah! What can old eyes see except an empty begging bowl?”

“—is turning away from this village back to the Plains.”

“Tell him to stay.”

Kim shook his head. “I know my Holy One, and his wrath if he is opposed,” he replied impressively. “His curses shake the Hills.”

“Pity they didn't save him from a broken head! I heard you were the tiger-hearted one who struck the Englishman. Let him dream a little longer. Stay!”

“Mountain woman,” said Kim, with a sternness that could not harden the soft lines of his young oval face, “these matters are too high for you.”

“Gods be good to us! Since when have men and women been anything other than men and women?”

“A priest is a priest. He says he will leave this very hour. I am his disciple, and I go with him. We need food for the road. He is an honored guest in all villages, but”—he broke into a bright boyish grin—“the food here is good. Give me some.”

“And what if I don’t give it to you? I am the mistress of this village.”

“ Then I will curse you—a little—not terribly, but enough to make you remember.” He couldn’t help smiling.

“You have already cursed me with your lowered eyelashes and uplifted chin. Curses? Why should I care about mere words?” She clenched her hands against her bosom... “But I wouldn't have you leave in anger, thinking ill of me—a gatherer of cow dung and grass at Shamlegh, but still a woman of substance.”

“I think nothing,” said Kim, “except that I am sorry to leave, for I am very tired; and that we need food. Here is the bag.”

The woman snatched it angrily. “I was foolish,” she said. “Who is your woman in the Plains? Fair or dark? I was fair once. Are you laughing? Once, long ago, if you can believe it, an Englishman looked upon me with favor. Once, long ago, I wore European clothes at the mission house over there.” She pointed toward Kotgarh. “Once, long ago. I was a Christian and spoke English—just like the Englishmen. Yes. My Englishman said he would return and marry me—yes, marry me. He went away—I had nursed him when he was sick—but he never came back. Then I saw that the Christian gods were lies, and I went back to my own people... I have never laid eyes on an Englishman since. (Don’t laugh at me. The spell has passed, little priest.) Your face and your walk and your manner of speaking reminded me of my Englishman, even though you are only a wandering beggar to whom I give alms. Curse me? You can neither curse nor bless!” She put her hands on her hips and laughed bitterly. “Your gods are lies; your deeds are lies; your words are lies. There are no gods under the heavens. I know it... But for a while I thought my Englishman had come back, and he was my god. Yes, once I played music on a piano in the mission house at Kotgarh. Now I give alms to priests who are heathens.” She ended with the English word and tied up the mouth of the brimming bag.

“I am waiting for you, disciple,” said the lama, leaning against the doorpost.

The woman swept his tall figure with her eyes. “He walk? He can’t cover half a mile. Where are those old bones going?”

At this, Kim—already troubled by the lama’s collapse and worrying about the heavy bag—completely lost his temper.

“What is it to you, woman of ill omen, where he goes?”

“Nothing—but it is something to you, priest with an Englishman's face. Will you carry him on your shoulders?”

“I am going to the Plains. No one must hinder my return. I have wrestled with my soul until I am strengthless. My stupid body is exhausted, and we are far from the Plains.”

“Behold!” she said simply, stepping aside to let Kim see his own utter helplessness. “Curse me. Perhaps it will give him strength. Cast a spell! Call upon your great God. You are a priest.” She turned away.

The lama had slumped limply, still clinging to the doorpost. You cannot strike down an old man and expect him to recover like a boy overnight. Weakness bowed him to the earth, but his eyes, fixed on Kim, were alive and pleading.

“It is all right,” said Kim. “It’s just the thin air weakening you. In a little while we will go! It’s mountain sickness. I’m a little sick to my stomach too”—and he knelt and comforted him with whatever simple words came to mind. Then the woman returned, more erect than ever.

“Your gods are useless, eh? Try mine. I am the Woman of Shamlegh.” She shouted harshly, and out of a cattle pen came her two husbands and three other men carrying a dooli, the rough native litter used in the hills for the sick and for state visits.

“These men”—she didn't deign to look at them—“are yours for as long as you need them.”

“But we aren’t going toward Simla. We won’t go near the Englishmen,” cried the first husband.

“They won’t run away like the others did, and they won’t steal baggage. You two take the rear pole, Sonoo and Taree.” They obeyed instantly. “Lower it now, and lift that holy man inside. I’ll look after the village and your virtuous wives until you return.”

“When will that be?”

“Ask the priests. Don’t pester me. Lay the food bag at his feet; it balances better that way.”

“Oh, Holy One, your Hills are kinder than our Plains!” cried Kim with relief as the lama tottered onto the litter. “It is a king’s bed—a place of honor and comfort. And we owe it to—”

“A woman of ill omen. I need your blessings just as much as your curses. This is my command, not yours. Lift and away! Here! Do you have money for the road?”

She beckoned Kim to her hut and bent over an old English cash box beneath her cot.

“I don’t need anything,” said Kim, feeling annoyed where he should have been grateful. “I am already heavily burdened with favors.”

Looking up with a curious smile, she placed a hand on his shoulder. “At least thank me. I am ugly and a mountain woman, but in your terms, I have gained merit. Shall I show you how the Englishmen give thanks?” Her hard eyes softened.

“I am only a wandering priest,” said Kim, his eyes lighting up in response. “You need neither my blessings nor my curses.”

“No. But for one tiny moment—you can catch up to the litter in ten strides—if you were an Englishman, shall I show you what you would do?”

“What if I guess?” said Kim, and putting his arm around her waist, he kissed her on the cheek, adding in English: “Thank you very much, my dear.”

Kissing is practically unknown among Asians, which may be why she leaned back with wide-open eyes and a terrified expression.

“Next time,” Kim continued, “you shouldn’t be so sure about your heathen priests. Now I say good-bye.” He held out his hand in the English fashion. She took it mechanically. “Good-bye, my dear.”

“Good-bye, and—and”—she searched for her English words one by one—“you will come back again? Good-bye, and—God bless you.”

Half an hour later, as the creaking litter jolted up the mountain path leading southeast from Shamlegh, Kim saw a tiny figure at the hut door waving a white rag.

“She has gained merit beyond all others,” said the lama. “For setting a man upon the path to Freedom is half as great as finding it herself.”

“Hmm,” said Kim thoughtfully, reflecting on the past. “It may be that I have gained merit too... At least she didn't treat me like a child.” He adjusted the front of his robe where the packet of documents and maps rested, stowed the precious food bag at the lama’s feet, placed his hand on the edge of the litter, and settled into the slow pace of the grunting husbands.

“These men also gain merit,” said the lama after three miles.

“More than that, they will be paid in silver,” replied Kim. The Woman of Shamlegh had given it to him, and it was only fair, he reasoned, that her men should earn it back again.
